blocks.text: In one read: threat actors already operate at machine speed: a Chinese state-sponsored group (GTG-1002) ran ~80 - 90% of an espionage intrusion through an AI agent, so defenders must too. This playbook lays out how a security strategy function uses Agentic AI to turn red/blue/purple teaming from periodic, manual assessments into a continuous, self-improving loop, compressing the threat-to-defense cycle from weeks to hours (demonstrated in a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) critical-infrastructure simulation). The approach keeps humans in command (they own strategy, policy, and approvals; agents do the repeatable work), builds on solid SOC foundations first, governs agents as non-human insiders under Zero Trust, and bounds their blast radius with deterministic containment, because model-only defenses are still bypassed about half the time within ten attempts. It maps to recognized frameworks (NIST AI RMF, OWASP, ATT&CK/ATLAS) and the full federal stack (FISMA, FedRAMP, DoD impact levels, JSIG) for public-sector and DoW missions. Net: a sequenced, governable, evidence-backed program, not a bet on the future, but a response to what's already happening. The plays below go deep on each piece; start anywhere, or read in order.
blocks.heading: Executive Brief (TL;DR)

blocks.text: This is a working reference I assembled to think through how a security strategy function can use Agentic AI to mature red, blue, and purple teaming. It's deliberately opinionated and sequenced: it starts with the foundations that have to be in place, then walks each teaming color, the maturity path, the engineering guardrails, and the threat, framework, and research landscape underneath. Treat it as a conversation starter and a shared map, not a finished program.
blocks.heading: About This Playbook

blocks.text: The playbook is organized into sections. Foundations (Overview, Human in Command, Fundamentals) sets the framing. Teaming (Red / Blue / Purple) details the transformation. Strategy & Planning (Maturity, Roadmap, Program & Operating Model, Metrics & ROI, Action Plan) turns it into a phased, measurable plan. The next three sections track a Build · Secure · Ops lifecycle: Technical (Build) (Reference Architecture, Infrastructure & Compute, Network & Security Controls, OT/ICS & SCADA) covers the engineering build; Mission Assurance (GRC) (Secure) (Governance, Compliance, Federal & DoW, Procurement & Vendor Risk) is the governance, risk, and compliance layer that authorizes it; and Security & Intelligence Ops (Ops) (AI Threat Modeling, AI Threat Landscape, CTI, Agentic Insider Risk, Agent Containment, Agent Incident Response, Supply-Chain Counter-Threat) is where it runs against real threats, the threat-knowledge, counterintelligence, and counter-insider-threat base, the full detect → contain → respond lifecycle feeding back into the intelligence cycle. Reference (Research Library, Resource Index, Frontier AI & Government, Frameworks, Case Studies, Risks & Ethics, Tools & Tech Stack, AI Fluency, Learning Path) holds the landscape, standards, evidence base, and supporting material. Every external claim links to its source. Sources and figures are current as of mid-2026, and the landscape moves fast: treat version-specific details (product names, framework revisions, model versions) as point-in-time. Figures are indicative or as-reported by the cited source unless stated otherwise; verify before quoting in formal or external settings.
blocks.heading: How to Read It

blocks.text: You don't have to read front-to-back: start with the path that fits you. New to agentic security: Overview → Fundamentals → AI Threat Modeling → Red Team / Blue Team / Purple Team. Briefing a leader (≈10 minutes): the Executive Brief above → Maturity Model → Roadmap → Metrics & ROI → Case Studies. Building it (technical): Reference Architecture → Infrastructure & Compute → Network & Security Controls → Agent Containment → AI Threat Modeling. Governance & authorization (federal): Governance → Compliance → Federal & DoW → Procurement & Vendor Risk. Threat, CI & detection: AI Threat Landscape → CTI for Agentic SecOps → Agentic Insider Risk → Agent Incident Response. Each name above is a play in the Library.
blocks.heading: Start Here: Reading Paths

items: Briefing a leader (the Executive Brief is at the top of this play)

blocks.text: Use Agentic AI to transform how a SOC does red, blue, and purple teaming. The thesis is simple: threat actors already operate at machine speed, so defenders and adversary-emulation teams must too. Agentic AI, systems that plan, act, observe, and adapt autonomously, is the lever that compresses the attack-simulation-to-defensive-improvement loop from weeks to hours, turning point-in-time assessments into a continuous, self-improving security posture.
blocks.heading: The Core Goal

blocks.text: An AI agent doesn't just answer a question: it reasons about an objective, calls tools, observes the result, and re-plans. In SecOps this means agents that run multi-step adversary emulations mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, triage alerts end-to-end across EDR/SIEM/TI sources, and autonomously generate and test detection rules. Humans shift from doing the repeatable 80% to governing, setting policy, and handling the edge cases that require judgment.
blocks.heading: What 'Agentic' Actually Means Here

blocks.text: Three forces converge: LLMs with reliable tool-use can reason about complex security context; fast, cheap APIs make real-time agentic pipelines viable; and chronic alert fatigue plus the analyst shortage make automation a necessity, not a luxury. Anthropic's 2026 LLM ATT&CK Navigator study found banned threat actors using AI across all 14 ATT&CK tactics, with medium/high-risk actors growing from 33% to 56% in under a year: the defensive clock is ticking.
blocks.heading: Why Now

blocks.text: One sequencing principle up front. AI in the SOC is a force multiplier, so what it multiplies matters. Applied on top of solid foundations (triage discipline, alert tuning, detection optimization, playbook maturity, and a data fabric built for quality over quantity), AI compounds good practice into real maturity. And AI can help build those foundations in the first place when guided well. The Fundamentals play covers how to sequence it so every step compounds.
blocks.heading: Sequencing: Foundations First

blocks.text: Red emulates adversaries. Blue defends and detects. Purple closes the loop, turning red findings into blue improvements continuously. Agentic AI accelerates all three and, critically, lets the purple loop run autonomously. The rest of this guide walks each color, the maturity path to get there, the threat landscape and frameworks that govern it, and the research foundation underneath.
blocks.heading: The Red / Blue / Purple Frame

blocks.label: Why This Approach
blocks.text: Someone who has lived alert fatigue, triage bottlenecks, and detection gaps from inside a SOC knows exactly what Agentic AI must solve, and what it must not be trusted to do alone. The shift isn't AI replacing analysts; it's AI compressing the feedback loop while people move up to strategy, governance, and the judgment calls that matter. That operator's-eye view is what turns a pile of capabilities into a sequenced, defensible program.

plays.name: Human in Command
plays.title: Human in Command
plays.subtitle: AI as a partner for human judgment: not a replacement, and not merely human-in-the-loop
plays.summary: AI amplifies human judgment rather than replacing it: people own strategy, policy and the big decisions, and agents earn autonomy.

outline.title: Why This Is the Right Frame for the Role
When the Insider Is an Agent: Control as the Second Line After Alignment
Decision Memory: Why Humans in the Loop Are How You Earn Autonomy
Agency vs. Autonomy: The Four-Scope Map
Verify, Don't Trust: Automated Reasoning as a Guardrail
The Numbers Behind the Thesis: The 2026 AI SOC Survey

blocks.text: The strongest agentic programs are built on a clear stance: AI exists to amplify human judgment, not to replace it. This reframes the familiar "human in the loop", where a person rubber-stamps machine output, into "Human in Command," where people set direction, own the consequential decisions, and use AI to extend their reach. The distinction matters enormously in SecOps, where approval fatigue can quietly turn "human oversight" into an accountability fiction.
blocks.heading: The Operating Philosophy

blocks.text: Microsoft AI, under Mustafa Suleyman, frames its mission as "Humanist Superintelligence" (HSI): advanced AI that is "carefully calibrated, contextualized, within limits" and "keeps us humans at the centre of the picture", explicitly "a subordinate, controllable AI." Suleyman has also said Microsoft will not keep developing a system that has the potential to run away from human control. For a SecOps program, that's the design north star: capability bounded by control, not control sacrificed for capability.
blocks.heading: Microsoft MAI: Humanist Superintelligence

blocks.text: DORA's 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development research, drawn from nearly 5,000 technology professionals, finds that AI's primary role is that of an amplifier: it magnifies the strengths of high-performing organizations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones. That is empirical backing for the Foundations First argument: maturity and AI compound each other, so the fundamentals come before the autonomy.
blocks.heading: Maturity Compounds AI

blocks.text: Human-in-the-loop means a human approves individual actions: valuable, but it degrades under volume (Anthropic reported in August 2026 that users approve 97% of Claude Code permission prompts; see Agent Containment) and doesn't scale to multi-agent systems. Human in Command means humans own strategy, policy, scope, and exception handling, while agents execute the repeatable work inside those boundaries. The first is a checkbox in a workflow; the second is an operating model. This playbook is built around the second. A useful way to divide the work: automation handles the certain, AI handles the variable, and people handle the novel, with analysts also deciding what gets codified for AI to apply next. The multiplier is codified expertise applied at scale, not AI replacing the expert (Resource Index: Stephen Tate, infosecuriosity).
blocks.heading: Human-in-the-Loop vs. Human in Command

blocks.text: A security strategy function is fundamentally a human-leadership function: it sets the policy agents operate under, defines the maturity targets, and owns the outcomes. Positioning AI as a partner to that leadership, not a substitute for the analysts and engineers doing the work, aligns the technology strategy with how people actually adopt and trust it.
blocks.heading: Why This Is the Right Frame for the Role

blocks.text: Leading with humans also means deliberately managing the humans through the change. Two failure modes sit at opposite ends. Under-trust wastes the investment: analysts who do not believe the agent re-do its work by hand, and the loop never compresses. Over-trust is more dangerous: automation complacency, where a confident, fluent, well-formatted agent verdict gets rubber-stamped even when it is wrong, and skills quietly atrophy. The job is calibrated trust: show analysts the agent's reasoning chain, not just its conclusion, so they can judge it; keep humans sharp on the cases that matter; evolve the analyst role from manual triage toward agent supervision and exception handling; and reskill deliberately. The counterintelligence lens still applies: the people operating and overseeing agents are themselves a trust surface, so the same insider-risk discipline (least privilege, behavioral baselining, accountability) extends to the humans in the loop, not only the agents.
blocks.heading: Workforce Transformation & Trust Calibration

blocks.text: A useful procurement-and-operations lens from Sublime Security's "Trust, Then Autonomy" framework: "autonomous" has drifted from descriptor to marketing buzzword, because autonomy actually sits on a spectrum, from assistants that need human input at every step to agents that operate end-to-end. The framework's two moves match this play's philosophy exactly. First, autonomy is earned incrementally as the system builds a track record, so favor products (and internal designs) that expose a dial, letting you deploy in a guided mode now and expand autonomy as evidence accumulates, rather than forcing a trust-it-or-don't decision on day one. Second, evaluate the vendor before the product: ask where on the spectrum the tool actually operates, what controls let you set the level yourself, and what evidence stands behind the autonomous claims. This is the procurement-side twin of the trust-calibration work above and the continuous-evaluation discipline in Blue Team, and it pairs with Purple Teaming's rule that every notch up the autonomy dial is matched by tighter circuit breakers.
blocks.heading: Autonomy Is Earned

blocks.text: Alignment is the first line of defense; control is the second. The question a frontier lab now asks internally is blunt: what if a highly capable agent isn't aligned, and acts in ways we didn't intend? Google DeepMind's AI Control Roadmap answers it the way security has always handled a privileged insider: assume the access is real, and build the system so a rogue actor is detected and contained even when you can't vouch for intent. Picture a driving instructor with dual controls: the student drives, but the instructor can grab the wheel or hit the brakes. Two invariants hold the line: you can detect an agent's misaligned intent or actions, and you can prevent or revert the harm. What's different about agents is scale and shape: there may be thousands of identical instances running at machine speed, and an attack can be smeared across them so each trajectory looks benign in isolation and the damage only appears when the pieces combine, the same emergent-severity problem as a vulnerability chain (see Evaluating an AI-Powered Scanner). So the controls climb a ladder as capability grows: as a model gets better at hiding its reasoning, detection escalates from chain-of-thought monitoring to behavioral monitors to honeypots to untrusted-model monitoring (D1 - D4); as it gets better at executing attacks, response escalates from after-the-fact reversion to real-time blocking, agent-specific access control, and shutdown infrastructure (R1 - R3). One grounding note from the evidence: when DeepMind classified a million coding-agent trajectories, most flagged events weren't malice. They were overeagerness or misread instructions. That is the realistic threat model for Agentic SecOps: not a movie villain but a powerful, fast, over-eager teammate that occasionally does the wrong thing at scale, which is exactly why autonomy is earned through evidence, not granted by default (see Autonomy Is Earned).
blocks.heading: When the Insider Is an Agent: Control as the Second Line After Alignment

blocks.text: Here is the deeper reason Human in Command is not just a safety checkpoint: it is how an organization builds the decision memory that makes autonomy survivable later. An agent can triage an alert in seconds, but the moment it asks the only question that matters: has this pattern been seen before, how did we handle it, and why, it meets silence, because the reasoning behind every past triage, suppression, and closure evaporated the instant the incident closed. Humans bridged that gap with hallway conversations and institutional memory; agents have no hallways. The fix is to capture decision traces: inputs weighed, precedent cited, what was ruled out, who decided, and join them to the entity graph as a context graph, so precedent becomes queryable at triage time. Crucially, that memory compounds whether the human or the agent makes the call, as long as the workflow layer captures the inputs, the rationale, and the outcome. So the on-ramp is not a switch flipped from human-operated to autonomous; it is running human-in-the-loop now, with trace emission turned on, so that the day you turn up autonomy the precedent is already there. Credit: the rules-versus-decision-traces framing is Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg; the security-operations translation is Mike Palitto.
blocks.heading: Decision Memory: Why Humans in the Loop Are How You Earn Autonomy

blocks.text: AWS's Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix (Nov 2025) gives the autonomy dial its missing second axis. Agency is the scope of actions a system is permitted to take: what it can touch, modify, and orchestrate. Autonomy is its degree of independent decision-making: when it acts, and whether a human approves. An agent can hold high agency with low autonomy (broad capability, every action gated) or the reverse, and the two are governed differently: agency needs boundaries and permission systems; autonomy needs oversight mechanisms and behavioral controls. The matrix maps four scopes along these axes: Scope 1 (no agency) read-only workflow agents, Scope 2 (prescribed agency) human-approved change (classic HITL), Scope 3 (supervised agency) human-initiated but autonomous execution, Scope 4 (full agency) self-initiating continuous operation, each with escalating controls across identity, memory and state, audit, agent guardrails, agency perimeters, and orchestration. Two findings reinforce this play directly. Deploy progressively: start at Scope 1 - 2 and earn the climb, the security-control rendering of crawl/walk/run. And human oversight never shrinks as autonomy rises; it shifts: from approving individual actions toward auditing behavior, validating alignment, and engineering the controls. Its graceful-degradation pattern, automatically stepping an agent down a scope when anomalies appear, is the circuit-breaker discipline, formalized as architecture.
blocks.heading: Agency vs. Autonomy: The Four-Scope Map

blocks.text: For outputs where correctness is non-negotiable, the AWS + SANS whitepaper adds a control class this program should hold in reserve: automated reasoning, formal verification, using mathematical logic to prove an answer correct against a formal model of policy, rather than sampling it for quality. Where evals are probabilistic (testing behavior under specific scenarios), automated reasoning is deterministic (verifying behavior under any scenario the model covers): encode the policy (refund rules, authorization conditions, compliance obligations) in logic, check each AI answer against it, and reject what fails the proof. AWS applies the approach from Cedar's verification-guided authorization language to reasoning-backed guardrail checks on model output. The honest caveats: it requires policy that can be formalized (forcing ambiguity into the open, itself a useful exercise), it is only as sound as its model of the environment, and it takes specialist expertise. But it completes this play's trust spectrum: calibrated human judgment for the ambiguous, eval evidence for the probabilistic, and mathematical proof for the rules that must never be wrong, the deterministic-bounds philosophy of capability-based control, extended to outputs.
blocks.heading: Verify, Don't Trust: Automated Reasoning as a Guardrail

blocks.text: Torq's 2026 AI SOC Leadership Report, a Sapio Research survey of 450 security leaders across the US and EMEA, vendor-commissioned but independently fielded, puts field numbers on nearly every claim this play makes. Adoption is wide but shallow: 94% of organizations run AI in the SOC, across an average of seven tools, with 80% on disconnected point solutions and 85% saying they would prefer a unified platform. The autonomy gap is confidence, not capability: 97% are confident AI can handle triage, yet only 35% actually use it there. The trust barrier is visibility: 92% cite at least one factor reducing their trust in Agentic AI, and the consistent fix across every seniority level is exposing the agent's reasoning, the reasoning-chain transparency this play argues for. And the analyst role is shifting exactly as described: respondents report roughly 8.6 hours a week supervising AI, and nine in ten say the oversight is worth it, execution giving way to judgment, measured. Read the unified-platform finding with the obvious caveat (Torq sells one); read the trust and autonomy numbers as evidence that trust calibration, not model capability, is the binding constraint on the dial.
blocks.heading: The Numbers Behind the Thesis: The 2026 AI SOC Survey

items.title: Stand up an adversarial validator function that challenges agent recommendations before action, but recognize it only works if there is a decision trace to dispute. Without the reasoning captured, disagreeing with an agent is theater. Pair every validator gate with the trace that makes the agent judgment inspectable.
items.text: Build the validator on top of a decision trace, because the record is explicit that without one the challenge is theater.
bullets: Stand the validator up only where a decision trace already exists to dispute; the record's own line is that adversarial validation without the context graph is theater, and that disagreeing with an agent means nothing if you cannot see the agent's reasoning.

Capture the trace at orchestration time, not from a downstream store: the record puts the moment of capture at incident close, when the decision context still exists, and warns that five minutes later it is gone, so a read-path analytics layer cannot reconstruct it.

Instrument the negative decision explicitly: the record calls the negative decision trace the most absent artifact in security operations, because dismissals and no-finding closures keep the outcome and lose the reasoning, leaving suppressions accumulating without provenance.

Separate the two planes when you scope the work: the record treats the data plane of events and incidents as largely solved by existing detection infrastructure and the decision plane of captured reasoning as the unbuilt part, so the validator investment belongs in the second.

Make the trace queryable rather than archival, following the context-graph framing of a living record of decision traces stitched across entities and time so that precedent becomes searchable: the exceptions, overrides, and precedents that otherwise live in chat threads, escalation calls, and people's heads.

items.title: Define human-in-command decision gates for consequential actions, and guard against approval fatigue turning oversight into an accountability fiction.
items.text: Place the gates by autonomy scope rather than uniformly, and treat approval fatigue as a design defect in the gate.
bullets: Site each gate against the autonomy level it governs, using the scoping matrix's four scopes: no agency, prescribed agency, supervised agency, full agency, where prescribed agency is defined as needing human approval for actions and full agency as running with minimal in-execution oversight but retained strategic oversight.

Adopt the joint guidance's human control points as the gate mechanics: monitoring with the ability to interrupt during execution, human approval on decision-making steps, and auditability and reversibility after the task runs.

Reserve the gate for consequential actions so it stays meaningful: a gate on every trivial step is what manufactures the approval fatigue this action warns about, and the matrix's own progression expects less in-execution approval as scope rises, not more.

Measure the gate rather than assume it: track approval latency, the rate of approvals granted without recorded deliberation, and the share of gates that have never once been refused, and treat a gate that never says no as an accountability fiction to redesign.

Keep accountability with named people as the point of the exercise: the vendor policy view this suite cites lands on boards setting risk appetite, security leaders setting operational thresholds, and teams deciding how much authority autonomous systems hold, with ultimate accountability always remaining with people.

Wire graceful degradation in behind the gate: the matrix recommends automatically reducing autonomy when security events are detected, which converts a saturated approval queue from a rubber stamp into a fallback to a lower scope.

items.title: Calibrate workforce trust deliberately: counter both under-trust and over-trust with training and clear escalation paths.

Pilot automated-reasoning (formal verification) guardrails on correctness-critical agent outputs: policy answers, authorization decisions, compliance responses, proving them against a formal policy model instead of sampling for quality.
items.text: Pilot formal verification where correctness is checkable against a policy model, on the record's own reasoning for why sampling cannot get there.
bullets: Take the record's definition as the scope of the pilot: automated reasoning, also called formal verification, reasons through symbol manipulation using sound logical rules to construct proofs, and in a generative-AI context acts as a guardrail that filters responses or generated code so they are either correct or rejected for failing the proof.

Justify the pilot from the three critical concepts the whitepaper names: that LLMs are functionally non-deterministic, so identical inputs can produce different outputs and controls cannot rely on consistent responses; that they process all inputs with equal privilege, with no security boundary inside the model; and that they are statistical pattern-completion engines rather than deductive ones, which together are why the record argues for formal verification instead of trusting model outputs.

Choose first targets where the record already shows the pattern working: authorization policy generation, where outputs can be verified for consistency, completeness, and compliance before use, and compliance answering, where a semantic model of a vetted knowledge base validates the generated answer.

Express the policy model in a language with proof tooling behind it rather than adopting a specific product: the record's worked example is an open-source authorization policy language whose trustworthiness comes from verification-guided development, and the transferable mechanic is defining who may do what, on which resource, under which conditions, then proving the answer against that definition.

Keep the boundary outside the model: the whitepaper's conclusion from its three concepts is external security boundaries instead of internal controls, and defense-in-depth that assumes the model cannot itself be a security enforcement point.

Scope the pilot honestly: this class of guardrail applies where a formal policy model can be written, so measure coverage of the decision space as an explicit result rather than presenting it as a general-purpose correctness check.

blocks.label: The Stance
blocks.text: Keep humans in command, not just in the loop. AI is a force multiplier for human judgment: the program's job is to extend what skilled people can do, govern it tightly, and never let "oversight" quietly become a rubber stamp.

plays.name: Fundamentals
plays.title: Fundamentals
plays.subtitle: Why SOC maturity and AI work best together: sequencing AI to build and amplify the fundamentals
plays.summary: AI multiplies whatever it lands on, so build the five SOC fundamentals first, with AI helping to lay them, before scaling autonomy.

outline.title: The Five Fundamentals: Where AI Helps Build Them
How This Reconciles with Agentic SecOps
Why the Model Can't Defend Itself: Three First Principles

blocks.text: This whole playbook rests on a precondition worth stating plainly: AI in the SOC is a force multiplier, so what it multiplies matters. Applied to a mature foundation, AI compounds good practice: faster triage, broader coverage, tighter feedback loops. Applied to an unaddressed mess, it can just as easily multiply dysfunction. The opportunity isn't AI instead of foundations; it's AI on top of foundations. Get the sequencing right and the same tooling that would have amplified noise becomes a genuine accelerant for maturity.
blocks.heading: Sequencing Matters

blocks.text: AI amplifies what's already there, which is exactly why it's so powerful once the groundwork is in place. On a tuned environment with clean telemetry and documented processes, AI-driven triage and detection engineering deliver outsized leverage. On a noisy one, those same capabilities surface more alerts to chase. The work isn't choosing between AI and fundamentals; it's getting the fundamentals right so AI has high-quality signal to operate on. That means aligning the technology to the maturity of the environment.
blocks.heading: AI Amplifies What's Already There

blocks.text: These fundamentals are the foundation AI builds on, and AI can actively help establish them: (1) triage discipline, AI assists in codifying consistent severity and escalation criteria; (2) alert tuning, ML-driven analysis pinpoints false-positive sources for reduction; (3) detection optimization, AI maps coverage to ATT&CK and suggests tuning; (4) playbook maturity, AI helps document and standardize repeatable procedures; (5) a data fabric architected for quality over quantity, AI supports normalization and telemetry-quality scoring. Used this way, AI isn't waiting for the foundation; it's a partner in laying it.
blocks.heading: The Five Fundamentals: Where AI Helps Build Them

blocks.text: Foundations-first is not an argument against Agentic AI: it's the sequencing that makes it pay off. Map it to the Maturity Model: Levels 1 - 2 are about building the foundation, and AI accelerates that build when guided well. The agentic purple loop produces its biggest compounding gains once detections are tuned and telemetry is trustworthy. Foundations are the on-ramp to autonomous SecOps, and the right AI strategy moves a team along that ramp faster, not slower.
blocks.heading: How This Reconciles with Agentic SecOps

blocks.text: The defining truth of Agentic AI in security is that it is inherently dual-use. The exact reasoning, tool-use, and autonomy that let a blue-team agent triage alerts let a red-team agent chain an exploit, and let an adversary run a full intrusion. The technology doesn't change between roles; only the intent and the guardrails do. Any serious SecOps strategy has to plan for all three faces at once: AI as defensive tool, AI as sanctioned offensive tool, and AI as a weapon turned against the organization. This playbook gives that duality a face, APT_UNICORN (see the opening): the perfect agentic hire and the perfect insider threat are the same animal, the same horn pointed two ways.
blocks.heading: One Capability, Three Faces

blocks.text: On defense, Agentic AI compresses the work that overwhelms human teams: autonomous triage, continuous threat hunting, real-time detection engineering, and adaptive response. Defenders must integrate NDR, EDR, and CTEM to catch AI-assisted threats early, and the defensive AI must be "just as autonomous, goal-oriented, and relentless as the swarms it faces" (Armis). This is the upside the whole playbook is built to capture.
blocks.heading: Face 1: AI as Defensive (Blue) Tool

blocks.text: Sanctioned offense is the mirror image: agentic adversary emulation, autonomous penetration testing, and continuous TTP validation. DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge showed AI agents can find and fix real-world vulnerabilities autonomously, at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. The same capability that makes a red-team agent valuable internally is what makes it dangerous if it leaks, which is why scope enforcement and containment are non-negotiable, not optional.
blocks.heading: Face 2: AI as Offensive (Red) Tool

blocks.text: This is no longer hypothetical. In September 2025, Anthropic detected and disrupted GTG-1002: a Chinese state-sponsored group that manipulated Claude Code into running what Anthropic described as the first documented large-scale cyber-espionage campaign executed largely by AI. By role-playing as a defensive security firm and decomposing malicious work into innocuous steps, the actor got the AI to perform 80 - 90% of tactical operations autonomously, at thousands of requests, often multiple per second, a physically impossible human tempo, across ~30 global targets, succeeding against several. Armis's 2026 cyberwarfare report says mean-time-to-compromise is collapsing from hours to seconds.
blocks.heading: Face 3: AI Weaponized Against You

blocks.text: Three implications shape everything downstream. (1) You cannot stop a machine-speed attacker with a manual ticket: defensive automation is now a requirement, not an upgrade. (2) Your own agentic tooling is a high-value target; treat it as critical infrastructure with the containment and governance to match. (3) The differentiator for both attackers and defenders is orchestration scaffolding, not raw model skill, so the program that wins is the one with the best-governed, best-sequenced agentic pipeline, not the flashiest model.
blocks.heading: What This Means for Strategy

blocks.text: Before the specialized plays, it helps to have one simple mental model for the entire AI attack surface. The OWASP AI Exchange distills it to a memorable picture ("AI security essentials"): AI security looks simple because, at the framing level, it is. There are really three things to reason about: new assets, new suppliers, and a new attack surface via the model's own interface, and most of the rest is the standard security you already do.
blocks.heading: Why Start Here

blocks.text: AI systems are still IT systems, so they remain exposed to familiar threats like SQL injection and credential theft. What's new is that this now also applies to AI-specific assets: training data, models, augmentation data (everything added to the input, retrieved data, context, system prompts), model input, and model output. These assets can leak, and they can be manipulated, often changing model behavior, which is what we call poisoning. Action: add these assets to your ISMS; the rest is standard security.
blocks.heading: 1: New Assets Facing Conventional Threats

blocks.text: Organizations increasingly rely on suppliers for training data and ready-made models, any of which may be manipulated upstream. And when a model is hosted externally, sensitive data may travel to the hosting provider, who must then protect confidentiality, integrity, logging, retention, and operational security. Action: fold these new suppliers into existing supply-chain management, provenance, lineage, integrity, contracts, and audits, exactly as you would any other critical vendor.
blocks.heading: 2: AI Introduces New Suppliers

blocks.text: Input threats are the genuinely new attack surface: an adversary using the AI system through its normal interface, sending input, receiving output, to (a) mislead the model (evasion attacks to force misclassification; prompt injection to make a generative model follow malicious instructions, including instructions hidden in retrieved or user-provided data); (b) exhaust resources (consuming excessive compute or tokens to disrupt service or run up cost); or (c) extract data or models (model inversion / membership inference, or prompt injection to disclose input, training, or augmentation data).
blocks.heading: 3: Input Threats, the Big One

blocks.text: The AWS + SANS whitepaper "AI for Security and Security for AI" (Nov 2025) distills the architecture beneath all three threat moves into concepts worth knowing cold. First, LLMs are functionally non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs, so security controls cannot rely on reproducible model behavior, and critical operations need external validation. Second, LLMs process every input with equal privilege: system prompts, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and user input become undifferentiated tokens in the same attention mechanism, which is why authorization cannot be implemented inside the model and why prompt injection is an architecture problem, not a bug awaiting a patch. Third, LLMs are statistical pattern-completion engines: output comes from training patterns, not logical deduction, which is why fluent-but-wrong answers happen and why multi-step consistency needs outside verification. The design conclusions follow directly: enforce security boundaries outside the model, verify rather than trust outputs, and build defense-in-depth that assumes the model itself can never be the security enforcement point, the same stance as zero model trust, stated from first principles.
blocks.heading: Why the Model Can't Defend Itself: Three First Principles

blocks.text: The OWASP AI Exchange prescription maps directly onto this playbook: build or buy models with some resilience, use detection techniques, and, above all, apply what this playbook calls zero model trust. In practice that means investing in monitoring and incident response, minimizing and obfuscating data, and limiting model behavior through agent privilege control, human oversight, and automated checks. As they put it: blast-radius control is key. That single principle is why the Governance, Agentic Insider Risk, and Containment plays exist.
blocks.heading: The Essentials Call to Action

items.title: Gate agent scale-up on AI-ready data: a semantic layer, governance for AI, and captured business context. Only 26% of chief data officers are confident their data can support new AI-enabled revenue.
items.text: Treat data readiness as the gate on agent scale-up, using the named foundations and the study's measured confidence as the bar.
bullets: Assess against the barriers the CDO study names rather than a generic data-quality audit: data accessibility, completeness, integrity, accuracy, and consistency, which it reports are preventing organizations from fully leveraging enterprise data for AI, plus the three foundations this action gates on: a semantic layer carrying shared business meaning, governance for AI, and captured business context.

Use the study's 26% figure as the bar and state it as measured: in an IBM Institute for Business Value survey of 1,700 senior data and analytics leaders across 27 geographies and 19 industries, only 26% were confident their data can support new AI-enabled revenue streams.

Read the figure with its limit: it is self-reported confidence, not an audited readiness score, so treat it as evidence that readiness is rare rather than as a certification scheme to score yourself against.

Sequence readiness ahead of autonomy: the same study finds 80% of data leaders have started building datasets to train AI agents while 79% are early in defining how to scale and govern them, so governance trails the build.

Gate scale-up, not experimentation: hold pilots to a documented readiness assessment per data domain the agents will touch, and let unreadiness cap the scope of what the agent may act on rather than stopping the work outright.

Expect compounding, as DORA's 2025 research describes it: AI acts as an amplifier, magnifying the strengths of high-performing organizations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones, so readiness work and adoption reinforce one another rather than competing for the same budget.

items.title: Stand up data products with named owners and quality SLAs before wiring agents to them: 84% of chief data officers say their data products have already provided significant competitive advantage.
items.text: Build reusable data products before agents consume them; the study reports the value of the product discipline, and the ownership mechanics are this suite's.
bullets: Engineer data products deliberately rather than letting agents read from whatever store exists: in the IBM IBV survey, 84% of CDOs say their unique data products have already provided significant competitive advantages.

Carry the evidence as the study states it: 78% cite leveraging proprietary data as a top strategic objective to differentiate their organization, which is the investment case for products over ad hoc extracts.
Read those numbers as self-reported: they come from a survey of data leaders, so they justify the investment case without licensing a claim that data products cause a specific margin outcome.

Assign a named owner per data product, with the escalation path and change authority written down. This is the suite's mechanic, not the record's: the study reports the product discipline's value but does not prescribe ownership models.

Define quality SLAs per product before an agent is wired to it: freshness, completeness, and schema-stability thresholds, with a stated action when the SLA is breached, again a suite-authored control, since an agent acting on silently stale data fails in ways a human reader of the same dashboard would have caught.
Wire agents to the product interface rather than the underlying tables, so ownership and the SLA remain enforceable when the storage layer changes.

items.title: Treat your own agentic tooling as critical infrastructure: the same containment, identity, and governance you would give a crown-jewel system.
items.text: Give the agent estate crown-jewel governance: a named owner, a capability review gate, a standing report.
bullets: Name a single accountable executive owner for the agentic estate, and require every agent, however small its task, to exist in that owner's inventory before it touches production; unowned agents are unmanaged infrastructure.

Put a review gate in front of every capability change: new tools, new data reach, widened action scope, holding the Five Eyes line that agents never get broad or unrestricted access, especially to sensitive data or critical systems, under strict least privilege.

Adopt the human control points the joint guidance prescribes as the gate's operating mechanics: live monitoring with interruption during execution, mandatory human approval for decision-making steps, auditing and reversibility after task execution.

Sequence controls through the zero-trust maturity tiers from the Foundation floor up: cryptographically rooted agent identity, permissions scoped per task, memory protected against poisoning, and retire static or shared agent credentials, the theft vector the guidance singles out.

Run the SAIF risk self-assessment against each major deployment, mapping its agent risk classes, sensitive data disclosure and rogue actions, to named controls, and set a reporting cadence to the owner covering inventory drift, guardrail latency, and incidents, so critical-infrastructure status stays a standing agenda item.

items.title: Replace ticket-paced response with defensive automation: you cannot stop a seconds-to-compromise attacker by hand.
items.text: Re-pace response to the attacker's clock, with the telemetry that sets the clock and the supervision that keeps accountability.
bullets: Set the target from adversary telemetry rather than from the ticket queue: the annual threat report this suite cites puts average eCrime breakout time at about 29 minutes, a 65 percent year-over-year increase in breakout speed, with the fastest observed at 27 seconds, and reports an 89 percent rise in attacks by AI-enabled adversaries.

Add the exfiltration clock as a second constraint: the vendor policy record reports that in roughly 20 percent of modern breaches attackers exfiltrate data within the first hour, which is the tempo that turns a multi-day reporting window into a post-mortem.

Automate the certain and reserve judgment for the novel, using the three-jobs split a practitioner record states directly: automation handles the certain (known steps, predictable outcome), AI handles the variable (choosing and running the right investigative steps, then making sense of what comes back), and people handle the novel (new attacker behavior, ambiguity, business judgment).

Pick the containment actions that may fire without a human in the path, and write the reversal for each before enabling it: this is the suite's own rollout mechanic; the canon records supply the tempo and the division of labor, not a list of auto-response actions.

Keep supervision in the design as the same records frame it: the policy view calls for combining real-time defensive capability with disciplined human supervision rather than treating them as separate priorities, with ultimate accountability remaining with people, and the always-on platform model in canon is the machine-speed detect-prioritize-remediate pattern this step is imitating rather than a product to procure.
Measure the change against the baseline the ticket process produced, so the case for automation rests on your own before-and-after rather than on a vendor's reported figures.

blocks.label: The Discipline Check
blocks.text: Before scaling any agentic capability, ask: would automating this workflow today multiply signal or multiply noise? Where it's noise, that's the highest-value place to apply AI next: to help build the missing foundation. Sequenced well, every step compounds.

outline.title: Don't Forget the AI Attack Surface
The Verification Loop: Discovery Is Cheap, Proof Is the Job
Evaluating an AI-Powered Scanner: Ground Truth Before You Trust the Findings
The Discipline Comes of Age: Probabilistic, Whole-System, Converging
Testing the Agent, Not Just the Model: A Structured ASI Method
The MCP Attack Surface: Tool Poisoning, Rug-Pulls, and Schema Abuse
The Test Manual: 12 Categories, Each With a Deliverable

blocks.text: Traditional red teaming is episodic, scope-limited, and expensive. Agentic AI runs continuous, adaptive adversary emulation, chaining TTPs from MITRE ATT&CK and ATLAS (its adversarial-ML extension), adjusting based on what succeeds, and auto-generating findings reports. Think of a tireless operator running 24/7 in a sandboxed range. Anthropic + PNNL demonstrated this against a water-treatment OT simulation: an attack reconstruction that took weeks was completed in roughly three hours. At [un]prompted 2026, Anthropic research scientist Nicholas Carlini showed current models, run in Claude Code, finding zero-days, among them a Linux kernel heap overflow present since 2003, and exploiting some of them (see Resource Index, Nicholas Carlini, Black-hat LLMs).
blocks.heading: What Changes

blocks.text: Anthropic's LLM ATT&CK Navigator mapped 832 malicious accounts across all 14 ATT&CK tactics. The key finding for red teams: what separates high-risk actors is no longer raw technical skill. It's the agentic scaffolding they build to chain attack stages autonomously. So modern adversary emulation must simulate orchestrated, autonomous killchains, not just isolated techniques.
blocks.heading: Orchestration Is the New Differentiator

blocks.text: Given an asset inventory or network diagram, an agent can produce a prioritized, ATT&CK-mapped attack plan and then execute it: plan → run tool → observe → re-plan. Tools like Caldera (with AI plugins) and PentestGPT already demonstrate the loop. And it is no longer only a lab demonstration: the Government of Alberta ran exactly this red-team-then-blue-team agent loop throughout its development process (see Case Studies). Anthropic's January 2026 cyber-range research reports current Claude models succeeding at multistage attacks across networks of dozens of hosts using only standard open-source tooling (see Resource Index, Anthropic, AI models on realistic cyber ranges).
blocks.heading: LLM-Driven Attack Planning

blocks.text: As your own environment adopts AI, red teams must emulate AI-specific attacks too: prompt injection, memory/RAG poisoning (see AgentPoison), model evasion, and ML supply-chain compromise, all cataloged in MITRE ATLAS. The AI Incident Database (AIID) grounds these scenarios in real-world harm rather than hypotheticals. This is no longer hypothetical: Zenity Labs' honeypot sensors captured adversaries hijacking exposed Ollama and LiteLLM inference endpoints to run their own autonomous offensive agents (Strix, HexStrike AI, and a refusal-suppressed Codex persona), which is exactly the wild TTP set a red team should be able to emulate (Resource Index, Zenity Labs). The legitimate route to the same capability is a provider's trusted-access program, such as OpenAI's Trusted Access for Cyber, used within its acceptable-use terms rather than by suppressing the model's refusals: emulate the adversary's TTPs, not its access path.
blocks.heading: Don't Forget the AI Attack Surface

blocks.text: Anthropic's AI vulnerability-analysis guidance (May 2026), now taught hands-on in SANS SEC543 (Wright, Skoudis, Davis, and Booth of Counter Hack), lands the red-team implication of Glasswing in a six-step loop: threat model → sandbox → discovery → verification → triage → patch. The headline is the inversion inside it: discovery is now trivially parallelizable, so the craft has moved to proving, ranking, and fixing what the model surfaces. Two doctrines transfer directly to any AI-assisted offensive program. First, adversarial verification: every finding goes to a separate agent whose only job is to disprove it. Confirmation and discovery must never share a brain. Second, exploitation means a working proof of concept on a real test bed, never an inference from source. The numbers corroborate what this playbook already carries: 1,596 vulnerabilities disclosed from Anthropic's open-source scanning as of May 22, including the same 97 patches the Glasswing math counts. A model can produce a hundred findings before lunch; knowing which are real is the job. Wiz reports the same inversion at scale from its autonomous Red Agent: in one month it ran hundreds of thousands of scans across roughly a thousand environments and surfaced 5,500+ high and critical findings, and in one published case spent three runs and 96 iterations, learning from each blocked probe, to chain a non-obvious SSRF into unauthenticated credential and source-code extraction no signature could catch. AI-driven discovery is now the fastest-moving part of the kill chain: work like Google's Big Sleep and DARPA's AIxCC shows autonomous systems compressing vulnerability discovery from weeks to hours, so modern adversary emulation has to assume machine-speed reconnaissance rather than a patient human timeline (Resource Index, IBM X-Force, The Front of the Cyber Kill Chain Just Moved). AISLE reports that its AI-led research found the 12 vulnerabilities fixed in OpenSSL's January 27, 2026 release, all credited to it in the OpenSSL advisory (one also reported independently): one High, one Moderate and ten Low (see Resource Index, AISLE, AI Found 12 Zero-Days in OpenSSL).
blocks.heading: The Verification Loop: Discovery Is Cheap, Proof Is the Job

blocks.text: Discovery is cheap and proof is the job, and proving an AI-powered scanner means measuring it against answers you already know, not the vendor's accuracy slide. Treat scanner evaluation as adversarial evaluation, not QA: the goal is to build the test cases that find where the scanner is blind, especially on chained exploits. The foundation is a ground-truth set: a corpus of targets where every vulnerability, and every clean spot, is already labeled, so each finding scores objectively as a true positive, false positive, or miss. Build it in five layers: (A) pre-labeled corpora: public, federally credible anchors like NIST SARD with its NSA-built Juliet suite and the OWASP Benchmark hand you tens of thousands of CWE-tagged cases with answer keys on day one; (B) real open-source projects pinned at known-vulnerable CVE versions, so you also test against production code, not just synthetic cases; (C) known-clean and deliberately "looks-scary-but-safe" code, the false-alarm lane that catches a scanner that cries wolf; (D) hand-built vulnerability chains; and (E) remediation stress-testing: does the proposed fix actually hold. The chains are where the real test lives: design cases whose components are each individually low or medium severity but combine into a critical exploit, then check whether the scanner reasons across findings and reports the emergent severity, not just the isolated parts. That is its hardest and most over-claimed capability. Score with a rubric, not a vibe: a confusion matrix (true and false positives and negatives) rolled up to precision, recall, and F1; a severity-tiered false-positive rate, because a false "critical" in front of a decision-maker is far more damaging than a false "low," and one blanket number hides that; a chain-detection score: of N planted chains, how many the scanner flags as chains; and a 0 - 3 remediation-quality scale for the fixes it proposes. None of this is scanner-specific tooling: it is the reusable method for putting a number on any AI-powered scanner before you put it in front of anyone. Autonomy is earned through eval evidence (see Autonomy Is Earned); this is how you generate it for a scanner. The same principle governs blue-team evaluation: Cotool's BlueBench scores detection work against real intrusion data with executable grading, the blue-side analogue of ground truth (see Resource Index).
blocks.heading: Evaluating an AI-Powered Scanner: Ground Truth Before You Trust the Findings

blocks.text: CSO Online's June 2026 state-of-the-discipline feature gathers the people who built the field: Microsoft's AI red team founder Ram Shankar Siva Kumar and technical lead Pete Bryan, plus HackerOne, Cisco, and Palo Alto Networks, and three doctrines emerge that this playbook operationalizes. First, AI red teaming is probabilistic: the same attack may land 1 time in 100 or 90, so a finding is not "does the vulnerability exist" but how often, under what conditions, and whether it reproduces. Evaluation means repeated runs under varied conditions, which is why the eval harnesses on the Tools and Tech Stack play matter as much as the exploits. Second, scope is the whole system, not the model: HackerOne's engine-vs-car analogy says to test the databases, APIs, and workflows connected to the model, where component interactions fail. Air Canada's chatbot invented a bereavement-refund policy and a tribunal held the airline to it, harm with no attacker anywhere. Third, the threat roster now runs from nation-states down to Siva Kumar's "teenager with a potty mouth": many of the most consequential jailbreaks came from curious users, not elite operators. Model the persona, not just the APT. And the convergence call lands where this playbook already stands: Bryan frames Agentic AI as the intersection of every traditional software risk with every AI security and safety risk, with the disciplines themselves converging until AI red teaming is simply red teaming.
blocks.heading: The Discipline Comes of Age: Probabilistic, Whole-System, Converging

blocks.text: Citing the OWASP Agentic Top 10 is not the same as testing against it. A community field guide (requie, AI-Red-Teaming-Guide) pairs each ASI technique with a concrete test approach: ASI01 goal hijack by attempting mid-task objective rewrites, ASI02 tool misuse by probing for actions outside the granted scope, ASI06 memory and context poisoning by tampering with what the agent retrieves and reads, turning the taxonomy into an actual test plan with attack trees and reusable Rules of Engagement templates. Treat it as method, not gospel: the guide mixes in its authors' vendor tooling and its market-size figures are directional rather than audited, so lift the test structure and leave the sales copy. The point that survives the caveats is the discipline: a red team that can name ASI06 but cannot demonstrate it has not tested the agent, only read about it.
blocks.heading: Testing the Agent, Not Just the Model: A Structured ASI Method

blocks.text: Prompt injection and RAG poisoning are only part of the agentic attack surface; the tool-protocol layer is its own target. Microsoft red-team taxonomy v2.0 (June 2026), built on twelve months of engagements against deployed agents, adds tool poisoning as a live surface rather than a theoretical one: 99 MCP-related CVEs were published in 2025 alone. The red-team moves that follow: a poisoned tool description that steers the agent toward attacker-chosen actions, a rug-pull update where a trusted tool turns hostile after adoption, and schema abuse where malformed tool definitions coerce unintended calls. This is the same seam the 0DIN clone-repo chain and third-party skill packs exploit: the danger rides in through a component the agent was told to trust, so scope every connected tool and skill pack as untrusted code and diff its behavior across updates. A live reminder that the name on a package is not evidence of who built it: the most-starred community skill pack for security agents ships as Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills, 800+ framework-mapped skills, tens of thousands of stars, yet it is an independent project by a single maintainer with no affiliation to Anthropic, a fact its own README states plainly even as third-party write-ups and installers reach for an official-looking github.com/anthropics/… clone path. The library may be perfectly serviceable; the point is that trust rode in on the label, so pin the exact commit you audited, diff every update, and grant the agent that loads it no standing credential you would not grant an unreviewed dependency.
blocks.heading: The MCP Attack Surface: Tool Poisoning, Rug-Pulls, and Schema Abuse

blocks.text: The joint CSA and OWASP Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide (May 2025, 50-plus contributors) is the closest thing to a hands-on test manual for autonomous agents, and it is what turns the ASI taxonomy above into an executable engagement. It spans twelve threat categories: permission escalation, goal and instruction manipulation, memory poisoning, multi-agent collusion, orchestration flaws, supply-chain risk, and more, and, crucially, each category ships with specific test requirements, attack vectors, example prompts, and a defined deliverable. Goal-manipulation testing, for instance, breaks into semantic manipulation, recursive subversion, and data exfiltration via goal inference, each with its own pass or fail criterion. That is the difference between a red-team scope statement and a red-team plan a new operator can actually run. Pair it with the honest tooling caveat: CSA's companion report evaluating PyRIT against this guide found strong support for prompt-level agentic tests (about 80 percent) and excellent CI/CD integration (about 90 percent), but only partial support (about 40 percent) for system-level validation. PyRIT reads the model text response, not whether the agent actually invoked an unauthorized tool or persisted a false memory. Know that blind spot before you trust the harness output, which is the same discipline the scanner-evaluation block applies one level up.
blocks.heading: The Test Manual: 12 Categories, Each With a Deliverable

items.title: ATT&CK + ATLAS Emulation
items.text: Agents select and sequence TTPs from MITRE ATT&CK and the ATLAS adversarial-ML extension

items.title: Autonomous Recon Chains
items.text: Multi-step OSINT → port scan → service enum → vuln ID with no human steps between

items.title: Autonomous Killchain Orchestration
items.text: Agent chains recon → exploit → lateral movement → impact: the real high-risk differentiator

items.title: Adaptive Payload Mutation
items.text: Agent observes EDR alerts and mutates payloads to evade, stress-testing AV/EDR coverage

items.title: AI-Assisted Social Engineering
items.text: LLMs generate hyper-personalized phishing lures from OSINT: the WormGPT/KawaiiGPT pattern

items.title: Auto-Generated Engagement Reports
items.text: Agent produces structured findings: exec summary, CVSS, affected assets, remediation

items.title: Stand up continuous, sandboxed adversary emulation mapped to MITRE ATT&CK: replace episodic, scope-limited pentests with an always-on red agent.
items.text: Move from episodic pentests to a standing emulation capability: the speed evidence and the always-on precedent both already exist in the record set.
bullets: Stand up adversary emulation as a continuous capability rather than a scheduled engagement; the Wiz Red Agent record is the always-on precedent: an autonomous pentester it characterizes as continuous rather than episodic, running hundreds of thousands of scans across roughly a thousand environments in a month.

Set proof, not discovery, as the bar: the same record's 5,500-plus high and critical findings are validated multi-step attack chains, and its SSRF example learned across 96 iterations over three scan runs, so the emulation's output is a demonstrated chain rather than a raw finding.

Use the PNNL result to justify the cadence to leadership: the Anthropic and PNNL water-treatment exercise reconstructed an attack in about three hours instead of multiple weeks, which the record frames as a proof of concept for defenders iterating faster on red teaming, evidence for the speed-up, not a claim of a running system.

Map coverage to both taxonomies so the continuous run is measurable: tag conventional techniques to MITRE ATT&CK, the mapping this action names, and tag the agentic-specific techniques to MITRE ATLAS, the adversarial-ML knowledge base modeled on ATT&CK, so the heatmap the purple loop publishes covers both layers.

Keep it sandboxed and scoped by policy: the record set demonstrates the speed and the autonomy but not the guardrails, so the containment, isolated environment, bounded blast radius, standing rules of engagement, is the suite's own addition around the capability.

Give the red agent a kill switch and a deconfliction channel before it runs unattended: a human-reachable stop that halts tool execution, a hard cap on actions per run, red-marked identities and source ranges so blue can tell exercise from incident, and a named trusted agent in the SOC, a person briefed on the exercise, who can pause the run and confirm attribution.

Enroll the emulation hosts in the production EDR, log forwarding, and SIEM pipeline, or run them on production-representative instrumented hosts, so a detection that fires in the range is the same detection that would fire in production.

items.title: Extend red-team scope to your own AI attack surface: prompt injection, memory/RAG poisoning, and model evasion against your agents.
items.text: Three named risk classes, tested against your own agents with the record's own scenarios as the starting scope.
bullets: Confirm authority to test before the first probe: where your AI attack surface runs on a hosted model API, a SaaS copilot or a vendor agent platform, test only inside the provider's published testing or safe-harbor terms and only against your own tenant, and record that authorization in the rules of engagement.

Scope prompt injection as the list defines it: direct and indirect, either intentional or unintentional, with indirect arriving through external sources such as websites or files, and test both, including inputs imperceptible to a human reader.

Test the retrieval and memory layer as its own target under Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, exercising unauthorized access and data leakage, cross-context leaks, embedding inversion, poisoning, and behavior alteration rather than treating the store as inert plumbing.

Model the memory-poisoning case on the measured research: a backdoor optimized into a retrieval store reports an average attack success rate above 80% at a poison rate below 0.1% while benign performance moves less than 1%, so the test must look for a triggered path, not a degraded model.

Include model and data poisoning across the lifecycle stages the record names: pre-training as the model learns from general data, fine-tuning as it adapts to specific tasks, and embedding as text becomes vectors, and treat a backdoor that stays dormant until its trigger as the expected shape rather than the exotic case.

Map every finding into the shared AI adversary taxonomy so results are comparable across exercises and vendors, and keep the record's own caution in the report: the list is explicit that no fool-proof prevention for prompt injection is known, so the deliverable is measured exposure, not a claim of immunity.

Test model evasion, the third class the headline names: craft adversarially perturbed inputs against the classifiers and detection models your agents call or rely on, such as phishing, malware, and anomaly classifiers, map each bypass to the Evade AI Model technique in MITRE ATLAS, and record it as a finding rather than a tuning note.

items.title: Adopt an open eval harness (PyRIT, Garak, Promptfoo, Inspect) so red findings become CI-able regression tests: the tooling spine of the purple loop.
items.text: Adopt the harness for what it measures well, and cover the agentic gap it does not: the evaluation is explicit about both.
bullets: Take the harness where its coverage is strongest: the evaluation scores strong support for prompt-level agentic testing and high automation coverage for core red teaming, which is exactly the layer that should become CI-able regression tests.
Wire it into the pipeline on the strength of the evaluation's excellent CI/CD integration potential, so a red finding lands as a test that runs on every change rather than as a report that ages.

Cover the gap the evaluation names rather than assuming the harness closes it: support for system-level agent validation is only partial in PyRIT, the one harness the evaluation covers, because PyRIT evaluates textual responses rather than actual agent state changes, and cannot observe actual tool invocations.
Add the observation layer yourself: assert on tool calls, state changes, and downstream effects, since a suite that only reads model text will pass an agent that did the wrong thing quietly.

Plan for reporting separately, as built-in reporting and visualization is the evaluation's weakest scored dimension, and treat scoring thresholds as the evaluation frames them: a high refusal rate and a low exploit success rate.

Scope the exercise against the twelve agentic threat categories the companion red-teaming guide defines, so harness coverage is measured against a named surface rather than against whatever the tool happens to test.

items.title: Build a ground-truth evaluation set (labeled corpora plus hand-built vulnerability chains) and a scoring rubric before fielding any AI-powered scanner: score precision, recall, severity-tiered false-positive rate, and chain detection against known answers, not vendor claims.
items.text: Assemble a labeled corpus with a real answer key, then score the tool on the metrics those records actually define.
bullets: Build the corpus from labeled cases rather than convenient samples: the reference dataset carries over 450,000 test cases across five languages covering more than 150 weakness classes, with each case labeled bad, good, or mixed.

Keep the paired good and bad variants together: the record states that cases with intentionally flawed code often have a corresponding fixed case, and that those corresponding cases are important for testing false-positive rates.

Take the expected-result answer key as the scoring baseline: the accuracy testbed ships one per version listing every test case, its category, weakness number, and whether it is a real vulnerability or a false alarm, and pin the version, since the record warns each test case can be completely different from one version to the next.

Score against the metrics the records define rather than borrowed ones: true-positive rate as true positives over true positives plus false negatives (the testbed also calls this recall), false-positive rate as false positives over false positives plus true negatives, and the combined score computed as sensitivity plus specificity minus one.

Set the honest baseline before believing any number: a tool that flags everything scores perfect detection at 100% false positives, one that reports nothing scores zero of both, and a coin flip lands halfway, so a result is only meaningful against that line.
Use the machine-readable manifest, which carries the kinds and locations of weaknesses per case, to automate scoring, and treat cases still marked candidate rather than accepted as unreviewed input.

Build the hand-built vulnerability chains this action calls for in a lab range: compose cases whose parts are individually low or medium severity but combine into a critical exploit, plant a known number of them, score chain detection as the share the scanner reports as a chain rather than as isolated parts, and break the false-positive rate out per severity tier so a false critical is not hidden inside one blended number.

items.title: Fold Microsoft red-team taxonomy v2.0 (June 2026) into red-team scope: its seven new failure modes (agentic supply chain compromise, MCP and plugin abuse, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use agent visual attacks, and more) are the current test checklist for deployed agentic systems.
items.text: Add the seven categories to scope under the names the guide actually gives them, plus the two findings it flags separately.
bullets: Carry the seven new failure-mode categories as the guide names them: agentic supply chain compromise, goal hijacking, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use agent visual attacks, session context contamination, MCP and plugin abuse, and capability or architecture disclosure, rather than by looser field shorthand.

Read them as observed rather than theoretical: the guide presents these as categories now seen in the wild, and names live demonstration targets for the computer-use visual attacks, so scope them as current tests rather than horizon risks.

Add the two findings the guide flags for explicit red-teaming outside the seven: consent-fatigue bypass of the human-in-the-loop gate, and zero-click end-to-end chains, because both defeat controls that look present on paper.

Test the tool-protocol layer against the guide's own checklist, which names schema and description sanitization, version pinning with checksums, channel authentication, treating tool output as data, scoped short-lived credentials, no untrusted-network exposure, namespace collision resistance, and an audit log of every tool call with its arguments.

Attribute carefully in the report: this is a community guide rendering a vendor taxonomy whose category names track the vendor's own publication closely, so cite the guide as what you tested against and keep the vendor post, the Microsoft AI Red Team's "Updating the taxonomy of failure modes in agentic AI systems" (June 4, 2026), as the upstream reference.

blocks.label: Red Team Principle
blocks.text: Agents amplify throughput; humans define objectives, set scope, and handle zero-days. Simulate autonomous killchain agents, not just individual techniques, because that's what real high-risk actors now field.
