plays.title: Agentic Blue Teaming
plays.subtitle: AI-driven detection, triage, and response at scale
plays.summary: Triage agents turn raw alerts into pre-analyzed cases, freeing analysts for judgment while hunting and detection scale up.

outline.title: The Post-Mythos SOC: Validation Becomes the Bottleneck
N-Day Is Becoming N-Hour: The Patch Gap Collapses
Harden the Analysis Pipeline: The Artifact Is Attacker-Controlled
Continuous Agent Evaluation: Are the Agents Still Good?

blocks.text: SOCs drown in alerts: thousands per day, most of them false positives. Tier-1 analysts spend most of their time on low-value triage, burning out and missing real threats. This is the lived reality Agentic AI attacks at the root: autonomous triage agents that ingest alerts, correlate context, and surface only what needs human judgment, freeing analysts for high-signal work.
blocks.heading: The Alert Fatigue Problem

blocks.text: A triage agent receives a SIEM alert → pulls the EDR process tree → queries threat intel (VirusTotal/MISP, by hash and indicator lookup only, never by uploading the artifact itself) → checks asset criticality in the CMDB → correlates with recent similar alerts → renders a verdict with a full reasoning chain. The analyst sees a pre-analyzed case, not a raw alert, compressing triage from tens of minutes to a few minutes. Microsoft reports that Defender XDR already contains attacks in progress through automatic attack disruption, in real time and without waiting for an analyst. Before any platform or agent is allowed to contain on its own, exclude the assets whose isolation is an outage (domain controllers, tier-0 and break-glass identities, critical servers), scope automated actions by asset criticality, and rehearse the undo path.
blocks.heading: Autonomous Triage Agents

blocks.text: Given a hypothesis ("Cobalt Strike beacon activity"), an agent writes hunt queries across Sentinel/Splunk/CrowdStrike, executes them, interprets results, and spawns sub-hypotheses. The same agents auto-generate Sigma/KQL/SPL detection rules from threat intel or fresh red-team TTPs: the input side of the purple loop.
blocks.heading: AI-Assisted Threat Hunting & Detection Engineering

blocks.text: Splunk's strategic read on the era (Dalling, June 2026) lands on this playbook's foundations-first thesis from the vendor side: frontier AI will not replace the SOC. It will expose every weakness in how the SOC operates today. The bottleneck moves from finding to validating. AI-assisted discovery surfaces possible weaknesses faster than ever; the constraint becomes whether the SOC can connect a finding to real assets, identities, and business services: what is normal here, which systems are exposed, what deserves action now. A technical finding without context is just noise, and the post-Mythos SOC "will not run on alert volume. It will run on confidence." Two details give the piece weight beyond the product positioning. First, Cisco sits inside both Anthropic's Project Glasswing and OpenAI's Daybreak (GPT-5.5) as a launch partner, the first cross-lab convergence point in this index: one vendor watching the frontier's own vulnerability-discovery work from inside both houses and turning offensive insight into defensive advantage. That work is already producing measurable results: Cisco reported scanning 1.8 billion lines of code across more than 25 languages in eight weeks, a job it pegged at roughly eight years of manual effort, at a false-positive rate under 3 percent by pairing frontier models with a human-guided harness, while pointedly declining to state how many vulnerabilities were found. Second, the detection-engineering implication: the old rhythm of slow content updates and manual tuning ages out, replaced by tight draft → test → refine → operationalize cycles, explicitly not a case for handing control to AI, but for using it to accelerate the work while human defenders stay responsible for quality, validation, and judgment, the same division Human in Command draws from the oversight side. The architecture argument (identity, network, and security operating as one system, because adversaries cross silos in minutes) is the Fundamentals data-fabric requirement restated for the era; the product layer underneath (Exposure Analytics, a Triage Agent in private alpha, Detection Studio, Cisco Data Fabric under the Splunk platform) is first-party vendor positioning, framed accordingly. The companion artifact is the stronger half: Cisco's "Shields Up" guidance, written directly off the April Mythos hold-back, traces the AI-enabled-attack record from the 2024 Microsoft/OpenAI research through TA547's LLM-generated PowerShell and models the near-future adversary. Both are in the Resource Index. The Purple Team play already declared point-in-time assessment dead in the post-Mythos environment; this is the same verdict, delivered from the SOC floor. Google's AI Threat Defense (May 2026) makes the same multi-model bet explicit from the platform side: its operating premise is that no single model catches everything, so it runs a collection of models across multiple passes under human supervision (Resource Index, Google, AI Threat Defense).
blocks.heading: The Post-Mythos SOC: Validation Becomes the Bottleneck

blocks.text: The bottleneck in this section's argument has a clock on it now. On June 8, 2026, Anthropic's red team published measured results on how much frontier models accelerate N-day exploit development: the weaponization of already-public patches against systems that haven't applied them yet. The finding reframes patch management as a defensive race: across 18 Firefox security patches, Claude Mythos Preview autonomously built 8 working code-execution exploits; across 21 Windows kernel patches, with no source code, working only from binary diffing, it produced 8 full privilege-escalation chains taking a low-privilege user to SYSTEM. The timing is the part to sit with: Mythos Preview had its first Firefox exploit within an hour of Mozilla shipping the patch, while the patched build was still 18 days from release, and it finished all eight Windows chains before Autopatch would have pushed the update to 90% of a fleet. Patch diffing, historically expert-weeks of scarce reverse-engineering talent (16 of 25 N-days took a month or more in Mandiant's 2020 analysis), now costs a few thousand dollars in API credits and an afternoon. For the SOC, three operational consequences follow. First, "N-day" timelines built on monthly cadences and multi-week staged rollouts no longer hold: the window between public patch and working exploit is now measured in hours, so emergency-patch criteria and exception-handling must assume it. Second, the systems this playbook's OT, ICS and SCADA and Federal and DoW plays already flag (fixed maintenance windows, vendor-locked firmware, uptime guarantees) move from "slow to patch" to "exposed by default," because the cost of weaponizing their patches has fallen toward zero. Third, the durable defense is upstream of patching speed: starve the bug supply (memory-safe languages, exploit-class mitigations like CFG and hardware shadow stacks) so there are fewer patches to lose the race on. This is the reaction-time-collapse thesis with a primary-source number attached: the same Daybreak/Mythos frontier the Vulnerability Storm tabletop rehearses, now quantified on the N-day side. Sysdig reports an intrusion that went from credentials exposed in public S3 buckets to AWS administrator in about eight minutes. The LLM-style code and hallucinated identifiers it left suggest, but do not prove, AI assistance (see Resource Index, Sergej Epp, 8 Minutes to Admin).
blocks.heading: N-Day Is Becoming N-Hour: The Patch Gap Collapses

blocks.text: Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta": any agent that combines (1) access to private data, (2) exposure to untrusted content, and (3) the ability to communicate externally is exploitable for data exfiltration via prompt injection, demonstrated against M365 Copilot, GitHub MCP, and Slack AI. Blue-team agents that ingest untrusted logs and emails must be architected to break at least one leg of this trifecta. Stripe's AI security lead described two guardrails in production. The first breaks the egress leg: web search with outside access disabled, third-party SaaS reached only through a central MCP proxy, and CI checks on agent services' egress settings. The second requires human confirmation for sensitive tools, driven by annotations every tool must carry (see Resource Index, Andrew Bullen, Breaking the Lethal Trifecta).
blocks.heading: Mind the Lethal Trifecta

blocks.text: Every section above points AI at attacker-shaped material: a SIEM alert, an EDR process tree, a suspect binary, a log line, a code diff. That artifact is untrusted input, and adversaries are already crafting it to break, derail, or sabotage the analysis itself. A field taxonomy (Thomas Roccia) names four classes now seen in the wild, usually combined: deception payloads, harmful-looking content (apparent weapon or exploit instructions) planted to trip your defensive AI's own safety guardrails so it refuses or aborts before reaching the real payload, the exact inversion CSO Online flagged in When AI Safety Constrains Defenders; fake system-prompt overrides, injected instructions hidden in comments or content to hijack the verdict (OWASP LLM01, covered throughout this playbook); context flooding, bulk repetitive text that overruns the context window to push the payload out of view while inflating cost and tripping rate limits (OWASP LLM10:2025, now LLM06:2026, Unbounded Consumption); and encoding evasion, ROT13, Base64, or foreign-language obfuscation that slips past filters and decodes only downstream. The countermeasures are the discipline you already apply to any hostile input: treat analyzed content as data, never instructions; normalize and decode before you analyze, not after; cap and segment input size; cryptographically sign the conversation context with an HMAC so an attacker cannot rewrite history or smuggle in fake system turns, the bypass Mandiant's red team demonstrated against a banking chatbot; and treat a guardrail refusal as a reason to escalate to a human, never a silent stop. A spike in refusals or oversized artifacts is itself an evasion signal worth a detection. MITRE ATLAS catalogs the underlying techniques; the muscle to counter them lives in this playbook's detection-engineering, evaluation, and containment loops. The agent that triages your alerts is itself a system that must be secured (Question A) even as it does the securing (Question B).
blocks.heading: Harden the Analysis Pipeline: The Artifact Is Attacker-Controlled

blocks.text: Deploying a defensive agent is the start, not the finish: its quality drifts as models update, prompts change, threats evolve, and data shifts. A security strategy function has to treat agent evaluation as a standing discipline: maintain a regression suite of known-good cases (past true and false positives, labeled incidents) and re-run it on every model or prompt change; track precision, recall, and verdict quality over time, not just at launch; watch for silent degradation (rising disagreement with analysts, confident-but-wrong verdicts, scope creep); and gate promotion of any agent change behind passing those evals, the same CI/CD rigor you would apply to detection content. An agent you stopped measuring is an agent you no longer trust. Joshua Saxe argued at [un]prompted 2026 that evaluation is the blocker. Security ground truth is noisy, so grade how an agent works (its evidence, reasoning and justification) against a rubric, calibrate an LLM judge on as few as about 100 labeled samples to start, and set a deployment bar before deploying (see Resource Index, Joshua Saxe, The Hard Part Isn't Building the Agent).
blocks.heading: Continuous Agent Evaluation: Are the Agents Still Good?

items.text: Analysts query in plain English; agent translates to KQL/SPL and interprets the results

items.text: LLM-driven response that adapts to novel incidents beyond rigid if/then playbooks

items.title: AI-Specific Threat Detection
items.text: Detect prompt injection, RAG leakage, model abuse per OWASP GenAI & AI Defense Matrix

items.title: Identity Assurance & Anti-Deepfake
items.text: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys), liveness + multi-modal biometrics, behavioral/continuous auth, NIST 800-63 IAL2/AAL2 proofing, and tight agent-identity (NHI) governance

items.title: Deploy autonomous Tier-1 triage (SIEM to EDR to threat-intel to CMDB correlation) to cut false-positive load and free analysts for high-value work.
items.text: Ship the governance before the autonomy: the field record's finding is that the constraint at this step is governance, not tooling.
bullets: Write the governance artifacts before triage fires autonomously, in the terms the field record names: defined rules of engagement, pre-approved policies, audit trails, and a clear organizational answer to who is responsible when an AI verdict is acted on.

Take the record's central finding as the sequencing rule: it reports the move from AI-assisted operations to partial autonomy as primarily a governance problem rather than a tooling one, so a capable triage engine does not by itself make the step available.

Establish the workflows in playbooks first: the same record relays the analyst-firm readiness criterion that operational workflows be established in playbooks before AI is introduced, which is also what gives the agent a defined correlation path across the detection, endpoint, intelligence, and asset-inventory sources this action names.

Expect a confidence-to-deployment gap and plan for it rather than around it: the survey record in canon reports 97 percent of leaders confident AI can handle triage against 35 percent actually using it there; it is published by an AI-SOC platform vendor and does not disclose its sponsorship on the page, so weigh it as directional.

Scope what the agent decides using the certain/variable/novel split: deterministic automation keeps the certain work (enrichment, ticket creation, blocking known-bad indicators), the agent takes the variable investigative reasoning, and analysts keep genuinely novel behavior and business judgment.

Baseline false-positive load and analyst time before cutover and re-measure after, so the freed-capacity claim in this action is evidenced by your own numbers rather than by vendor-reported customer outcomes; run the agent in recommend-only mode first and measure its agreement with analyst verdicts per alert class, then after cutover re-adjudicate a fixed weekly sample of agent-closed alerts and publish the false-negative rate next to the auto-close rate.

At cutover, stand up a baseline regression suite of known-good triage cases (past true and false positives, labeled incidents) and rerun it on every model, prompt, or detection-content change before the agent closes alerts again; this is the suite's own gate, the first slice of continuous agent evaluation.

items.title: Audit every defensive agent against the lethal trifecta (private-data access, untrusted input, external comms), and break at least one leg.
items.text: Inventory the three legs per agent, then break the cheapest one with a control the guidance actually names.
bullets: Build the inventory one agent at a time, recording what private data it can reach, what untrusted content enters its context, and what external communication it can perform: the combination is the finding, so an agent is only cleared when one leg is demonstrably absent.

Break the data leg first where you can: minimize sensitive data in agent context, classify documents before they enter it, and redact restricted content at the point of inclusion rather than trusting the model to withhold it.

Break the input leg by treating all external data as untrusted: user messages, retrieved documents, API responses, emails, sanitizing it before it reaches context and marking clear boundaries between instructions and data.

Break the action leg with per-tool permission scoping and separate tool sets for different trust levels, escalating high-impact or irreversible calls to explicit approval, and binding that approval to the exact action rather than to the session.

Prove the break instead of asserting it: run the abuse cases as tests, an unauthorized tool denied even when the model asks confidently, a low-trust path unable to escalate, and log the structured decision metadata that shows which control fired.

items.title: Run continuous agent evaluation: re-baseline detection agents as models, prompts, threats, and data drift.
items.text: Build the evaluation as infrastructure across the playbook's five layers, so a re-baseline is a rerun rather than a rebuild.
bullets: Treat evaluation as infrastructure with the five layers the playbook names: evaluate, isolate, connect, run, and scale, because a re-baseline is only cheap when the harness beneath it is already reproducible.

Isolate deliberately along the three independent dimensions the record defines: tooling, host isolation, and network isolation, so a detection agent under evaluation cannot reach anything its production twin would.

Standardize the provider connection rather than the model, since the record counts more than forty model providers each with different APIs, authentication schemes, and capabilities: that abstraction is what lets a model swap become a config change.

Run the loop the record names ("design", "run", "analyse", "understand") against the regression suite this play describes, labeled past true and false positives scored on precision, recall and agreement with analyst verdicts, and re-enter it on the triggers the program defines, since the record prescribes no interval and none should be invented on its authority.

Scale on shared components rather than bespoke suites, following the record's own pattern of contributed evaluation components and a large shared benchmark collection, so each re-baseline inherits work instead of repeating it.

items.title: Instrument time-to-validate alongside time-to-detect: gate AI-surfaced findings on environment context (assets, identities, exposure) before action, and treat a growing validation backlog as the bottleneck signal it is.
items.text: Instrument the validation half of the loop the record says is now the bottleneck, and gate action on environment context the way it describes.
bullets: Take the record's thesis as the reason for the metric: it argues the bottleneck must move from finding to validating, so a program that measures only detection speed is measuring the half that is no longer scarce.

Gate on context before action in the record's own terms: a technical finding without context is just noise, and the move it describes is from this looks important to this is relevant now, and here is why, which is what connecting a finding to assets, identities, and exposure buys.

Adopt confidence as the operating measure: the record's landing point is that the future SOC will not run on alert volume but on confidence, which is what a validation gate produces and a raw alert count does not.

Tighten the content loop the record names: tighter cycles for how detection content is drafted, tested, refined, and operationalized, so validation failures feed back into detection quality rather than only into the queue.

Define time-to-validate and the backlog threshold locally: the record establishes validation as the constraint but does not name this metric or set a number, so the definition, owner, and alerting threshold are this suite's instrumentation of the record's thesis.

Treat a growing validation backlog as a staffing-and-governance signal, and pair it with the accountability precondition the autonomous-SOC record sets, a clear organizational answer to who is responsible when an AI verdict is acted on, so the backlog has somewhere to escalate.

items.title: Re-scope emergency-patch criteria for the N-hour window: assume a public patch can be weaponized within hours (a frontier model built a working exploit inside an hour of a patch release), prioritize internet-facing and hard-to-patch OT/ICS systems, and push the durable fix upstream, memory-safe components and exploit-class mitigations that retire whole bug families.
items.text: Rebuild the emergency-patch decision around hours-scale weaponization, with the four-criteria triage as the sorter.
bullets: Reset the planning assumption to the measured record: a frontier model produced its first working exploit about an hour after patch release, and a month of patches became working exploits in an afternoon for a few thousand dollars, so the defended window is hours, not weeks.

Sort the emergency queue on BOD 26-04's four criteria: Asset Exposure, KEV Status, Exploit Automation, Technical Impact, with internet-facing systems first and slow-cycle estates close behind; the research names industrial control systems, medical devices, and IoT on fixed maintenance windows or vendor-locked firmware as where exposure concentrates.

Compress release-to-deploy for the IT estate: the monthly-cadence, staged-rollout playbook no longer holds there, so take the vendor-side shift to roughly weekly dot-releases, which the research cites as progress, as the pace to match, and pre-authorize the emergency path so deployment never waits on a meeting; keep OT systems, medical devices, and vendor-locked firmware on step 4's compensating controls, because an untested patch there is an outage.
Hold pre-staged compensating controls ready for the windows that cannot close: egress cutoff, identity revocation, isolation, so unpatchable hours are covered by procedure rather than improvisation.

Shrink the emergency lane structurally: migrate critical components to memory-safe languages and adopt exploit-class mitigations that retire whole bug families at once, the durable fixes the research points upstream.

blocks.label: Blue Team Principle
blocks.text: Aim for human-machine teaming, not a lights-out SOC: AI handles breadth and speed, humans handle depth and judgment. Set explicit escalation thresholds, and red-team your own agents for prompt injection before they touch production.

plays.name: Purple Team
plays.title: Agentic Purple Teaming
plays.subtitle: The continuous, self-improving feedback loop: the heart of the strategy
plays.summary: The heart of the strategy: red executes, blue detects, both close the gap, and agents run the loop with autonomy as a dial.

outline.title: Autonomy Is a Dial, Not a Cliff
You Can't Escape Gödel: The Case for Continuous Defense Gets a Proof
Gap Analysis Across ATT&CK and ATLAS

blocks.text: Not just red and blue in one room. It's a structured loop: red executes a TTP, blue tries to detect it, both analyze the gap, and controls improve immediately, then repeat. Done by hand it's slow and costly. With Agentic AI the loop runs continuously and autonomously, which is what makes "continuous purple teaming" a credible maturity strategy rather than a slogan. It's also where named practitioners are converging: AI-security researcher Disesdi Susanna Cox argues that point-in-time "AI red teaming" is giving way to a purple paradigm, adversarial testing and threat modeling working as two halves of one loop (see her work in the Resource Index and AI Threat Modeling). Block reports red-teaming its own open-source agent, goose, end to end. Calendar-invite injection failed, a poisoned recipe reached the goose team and ran, the blue team caught the payload, and the fixes shipped: Unicode stripping, recipe warnings and a command allowlist (see Resource Index, Block, Operation Pale Fire).
blocks.heading: What Purple Teaming Actually Is

blocks.text: A useful framing for leadership conversations: the level of autonomy in the loop is a dial you turn deliberately, not a switch you flip. Crawl is manual: humans run the red/blue handoffs, AI mostly assists with analysis. Walk is scheduled with AI assist: agents run the loop on a cadence, humans review every change before it promotes. Run is end-to-end: the loop closes autonomously at machine speed, with human review reserved for the decisions that warrant it (novel findings, high-impact changes, anything touching production controls). The point isn't to reach "run" everywhere as fast as possible; it's to turn the dial up only where the environment is mature, the controls are bounded, and the evidence supports it, which is exactly what the Maturity Model and Roadmap sequence. This gradient also pairs with the safety controls below: the more autonomy you grant, the more the circuit breakers and containment boundaries (see Agent Containment) have to be doing the work.
blocks.heading: Autonomy Is a Dial, Not a Cliff

blocks.text: (1) Red agent selects a TTP from ATT&CK/ATLAS or a threat-intel feed; (2) executes it in a sandbox or controlled environment; (3) blue detection agent checks whether SIEM/EDR fired; (4) a purple orchestrator agent root-causes any gap; (5) a detection-engineering agent writes a new Sigma/KQL rule; (6) the rule is tested and promoted; (7) coverage metrics update on the ATT&CK/ATLAS heatmap. Humans review, approve, and govern the cycle.
blocks.heading: The Agentic Purple Loop

blocks.text: Annual or quarterly assessments are snapshots; environments change daily. Agentic purple teaming runs simulations against your live detection stack continuously, measures coverage in real time, and tracks improvement with quantitative metrics rather than checkbox compliance. MIT's AI Risk Repository, via its 272-expert Priority Risks Delphi study, finds that under current trajectories 18 of 24 AI risk domains carry ≥10% catastrophic-outcome probability within five years: the tempo of risk demands continuous validation. Industry has caught up to the premise: Cisco's infrastructure-and-security lead calls the harden-and-hope posture, locking down a system and trusting it for 18 months, dead for good in the post-Mythos environment (CSO Online, Jun 2026); point-in-time is no longer a defensible stance, it is a lapsed one.
blocks.heading: Continuous Validation vs. Point-in-Time

blocks.text: On June 9, 2026, the section above gained a mathematical footing. NIST announced that its senior scientist Apostol Vassilev had published a peer-reviewed mathematical proof (IEEE Security & Privacy, May 2026) extending Gödel's incompleteness theorems to AI guardrails: a guardrail set is a formal system built on finitely many rules, natural-language input makes the space it must police effectively unbounded, and so, structurally, not because anyone wrote the rules badly, "there is no finite set of guardrails that is universally robust against adversarial prompts." The paper formalizes guardrails as a checker function and proves that for any such checker, some constraint exists that it will enforce incorrectly against some adversarial input; finite context windows only tighten the bound. The empirical record this playbook already carries now has its explanation: the ~50% adaptive-bypass rate, the 24-of-25 trusted-user exfiltration, OWASP ranking prompt injection first three editions running, and the refuse-then-comply fine-tuning attack the CSA's companion note cites at 72% and 57% success against frontier models are not engineering shortfalls awaiting a patch. They are what incompleteness looks like in production. The constructive half is just as load-bearing. The proof hands attackers no recipe; hardening forces them toward zero-day-style prompt discovery, historically a nation-state-priced activity, so the rational defensive goal shifts from impossible completeness to economics: make finding the next exploit cost more than the adversary's resources. Vassilev's prescribed model is, element for element, this playbook's architecture: standing red teams continuously hunting adversarial prompts (this loop), continuous guardrail updates as evasions surface (the detection-engineering and VulnOps cadence), and operational resilience that limits impact and recovers fast when, not if, an exploit lands (Agent Containment and Agent Incident Response). The CSA's enterprise read closes the governance loop: point-in-time audits "systematically underestimate residual risk" because they measure control presence at assessment time rather than the discovery-to-update cadence that actually determines posture, the same argument the cATO thread makes from federal authorization, now with a theorem under it, and its architectural prescription is gateway-layer guardrails, input and output, hot-updateable without redeploying the application. One discipline note for the briefing deck: the proof concerns model-layer guardrails. It is the mathematical case for what Blue Team and Agent Containment conclude operationally: deterministic, environment-layer bounds are the controls that hold when the model layer provably cannot.
blocks.heading: You Can't Escape Gödel: The Case for Continuous Defense Gets a Proof

blocks.text: When a TTP succeeds undetected, the agent reasons about why: missing log source? absent rule? over-broad suppression? known evasion variant? Crucially, standard ATT&CK coverage doesn't capture AI-specific techniques, so purple teams must map coverage against MITRE ATLAS too, validating that AI-enabled threats are tested, not just traditional ones.
blocks.heading: Gap Analysis Across ATT&CK and ATLAS

blocks.text: A concrete, RAITE-aligned loop you can run: red clones an employee's voice from public audio and calls the help desk to take over their account; blue checks whether the account-recovery and MFA-reset workflow detects or stops it; purple measures the gap and closes it. Measure three things: time-to-detect (first malicious recovery attempt to SOC alert), false-accept rate under adversarial pressure (how often the cloned identity is accepted), and coverage delta (detections that existed before vs. after). It extends RAITE's red-acts / blue-acts alternation with a purple measurement step, exercises a model (voice liveness) and a human workflow at once, and scales straight to the agentic case: swap the human help desk for an AI account-recovery agent and re-run. Keep any live demo to consented, internal targets and synthetic identities only.
blocks.heading: Worked Example: Deepfake Voice → Help-Desk

blocks.text: An emerging pattern that turns CTI directly into purple-team exercises: instead of hand-building a scenario from an advisory, put an agent in the adversary's seat. It ingests the threat intelligence for a named actor (e.g., a CISA advisory on APT28/GRU targeting logistics), maps it to a structured ATT&CK technique set, and emulates THAT actor in a sandboxed range, not a generic attacker. Red emulation feeds blue detection; the loop reruns the day new intel drops. This is a real, named discipline as of 2026: academic systems (RedTeamLLM, Incalmo, hierarchical LLM-RL red teamers) and CTI-to-emulation tooling (IntelEX and eLLM-CTI for extraction; Aurora, which raises CTI-technique fidelity ~30% and substitutes available tooling while preserving chain logic; Microsoft's CTI-REALM for checkpoint-scored evaluation) have made each step buildable. Three controls keep it on the right side of the playbook's own doctrine: hard sandboxing and an explicit human authorization gate (it is an autonomous offense capability: guardrails travel with the capability, not the intent); CTI-grounding plus a separate evaluator agent tasked to disprove off-script actions (the verification doctrine from Red Team: this prevents hallucinated TTPs from corrupting the emulation); and fidelity scoring against the source advisory so you can prove you emulated the actor, not "generic attacker." The right framing is Intelligence-Driven Agentic Adversary Emulation, TTP-grounded, sandbox-bound, fidelity-evaluated, human-authorized. A standalone concept brief accompanies this playbook.
blocks.heading: Worked Example: Intelligence-Driven Adversary Emulation

blocks.text: The CSA's Mythos-ready guidance asks programs to rehearse the storm, not the incident, so run it. In one morning, three injects land: (1) an indirect prompt injection through a vendor email turns a triage agent into an exfiltration channel; (2) Glasswing-class scanning publicly drops a working exploit for a library inside your detection stack; (3) the OT historian starts answering queries it should never receive. Red plays all three from prepared cards; blue must triage under the contain-first doctrine: cut agent egress and revoke its identity first (Agent Containment), preserve memory and tool logs before any restart (Agent Incident Response), and hold the Purdue 3.5 boundary while the historian anomaly is scoped (OT, ICS & SCADA). Purple measures three things: time-to-containment per incident, whether evidence survived responder actions, and where the single on-call analyst became the bottleneck, the storm's real lesson. End on the CSA question: which of the three would you have deprioritized, and what would it have cost? Feed every gap back as a detection, an authorization change, or a staffing decision: the same close-the-gaps mechanics as the maturity self-assessment. The full written scenario set (this storm plus two more) lives in the study guide, Part 7.
blocks.heading: Worked Example: The Vulnerability Storm (Tabletop)

items.text: Continuous simulation of ATT&CK techniques against the live detection stack; ATLAS techniques join as the AI-specific detections mature (see Blue Team)

items.title: Coverage Gap Analysis
items.text: Agent identifies which techniques lack detection and root-causes why

items.title: Auto-Generated Detections
items.text: Missed technique → agent writes Sigma rule → tests → promotes to production

items.title: Quantitative Coverage Metrics
items.text: Real-time ATT&CK/ATLAS heatmap, graded share of in-scope techniques with validated detections, updated continuously

items.title: Detection Drift Monitoring
items.text: Agent flags when previously working detections degrade due to environment changes

items.title: Threat-Intel-Driven Prioritization
items.text: Agent prioritizes TTPs from CTI actor profiles (ATT&CK Groups, advisories, TI feeds), with ATLAS case studies and AIID trends for AI-specific techniques

items.title: Run the agentic purple loop continuously against your live detection stack (red TTP to blue detect to gap to fix) instead of annual snapshots.
items.text: Continuous by the guide's own instruction, scoped by its twelve categories, with the blue half wired by the program.
bullets: Run the red half on the continuous ATT&CK and ATLAS emulation the Red Team play stands up, and add the guide's twelve agentic threat categories (authorization and control hijacking, checker-out-of-the-loop, critical system interaction, goal and instruction manipulation, hallucination exploitation, impact chain and blast radius, and the rest) as the rotating scope for the agent estate itself, so coverage of both layers is a schedule rather than a preference.

Run the loop before and after deployment as the record directs, on the reasoning it gives: agents should be treated no differently than any other code in production, which makes the annual snapshot the anomaly, not the continuous cadence.

Structure each iteration on the guide's four phases: preparation, execution, analysis, reporting, reusing its per-category test requirements and actionable steps so runs are comparable rather than bespoke.

Close the blue half the program owns: the guide stops at findings informing system hardening and design decisions, so route every detection gap into detection engineering with an owner and a due date, because that handoff is yours to build and not the record's.

Track the loop with the metrics the guide suggests teams agree on: time to detect and block unauthorized access, share of successful exploits against attempts, time to containment, and undetected malicious actions per run, and map results into the shared AI adversary taxonomy for comparability.

Deconflict every run through the kill switch and deconfliction channel set up in the Red Team play's continuous-emulation action, and tag sanctioned detections so they score as coverage rather than open as incidents or trip automated containment.

items.title: Validate identity-verification controls with the deepfake-voice to help-desk loop (RAITE-aligned), on consented internal targets and synthetic identities only.

Audit every deployed AI system for static, non-updating guardrail configurations: anything not adversarially tested since deployment, or with controls baked into application code, is elevated risk; move enforcement to hot-updateable gateway layers, input and output.
items.text: Inventory guardrails like attack surface: anything static since deployment is presumed stale.
bullets: Enumerate every deployed AI system's guardrail set: system prompts, input filters, output checks, tool allowlists, with owner, enforcement point, and last adversarial test date; the proof's result is that no finite guardrail set is universally robust, so an unchanged configuration is a finding, not a comfort.
Flag the two elevated-risk classes for first remediation: guardrails never adversarially tested since deployment, and enforcement baked into application code where it cannot move at attack speed.

Relocate enforcement to hot-updateable layers on both sides of the model: every prompt preprocessed before inference, every output postprocessed before release, treating system prompts as the tactical, incomplete mitigation the SANS guidance says they are.

Stand up the operating loop the proof prescribes: a standing red-team function hunting new adversarial prompts, guardrail updates shipped as weaknesses surface, and resilience planning that assumes exploit-when-not-if.

Measure the program economically: the stated defensive goal is a state where finding a new exploit costs more than the attacker's resources, so track guardrail-update latency as the number that moves that ratio.

blocks.label: The Strategy in One Line
blocks.text: Continuous agentic purple teaming IS the maturity strategy: a self-improving posture where the attack-to-defense feedback loop runs automatically, governed by the security strategy function. (The continuous purple-loop diagram and its value-stream map are in the Reference Architecture play, under Use Case & Value Stream Map.)

plays.name: Maturity Model
plays.title: SecOps AI Maturity Model
plays.subtitle: The roadmap from manual operations to autonomous, adaptive SecOps
plays.summary: A four-level ladder from AI-assisted work to autonomous SecOps, so you can place your SOC and see what the next level asks.

items.title: AI-Assisted
items.text: Humans do the work; AI gives recommendations and generates content on request.
bullets: Claude/ChatGPT for writing detection rules or IR playbooks
Security Copilot for report drafting
Natural-language → KQL query generation
LLM-assisted phishing-lure analysis
items.meta: AI is a research assistant; workflow stays human-driven. Most Tier-1 SOC analysts operate here today.

items.title: AI-Augmented
items.text: AI handles defined subtasks autonomously inside human-supervised workflows.
bullets: SOAR playbooks calling AI APIs for alert enrichment
AI triage scoring in the SIEM alert queue
Automated threat-intel summarization to analysts
AI-suggested detection rules in the engineering pipeline
items.meta: AI is embedded in the toolchain; analysts spend less time on low-value tasks; clear human review gates exist.

items.title: Agentic Pipelines
items.text: Multi-step agents own end-to-end workflows with human oversight at key decision points.
bullets: Triage agent: alert → enrich → verdict → ticket, end-to-end
Hunt agent: hypothesis → query → interpret → sub-hypothesis
Red agent: recon → exploit chain → report
Purple loop: TTP sim → detection check → gap analysis → rule gen
items.meta: Agents handle full case workflows; humans review, approve, and escalate. All agent runs are logged and auditable.

items.title: Autonomous SecOps
items.text: Agents run continuously, self-direct on the threat landscape, and improve controls automatically. Humans set policy and review exceptions.
bullets: Continuous purple loop running 24/7 against production detections
Self-improving detection: agents generate, test, and promote rules
Hunt focus reallocated from CTI actor activity and AIID trends
Autonomous IR for defined low-risk incident classes, fully audited
items.meta: Posture improves passively; coverage metrics trend up without manual sprints; human role is governance, policy, and edge cases. This is the target state for a mature Agentic SecOps program. Validate progress against external benchmarks: Anthropic's three-tier Zero Trust framework (Foundation → Enterprise → Advanced, the eBook's tier names; its blog summary says Foundation, Advanced, Optimized) and the SANS 5-stage AI Security Maturity Model, both in the Frameworks play, plus, as of June 2026, the Carnegie Mellon SEI AI Adoption Maturity Model (see the callout below), and SentinelOne's Autonomous SOC Maturity Model, revisited in July 2026 with 18 months of field deployment data (Resource Index, SentinelOne, The Autonomous SOC, Revisited).

blocks.label: Benchmark Against the Field: CMU SEI
blocks.text: In June 2026, the Carnegie Mellon Software Engineering Institute (the home of CMMI), in collaboration with Accenture, released the AI Adoption Maturity Model: a research-validated framework built from a review of 100+ existing maturity efforts, ~25 executive interviews, ~600 practitioners surveyed, and Fortune 500 pilots. It assesses eight dimensions: organizational strategy; workforce & culture; workflow re-engineering; risk & governance; data; engineering; operations; and technology ecosystem, toward two high-level goals (organizational change and AI lifecycle engineering), and ships with an assessment tool for baselining and periodic re-assessment. Use it as the externally validated anchor for this ladder: the levels above are the SecOps-specific climb; the SEI model is the enterprise-wide maturity frame that climb nests inside. (Figures and specifics are as published by the SEI at launch: verify before quoting.)

plays.name: Roadmap
plays.title: Implementation Roadmap
plays.subtitle: A phased, foundations-first path from assessment to autonomous purple teaming
plays.summary: A phased path from assessment and baseline to scaling toward autonomy, each phase with key moves and an exit criterion to meet first.

blocks.text: A pragmatic sequence mapped to the Maturity Model. Each phase has an objective, the key moves, and a measurable exit criterion before advancing. Timelines are indicative: the gates matter more than the calendar.

items.title: Assess & Baseline
items.text: Establish an honest baseline before introducing any automation.
bullets: Inventory current detections and map coverage to MITRE ATT&CK (and ATLAS for AI assets)
Measure the real false-positive rate and mean time to triage
Document existing triage criteria and response playbooks as-is
Audit telemetry quality and data-fabric gaps
items.meta: A documented coverage heatmap, FP-rate baseline, and a prioritized foundations backlog.

items.title: Strengthen Foundations (AI-Assisted)
items.text: Use AI to help fix fundamentals: the work that makes everything after it pay off.
bullets: AI-assisted alert tuning to cut false positives at the source
Codify triage discipline and severity/escalation criteria with AI support
Generate and backfill detections for high-priority ATT&CK gaps
Stand up telemetry-quality scoring; normalize the data fabric
items.meta: Measurable FP reduction, documented triage standard, and a trustworthy telemetry baseline.

items.title: Embed AI in the Workflow
items.text: Move from AI-on-request to AI embedded in supervised workflows.
bullets: Deploy an autonomous triage agent with human review gates
Pilot an AI threat-hunting agent on a bounded hypothesis set
Integrate AI enrichment into SOAR playbooks
Establish agent containment guardrails (sandboxing, egress, least privilege)
Stand up 'VulnOps' as a standing capability: continuous, AI-accelerated vulnerability triage matched to the shrinking disclosure-to-exploit window (per CSA's 'AI Vulnerability Storm')
items.meta: Triage time materially reduced; agents auditable; containment controls verified by red-team test.

items.title: Stand Up the Purple Loop
items.text: Connect red emulation and blue detection into a continuous, measured loop.
bullets: Automate ATT&CK/ATLAS TTP emulation against the live detection stack
Wire gap analysis → auto-generated Sigma/KQL rules → test → promote
Publish a live coverage heatmap and trend metrics to leadership
Prioritize TTPs by current threat-actor profiles (ATT&CK Groups, advisories, TI feeds), with ATLAS and AIID for AI-specific techniques
items.meta: A running purple loop with weekly coverage improvements and an auditable change trail.

items.title: Scale Toward Autonomy
items.text: Let the loop run continuously; humans govern, set policy, and handle exceptions.
bullets: Expand autonomous response to defined low-risk incident classes
Continuous 24/7 purple validation with drift monitoring
Quarterly governance review against NIST AI 600-1 and the AI Defense Matrix
Reallocate analyst time to threat strategy and edge-case judgment
items.meta: Coverage trends up without manual sprints; human role is governance and exceptions.

blocks.label: Governance Note
blocks.text: Every phase advances only when its exit criterion is met: gates over calendar. Risk governance (acceptable use, agent identities, logging) starts in Phase 0 and runs in parallel through every phase; containment guardrails come online with the first agents in Phase 2, never bolted on at the end.

plays.name: Program and Operating Model
plays.title: Program & Operating Model
plays.subtitle: The management view: first 90 days, who owns what, build-vs-buy, and the workforce plan
plays.summary: The management view: the first 90 days, who owns what, build versus buy, and a workforce plan for the analysts.

blocks.text: The roadmap says what to build; this is how to run it as a program. A useful way to show leadership this is a balanced program, not just a tech purchase, is the classic People / Process / Technology lens, with Data as a fourth pillar that Agentic AI makes non-negotiable. The rest of this play covers the questions senior leadership tends to ask first: near-term wins, ownership, cost posture, and people. For the people-and-process redesign itself, watch Anton Chuvakin and Augusto Barros' framework-in-progress, Stop Building a 2003 SOC with AI (Resource Index, Anton Chuvakin, Stop Building a 2003 SOC with AI), which opens with the same warning this play is built on: keep 2003 processes, and AI yields a somewhat better 2003 SOC.

blocks.alt: Security org chart: today vs future

items.title: People
items.text: Human-in-command operators set strategy, hypotheses, and exceptions; analysts are upskilled and redeployed to judgment work, not replaced. Covered in Human in Command and the workforce plan below: AI as a partner for human judgment.

items.title: Process
items.text: The continuous purple loop, governance control plane, phased roadmap, and continuous control validation. Process is what turns capability into repeatable, auditable outcomes: the Maturity, Roadmap, Governance, and CTI plays.

items.title: Technology
items.text: Agentic platforms, the model layer, and deterministic containment. Powerful, but bought-and-integrated rather than the source of advantage: the Tools and Tech Stack and Agent Containment plays.

items.title: Data
items.text: Agentic SecOps runs on telemetry and context, so data quality is foundational, and a genuine attack surface. Bad or poisoned data degrades or hijacks AI (data/model poisoning, RAG manipulation). Hence the data fabric in Foundations, provenance in SAIF, and the poisoning risks in Risks & Ethics.

items.title: Days 1 - 30 · See clearly
items.text: Stand up the coverage/FP baseline (Phase 0) and ship one low-risk, high-visibility AI assist, e.g., AI-drafted alert summaries, to build momentum and trust.

items.title: Days 31 - 60 · Fix a real pain
items.text: Target the noisiest alert source with AI-assisted tuning; report the before/after to leadership in business terms. Early credibility funds the rest.

items.title: Days 61 - 90 · Prove the loop
items.text: Run a single TTP through emulation → detection check → rule update, with humans in command. Demonstrates the model works before scaling investment.

items.title: Throughout · Govern from day one
items.text: Establish agent identities, least-privilege scope, logging, and an acceptable-use boundary now, not after agents are everywhere.

items.title: Security Strategy
items.text: Owns the roadmap, maturity targets, governance posture, and the 'what do we automate next' decision. Sets acceptable-use and human-in-command policy.

items.title: Detection Engineering / Blue
items.text: Builds and tunes detections, owns the rules the purple loop generates, runs day-to-day blue agents under review.

items.title: Red / Adversary Emulation
items.text: Owns sanctioned TTP emulation and scope; validates that detections and containment actually hold.

items.title: Security Leadership / AO
items.text: Owns risk acceptance, ATO/cATO authorization, and sign-off on high-impact autonomous actions. Consulted on exceptions.

items.title: Platform / Cloud & IAM
items.text: Provides the agent identities, SSO/IAM, egress controls, and sandboxes the program depends on.

items.title: Legal / Privacy / Compliance
items.text: Advises on regulatory obligations, data handling, and acceptable-use boundaries; informed on incidents.

items.title: CTI / Threat Intelligence
items.text: Owns the actor profiles and intel feeds that prioritize the purple loop's TTP queue, and grades emulation fidelity against the source advisory.

items.title: Organize around outcomes, not tasks
items.text: Today's security orgs are built around functions: AppSec, Cloud, SOC, GRC, Identity, because people do the work. As agents absorb the routine work, that logic weakens: the durable structure organizes around outcomes instead, security strategy and risk, AI and automation engineering, security operations, engineering enablement, and trust and business resilience. The RACI above is the near-term control plane; the direction of travel is a chart drawn around what the org delivers rather than the tools it runs, with the leader's value shifting from alert throughput to judgment, knowing what the risk actually is and where a human still belongs in the loop.

items.title: Buy the platform layer
items.text: Use accredited commercial AI-SOC platforms (the CSP/vendor stack) for triage, detection, and orchestration rather than building from scratch: faster, and they arrive with authorization lineage (GovCloud/IL where relevant).

items.title: Build the integration & loop
items.text: Your proprietary value is the continuous purple loop, the foundations work, and the governance/evidence layer wired to your environment, not the base model.

items.title: Cost posture
items.text: Budget against baselined outcomes (FP reduction, coverage gain, analyst hours freed). Watch token/compute consumption and approval-fatigue overhead as scale grows.

items.title: Avoid lock-in & silver bullets
items.text: Favor model-agnostic control layers; be skeptical of vendors selling 'agentic auto-fix' as a complete solution (see Risks: Security Theater).

items.title: Reframe roles, don't cut them
items.text: Position AI as removing toil so analysts move to investigation, threat hunting, and strategy: the 'partner, not replacement' message, made concrete.

items.title: Upskill for AI fluency
items.text: Train analysts to review and challenge AI reasoning (not rubber-stamp), and to recognize AI failure modes. The AI Fluency play is a starting glossary.

items.title: Guard against skill atrophy
items.text: Keep core skills sharp with manual exercises so the team can operate when AI is wrong or unavailable (see Risks: Overreliance).

items.title: Bring people along
items.text: Change lands when people understand the rationale and see early wins. Tie the rollout to relief from their worst daily pain points.

blocks.label: Program Principle
blocks.text: Win trust early with one visible quick win, make ownership explicit so nothing falls through the cracks, buy the platform and build the loop, and treat the workforce as partners to bring along, not costs to cut. Govern from day one, not after scale.

plays.name: Metrics and ROI
plays.title: Metrics & ROI
plays.subtitle: Measuring whether the program works: quality, speed, coverage, and force multiplication
plays.summary: Speed, quality, coverage and cost measures that show whether the program works, with every speed metric paired to a quality metric.

blocks.text: Without metrics you can't tell whether a SOC is protecting the organization or just generating reports. These are the measures that prove the program is working and justify continued investment. Benchmarks are indicative industry ranges (2026): set your own targets against your Phase 0 baseline. Pair every speed metric with a quality metric so you're not just failing faster. For a concrete external benchmark, SentinelOne reports 75% faster investigations, 4x more threats handled and 42% fewer false positives among customers running its Autonomous SOC, figures from an IDC study SentinelOne sponsored (Resource Index: SentinelOne, The Autonomous SOC, Revisited; vendor-reported, verify before quoting).

items.title: Mean Time to Detect (MTTD)
items.text: Time from malicious activity start to detection. The leading indicator that predicts where MTTR lands.

items.title: Mean Time to Respond (MTTR)
items.text: Detection to first containment. Keep severity-tiered targets and measure the reduction against your Phase 0 baseline.

items.title: Mean Time to Contain (MTTC)
items.text: Confirmed threat to neutralized. Automated playbooks collapse this most dramatically: the highest-visibility ROI.

items.title: Alert-to-Triage Time
items.text: Agentic triage should cut the minutes a human spends on each alert while keeping a consistent depth. Measure it against your Phase 0 baseline.

items.title: AI Decision Accuracy
items.text: Share of agent triage verdicts that are correct. The guardrail against automating mistakes: track it before trusting throughput.

items.title: False Positive Rate
items.text: A spike signals detection rules are degrading. Use severity-tiered thresholds, not one blanket number, and measure it against a labeled regression set with an eval harness (Promptfoo, CyberSecEval), not by eyeball.

items.title: False Negative Rate
items.text: How often real threats are dismissed as benign: the most dangerous and hardest-to-see failure mode. Production truth is unobservable, so measure it on the purple loop (emulated TTPs the agent auto-closed) and on sampled re-review of auto-closed alerts.

items.title: Escalation Rate
items.text: Share of cases needing human review. Too high wastes the automation; too low may mean over-trusting the agent.

items.title: ATT&CK / ATLAS Coverage %
items.text: Share of in-scope techniques with a detection validated by emulation, graded (telemetry, alert, prevention) rather than counted because a rule exists. The primary output of the purple loop; trend it weekly.

items.title: Automation / Auto-Close Rate
items.text: Share of alerts resolved without human touch. Shows how much analyst time is freed for high-value work.

items.title: Analyst Force Multiplication
items.text: The clearest 'AI as partner, not replacement' metric: capacity gained and where it went, not alerts closed.
items.meta: Analyst hours redeployed to hunting, engineering, and purple work

items.title: Detection Drift / Repeat-Incident Rate
items.text: Detections degrading over time, and incidents recurring: the cleanest signal of postmortem and tuning discipline.

items.title: Cost per Investigated Alert
items.text: All-in agentic cost (tokens, infra, licenses) per alert vs. the Phase-0 loaded analyst-hour. The unit economics that justify scale-up.

items.title: Token Spend per Workflow / Agent
items.text: Loop multiplication makes spend non-linear; token budgets and loop caps (see Infrastructure & Compute) are the guardrail of record.

items.title: Small-Model Resolution Rate
items.text: Share of tasks resolved by cached or small-model tiers before frontier-model escalation: the cleanest running-cost lever.

items.title: Cost-per-Task Regression Gate
items.text: Include $/task in the eval suite: model and prompt changes gate on cost the same way they gate on accuracy.

items.title: Idle / Orphaned Agent Spend
items.text: Compute and credentials consumed by agents with no owner or recent tasking: the FinOps face of NHI offboarding (see Agentic Insider Risk).

blocks.label: Reporting Principle
blocks.text: Leadership doesn't want to hear that MTTR dropped 15 minutes: they want to know what that saved and what risk it retired. Translate every metric into business terms, baseline at Phase 0, and report the trend. "Show, don't tell": observable workflows and reproducible outcomes beat vendor claims.

plays.name: Action Plan
plays.title: Action Plan
plays.subtitle: Every recommended action in the playbook, aggregated and sequenced: Now, Next, Later
plays.summary: Every recommended action in the playbook in one sequenced list, Now, Next and Later, each linked back to the play it comes from.

blocks.text: Now means start immediately; Next, once the Now items are moving; and Later, as the program matures.

items.title: Define human-in-command decision gates for consequential actions, and guard against approval fatigue turning oversight into an accountability fiction.
Gate agent scale-up on AI-ready data: a semantic layer, governance for AI, and captured business context. Only 26% of chief data officers are confident their data can support new AI-enabled revenue.
Treat your own agentic tooling as critical infrastructure: the same containment, identity, and governance you would give a crown-jewel system.
Deploy autonomous Tier-1 triage (SIEM to EDR to threat-intel to CMDB correlation) to cut false-positive load and free analysts for high-value work.
Audit every defensive agent against the lethal trifecta (private-data access, untrusted input, external comms), and break at least one leg.

Instrument time-to-validate alongside time-to-detect: gate AI-surfaced findings on environment context (assets, identities, exposure) before action, and treat a growing validation backlog as the bottleneck signal it is.

Re-scope emergency-patch criteria for the N-hour window: assume a public patch can be weaponized within hours (a frontier model built a working exploit inside an hour of a patch release), prioritize internet-facing and hard-to-patch OT/ICS systems, and push the durable fix upstream, memory-safe components and exploit-class mitigations that retire whole bug families.

Audit every deployed AI system for static, non-updating guardrail configurations: anything not adversarially tested since deployment, or with controls baked into application code, is elevated risk; move enforcement to hot-updateable gateway layers, input and output.
Diagram your actual agent dataflows against this reference: every tool, credential, data store, and egress path each agent can reach. The gap between the diagram and reality is your blast radius.

Pick one high-volume, low-blast-radius workflow as the first production use case and instrument it end-to-end: baseline the manual value stream before the agent touches it, or you'll never prove the gain.
Choose the hosting model by data sensitivity: managed API by default, self-hosted open models where residency/control demands it.
Make egress filtering the priority control: default-deny outbound with DNS/destination allowlisting so a compromised agent cannot reach attacker infrastructure.
Make Human in Command a hard line for any agent that can actuate a physical process: no autonomous actuation in OT.
Enforce the IT/OT boundary (Purdue Level 3.5 DMZ) as the most consequential authorization boundary: no unmediated agent crossings.

Give every suppression and tuning change a lineage record: who authorized it, what incident or decision prompted it, when it should be reviewed, and what conditions must hold for it to remain valid. Suppressions without provenance are technical debt that accrues silently until a breach review asks why an alert was never seen and no one can answer.
Anchor the program to NIST AI RMF + GenAI Profile (with OWASP and MITRE) so risk reduction is demonstrable, not a private rulebook.
Give every agent its own scoped, least-privilege, short-lived identity, not shared service credentials.

Adopt tool-arrangement reviews as the governance gate: for every agent deployment, record what it may do, which tools and data it can reach, how memory is handled, and how updates land, and treat any change to that arrangement as the approval record.
items.meta: Dux et al. · Governance by Design, Apr 2026

items.title: Map every AI system against EU AI Act roles (provider vs. deployer) and Annex III high-risk criteria: the 2026 Omnibus defers high-risk duties to Dec 2, 2027, but transparency obligations have applied since Aug 2, 2026 and the mapping gates everything else.

When using an LLM to threat-model an AI system, treat the assistant itself as in-scope: isolate its context, verify every architecture document fed to it, and never let an unreviewed artifact drive the model. A crafted input loaded as context can steer the assistant toward a threat model that is confidently but structurally wrong.

Cap AI-generated threat batches and require per-item human adjudication; sample for hallucinated or duplicate threats before they reach the register. When a model emits forty scenarios in ninety seconds, fluency and volume get mistaken for validity, and acceptance by omission is how fictional threats become tracked work.
Add role-based jailbreaks ("respond as a trusted analyst") and instruction-chaining to red-team prompt suites: the same social framing GTG-1002 used to decompose malicious work into innocuous steps.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Ground threat models in live source code rather than documentation and keep them continuously updated, schema-validated, and cataloged across products, so kill-chain viability and incident-scope questions resolve in minutes against real code instead of hours of cross-team analysis when a zero-day lands.
items.meta: Purple Book · Snapshots to Living Intelligence, Jun 2026

items.title: Bring agents into ICAM as governed non-human identities (NHIs): the agentic-specific move this playbook draws from the DoW Zero Trust mandate.
Map every agent to its authorization boundary and Impact Level (IL2-IL6) before it touches federal data.
Harden remote hiring against fabricated personas: liveness checks in interviews, detection of reused AI-generated headshots across applicants, and awareness of real-time voice modulation.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Pre-stage compensating controls for unpatchable windows: egress cutoff, identity revocation, sandbox isolation, as pre-planned procedures, not reactive improvisation.

Baseline every agent deployment against the Five Eyes 'Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services' guidance: audit what each agent can reach (least privilege), anchor agents to verified short-lived credentials, and adopt its containment-over-efficiency defaults.
items.meta: Five Eyes · Careful Adoption of Agentic AI, May 2026

items.title: Adopt BOD 26-04's four-criteria triage for your own vulnerability program even outside the Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB): asset exposure, KEV status, exploit automatability, post-exploitation impact, with a three-day class plus forensic triage for the worst, fixed-day classes of 3, 14, and 60 days in between, and fix on system upgrade for the lowest.

Require agents to surface the full effect of a setup or recovery command before running it, including the contents of any script it invokes and anything that script fetches at runtime (DNS, HTTP, package hooks), not just the command string. A pre-authorized step is not a safe step.

Treat setup instructions and scripts in unfamiliar repos as untrusted code regardless of what the AI tool recommends. Run agent-driven first-time setup in a sandbox with no standing secrets and egress control, so a fetched payload lands in a throwaway shell with nothing to steal.

Replace freeform closure comments with a structured close artifact on every analyst-closed incident: what inputs were weighed, what precedent was cited, what was ruled out and why, and who or what made the call. The outcome already survives as the incident state; this captures the reasoning before it evaporates. Needs no new platform: a comment template or SOAR variable is enough to start.
Write agent-specific IR runbooks: the agent itself can be the incident, and containment must move at agent speed.
Instrument detection for agent-gone-wrong signals: egress anomalies, unexpected privilege escalation, off-pattern tool use, abnormal looping, and runaway token or compute consumption.

Enable AI-investigation telemetry before you need it: AI interaction audit logging, the SIEM's AI connectors, and agent-inventory risk queries, and adopt the scope → context → signal investigation sequence.
items.meta: Microsoft AeGIS · AI Investigation Playbook, Jun 2026

items.title: Maintain an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM): you cannot govern uninventoried models, services, and agent frameworks.

Audit direct and transitive dependencies against the 281 open-source projects with Glasswing-disclosed vulnerabilities as of May 22, 2026: prioritize anything internet-facing or handling auth, crypto, or protocol parsing.
Treat available Glasswing patches (97 confirmed as of May 22, 2026) as emergency changes, not scheduled maintenance: median disclosure-to-exploit has collapsed to hours.
Adopt MITRE ATLAS as the shared taxonomy for AI-specific threats: adversarial data, model evasion, ML supply-chain compromise, model inversion.
Hunt for AI-assisted tooling tells in suspect code: emoji status markers, conversational in-line comments, overly descriptive or inconsistent naming, and over-engineered modular structure.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Stand up an adversarial validator function that challenges agent recommendations before action, but recognize it only works if there is a decision trace to dispute. Without the reasoning captured, disagreeing with an agent is theater. Pair every validator gate with the trace that makes the agent judgment inspectable.
Calibrate workforce trust deliberately: counter both under-trust and over-trust with training and clear escalation paths.
Stand up data products with named owners and quality SLAs before wiring agents to them: 84% of chief data officers say their data products have already provided significant competitive advantage.
Replace ticket-paced response with defensive automation: you cannot stop a seconds-to-compromise attacker by hand.
Stand up continuous, sandboxed adversary emulation mapped to MITRE ATT&CK: replace episodic, scope-limited pentests with an always-on red agent.
Extend red-team scope to your own AI attack surface: prompt injection, memory/RAG poisoning, and model evasion against your agents.
Adopt an open eval harness (PyRIT, Garak, Promptfoo, Inspect) so red findings become CI-able regression tests: the tooling spine of the purple loop.

Build a ground-truth evaluation set (labeled corpora plus hand-built vulnerability chains) and a scoring rubric before fielding any AI-powered scanner: score precision, recall, severity-tiered false-positive rate, and chain detection against known answers, not vendor claims.

Fold Microsoft red-team taxonomy v2.0 (June 2026) into red-team scope: its seven new failure modes (agentic supply chain compromise, MCP and plugin abuse, inter-agent trust escalation, computer-use agent visual attacks, and more) are the current test checklist for deployed agentic systems.
Run the agentic purple loop continuously against your live detection stack (red TTP to blue detect to gap to fix) instead of annual snapshots.
Validate identity-verification controls with the deepfake-voice to help-desk loop (RAITE-aligned), on consented internal targets and synthetic identities only.

Instrument the agent orchestration layer to emit a structured decision trace at commit time: inputs consumed, alternatives weighed, precedent cited, what was ruled out, the recommendation, and who or what made the call, persisted as a peer artifact to events and joined to the entity graph. Then expose precedent retrieval to agents so the next decision can query the prior ones. Capture has to happen at orchestration time; once data lands downstream via ETL the reasoning is already gone.
Stand up the gateway pattern: route all agent tool-calls through a policy-enforcing proxy with logging, allow-lists, and rate caps, so the architecture's control points exist in one place.
Keep authorization outside the model: bind each agent session to the user who started it, scope tokens per hop, and give the policy decision point the delegation chain it needs to say no.
items.meta: CoSAI · Zero Trust for AI Systems, Sep 2026

items.title: Treat every MCP connection as a trust boundary: close the gaps the protocol leaves open by binding each session to an authenticated identity and enforcing authorization at the server, accept dynamically discovered tools only after verifying their origin, and run MCP processes sandboxed and least-privileged.
items.meta: NSA · MCP Security Design Considerations, May 2026

items.title: Maintain a scored use-case backlog (value × data-readiness × blast-radius) and let the metrics from the first use case pull the next one, not enthusiasm.
Put cost-control levers on agent loops (token budgets, loop caps): agent-loop multiplication makes spend non-linear.
Front agents with an AI firewall / LLM gateway to inspect prompts and responses for injection and exfiltration.
Microsegment agent workloads behind private endpoints to contain lateral movement and blast radius.
Define the delegation operating model across red/blue/purple while holding the governance line centrally.
Design the architecture as a common control core instantiable at multiple levels (CUI to classified): build to the highest applicable bar.
In classified enclaves, make isolation the first control: air-gap/cross-domain solutions and JSIG controls for SCIF-operated systems.

Hunt for persona-fabrication indicators post-hire: resumes suspiciously aligned to posting language, AI-polished communications inconsistent with live performance, identity-document photo reuse. Route those HR-observable indicators through the insider-threat program under a documented legal basis with HR and privacy sign-off, aimed at behavior rather than individuals, and have the SOC hunt the signals it can query: remote-management or KVM-over-IP tooling on the issued laptop, sign-ins from geographies inconsistent with the claimed location, and concurrent sessions across personas.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Run the full NHI lifecycle on every agent: owner of record and expiry at provisioning, automatic rotation, and offboarding sweeps for residual grants and orphaned identities.

Treat agent memory, retrieved context, hooks, and local config as attack surface (OWASP ASI06): enforce provenance on what enters persistent state, separate trust tiers so untrusted content cannot reach high-trust layers, and add visibility into what persists across sessions. The MemoryTrap pattern turned a routine dependency install into cross-session compromise.
Apply signature-reduction / managed-attribution doctrine to sanctioned offensive agents in a UTS environment: manage observability, do not assume anonymity.
For OT/ICS assets on quarter-to-year patch cycles, define per-system exposure-reduction playbooks: the operative question is what you deploy now, not how fast you patch.

Prototype a closed-loop exposure-management pattern (BOD 26-04's four criteria prioritize findings, agents draft remediations, a human adjudicates, deployment automates with rollback), and benchmark build-vs-buy against a commercial execution layer such as Palantir Apollo.

Tabletop the storm, not the incident: exercise multiple simultaneous high-severity incidents landing in the same week, with critical-incident playbooks pre-written and remediation automated as far as possible.
Gate post-incident return-to-duty on the agent's eval regression suite, with the incident added as a permanent test case: an agent that caused an incident re-earns production, it doesn't resume it.
Vet both the artifact and the provider, model provenance/training and the vendor security posture, before adoption.
When a product claims "autonomous," locate it on the autonomy spectrum and demand the controls to set the dial yourself: autonomy is earned through evidence, not granted by a datasheet.

Make continuous safety operations a procurement gate: require AI vendors to evidence ongoing adversarial testing, guardrail update cadence, and a disclosure process. A static safety configuration is elevated supply-chain risk under the Gödel result.

Inventory and govern the agent configuration surface, instruction files (AGENTS.md), persona files (SOUL.md), system prompts, and the skills, tools, and memory a swarm shares: version-control it, access-control it, integrity-check it, and review-gate every change, and bring it into threat-modeling and supply-chain review. Whoever edits these files, or poisons a shared resource the agents read, redirects the agents.
Audit vulnerability-management tooling for NVD/CVSS dependency and add vendor advisories + CTI as primary triage signals: NVD can no longer enrich everything it receives.
Add deepfake-KYC and synthetic-identity onboarding bypass to your fraud and identity threat models.
Wire CTI to drive operations across three altitudes: tactical to detection/emulation, operational to hunting, strategic to roadmap.

Pilot automated-reasoning (formal verification) guardrails on correctness-critical agent outputs: policy answers, authorization decisions, compliance responses, proving them against a formal policy model instead of sampling for quality.
items.meta: AWS + SANS · AI for Security, Nov 2025

items.title: Run continuous agent evaluation: re-baseline detection agents as models, prompts, threats, and data drift.
Stand up continuous control validation (the compliance analogue of the purple loop) producing a living audit trail.
Pursue ISO/IEC 42001 certification for defensible, third-party AI-management assurance.

Re-baseline the adversary assumptions behind threat models and emulation plans quarterly as adversary agentic adoption matures: Microsoft already observes early threat-actor experimentation with Agentic AI.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Move toward continuous ATO (cATO): authorization at machine speed instead of point-in-time.
Use pattern-of-life baselining (the tradecraft mirror of UEBA) to flag agents deviating from normal behavior.
Close the loop automatically: every agent incident root cause opens a purple-loop item that produces a detection, a validation test and a regression case, with repeat-incident rate as the metric.
Report mean-time-to-remediate alongside discovery volume so leadership sees the patching deficit, not just the find count.
Mature CTI against the SANS AI Security Maturity Model (Protect/Utilize/Govern) rather than by feel.

plays.name: Reference Architecture
plays.title: Reference Architecture
plays.subtitle: The agentic security architecture read two ways: defensive design and the attacker's view, layer by layer
plays.summary: A seven-layer reference architecture, read as defensive design and as the attacker's view, with six principles applied at every layer.

outline.title: Six Principles, Applied at Every Layer
The Pattern on a Microsoft Estate

blocks.text: A reference architecture is only useful if it survives contact with an adversary, so this one is built to be read two ways at once: how you design an agentic system to be defensible, and how an attacker takes that same design apart. Every defensive pattern here carries its attacker's-eye counterpart, because a control you cannot see being bypassed is a control you cannot trust. The organizing spine is CSA's MAESTRO seven-layer decomposition, the same model the AI Threat Modeling play uses to enumerate threats, so the architecture and the threat model share one map instead of two competing ones. It is deliberately vendor-neutral: the pattern is what transfers across a commercial SOC, a federal enclave, and an OT-adjacent estate, not the product names. A concrete Microsoft instantiation is kept at the end as one worked example, because an abstract layer model that never touches a real stack is hard to build against.

Six principles recur at every layer, and the layer-by-layer treatment is largely their application. Bounded autonomy: an agent's permitted scope of action is set by design, not discovered at runtime, and autonomy is earned in stages, never granted by default (the AWS agency-versus-autonomy scoping matrix; see Human in Command). Least privilege, per identity: every agent is a distinct non-human identity with a scope bound to its purpose, never a shared key or a borrowed human credential (see Agentic Insider Risk). Progressive permissioning: capability climbs only as the system earns trust through evidence, the security-control rendering of crawl / walk / run. Defense in depth: no single layer is load-bearing for safety; breaching one boundary meets another control at the next. Zero model trust: the model is never the enforcement point, because an LLM processes system prompts, retrieved content, tool output, and user input as undifferentiated tokens at equal privilege, so authorization cannot live inside it (the AWS and SANS first principles; see Fundamentals), and prompt injection is an architecture problem, not a patchable bug. Deterministic environment-layer bounds: where the model provably cannot hold a line, and a peer-reviewed result now proves no finite guardrail set is universally robust (the Vassilev Gödel proof; see Purple Team), a non-LLM reference monitor enforces the bound outside the model.
blocks.heading: Six Principles, Applied at Every Layer

blocks.text: Treat the model as a trust boundary, not a trusted component. Defensive design places guardrails, input and output, at a gateway where they can be hot-updated without redeploying the application, the CSA's gateway-layer prescription; signs and provenance-checks model weights; and pairs every probabilistic guardrail with a deterministic bound, because the guardrail alone is not sufficient. The attacker's view is why: prompt injection turns the model's own equal-privilege token stream against it, direct or hidden in retrieved and tool-returned content; jailbreaks defeat guardrails at rates near fifty percent under adaptive attack; and model extraction, inversion, and refuse-then-comply fine-tuning attacks target the weights and behavior themselves.
