The design conclusion is the layer's founding assumption, the model can be steered, so the controls that matter are the ones around it, not inside it.
blocks.heading: Layer 1: Foundation Models

blocks.text: The agent's data plane, training and fine-tuning data, retrieved and augmentation content, and persistent memory, is where poisoning enters and where sensitive data leaks. Defensive design isolates each agent's memory, treats all retrieved and augmentation content as untrusted until validated, versions and scans data the way software dependencies are controlled (treating data as code), and enforces fine-grained access control at the data plane so the agent sees only what its task and its user's permissions allow. The attacker works the same surface in reverse: memory poisoning plants durable manipulations that resurface across sessions (the AgentPoison technique; see Risks & Ethics), poisoned retrieval steers the model toward attacker-chosen behavior, and the model becomes an exfiltration channel for the very data it was given. Provenance and integrity attestation on data sources (SLSA-style) is the control that makes "untrusted until validated" enforceable rather than aspirational (see Supply-Chain Counter-Threat).
blocks.heading: Layer 2: Data Operations

blocks.text: This is the orchestration and tool-calling layer, and the highest-leverage control is the gateway: route every agent tool-call through a policy-enforcing proxy with allow-lists, rate caps, and full logging, so the architecture's control points sit in one place rather than scattered across integrations. Tools are granted least privilege, ideally through OAuth-style delegation rather than standing credentials, and the agent's agency, the scope of what it may touch and orchestrate, is set explicitly and separately from its autonomy (the AWS scoping matrix). The attacker's view names what the gateway defends against: tool abuse and excessive agency (OWASP LLM06:2025, LLM03:2026); the lethal trifecta of private-data access plus untrusted content plus external communication, which turns a helpful agent into an exfiltration path; confused-deputy escalation, where the agent wields more authority than the user it serves; and authorization-boundary transitions that sequence individually permitted operations into a combined effect no one authorized (see Federal & DoW). The durable adversary advantage is architectural, scaffolding that chains attack stages with minimal human input, which is exactly why the gateway, not the model, is the enforcement point.
blocks.heading: Layer 3: Agent Frameworks

blocks.text: This layer decides how much damage a compromised agent can do, and it is where containment becomes physical. Defensive design sandboxes the agent as untrusted by default, isolates it in a network enclave with microsegmentation so out-of-scope resources are not even reachable, and filters egress so exfiltration paths are closed (see Network & Security Controls). The strongest form of the trust boundary, and the one genuine gap this playbook carried until now, is hardware confidential computing: running the model and the agent's computation inside a Trusted Execution Environment, a hardware-encrypted enclave the host operating system, hypervisor, and cloud operator cannot read into, with remote attestation that cryptographically proves which code ran on which input. A systematic survey of confidential computing for Agentic AI (Forough, Kogias and Haddadi, 2026) maps six hardware platforms onto agent security and confirms it is now practical: NVIDIA H100 confidential computing runs at a throughput penalty of roughly four to eight percent under the benchmarked workloads. It is also honest about the limits, and so is this layer. Confidential computing is not a fix for prompt injection; partial-TEE optimizations have already been shown to leak model weights; and no established framework yet binds these primitives into an end-to-end substrate for production agents. The attacker's view is the reason the layer exists, sandbox escape, lateral movement across a flat network, and the cloud-operator or host adversary who reads sensitive prompts and memory straight out of unprotected infrastructure, and confidential computing is the control that removes that last adversary from the trust model without pretending to remove the others.
blocks.heading: Layer 4: Deployment & Infrastructure

blocks.text: You cannot investigate what you did not log, so defensive design traces every agent step, tool call, and decision, and, the harder half, captures the reasoning behind each triage and action, not just the resulting events (the decision plane, distinct from the data plane the SIEM already delivers; see Human in Command). Anomaly detection tuned for agents, in-deployment honeypots, and continuous control validation, the purple loop pointed at controls rather than only detections, turn the logs into live assurance instead of an after-the-fact archive. The attacker's view is a catalog of ways to go dark: obfuscated reasoning and actions smeared across instances so each trajectory looks benign in isolation and the harm appears only when the pieces combine; and, more corrosively, tampering with the evidence itself, since an agent that can generate synthetic logs and forged trails attacks non-repudiation directly (see Agentic Insider Risk). The defensive answer is tamper-evident, append-only, hash-chained logging protected as a crown jewel, so the trail the whole layer depends on cannot be silently rewritten.
blocks.heading: Layer 5: Evaluation & Observability

blocks.text: This is the identity and policy control plane, and in an agentic architecture it is first-class, not an afterthought. Every agent is a distinct non-human identity with a full lifecycle: provisioned just-in-time with a named human owner and an expiry, credentialed with short-lived verifiable tokens (OAuth 2.0 / OIDC, patterns like SPIFFE/SPIRE), rotated automatically, and offboarded with residual-grant sweeps (the OWASP NHI Top 10 ranks improper offboarding first; see Agentic Insider Risk). Identity propagates end to end: a tool call runs under the calling user's identity, not the agent's, whenever users differ in permission (Google's SAIF Agent-Auth-versus-User-Auth decision), so the agent never becomes the over-privileged middleman. Governance is expressed as architecture rather than paperwork, an agent's effective policy is the set of tools and data placed within its reach, which makes the arrangement diagram itself the control (the Governance-by-Design finding that tool arrangement is policy; see Governance). The attacker's view is the confused deputy and its relatives: a shared or borrowed credential that breaks attribution, privilege creep that accretes standing access across tasks, an orphaned agent left as an unowned privileged insider on permanent payroll, and Agent-Auth misuse that lets the agent act with more authority than its user holds. Hardware-rooted identity, a Pluton-style root of trust binding agent identity in hardware with continuous attestation (as Build 2026 coverage reported for Microsoft's Project Solara; see Frontier AI & Government), is where this layer is heading.
blocks.heading: Layer 6: Security & Compliance

blocks.text: The outermost layer is the one single-component models miss: agents that discover, trust, and delegate to other agents, tools, and marketplaces. Defensive design draws explicit trust boundaries between agents, authorizes agent-to-agent (A2A) interaction the way it authorizes any other privileged call, and extends supply-chain assurance, provenance, signing, and vetting, to the tools, connectors, and peer agents an agent is allowed to reach. The attacker's view is where cross-layer meets multi-agent: agent impersonation and marketplace manipulation at the ecosystem boundary, and, the failure mode with no analogue in single-agent systems, a compromised agent prompt-injecting its peers, so a contextual misalignment spreads as a wave faster than targeting can isolate it (the diffuse, distributed kill chain the frontier-lab control research models directly; see Human in Command). Containing it takes the same discipline as the rest of the stack: bounded A2A authority, per-agent identity and attribution, and observability with enough cross-agent visibility to see the wave forming.
blocks.heading: Layer 7: Agent Ecosystem

blocks.text: The reason to hold both lenses at once is that the most dangerous attacks do not stay in a layer. MAESTRO's central insight, and the discipline this architecture inherits, is that single-component threat models miss the paths that cascade: an infrastructure compromise (L4) that reaches into the data and model layers (L2, L1); a goal-misalignment cascade that begins as a subtle reasoning failure and ends as an exfiltration; ecosystem-layer impersonation (L7) that becomes privilege escalation once a trusted-looking peer is inside the boundary. A defense that is strong at every layer independently can still be defeated by a path that crosses them, which is why the spine is defense in depth: the goal is not a perfect layer but a stack where breaching one boundary forces the attacker into another control, visibly, before the pieces combine. The AI Threat Modeling play carries the layer-by-layer threat enumeration this architecture is designed to answer.
blocks.heading: Cross-Layer Attack Paths

blocks.text: The pattern above is vendor-neutral, but a layer model that never touches a real stack is hard to build against, so here is one concrete instantiation on a Microsoft estate. Read it as an example of the pattern, not the pattern itself. Microsoft Sentinel serves the data and orchestration plane; Defender XDR provides cross-domain detection (L5); Security Copilot supplies agentic reasoning; and Agent 365 with Entra Agent ID is the identity and governance control plane that gives each agent an identity, a least-privilege scope, and a blast-radius boundary (L6). The frontier of the same pattern is hardware-rooted: Build 2026 coverage reported that Project Solara binds agent-device identity to Entra through a Pluton root of trust and adds continuous Agent Attestation (L4 and L6). Any equivalent stack that satisfies the layer controls, a gateway that brokers tool-calls, per-agent identity, environment-layer containment, confidential-compute options, and end-to-end observability, instantiates the same architecture. Product names and capabilities are current as of mid-2026; confirm against vendor docs before designing. The stacked-layer diagram shows what sits where; the zero-trust control-plane flow shows how a single request is policed end to end.
blocks.heading: The Pattern on a Microsoft Estate

blocks.text: POC scenario: a new ransomware TTP (a novel living-off-the-land lateral-movement technique) is reported by threat intelligence. The question every SOC faces, 'are we covered, and if not, how fast can we be?', is exactly what the agentic purple loop answers. Below, the same scenario is shown first as the continuous loop, then as a Value Stream Map contrasting the traditional manual cycle with the agentic one.
blocks.heading: A Worked Proof-of-Concept

blocks.alt: Value stream map: lead time per TTP

items.title: Instrument the agent orchestration layer to emit a structured decision trace at commit time: inputs consumed, alternatives weighed, precedent cited, what was ruled out, the recommendation, and who or what made the call, persisted as a peer artifact to events and joined to the entity graph. Then expose precedent retrieval to agents so the next decision can query the prior ones. Capture has to happen at orchestration time; once data lands downstream via ETL the reasoning is already gone.
items.text: Emit the trace as a first-class artifact at decision time, with the fields the record names and a retrieval path so the next decision can read the last one.
bullets: Emit the trace with the questions the record itself poses as the schema: what inputs were consumed, what queries were executed, what alternatives were considered, what precedent was cited, what was ruled out and why, the final recommendation and outcome, and who or what made the call.

Persist it alongside events rather than under them: the record's design writes traces as a peer table to events with the same retention, the same query surface, and the same access controls, which is what keeps a trace as durable as the alert that triggered it.
Join traces to the existing entity graph so a decision is reachable from the asset, identity, or incident it concerns, rather than sitting in a parallel store nobody queries.

Expose precedent retrieval to the agents: the record's stated goal is that the next decision can read the prior decisions and that the graph becomes queryable at triage time, with its worked example a tool an agent invokes to query prior decisions for a given alert pattern.

Capture at orchestration time, not downstream: the record puts the moment at incident close, when the decision context still exists, and warns that five minutes later it is vapor, which is why an ETL or read-path layer cannot reconstruct it.

Read the record's implementation as one worked example rather than a required stack: it demonstrates the pattern on a specific SIEM and its data lake, and the transferable requirements are peer-artifact persistence, entity-graph joins, and query-time retrieval on whatever platform already holds your incidents.

items.title: Diagram your actual agent dataflows against this reference: every tool, credential, data store, and egress path each agent can reach. The gap between the diagram and reality is your blast radius.
items.text: Model the estate against the framework's seven layers, then work the cross-layer threats it names separately.
bullets: Decompose each agent against the framework's seven-layer reference architecture rather than against a free-form box diagram, so two reviewers decomposing the same system arrive at the same picture.

Walk the framework's own step sequence: identify the layers in play, enumerate the threats at each, assess risk, plan mitigations, then treat the model as a living artifact rather than a one-time deliverable.

Record per layer what the diagram is for: the tools, credentials, data stores, and reachable destinations each agent actually holds. The framework supplies the layers, and the inventory beneath them is yours to fill.

Work the cross-layer threats the framework names specifically, which it lists apart from the per-layer sets: supply chain attacks, lateral movement, privilege escalation, data leakage, and goal-misalignment cascades.
Diff the model against reality on a cadence and after every capability change, treating divergence between the diagram and the deployment as the finding rather than as a documentation debt.

items.title: Stand up the gateway pattern: route all agent tool-calls through a policy-enforcing proxy with logging, allow-lists, and rate caps, so the architecture's control points exist in one place.
items.text: Make the proxy a real policy enforcement point in the zero-trust sense, then put the tool-access controls behind it.
bullets: Build the proxy as the architecture's policy enforcement point and hold it to the zero-trust standard the record sets: enterprise resources should not be reachable without accessing a PEP, so a tool reachable around the proxy is a gap in the pattern, not an exception to it; run the proxy fail-closed and redundant, with every deny alerting, so an outage of the proxy stops the agents rather than unguarding them.

Keep the enforcement decision out of the enforcement path: the record separates the policy engine that decides from the policy administrator that executes the decision, so the proxy asks and enforces rather than deciding locally per integration.

Apply the tool-access controls at that choke point in the order the agent guidance gives them: tool allow-listing, parameter validation, sandboxed execution, and approval escalation for actions that clear the risk line.

Treat rate caps as timing, not as a barrier: the guidance is explicit that rate limits are friction that buys time and does not stop a determined agent, so pair every cap with an alert and an authorization control that actually denies.

Log at the proxy so the record of what was attempted, allowed, and denied exists in one place, and carry the record's own carve-out that some infrastructure, DNS among it, must stay reachable rather than hidden behind the pattern.

items.title: Keep authorization outside the model: bind each agent session to the user who started it, scope tokens per hop, and give the policy decision point the delegation chain it needs to say no.
items.text: Fix the confused deputy by making every agent request carry the user, the agent and the delegated scope to a decision point the model can't influence.
bullets: Treat the model as untrusted: CoSAI places the LLM inside an AI threat boundary where prompt injection and poisoned context can steer it, so guardrails and prompt firewalls are mitigations, not a permission system, and no authorization decision is delegated to the model.

Start at the initial rung: bind the agent session to the authenticated user and authorize every request at the gateway against that user's permissions, not the agent's broad service identity, so the agent can never reach what the user cannot.

Move to token exchange at each hop, using OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693): swap the user's token for a short-lived, downstream-specific token that carries both the user and the agent, so a broad token is never reused across unrelated resources and the audit trail shows an agent acted on the user's behalf.

Reach the advanced rung: give the policy decision point three things on every request (the chain of delegation, the agent's identity and delegated scope, and whether this exact action and its parameters fall inside that scope), and have the enforcement point, not the agent, write the audit record.

Close the gap Zero Trust leaves open: a misaligned agent can still misuse access the user legitimately holds, so require contingent authorization, such as a human approval bound to the exact action, for high-impact steps like sending sensitive data outside the organization.
items.meta: CoSAI · Zero Trust for AI Systems, Sep 2026

items.title: Treat every MCP connection as a trust boundary: close the gaps the protocol leaves open by binding each session to an authenticated identity and enforcing authorization at the server, accept dynamically discovered tools only after verifying their origin, and run MCP processes sandboxed and least-privileged.
items.text: The NSA information sheet finds that MCP neither binds sessions to identities nor requires authorization; close those gaps at deployment, then apply its recommendations.
bullets: Draw the trust boundaries and data-classification zones every MCP connection crosses.

This step is the playbook's answer to the gaps the information sheet names (no session-to-identity binding, optional authorization, no token lifecycle), not one of its recommendations: bind each session to an authenticated identity and enforce authorization at the server, with scoped tokens that have a defined refresh and revocation path.
Accept dynamic tool discovery only with origin verification or an authorization check, and validate tool parameters.
Run MCP server and agent processes sandboxed with least privilege, and sign messages with time-bound signatures and replay protection.
Treat every tool and model output as untrusted input to the next step, and log each tool invocation with the identities involved.
items.meta: NSA · MCP Security Design Considerations, May 2026

items.title: Pick one high-volume, low-blast-radius workflow as the first production use case and instrument it end-to-end: baseline the manual value stream before the agent touches it, or you'll never prove the gain.
items.text: Pick the first use case at a low scope and baseline the manual stream first: the matrix supplies the climb, the baseline discipline is the suite's.
bullets: Start at the bottom of the autonomy ladder: the scoping matrix recommends starting with scope 1 or 2 implementations and advancing through the scopes as organizational confidence and security capability mature, which is what makes a first use case low-blast-radius by construction.

Hold the low-risk-first line the joint guidance sets, where expansion is earned through demonstrated performance rather than assumed, and containment and reversibility are prioritized over efficiency while evaluation methods are still maturing.

Baseline the manual value stream before the agent touches it: cycle time, touch count, rework rate, and cost per unit of work. The matrix and the joint guidance govern how much agency to grant; neither prescribes use-case selection or baselining, so this measurement discipline is the suite's own and is the only thing that later proves the gain.
Instrument the agent path with the same measures as the manual path, so the comparison is like-for-like rather than a new dashboard next to an old anecdote.

Assess maturity on a published scale rather than by feel, using the adoption maturity model in canon: eight dimensions including workflow re-engineering, risk and governance, data, and operations, rated across five levels, and re-rate after the first use case to decide whether the next scope step is earned.

Set the expansion gate in advance: name the metric thresholds and the security events that trigger a fall back to a lower scope, which the matrix describes as automatically reducing autonomy when security events are detected.

items.title: Maintain a scored use-case backlog (value × data-readiness × blast-radius) and let the metrics from the first use case pull the next one, not enthusiasm.
items.text: Run the backlog as a scored portfolio whose axes each trace to a canon authority, and let measured results promote the next item.
bullets: Define each axis before scoring anything: value from the baselined manual stream, data-readiness from the readiness foundations this suite already gates on, and blast radius from the autonomy scope the use case would need.

Anchor the data-readiness axis on the sequencing evidence rather than on intuition: the AI-readiness study's arc is that letting AI systems initiate actions requires a fundamental shift in how data is managed, which is why an unready domain scores low regardless of how attractive the use case looks.

Anchor the blast-radius axis on the scoping matrix's four scopes and its six security dimensions: identity context; data, memory, and state protection; audit and logging; agent and model controls; agency perimeters and policies; and orchestration, so the score reflects what the use case would actually be permitted to do.

Govern the backlog as portfolio risk work under the AI RMF functions, with MAP establishing context and risk per candidate and GOVERN carrying the accountability and cadence, so scoring is a standing process with an owner rather than a one-off spreadsheet.

Promote on evidence from the previous use case: hold the scoring rubric, the review cadence, and the promotion thresholds in one document, and require the measured result of the last item before the next one starts.
Re-score on a schedule, since data readiness and blast radius both move as domains are remediated and as agents gain scope; a backlog scored once is a snapshot that quietly becomes wrong.

blocks.label: Architecture Principle
blocks.text: Read every layer twice: once as the blueprint, once as the attacker's map of it. The model is a trust boundary, the gateway is the enforcement point, identity is the control plane, containment is physical, and no single layer is load-bearing. A defensive pattern without its attacker's-eye counterpart is a diagram, not an architecture.

plays.name: Infrastructure and Compute
plays.title: Infrastructure & Compute Factors
plays.subtitle: Engineering considerations for standing up Agentic AI: compute, cost, hosting, and storage
plays.summary: The engineering factors behind deploying agents: token economics, compute, hosting, storage and scaling, as factors to baseline.

blocks.text: The engineering reality behind the strategy. These are the infrastructure and cost factors to weigh when deploying Agentic AI for security. Vendor names (Azure, AWS, GCP) appear as examples; the factors are platform-general. Specific prices and specs move fast: treat figures as factors to baseline, not fixed quotes. Performance research on agentic systems (the Georgia Tech and Intel CPU-centric study) makes the same point: in a production agent system the execution stack (orchestration, retrieval, tools, gateway, data, infrastructure) is where runtime and cost actually concentrate, not the model; the attack surface concentrates there too, so right-sizing and instrumenting that stack end-to-end is a security concern as much as a performance one.

blocks.heading: Tokenization & Token Economics

items.title: Input vs. output tokens
items.text: Both are billed; output is often priced higher. Large log/alert context inflates input tokens on every agent step

items.title: Context window limits
items.text: Models cap total tokens (context). Long investigations may need summarization/chunking to stay within window

items.title: Agent loop multiplication
items.text: An agent that plans→acts→observes→re-plans consumes tokens each cycle: multi-step runs cost far more than one call

items.title: Cost-control levers
items.text: Prompt caching, retrieval (RAG) over stuffing context, model-tiering (cheap model for triage, strong for analysis), batching, output limits

items.title: Predictability
items.text: Token spend is variable by nature; set budgets/alerts and baseline cost-per-investigation against Phase 0

blocks.text: LLMs price and meter work in tokens (~4 characters / ~0.75 words each), for both input (prompt + context) and output. In Agentic SecOps this matters more than in chat: agents loop, re-prompt, and carry large context (logs, alerts, telemetry), so token volume, and cost, compounds fast. Understanding token flow is the single biggest lever on running cost.

blocks.heading: GPU / TPU & Compute Power

items.title: Inference vs. training
items.text: Security teams almost always do inference (running models), not training. Inference is far cheaper but still GPU-backed

items.title: Managed API (default)
items.text: Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI): the provider owns the GPUs/TPUs; you pay per token. Fastest path, least ops

items.title: Self-hosted open models
items.text: Llama/Mistral on your own GPUs: chosen for air-gap/classified or high-volume cost control; needs MLOps, scaling, patching

items.title: GPU sizing & availability
items.text: If self-hosting: VRAM determines model size you can run; high-end GPUs are scarce/expensive and may need reservation

items.title: Latency budget
items.text: Interactive triage needs low latency; batch hunting can tolerate more. Hardware and region choice affect both

blocks.text: AI workloads run on accelerated hardware: GPUs (NVIDIA H100/A100 etc.) or TPUs (Google). For most SecOps teams the right answer is consuming models as a managed API (no GPUs to own); self-hosting open models is the exception, driven by data-sensitivity or cost-at-scale, and brings real infrastructure burden.

blocks.heading: Hosting & Deployment Model

items.title: SaaS security platforms
items.text: Security Copilot, Google AI Threat Defense: least integration burden, provider-run, fastest to value

items.title: PaaS model endpoints
items.text: Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI): your apps/agents call governed model APIs in your tenant

items.title: Self-hosted / dedicated
items.text: Full control for sensitive data; you own scaling, availability, patching, and the GPU fleet

items.title: Federal hosting tiers
items.text: GovCloud / air-gapped regions; impact level (IL2 - IL6) dictates dedicated infra and US-person access (see Federal & DoW)

items.title: Region & residency
items.text: Data-residency and sovereignty requirements constrain which regions/clouds are eligible

blocks.text: Where the agentic stack runs shapes cost, control, and compliance. The spectrum runs from fully managed SaaS (Security Copilot) through PaaS model endpoints (Azure OpenAI / Bedrock / Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform) to self-hosted/air-gapped. For federal work, the data's impact level (see Federal & DoW) often forces the choice.

blocks.heading: Storage & Data Pipeline

items.title: Telemetry volume & retention
items.text: SIEM ingestion (e.g., Sentinel) is often priced by GB/day; retention tiers (hot/warm/cold/archive) balance cost vs. access

items.title: Data lake / analytics store
items.text: A queryable lake (Sentinel data lake, Log Analytics) is what agents reason over; schema and normalization matter

items.title: Vector stores for RAG
items.text: Embeddings/vector DBs power retrieval-augmented agents; sizing and freshness affect relevance and cost

items.title: Data quality & provenance
items.text: Garbage in → bad AI out. Integrity and provenance controls protect against poisoning (see Risks & Ethics)

items.title: Egress & transfer costs
items.text: Cloud data-egress and cross-region transfer carry fees; co-locating compute with data reduces both

blocks.text: Agentic SecOps is data-hungry: it reasons over logs, alerts, and telemetry, so the storage and data-pipeline layer is foundational (and a cost center). This is also where data quality lives, which directly affects AI output and is an attack surface (poisoning).

blocks.heading: Scaling, Availability & Ops

items.title: Rate limits & quotas
items.text: Managed model APIs impose token-per-minute / request quotas; high-volume SOCs must plan capacity and quota increases

items.title: Throughput & autoscaling
items.text: Alert surges (incidents) spike demand; provisioned throughput or autoscaling prevents the agents stalling when needed most

items.title: Availability & failover
items.text: Multi-region/redundancy for a capability the SOC now depends on; degraded-mode plan if the model is unavailable

items.title: Observability / tracing
items.text: Trace agent steps, tool calls, token spend, and decisions: for debugging, cost, and audit (ties to governance)

items.title: Model lifecycle
items.text: Versions deprecate and update; regression-test prompts/agents against new model versions before promoting

blocks.text: Production Agentic SecOps must scale with alert volume and stay available during incidents, exactly when load spikes. The operational (MLOps/LLMOps) burden is real and easy to underestimate in a POC-to-production transition.

items.title: Choose the hosting model by data sensitivity: managed API by default, self-hosted open models where residency/control demands it.
Put cost-control levers on agent loops (token budgets, loop caps): agent-loop multiplication makes spend non-linear.
items.text: The record's named consumption controls first, with per-session cost tracking as the signal that a loop has gone non-linear.
bullets: Apply the controls the record actually names for unbounded consumption: rate limiting and user quotas per source entity, dynamic resource-allocation management so no single request starves the rest, timeouts and throttling on heavy operations, and a cap on queued actions.

Validate input size before inference rather than after, since the record's first named strategy is strict input validation against size limits and its first attack scenario is a single uncontrolled input size: one unusually large input driving excessive memory and CPU load.

Instrument spend where it accrues: track token usage and cost per session and per user, and alert on the trajectory. An agent loop multiplies calls, so the useful signal is the rate of accrual inside one task, not the monthly invoice.

Treat cost as an availability and abuse signal, not only a finance one: the record names denial of wallet as an attack that exploits per-use pricing, so a spend anomaly is triaged like a security event and can stop the loop.

Sandbox the agent's reach to network resources, internal services, and APIs, and degrade gracefully under load rather than failing hard, so a runaway loop is contained by the architecture instead of by the bill.

Cap the loop itself, not only the queue: set a maximum number of iterations and tool calls per task, a retry limit, and a circuit breaker that halts execution when a threshold is crossed, which applies the token, cost, retry, and tool-chain limits the OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet tells teams to enforce.

blocks.label: Integration Principle
blocks.text: Default to managed model APIs unless data-sensitivity or scale forces self-hosting: the GPU/MLOps burden is the most underestimated cost in moving from POC to production. Token economics is the biggest running-cost lever, and the data pipeline is both the foundation and an attack surface. Size for incident-time spikes, because that's when the SOC needs the agents most.

plays.name: Network and Security Controls
plays.title: Network & Security Controls
plays.subtitle: The technical security plumbing: firewalls, egress, monitoring, identity, and segmentation for Agentic AI
plays.summary: Firewalls and AI gateways, egress filtering, segmentation, monitoring and identity controls that bound an agentic deployment.

blocks.text: The domain-security technical controls that bound and protect an agentic deployment, including the firewall, network-monitoring, and IAM controls a SOC works with day to day. These make the playbook's containment and Zero Trust principles concrete in network and infrastructure terms. Vendor features named as examples.

blocks.heading: Firewalls & AI Gateways

items.title: Network firewall / NGFW
items.text: Controls north-south traffic to/from the agent infrastructure; rules enforce what hosts and services are reachable

items.title: Egress filtering (critical)
items.text: Restricting outbound destinations is the concrete Lethal Trifecta defense: it blocks an agent's path to exfiltrate data

items.title: Web Application Firewall (WAF)
items.text: Protects agent-facing apps/APIs from web attacks; pairs with API gateway rate-limiting

items.title: AI firewall / LLM gateway
items.text: Emerging layer (e.g., in SAIF, vendor gateways) inspecting prompts/outputs for injection, PII, and policy: applied in front of the model

items.title: Cloud firewall services
items.text: Azure Firewall, AWS Network Firewall, GCP Cloud Firewall: managed enforcement points in cloud deployments

blocks.text: Two firewall layers matter for Agentic AI. The traditional network firewall (and WAF) still governs what the infrastructure can reach, and a newer category, the 'AI firewall' / LLM gateway, inspects prompts and model traffic for injection, data leakage, and policy violations. Firewalls are a primary blast-radius control.

blocks.heading: Network Architecture & Segmentation

items.title: Private endpoints / VNet
items.text: Keep model and data traffic on private networks (Private Link, VPC endpoints) rather than the public internet

items.title: Microsegmentation
items.text: Isolate the agent enclave so a compromised agent can't move laterally: the network expression of blast-radius control

items.title: API gateway
items.text: A single governed ingress/egress point for agent and tool calls: auth, rate-limiting, logging, and policy in one place

items.title: Cross-domain / air-gap
items.text: For classified work, cross-domain solutions govern any movement between levels; no path to commercial internet (see Federal & DoW)

items.title: DNS & egress allowlisting
items.text: Allowlist the specific destinations agents may reach; default-deny everything else

blocks.text: How the agent stack is placed on the network determines its reach if compromised. Private connectivity, segmentation, and microsegmentation are how Zero Trust and containment are realized at the network layer, keeping agents in a bounded enclave rather than flat-networked to everything.

blocks.heading: Network Monitoring & Detection

items.title: IDS / IPS / NDR
items.text: Detect/prevent malicious network activity; network detection & response complements endpoint and identity signals

items.title: Flow & traffic logging
items.text: NetFlow/VPC flow logs and firewall logs feed the SIEM; baseline normal agent egress to spot anomalies

items.title: Agent behavior monitoring
items.text: Watch for an agent reaching unexpected destinations or escalating activity: non-human-insider detection (see Agentic Insider Risk)

items.title: Log pipeline to SIEM
items.text: Reliable, tamper-evident log shipping into Sentinel/Splunk/Google SecOps; logging is also an audit/compliance control

items.title: Egress anomaly detection
items.text: Sudden volume or new destinations from an agent can signal exfiltration: a key Lethal Trifecta tripwire

blocks.text: You can't defend what you can't see, and agentic traffic adds new things to watch (agent egress patterns, tool calls, model API usage). Network monitoring, IDS/IPS, and the logging pipeline feed both the SOC's detections and the agents' own telemetry. Monitoring the agents is as important as monitoring with them.

blocks.heading: Identity, Access & Secrets

items.title: SSO / IAM
items.text: Single sign-on and centralized IAM govern who (and which agent) can invoke what: the access control plane

items.title: Non-human / agent identity
items.text: Each agent gets a unique identity (e.g., Entra Agent ID), not a shared key, so actions are attributable and revocable

items.title: Least-privilege scoping
items.text: Permissions start at zero; grant only what the agent's task needs (see Agentic Insider Risk)

items.title: Secrets management
items.text: API keys, tokens, and credentials in a vault (Key Vault / Secrets Manager), never hardcoded in prompts or scaffolding

items.title: Conditional access / MFA
items.text: Context-aware access policies for human operators; step-up auth for high-impact agent actions

blocks.text: Identity is the new perimeter, and agents need their own. SSO/IAM, non-human identities, least-privilege scoping, and secrets management are how an agent is authenticated, bounded, and held accountable. This is where 'agents as insiders' becomes a concrete technical control. The same logic now reaches the capability itself: OpenAI's Trusted Access for Cyber gates frontier cyber access on phishing-resistant MFA (June 1, 2026 onward), making who may wield the model an identity decision, not just what the model allows (Resource Index, OpenAI, Trusted Access for Cyber).

blocks.heading: Post-Quantum Readiness (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later)

items.title: Harvest now, decrypt later
items.text: Recorded agent traffic and retained logs are a future-readable archive unless channel crypto migrates: long-lived secrets age worst

items.title: ML-KEM in transit
items.text: FIPS 203 key encapsulation for agent channels and machine-to-machine sessions: the in-flight half of the migration

items.title: Crypto-agile agent identity
items.text: Design certificate and workload-identity plumbing so signatures migrate to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) without re-architecting the identity layer

items.title: PQC-signed audit trails
items.text: Tamper-evident logs must stay provable decades out: SLH-DSA/ML-DSA signatures keep the forensic record trustworthy post-quantum

blocks.text: Harvest-now-decrypt-later applied to the agentic estate: an adversary recording encrypted agent traffic today (tool calls, credential exchanges, machine-to-machine sessions) and holding long-retained tamper-evident logs decrypts them later unless channel cryptography and signatures migrate. The quantum-safe primitives exist: NIST finalized FIPS 203 (ML-KEM key encapsulation), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) signatures in August 2024, NIST IR 8547 (draft) sequences the federal transition toward NSM-10's 2035 target, and NSA's CNSA 2.0 sets the National Security Systems mandate (see Federal & DoW Standards in the Resource Index). For agents the work is concrete: crypto-agility in agent identity so certificates can migrate to ML-DSA without re-architecting; ML-KEM in transit for agent channels; and PQC signatures on audit trails, so the tamper-evident record that agent forensics leans on stays provable after a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives.

blocks.heading: Runtime Protection & Containment

items.title: Sandboxing / isolation
items.text: Run agents in sandboxed, ephemeral environments (gVisor, containers, VMs) so out-of-scope resources aren't reachable

items.title: Container & workload security
items.text: Harden and monitor the containers/hosts agents run in; CSPM/CWPP for cloud posture

items.title: Runtime threat protection
items.text: Defender / GuardDuty-class services detect and block malicious behavior at runtime, including agent hosts

items.title: Capability-based limits
items.text: Constrain agent tool access at the platform layer (cf. DeepMind CaMeL): deterministic, not model-dependent

items.title: Kill-switch & rollback
items.text: Ability to disable an agent, revoke its identity, and roll back changes fast: incident response for agents

blocks.text: The environment layer is the control that doesn't depend on the model behaving. Sandboxing, container isolation, and runtime protection bound what an agent can do even if it's misled: the deterministic backstop behind the whole containment thesis.

items.title: Make egress filtering the priority control: default-deny outbound with DNS/destination allowlisting so a compromised agent cannot reach attacker infrastructure.
items.text: Default-deny egress is the control that holds when the model layer fails, but the record shows an approved-domain path can still be abused, so allowlist governance is the real work.
bullets: Default-deny outbound and allowlist by destination, following the record's own posture: the containment retrospective runs its agent sandbox with network denied by default and names egress controls as the defense that holds when model-layer protections fail.

Treat destination allowlisting as necessary but not sufficient: the same record documents an exfiltration that rode an approved domain the proxy waved through, so the allowlist needs per-agent scoping and identity or content checks, not a bare domain match.

Govern the allowlist as a controlled surface with an owner, a change gate, and proxy logging of every allowed and blocked flow, since an over-broad approved-domain entry is the exact failure mode the record demonstrates; for agents already running, build the first allowlist from a log-only observation window, then enforce with a time-boxed break-glass path and an alert on every deny.

Anchor the posture in zero trust: SP 800-207's tenet that trust is never implicit from network location makes outbound reach a per-session policy decision rather than a property of sitting inside the perimeter.

Map the control to the objective it blunts: MITRE ATLAS's Exfiltration column is what default-deny egress is contesting, so the allowlist and its break-glass path are tuned to that goal rather than to generic outbound convenience.

items.title: Front agents with an AI firewall / LLM gateway to inspect prompts and responses for injection and exfiltration.
items.text: Front the agent with a guardrail layer that inspects both directions, using the risks the record actually names and adding the exfiltration check it does not.
bullets: Inspect inputs and outputs both, which is the record's own recommendation: thorough checking and filtering of all inputs to and outputs from the model, against content guidelines set for your use case and audience.

Scope the injection defense to the risks the guardrail record asserts it detects and prevents: prompt injection, insecure code, and risky tool interactions, orchestrated across its guard models, with the firewall described as agnostic to the agentic framework.

Add exfiltration inspection as the suite's requirement rather than the record's: the guardrail suite names injection, insecure code, and risky tool interactions but does not assert data-exfiltration detection, so egress content checks and destination controls are a separate layer you specify.

Carry the record's own hedge into the design: it states there is no one-size-fits-all guardrail detection that prevents all risks, and recommends combining its system-level tools with other guardrails, which is why the gateway is one layer rather than the control.

Consider a managed equivalent where the estate is already there: the managed-service record in canon offers prompt-attack detection, sensitive-data redaction, and contextual grounding as model-agnostic safeguards, with its published blocking rate stated as the vendor's own figure.

Benchmark the layer instead of trusting it, using the open evaluation suite the record ships: its prompt-injection tests measure whether a system recognizes which part of an input is untrusted and how resilient it is to text and image injection techniques.
Treat injection as an open frontier problem, the framing the third canon record uses, and pair the gateway with least-privilege tool scoping so a bypass does not become an action.

Operate the gateway as a detection source and decide its fail mode: forward every block, flag, and redaction event with the agent identity to the SIEM, alert on repeated injection attempts against one agent, and write down fail closed for agents that can act and a defined degraded mode for read-only assistants.

items.title: Microsegment agent workloads behind private endpoints to contain lateral movement and blast radius.
items.text: Segment as an architecture choice, with the zero-trust tenets, not the network diagram, deciding what the segments mean.
bullets: Choose the approach deliberately: micro-segmentation is one of the record's three zero-trust architecture approaches rather than one of its seven tenets, so adopt it as a design decision and say what it is buying, blast-radius containment for agent workloads.

Put each agent workload class in its own segment behind private endpoints, and set the boundary from what the workload must reach: the tenets grant access per session and per resource, never to a zone by virtue of sitting inside it.

Secure the traffic regardless of where it sits, since the record removes network location as a source of trust; internal agent-to-service calls get the same authentication and protection as anything crossing the perimeter.

Front each segment with an enforcement point so segmentation and authorization are the same decision, and keep the record's exception in view: some infrastructure components must remain reachable rather than hidden.
Re-evaluate segments on a cycle, treating the estate as the record does: no asset inherently trusted, posture continuously assessed, and access re-decided as workloads and their reach change.

blocks.label: Network & Security Principle
blocks.text: Make the principles physical: egress filtering and segmentation are how 'bound the blast radius' becomes real, unique agent identities with least privilege are how 'agents as insiders' becomes enforceable, and runtime sandboxing is the backstop that doesn't rely on the model behaving. Firewalls, network and the newer AI gateway, sit at the center of all three, which is why they're load-bearing, not legacy.

plays.name: OT, ICS and SCADA
plays.title: OT, ICS & SCADA Security
plays.subtitle: Securing Agentic AI where it meets physical infrastructure: water, power, utilities, and facility control systems
plays.summary: In OT, safety and availability come first, so the bar for agent autonomy rises sharply and the IT/OT boundary is the hard line.

outline.title: Why OT Is a Different Discipline
The OT Standards Stack: NIST 800-82, IEC 62443 & Purdue
CISA Guidance: Securing AI in OT (2025)
CISA Zero Trust for OT & CI Fortify (2026)
Federal Control-System Authorization: PIT, FRCS & UFC 4-010-06
Agentic AI in OT: Human in Command Is Non-Negotiable
The IT/OT Boundary Is the Hard Line

blocks.text: Operational technology (OT), meaning the industrial control systems (ICS), SCADA, distributed control systems, and PLCs that monitor and run physical processes, inverts the priorities of IT security. In IT, confidentiality usually leads; in OT, safety and availability come first, because the failure mode isn't a data breach, it's a flood, a power loss, a damaged pump, or a threat to human life. This is exactly the challenge that distinguishes a critical-infrastructure operator from a typical IT shop: because such operators build and run physical infrastructure (water, power, pipelines, utilities, facilities), they carry a large OT footprint, and the cybersecurity guidance that governs them applies to facility-related platform IT such as industrial control systems, utility monitoring and control, electronic security systems, building automation, and SCADA. These environments add constraints IT rarely faces: legacy systems that run for decades and can't be casually patched, proprietary protocols (Modbus, DNP3) with little built-in authentication, fragile devices that active scanning can crash, and uptime requirements measured against physical consequence rather than convenience. The result is that everything in this playbook applies, but the trade-offs shift, and the bar for autonomy rises sharply.
blocks.heading: Why OT Is a Different Discipline

blocks.text: Three references anchor OT security and complement the NIST spine the rest of this playbook uses. NIST SP 800-82 (Guide to Operational Technology Security, Rev. 3) is the US baseline: it adapts the SP 800-53 control families with ICS-specific guidance and a tailored control overlay, organized around consequence-driven risk. (Revalidation note: Rev. 3 is current; NIST opened the Rev. 4 revision in January 2026 and released the Rev. 4 initial public draft on September 21, 2026, with comments due November 30, 2026. The draft is restructured around CSF 2.0 and expands OT sector coverage. Treat Rev. 3 as current and watch for the Rev. 4 final.) ISA/IEC 62443 is the international standard for industrial automation and control systems; it fills in the technical detail with a zones-and-conduits architecture and a Security Level model (SL-1 accidental exposure through SL-4 state-level adversaries with deep OT expertise) that maps controls to the threat you must withstand. The Purdue Model provides the segmentation backbone: hierarchical levels (0 - 5) from the physical process and safety systems up through control, supervisory, site operations, and enterprise IT, with a hardened IT/OT boundary (often a Level 3.5 DMZ) preventing enterprise-level systems from talking directly to controllers. NIST 800-82 Rev. 3 explicitly recommends firewall rules that stop Level 4 devices from directly reaching Levels 2/1/0, and suggests making outbound rules as stringent as inbound: the same egress discipline this playbook applies to agents, here enforcing physical-process isolation.
blocks.heading: The OT Standards Stack: NIST 800-82, IEC 62443 & Purdue

blocks.text: In December 2025, CISA, the NSA, the FBI, and international partners (Australia, Canada, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the UK) published "Principles for the Secure Integration of AI in Operational Technology": a cross-government baseline for putting ML, LLMs, and AI agents into systems that control physical processes. It rests on four principles: understand the AI-specific risks, assess the business case before adopting, build a governance framework, and embed safety and security, human oversight included. It maps directly to a critical-infrastructure mission: it warns that AI in OT couples cyber, safety, and reliability risk; that OT vendors embedding AI often hold privileged access to control workflows (a supply-chain concern, see Supply-Chain Counter-Threat); and that autonomy must never outrun a human's ability to intervene in a physical process. Read it alongside the OT standards stack above.
blocks.heading: CISA Guidance: Securing AI in OT (2025)

blocks.text: On April 29, 2026, CISA, with the Department of War, Department of Energy, FBI, and Department of State, and technical contributions from NIST, published "Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology," a joint guide that does for OT what zero trust did for IT: stop trusting the network, and design controls on the assumption that an adversary is already inside. Its core moves are exactly this playbook's posture, now federal guidance for physical infrastructure: validate every access request on identity, context, and risk rather than network location; treat segmentation as a dynamic, enforceable policy rather than a one-time architectural decision; and layer identity-aware access and continuous evaluation on an assume-breach footing. Critically, the guide is honest about OT's constraints: it acknowledges that blanket application of IT-style zero trust to OT is "neither reasonable nor feasible," which is why the Purdue boundary, passive monitoring, and bounded autonomy above still hold. Six days later, CISA's CI Fortify initiative (May 5, 2026) pushed the same logic into resilience. Assume hostile actors retain a foothold and that internet, vendors, and upstream services may be unreliable in a crisis, and build two capabilities now: isolation (deliberately severing OT from outside and business networks) and recovery (rapidly restoring vital compromised systems while isolated, with tested recovery plans and practiced local and manual operations). The threat driving this is not hypothetical: alongside Volt Typhoon's pre-positioning (below), CISA advisory AA26-097A (April 2026) documented Iranian-affiliated actors manipulating PLC project files and HMI displays in US water, energy, and government facilities to cause real operational disruption. For a critical-infrastructure operator the takeaway compounds the rest of this play: the federal government is now telling you to assume the adversary is inside the OT network and to enforce identity-centric access and deterministic isolation around it, precisely the assume-breach, identity-first, blast-radius-bounded approach this playbook applies to Agentic AI (see Agentic Insider Risk, Agent Containment, and Federal & DoW).
blocks.heading: CISA Zero Trust for OT & CI Fortify (2026)

blocks.text: Control systems sit in a distinct federal authorization lane from ordinary IT. DoD Instructions 8500.01 and 8510.01 categorize them as Platform IT (PIT), a "special purpose" RMF category for systems that aren't traditional IT, using tailored control sets and requiring an Authorizing Official who actually understands the control-system engineering. UFC 4-010-06 (Cybersecurity of Facility-Related Control Systems) is the design guidance written for the architects, engineers, and integrators who build these systems, applying the RMF to facility-related control systems (building control, utility control, electronic security, fire and life safety). Implementing agencies typically layer their own guide specifications on top of UFC 4-010-06 for the control systems they design or build. The practical link to the rest of this playbook: an OT capability is authorized as PIT under the RMF, so the authorization-boundary and cATO discipline from the Federal and DoW play applies, but the boundary now wraps a cyber-physical system, and the AO is balancing residual cyber risk against operational and safety consequence, not just data sensitivity.
blocks.heading: Federal Control-System Authorization: PIT, FRCS & UFC 4-010-06

blocks.text: OT threats are tracked in their own knowledge base, MITRE ATT&CK for ICS, which catalogs adversary techniques against control systems, paired with MITRE ATLAS for the AI-specific layer. The marquee cases show why the stakes are physical: TRITON/TRISIS specifically targeted a plant's Safety Instrumented System, the last-resort safety layer; PIPEDREAM (developed by the actor CHERNOVITE) is a modular ICS attack framework able to execute a large share of known ICS techniques across multiple vendor devices; and Volt Typhoon, a PRC state-sponsored actor, has been assessed by CISA as pre-positioning inside US critical infrastructure, using living-off-the-land techniques to stay stealthy, to enable disruptive or destructive attacks on OT in a future conflict. For a critical-infrastructure operator, this means the adversary is not hypothetical and not purely after information: the goal may be the ability to disrupt the physical mission. That reality is the strongest possible argument for the playbook's assume-breach, continuous-monitoring, and bounded-autonomy stance, applied to the OT environment. A live example: at RAITE 2026 (see Case Studies), a red team combined physical access with a purpose-built ICS exploit to subvert security cameras, disable a water pump, and simulate a contaminant strike on a water tank, exactly the IT-meets-physical attack this discipline exists to stop.
blocks.heading: The OT Threat Landscape

blocks.text: The playbook's human-in-command principle is important everywhere; in OT it is a hard line. An agent that can actuate a physical process (open a gate, change a setpoint, trip a breaker) can cause irreversible physical harm, so the default posture is that agents are read-only and advisory in OT: they observe, correlate, enrich, and recommend, while humans retain every actuation decision. AI must never be placed in the control loop of a Safety Instrumented System or be allowed to override a safety function. Where AI genuinely helps in OT, it does so non-intrusively: passive, protocol-aware anomaly detection on a network tap (never active scanning that could disrupt a fragile PLC), baselining normal process and traffic patterns, triaging alerts, accelerating retrospective incident analysis, and threat-informed defense mapped to ATT&CK for ICS, an approach some now call agentic threat-informed defense for operational control. The agent earns trust the way every other control system does: by demonstrating safe, bounded behavior under oversight before its scope is ever widened.
blocks.heading: Agentic AI in OT: Human in Command Is Non-Negotiable

blocks.text: If the authorization boundary is the key concept in the Federal and DoW play, the IT/OT boundary is its most consequential instance. The Purdue Level 3.5 DMZ between enterprise IT and the control network, reinforced by firewalls, strict access control, and where warranted unidirectional data diodes that physically permit one-way flow only, is what keeps an enterprise compromise from reaching the systems that move water and power. An AI agent must respect that boundary absolutely: an agent operating in enterprise IT should never hold a path to actuate OT, and any monitoring data crossing from OT to IT should travel one-way, out of the control network, never the reverse. This is the containment thesis at its most literal: the blast radius being bounded is physical infrastructure. In RMF terms, draw the OT authorization boundary tightly around the control system, treat every crossing as a conduit to be secured to the level of the most critical zone it touches, and make deterministic, environment-layer enforcement (not model behavior) the thing that holds the line between a cyber incident and a physical one.
blocks.heading: The IT/OT Boundary Is the Hard Line

items.title: Make Human in Command a hard line for any agent that can actuate a physical process: no autonomous actuation in OT.
items.text: Hold the human-in-command line for actuation, on joint guidance that limits and cautions: the absolute prohibition is this suite's hardening of it.
bullets: Start from the joint guidance's own position: it advises limiting active control of OT infrastructure by AI without a human in the loop, to account for safety concerns and latency limitations, and urges caution with active AI systems directly influencing control because problems can escalate before operators become aware of them.

Note what the suite is adding: this action states a hard line of no autonomous actuation, while the guidance limits and cautions rather than prohibiting outright. The guidance is advisory, describing principles owners and operators can follow, and the authoring agencies encourage rather than direct. The absolute rule is the suite's choice, taken deliberately for physical-process risk.

Where AI does touch control logic, apply the guidance's named mechanism: safety thresholds, alternative sensor output, or state changes that add human-in-the-loop intervention points, so oversight is engineered into the loop rather than left to operator vigilance.

For advisory rather than actuating systems, route recommendations through the existing change-management process, which is how the guidance describes implementing human-in-the-loop decision-making for more passive AI.

Require the failsafe path the guidance calls for: mechanisms that revert to traditional automation or to manual for any AI-enabled system process, with new AI failure states written into existing functional-safety and incident-response procedures.

Cap the autonomy formally using the scoping framework in canon, whose prescribed-agency scope is defined as requiring explicit human approval for actions of consequence: that is the ceiling an actuation-capable agent sits under, with the scoping framework itself advisory rather than binding.

Harden the access rule with the joint agentic guidance in canon, which holds that agents should not receive broad or unrestricted access to critical systems, and keep the guidance's own anchor in view: humans are ultimately responsible for functional safety.

items.title: Enforce the IT/OT boundary (Purdue Level 3.5 DMZ) as the most consequential authorization boundary: no unmediated agent crossings.
items.text: Make the IT/OT boundary the enforcement point for agent traffic; the mediation mechanics are the suite's, the push-based and DMZ language is the guidance's.
bullets: Inventory every path by which an agent could reach OT, including read paths, and record which system initiates each connection: this crossing inventory is the suite's own mechanic and is the precondition for mediating anything.

Prefer push-based data flow, which the joint guidance explicitly encourages: data pushed out of the OT network for AI systems to use, without persistent access into the OT network. An agent that never holds a session into OT cannot cross the boundary at all.

Where a connection is unavoidable, route it through the mediation layer the guidance names: it expects new connection paths such as remote access to be approved and to work through the existing demilitarized zone or jump-host infrastructure, and to be verified against existing device-management policy.

Note the framing difference: this action calls the boundary Purdue Level 3.5, a convention from the industrial-control literature rather than from the joint guidance, whose own Purdue table runs Level 0 through Level 3 and then Levels 4 and 5 without a 3.5 designation. The layer is the same; the label is the suite's.

Forbid unmediated agent sessions below the boundary as a written rule with a named approver, and treat any direct agent-to-controller path as an exception requiring the failsafe and rollback story before it is granted.

Anchor the boundary in zero-trust terms so it is a policy decision rather than a topology assumption: the architecture standard in canon holds that trust is never implicit from network location, which is what makes the crossing an authorization event rather than a routing detail.
Monitor the boundary as a detection surface, with the guidance's logging expectation that AI decisions are trackable and the logged AI identity is distinct from typical machine or user identifiers.

Have the red team prove the boundary offensively, but only off the plant: run agent-mediated crossing attempts against a replica built on virtualized controllers or hardware in the loop, map the emulation to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS, and never emulate against live OT, since the joint guidance lists AI red teaming among its oversight mechanisms and starts testing on infrastructure designed for it.

blocks.label: OT Principle
blocks.text: In OT, safety and availability lead, not confidentiality. Keep agents read-only and advisory by default; never put AI in the loop of a safety system; monitor passively, never scan actively. Treat the IT/OT boundary (Purdue 3.5, data diodes where warranted) as a hard authorization boundary enforced deterministically: the blast radius here is physical. Authorize control systems as PIT under UFC 4-010-06 (and your agency's implementing bulletin), with an AO who understands the engineering. (Informational, not engineering or authorization guidance: confirm with your AO and control-system engineers.)

plays.name: Governance
plays.title: Security Governance
plays.subtitle: The control plane that makes Agentic SecOps auditable, compliant, and defensible
plays.summary: Governance as the control plane: every agent action authorized, scoped, logged and reviewable, and mapped to a framework.

outline.title: Why Governance Is the Center of Gravity
The Disclosure Gap: Evidence from the MIT AI Agent Index
Identity, Access & the Classic Controls Still Matter
Governance by Design: The Tool Arrangement Is the Policy

blocks.text: Agentic capabilities are only as trustworthy as the governance around them. For a security strategy function, governance isn't paperwork that slows delivery: it's the control plane that lets you ship high-utility automation safely and prove to auditors, leadership, and regulators that risk-reducing behaviors are enforced. The goal: every agent action is authorized, scoped, logged, and reviewable, and every control maps to a recognized framework.
blocks.heading: Why Governance Is the Center of Gravity

blocks.text: Independent evidence says the governance gap is real, not hypothetical. The MIT AI Agent Index, an external transparency survey of thirty deployed agents, found autonomy spanning five levels while safety disclosure lagged badly: of the thirteen agents at frontier autonomy, only four disclosed any agentic safety evaluation at all, and nearly the whole population runs on the same three model families. For a governance program the reading is direct: the market is shipping autonomy faster than it is shipping evidence, so a buyer's or operator's governance cannot outsource assurance to vendor disclosure. Demand the evals in procurement, require the disclosure in vendor risk, and treat an agent with frontier autonomy and no published safety evidence as exactly what the index suggests it is: an unassessed risk.
blocks.heading: The Disclosure Gap: Evidence from the MIT AI Agent Index

blocks.text: Don't invent a private rulebook. Anchor the program to established standards so compliance is demonstrable: the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its GenAI Profile (AI 600-1) for the GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE lifecycle; the AI Defense Matrix (NIST CSF 2.0-aligned) for control coverage across AI asset classes; OWASP LLM Top 10 and the OWASP AI Exchange for technical controls; and MITRE ATT&CK/ATLAS for measurable detection coverage. Mapping controls to these frameworks turns "we're secure" into "here is the evidence."
blocks.heading: Map to Recognized Frameworks

blocks.text: Agentic AI rides on top of conventional security plumbing, not instead of it. Agents need their own identities, scoped with least privilege and ideally OAuth-style delegation. An over-permissioned agent is OWASP LLM06:2025 (Excessive Agency, LLM03 in the 2026 list) waiting to happen. Single sign-on (SSO) and strong IAM govern who and what can invoke agents; firewalls and egress controls bound where agents can reach. Microsoft's Zero Trust for AI guidance shows this concretely: the vendor says Entra now assigns agents their own identities and applies Conditional Access to them, including risk-based policies that block risky agents, though Entra's agent risk detections currently run offline rather than in real time. The AI Defense Matrix treats agent identities, AI traffic, and runtime AI data as first-class asset classes precisely because the old controls are load-bearing in the new world.
blocks.heading: Identity, Access & the Classic Controls Still Matter

blocks.text: Compliance to risk-reducing behaviors shouldn't be an annual attestation: Agentic AI lets it be continuous. The same purple loop that validates detections can validate controls: continuously test that least-privilege holds, that egress restrictions block exfiltration paths, that logging captures every agent decision, and that drift hasn't quietly degraded a control. Continuous control validation is the compliance analogue of continuous detection validation, and it produces a living audit trail instead of a point-in-time snapshot.
blocks.heading: Risk-Reduction Behaviors, Made Continuous

blocks.text: Leading this effort means delegating cleanly across the red/blue/purple functions while holding the governance line. A workable split: detection-engineering owns rule generation and promotion gates; red-team owns sanctioned emulation within enforced scope; blue-team owns triage and response with defined escalation thresholds; and the strategy function owns policy, framework mapping, exception review, and the metrics that go to leadership. Agents do the repeatable work inside each lane; humans own the lane boundaries and the cross-lane governance.
blocks.heading: An Operating Model for Delegation

blocks.text: An April 2026 paper, "Governance by Design: Architecting Agentic AI for Organizational Learning and Scalable Autonomy" (Dux, Alaimo, Roussiere & Mishra), supplies the doctrine this play's controls add up to. Studying a large IT services firm's staged 2025 rollout of an agentic system wired into enterprise tools, the authors found that effective governance was not a policy layer reviewed after the fact; it was implemented through the concrete architectural and working arrangements of the system itself: what the agent is allowed to do, which tools and data it can reach, how memory is handled, and how improvements are introduced over time, distilled into seven lessons for operationalizing and scaling. The idea worth stealing is what this playbook calls tool arrangement: an agent's effective policy is the set of tools and data sources placed within its reach, which makes the arrangement diagram a governance artifact, not an engineering convenience. It is the same conclusion the Five Eyes guidance reaches from the threat side (containment over efficiency), the AWS scoping matrix reaches from the autonomy side (agency earned in stages), and SAIF's identity-propagation pattern reaches from the identity side: governance you cannot bypass, because it is load-bearing architecture. For this program it converts governance review from a document audit into an architecture review: to change what an agent may do, you change what it can touch, and the diff is the approval record.
blocks.heading: Governance by Design: The Tool Arrangement Is the Policy

items.title: Give every suppression and tuning change a lineage record: who authorized it, what incident or decision prompted it, when it should be reviewed, and what conditions must hold for it to remain valid. Suppressions without provenance are technical debt that accrues silently until a breach review asks why an alert was never seen and no one can answer.
items.text: Give suppressions the four lineage fields the record names, so a tuning decision stays auditable instead of silently outliving its reason.
bullets: Attach the four fields the record specifies to every suppression and tuning change: an authority (who approved this), a precedent link (what incident or decision prompted it), an expiration (when this should be reviewed), and a scope (what conditions must hold for the suppression to remain valid).

Treat the expiration as the control that does the work: a suppression without a review date is the silent-accrual case this action describes, where the outcome persists long after the reason for it stopped applying.

Capture the reason at the moment of the change, following the record's central finding that reasoning evaporates at close and cannot be recovered downstream; a suppression is exactly the decision whose justification is never written down.

Make the record queryable at review time so a breach review can ask why an alert was never seen and get an answer: the record's framing is that suppressions accumulate without provenance until someone runs that report and nobody can answer.

Place the lineage record in the decision plane rather than the data plane: the record treats events and incidents as largely solved and the captured reasoning as the unbuilt part, and a suppression's justification belongs in the second.

Wire the review cadence and accountability into the AI RMF functions already governing the program, with GOVERN carrying the named owner and the schedule so expirations are actually worked rather than merely recorded.

items.title: Anchor the program to NIST AI RMF + GenAI Profile (with OWASP and MITRE) so risk reduction is demonstrable, not a private rulebook.
items.text: Adopt the four functions as the program's spine, then use the GenAI profile's keyed actions as the generative-specific layer.
bullets: Structure the program on the framework's four functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE, each broken into categories and subcategories that state outcomes, and treat GOVERN as cross-cutting rather than as a stage that completes.

Sequence as the record itself suggests: institute the GOVERN outcomes, then start with MAP and continue to MEASURE and MANAGE, while holding its own caveat that the actions are not a checklist and the functions may be performed in any order across the lifecycle.

Use MAP to reach the go/no-go point the framework names: enough contextual knowledge of system impacts to decide whether to design, develop, or deploy at all, and record that decision where it can be audited.

Layer the generative-specific work through the profile's suggested actions, which are keyed by Action ID to individual framework subcategories and tagged to the risks they address, so generative work extends the same structure instead of forking it.

Test before deployment and regularly in operation as MEASURE directs, and document risks that cannot be measured quantitatively together with the reason they cannot: an unmeasured risk that is written down is governed; one that is silent is not.

Express the target as a profile rather than a maturity score: the framework defines current and target profiles but prescribes no templates, no tiers, and no certification, and is voluntary by its own terms; pin the framework version the program adopts, since NIST states that AI RMF 1.0 is being revised under the White House AI Action Plan.

items.title: Give every agent its own scoped, least-privilege, short-lived identity, not shared service credentials.
items.text: One identity per component, permissions to the task, credentials that expire, and an owner who survives the org chart.
bullets: Issue a unique identity per logical component as the list requires, and audit for reuse: a service account shared across pods, or one key spanning several integrations, is the named risk rather than a convenience.

Scope permissions to only what the specific task requires, add organization-level deny policies against excessively permissive configurations, and route the exceptions through temporary, on-demand elevation inside a defined window instead of standing rights.

Retire long-lived secrets on the list's own terms, credentials that never expire or expire too far out, by automating rotation and issuing short-lived credentials from cloud-native mechanisms, without inventing an interval the record does not state.

Re-authenticate rather than trust the session: require fresh verification when an agent identity reaches sensitive resources or performs high-risk operations, and pair the identity with a cryptographically anchored form so the actor is provable.

Give every identity a named owner and an end date at issuance; the recertification cadence, the offboarding sweep and the orphan hunt are the Next-phase lifecycle action on the Agentic Insider Risk play.

items.title: Define the delegation operating model across red/blue/purple while holding the governance line centrally.
items.text: Delegate the doing, keep the deciding: accountability structures named centrally, authority written down per team.
bullets: Write the delegation down as a table of decisions rather than a table of teams: for each decision, scope a test, accept a finding, sign off a control, halt a campaign, name who holds it and who merely executes it.

Keep accountability structures central, in the governance function the framework treats as cross-cutting, so that delegating execution to red, blue, and purple never delegates the risk-acceptance decision alongside it.

Give each team its standing authority in writing: what it may run without asking, what needs sign-off, and what is prohibited, so speed comes from pre-agreed boundaries rather than from case-by-case escalation.
Route findings back through one register regardless of which team raised them, so the risk picture is assembled centrally even though the work is distributed.
Re-read the model on a cadence and after any incident, treating the delegation itself as a control that can drift as teams, tooling, and autonomy levels change.

items.title: Adopt tool-arrangement reviews as the governance gate: for every agent deployment, record what it may do, which tools and data it can reach, how memory is handled, and how updates land, and treat any change to that arrangement as the approval record.
items.text: Review the arrangement, not the model: the paper's four dimensions become the record, and a change to any of them is the thing you approve.
bullets: Record the four dimensions the paper names as the arrangement: what the system is allowed to do, which tools and data it can use, how memory is handled, and how performance improvements are introduced over time. The paper frames governance as implemented through concrete architectural and working arrangements rather than as a compliance layer applied to a finished system.

Put approval gates on high-impact actions, which is the paper's fourth lesson: embed oversight into the workflow, because checking outputs only at the end is often too late or too costly; in its case study no complex task runs without the user first reviewing the plan and source scope.

Make memory an explicit governed decision, its fifth lesson: what the system remembers determines how errors propagate, the case organization chose not to retain long-term memory across sessions unless explicitly allowed, and where persistent learning is enabled the paper advises a way to review and roll back those learnings.

Treat a change to the arrangement as the approval record by requiring behavior versioning and formal approval controls alongside logging: the paper ties accountability to exactly that combination as autonomy rises.
