Use the paper's design-choice enumeration as the review checklist: what tasks are permissible, how much autonomy is granted, which workflows are allowed, what data and tools the system can access, what is logged and retained, and when changes to behavior are introduced.

Weigh its evidentiary status honestly: it is a qualitative case study of a single organization's agentic rollout, so the dimensions and lessons are transferable structure rather than a validated control set, and the review gate itself is the suite's operationalization.
items.meta: Dux et al. · Governance by Design, Apr 2026

blocks.label: Governance Principle
blocks.text: Authorize, scope, log, review: for every agent and every action. Map each control to a recognized framework so compliance is evidence-based, and make control validation continuous so the audit trail is always current. Governance is what lets the program move fast without losing the right to.

plays.name: Compliance
plays.title: Regulatory & Compliance Landscape
plays.subtitle: The external obligations that turn AI governance from good practice into a legal requirement
plays.summary: The EU AI Act, NIS2, DORA, ISO 42001 and the US picture: the dated obligations your controls and audit trail must satisfy.

outline.title: Why This Belongs in a SecOps Strategy
EU AI Act: High-Risk Obligations & the 2026 Omnibus Shift
EU AI Act, Operationally: What It Asks of a SecOps Program
NIS2 & DORA: Cyber Risk and Resilience
ENISA's FAICP: The EU's Layered Good-Practices Framework
ISO 42001 & STAR for AI: Certifiable Assurance
Turning Compliance Into an Operating Advantage

blocks.text: AI governance has become a Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC) function, and GRC maturity is a strong predictor of regulatory readiness. And maturity is the right lens precisely because frameworks alone are weak: independent 2026 benchmarking of frontier labs (see the FLI AI Safety Index) found that published safety frameworks sometimes lack quantitative thresholds, genuinely independent audits, and clear decision authority. A framework on paper is not an enforced one, which is why continuous control validation matters more than the document. For a security strategy function, the compliance landscape isn't a side concern: it sets hard, dated obligations that the program's controls, documentation, and audit trail must satisfy. The good news: the governance and continuous-validation approach in this playbook produces exactly the evidence these regimes demand.
blocks.heading: Why This Belongs in a SecOps Strategy

blocks.text: The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) entered into force August 2024 with staggered deadlines: prohibitions and AI-literacy duties from February 2025, general-purpose AI (GPAI) model obligations from August 2025, and the broadest layer, high-risk system obligations, originally from August 2, 2026. That last date has now moved: the Digital Omnibus on AI, adopted July 8, 2026 as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and in force since late July 2026, defers high-risk obligations for stand-alone Annex III systems (for example, critical-infrastructure safety components, credit scoring, access to essential public services, and employment) to December 2, 2027, and for AI embedded in regulated products to August 2, 2028, driven by delayed harmonized standards and authority designations, not a retreat from the obligations themselves. One caution keeps this from being a reprieve: transparency obligations, including deployer duties, still apply from August 2, 2026, with a four-month transitional period for generative systems already on the market. The substance is unchanged: provider obligations under Articles 9 - 17 include a continuous, documented risk-management system, data governance, technical documentation, human oversight, and post-market monitoring, with high-risk systems registered in the EU database before market placement; penalties reach €35M or 7% of global revenue, and non-EU organizations are in scope if their AI affects EU users. (Status as of July 2026: re-verify before relying on dates.)
blocks.heading: EU AI Act: High-Risk Obligations & the 2026 Omnibus Shift

blocks.text: Strip the regulation to its SecOps to-do list and it maps almost one-to-one onto this playbook. First, role and scope mapping: determine for each AI system whether you are provider or deployer (the duty sets differ) and screen it against Annex III. The mapping gates everything else and costs little. Second, adversarial robustness: Article 15 requires high-risk systems be accurate, robust, and cyber-resilient against attacks including data poisoning and adversarial inputs. The continuous purple loop and AI red-teaming in this playbook are exactly the evidence-generating machinery for that clause, and GPAI models with systemic risk carry explicit adversarial-testing and incident-reporting duties of their own. Third, logging and traceability: Article 12 requires automatic event logging across the lifecycle, and deployers must retain those logs (at least six months under Article 26). The agent action-trail and observability work in Governance and Agent IR satisfies this by design. Fourth, incident response: Article 73 requires serious-incident reporting on regulator timelines (a 15-day outer bound, compressing to as little as 2 days for critical-infrastructure incidents), which means the agent-incident runbooks here need a regulatory-notification branch, not just a technical one. The strategic read: the Omnibus bought calendar time on Annex III, but every one of these capabilities is already justified on security grounds. Build them once, and the compliance evidence falls out as a by-product.
blocks.heading: EU AI Act, Operationally: What It Asks of a SecOps Program

blocks.text: NIS2 (Directive 2022/2555) applies cybersecurity risk-management and incident-reporting duties to 160,000+ entities across 18 sectors (Annex I high criticality, Annex II other critical), with management accountability, supply-chain oversight, and breach-notification timelines; maximum fines of at least €10M or 2% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher, for essential entities (€7M or 1.4% for important ones), and national authorities have begun the first enforcement actions. DORA adds operational-resilience requirements for financial entities. Crucially, NIS2 and the EU AI Act overlap for operators of essential services: a "high-risk" classification in your sector becomes a flag for NIS2 too, creating a compounding, not duplicative, compliance load.
blocks.heading: NIS2 & DORA: Cyber Risk and Resilience

blocks.text: Between the EU's regulation and a team's controls sits ENISA's Multilayer Framework for Good Cybersecurity Practices for AI (FAICP), the EU cybersecurity agency's answer to "what do we actually do." It stacks three layers: a foundation of classic ICT security (the estate the AI runs on), an AI-specific layer for the properties machine learning adds (data poisoning, model attacks, lifecycle controls), and a sector-specific layer where domain regulation bites. The structure is the point: it says out loud that AI security is layered on top of, not instead of, the security program you already run, which is the same posture this playbook takes. For an EU-exposed program it is the natural bridge document: AI Act obligations above, NIS2 resilience alongside, FAICP translating both into practice.
blocks.heading: ENISA's FAICP: The EU's Layered Good-Practices Framework

blocks.text: In the US, the approach is framework-led rather than a single statute: the NIST AI RMF and its GenAI Profile (AI 600-1) provide the lifecycle structure, with a Critical-Infrastructure profile concept note added in 2026. Under the EU AI Act, providers of general-purpose models (Claude, Gemini, GPT, Llama) face transparency obligations, with additional duties for systemic-risk models. The practical takeaway for a delivery program: design to the strictest applicable regime, map controls once to a recognized framework, and reuse that evidence across audits.
blocks.heading: The US & Framework Picture

blocks.text: Beyond regulation, there's a fast-emerging layer of voluntary, certifiable AI assurance worth knowing. ISO/IEC 42001 is the leading management-system standard for AI (an AI Management System, analogous to ISO 27001 for infosec), giving an organization an auditable governance backbone. The Cloud Security Alliance's STAR for AI extends its long-running STAR assurance registry to AI: an organization assesses itself against the AI Controls Matrix using the AI-CAIQ questionnaire (Level 1, self-attested) and can pursue third-party validation (higher levels), with a Catastrophic Risk Annex on the roadmap, all aligned to NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, and ISO 42001. The practical point for a federal or enterprise program: the same control evidence the continuous purple loop already produces can feed an ISO 42001 AIMS and a STAR for AI submission, turning security work into a recognized, third-party-checkable trust signal for customers, partners, and authorizing officials, without standing up a separate compliance track. (See the AICM entry in Frameworks.)
blocks.heading: ISO 42001 & STAR for AI: Certifiable Assurance

blocks.text: Continuous control validation, the compliance analogue of the purple loop, produces a living audit trail (model cards, data-provenance records, risk assessments, agent action logs) that satisfies these regimes by default rather than scrambling before an audit. Sequenced this way, compliance stops being a brake on delivery and becomes proof that the program is trustworthy. For practitioners, the ability to demonstrate audit-ready AI governance is itself a differentiator.
blocks.heading: Turning Compliance Into an Operating Advantage

items.title: Map every AI system against EU AI Act roles (provider vs. deployer) and Annex III high-risk criteria: the 2026 Omnibus defers high-risk duties to Dec 2, 2027, but transparency obligations have applied since Aug 2, 2026 and the mapping gates everything else.
items.text: Build the register first, role and Annex III exposure per system, because every downstream duty keys off that mapping.
bullets: Inventory every AI system in scope and record the organization's role per system, provider (developing the system or placing it on the market under one's own name) or deployer (using it under one's own authority), since the Act's duties attach to the role, and one organization can hold both across systems.

Screen each system against Annex III's eight high-risk areas as the record lists them: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers management and access to self-employment; access to essential private and public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; administration of justice and democratic processes.

Date every obligation off the enacted Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744: Annex III high-risk duties at December 2, 2027, embedded-product AI at August 2, 2028, and Article 50 transparency holding at August 2, 2026 with a four-month transitional period for generative systems already on the market.

Where a security system touches an Annex III area (safety components for critical infrastructure, or monitoring that reaches into employment contexts), record the classification reasoning per system; the mapping, not the security label, decides.
Re-run the mapping on a set cadence and at every material system change, keeping the register as the living evidence base the transparency and high-risk duties will be examined against.

items.title: Stand up continuous control validation (the compliance analogue of the purple loop) producing a living audit trail.
items.text: Assess controls on an ongoing basis against a written monitoring strategy, and let the evidence accumulate as the trail.
bullets: Write the continuous monitoring strategy first, because the framework makes it the thing that governs everything downstream: it sets the minimum monitoring frequency for implemented controls and defines the ongoing control-assessment approach.
Assess all controls on an ongoing basis after the initial authorization rather than re-testing everything at a fixed annual point, taking each control's frequency from that strategy.

Automate where the volume justifies it: the record's stated benefit is greater frequency, volume, and coverage of assessments, supporting near-real-time risk management, while holding its caveat that automated output alone may not suffice for a risk determination.

Keep the authorization artifacts live rather than periodic: update security and privacy plans, assessment reports, and plans of action and milestones on an ongoing basis, which is what makes the trail a living record instead of a snapshot.

Report posture on an event-driven, time-driven, or combined cadence, summarizing at minimum what changed in those artifacts since the last report, so the audit trail is generated by the process rather than assembled for an audit.

items.title: Pursue ISO/IEC 42001 certification for defensible, third-party AI-management assurance.
items.text: Run one control set that already crosswalks to the standard, evidence it once, and submit through the published assurance path.
bullets: Adopt a single AI control set as the working spine rather than answering each regime separately: the v1 release of the matrix carries 243 control objectives across 18 security domains, with mappings that include ISO 42001 alongside ISO 27001, the NIST AI RMF, and the BSI AIC4 catalog.
Use the published crosswalk as the evidence multiplier: one implemented control answers to several regimes at once, which is what makes third-party assurance defensible rather than duplicative.

Self-assess with the matrix's own questionnaire, the consensus assessment initiative questionnaire for AI, so the gap list is generated against the control objectives instead of against an internal opinion.

Submit through the published assurance path, following the STAR for AI Level 1 submission guide as the documented entry point; then scope the AI management system, appoint an accredited certification body, and schedule the stage 1 and stage 2 audits, since certification against the standard itself is a separate accredited-body activity the STAR submission does not deliver.

Track the version you are working to, since the matrix moved to a v1.1 release with a changed control-objective count while holding the same 18 domains: a gap list built against the older release goes stale silently.

blocks.label: Compliance Principle
blocks.text: Design to the strictest applicable regime, map controls to a recognized framework once, and let continuous validation keep the evidence current. The 2026 Omnibus, enacted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, deferred the EU AI Act's Annex III high-risk date to December 2027, but transparency duties have applied since August 2, 2026, GPAI obligations and NIS2 enforcement are already live, and the regulators' own message is that implementation should be underway now. (This is informational, not legal advice; confirm specifics with counsel.)

plays.name: Federal and DoW
plays.title: Federal & DoW Considerations
plays.subtitle: How Agentic AI security maps to federal authorization, DoD impact levels, and the Pentagon's AI push
plays.summary: How agentic AI fits federal authorization: FISMA, FedRAMP, DoD impact levels, continuous ATO, CUI and classified networks.

outline.title: Why This Matters for a Federal Program
FISMA, FedRAMP & the NIST Control Spine
ATO & Continuous ATO: The Authorization Model for Machine-Speed Ops
DoD Zero Trust Strategy & ICAM (the Identity Foundation)
Agents as Non-Human Identities in ICAM
The June 2026 EO & the National Threat-Model Mandate
Responsible-Use Boundaries Are Part of the Deal
Data Sensitivity Changes the Whole Calculus
Designing for the Highest Applicable Bar

blocks.text: In the federal public sector, a security program is judged not only on whether it works but on whether it's authorized. FISMA (the Federal Information Security Modernization Act) requires agencies to secure information systems against a NIST-defined control baseline; FedRAMP standardizes the authorization of cloud services; and for Department of War (DoW) customers, the DISA Cloud Computing SRG adds defense-specific requirements on top. Any Agentic AI capability supporting federal, and especially DoW/Army, missions has to live inside this authorization scaffolding from day one, not be retrofitted into it. The good news: the governance, continuous-validation, and Zero Trust approach in this playbook produces much of the evidence these regimes demand.
blocks.heading: Why This Matters for a Federal Program

blocks.text: These regimes share a common backbone: NIST. FISMA authorization runs on the NIST Risk Management Framework (SP 800-37) and the SP 800-53 control catalog, beginning with system categorization under FIPS 199 (the standard that sets a system's Low / Moderate / High impact level from its confidentiality, integrity, and availability needs: the input that drives which control baseline applies); FedRAMP is essentially a standardized, cloud-specific application of those same controls with continuous monitoring built in (on its Rev5 path; FedRAMP 20x, its successor, is out of pilot, and FedRAMP will stop accepting new Rev5 certifications on June 11, 2027). CUI handling adds NIST SP 800-171 for non-federal systems. Because this playbook already maps controls to the NIST AI RMF, CSF 2.0, and SP 800-207 (Zero Trust), a federal program can reuse that mapping as the AI-specific overlay on its existing FISMA/FedRAMP authorization rather than starting a separate compliance track.
blocks.heading: FISMA, FedRAMP & the NIST Control Spine

blocks.text: For DoW missions, the DISA Cloud Computing SRG sorts systems by Impact Level based on data sensitivity and the damage from compromise. IL2 covers public/non-critical data (and is granted by reciprocity to FedRAMP Moderate). IL4 covers Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) and other mission-critical data. IL5 covers higher-sensitivity CUI and unclassified National Security Systems, requiring dedicated infrastructure and U.S.-person-only access. IL6 covers classified information up to SECRET, hosted on the SIPRNet side. The practical point for Agentic AI: the impact level of the data an agent can touch dictates where it can run, who can operate it, and which control baseline applies, so determine the IL before designing the agent, not after. (Facility-related control systems and other OT follow a distinct lane: DoW categorizes them as Platform IT (PIT) with tailored controls under UFC 4-010-06, often implemented through an agency's own guide specifications. See the OT, ICS and SCADA play.)
blocks.heading: DoD Cloud Impact Levels (IL2 - IL6)

blocks.text: Federal systems need an Authorization to Operate (ATO) before going live: a formal, risk-based decision under FISMA and the NIST RMF, traditionally a point-in-time assessment valid for up to three years. That cadence simply cannot govern an agentic SOC that changes and acts at machine speed, which is why Continuous ATO (cATO) is the natural fit. Per the DoD CIO's cATO guidance, an Authorizing Official grants cATO only when three competencies are demonstrated: ongoing visibility of cybersecurity activity inside the system authorization boundary via robust continuous monitoring of RMF controls; the ability to conduct active cyber defense and respond to threats in real time; and adoption of an approved DoD Enterprise DevSecOps reference design. Read that list against this playbook: the continuous purple loop is the continuous monitoring; agentic detection-and-response is the active cyber defense; and the Build·Secure·Ops lifecycle is the DevSecOps spine. The same control-validation that proves least-privilege, egress limits, and logging hold over time produces the live evidence a cATO depends on, so framing the program as a cATO enabler turns a security capability into an authorization accelerator, language that resonates with federal leadership. (cATO is a DoW implementation of the RMF's "ongoing authorization"; a DoD CISO-approved cATO has no expiration so long as the real-time risk posture is maintained. Since its announcement on September 24, 2025, the Department of War's Cybersecurity Risk Management Construct (CSRMC) has succeeded the RMF inside the Department, carrying "Continuous Monitoring and ATO" forward as one of its ten core principles, aimed at a constant ATO posture.)
blocks.heading: ATO & Continuous ATO: The Authorization Model for Machine-Speed Ops

blocks.text: The authorization boundary, the set of components under one AO's management that an ATO actually covers, is the federal concept Agentic AI most directly stresses, and it's the bridge between this playbook's containment thesis and the compliance world. Two problems arise. First, agents don't respect the boundary the way a fixed application does: because they interpret goals and chain tools, they can attempt "authorization-boundary transitions", sequencing individually permitted operations so the combined effect bypasses controls, or using the output of one allowed function as unauthorized input to another (the federal-authorization framing of the lethal trifecta and excessive-agency risks elsewhere in this playbook). Second, agent identity and reach often extend past where the boundary's controls stop: an agent calling an external model, a tool in another enclave, or a data source at a different impact level effectively pulls activity outside the authorized boundary unless it's deliberately bounded. The defensive answer is the same one the playbook makes on engineering grounds and that the research literature now makes on impossibility grounds: probabilistic compliance is not security, so authorization must be enforced deterministically at the environment layer, a non-LLM reference monitor mediating tools, information flow, and privilege, not left to the model's good behavior. In RMF terms: draw the agent's authorization boundary explicitly, keep its actions and data within the impact level it's authorized for, route any cross-boundary or cross-domain interaction through approved connections (and cross-domain solutions where classification levels differ), and treat blast-radius containment as the technical instantiation of the boundary. This is also where the federal direction of travel is moving: the CDAO's "AI-first" agenda explicitly pursues cross-domain data flows and rapid ATO reciprocity to reduce accreditation friction for AI, and the NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative (launched February 2026), whose request for information on agent security closed in March 2026, is developing security guidance for exactly these autonomous-agent deployments.
blocks.heading: Authorization Boundaries & Agentic Operations

blocks.text: Identity is where the federal Zero Trust mandate begins, and where Agentic AI most needs deliberate design. The DoD Zero Trust Strategy organizes the mandate into seven pillars: User, Device, Application & Workload, Data, Network & Environment, Automation & Orchestration, and Visibility & Analytics, spanning 45 capabilities and 152 activities, with the Target-Level baseline due by FY2027 and the Advanced Level by FY2032, across both NIPRNet and SIPRNet. The User pillar is anchored on ICAM (Identity, Credential, and Access Management): continuous verification of identity, strong authentication, and least-privilege access. Identity is treated as the first pillar for a reason: every subsequent control (device, network, data) depends on reliably knowing who, or what, is asking. The leverage for an agentic program is that the other pillars line up with controls this playbook already covers: the agentic SOC itself is the Automation & Orchestration pillar; continuous logging and the purple loop are Visibility & Analytics; agent enclaves and microsegmentation are Network & Environment and Application & Workload; and data-centric bounding is the Data pillar. That mapping lets the program be framed as advancing the DoW's Zero Trust Target-Level goals rather than as a separate, competing initiative, and a true ZT posture means trust is never static: an identity, device, or workload is trusted only as long as it behaves exactly as expected, in real time.
blocks.heading: DoD Zero Trust Strategy & ICAM (the Identity Foundation)

blocks.text: The agentic-specific move is to bring agents into ICAM as non-human identities (NHIs). NHIs (service accounts, API keys, machine tokens, and now autonomous agents) already outnumber human identities by an estimated 40:1 to over 100:1 in many environments, according to vendor identity-security surveys, and traditional IAM and PAM were never designed for actors that interpret goals, chain tools, and act across systems in seconds. The approach is an identity lifecycle for agents that parallels the human ICAM lifecycle but is built for machine speed and runtime context: (1) discover and inventory every agent and machine identity: you can't govern what you can't see, and the discovery exercise alone tends to surface the most over-privileged identities; (2) give each agent a unique, attributable identity with a defined lifecycle (creation, credential rotation, and deprovisioning), never shared or anonymous service accounts; (3) credential it with short-lived, verifiable credentials (OAuth 2.0 / OIDC), and prohibit cross-agent privilege delegation unless explicitly authorized; (4) enforce least privilege plus just-in-time access, so an agent holds only the permissions it needs, only while it needs them; and (5) wire agent identity telemetry into Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) feeding the SIEM/SOAR, so a session can be terminated the moment behavior diverges from baseline. This is the federal-identity expression of the playbook's Agentic Insider Risk and Agent Containment theses: the same non-human-insider model, instantiated through the DoD ICAM and User-pillar lens. (Map to your component's Zero Trust execution plan and AO expectations; specific DoD ICAM tooling and ZT activity tallies evolve.)
blocks.heading: Agents as Non-Human Identities in ICAM

blocks.text: The June 2, 2026 Executive Order 14409 ("Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security") sharpens the federal picture: it directs agencies to develop a classified benchmarking process for the cyber capabilities of AI models and to set the threshold for a "covered frontier model," with the Director of NSA, in consultation with the National Cyber Director, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology, CISA, and the Department of War, making the determinations. The practical implication, as practitioners have noted, is that you can't benchmark or designate what you haven't modeled: this effectively tasks the IC with building a cohesive national AI threat model. For defenders, that makes use-case-driven AI threat modeling (see the AI Threat Modeling play) a directly relevant, in-demand capability, and it reinforces the EO's voluntary, security-conscious posture over mandatory licensing.
blocks.heading: The June 2026 EO & the National Threat-Model Mandate

blocks.text: The federal direction of travel is unambiguous. In July 2025 the DoD's Chief Digital and AI Office (CDAO) awarded prototype agreements with a $200M ceiling each to Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and xAI to build Agentic AI workflows across mission areas, taking a commercial-first approach. On March 3, 2026 the Department of War designated Anthropic a supply chain risk, and on September 25, 2026 the D.C. Circuit denied Anthropic's petitions for review. Vendor-specific accreditations have followed (e.g., GovCloud IL5 authorizations; air-gapped cloud reaching IL6 for classified workloads), and tailored government model variants now operate in sensitive environments. Agentic security tooling is following the same path: Microsoft reports that its MDASH scanning system has been in preview in Azure Government for select US government customers and authorized partners since September 8, 2026. For practitioners, this validates the thesis: the question leadership is asking is no longer "should we use Agentic AI," but "how do we adopt it responsibly and get it authorized." (Specific awards, levels, and vendor statuses change: verify current details before quoting in any formal setting.)
blocks.heading: The Pentagon's AI Push (Adoption Signal)

blocks.text: The Pentagon-frontier-lab relationship has also surfaced a governance lesson worth carrying into any federal program: usage boundaries matter and can become contractual flashpoints. Public reporting in early 2026 described a dispute over model-use restrictions (fully autonomous weapons and domestic mass surveillance); on March 3, 2026 the Department of War designated the vendor a supply chain risk, and on September 25, 2026 the D.C. Circuit denied the vendor's petitions for review. Whatever one's view, the takeaway for a program lead is concrete: define acceptable-use boundaries, human-in-command controls, and escalation paths up front, document them, and align them with mission and law, so they're a deliberate design choice rather than a late surprise.
blocks.heading: Responsible-Use Boundaries Are Part of the Deal

blocks.text: Most commercial AI security guidance assumes internet-connected, unclassified systems. Federal reality is a spectrum: from CUI on moderate systems, to higher-sensitivity CUI and unclassified National Security Systems, to classified networks up to SECRET and above. As data sensitivity rises, the constraints tighten: isolation, personnel vetting, where data may physically reside, and what may connect to what. An agentic capability that's appropriate on an IL4 CUI system may be entirely off-limits on a classified enclave without a different design and a different authorization.
blocks.heading: Data Sensitivity Changes the Whole Calculus

blocks.text: Controlled Unclassified Information is the most common sensitivity level a federal program touches day-to-day. For Agentic AI, the core obligations carry straight over from this playbook's data-handling and governance guidance: minimize what enters the model's context, strip or tokenize sensitive fields where possible, keep CUI inside authorized boundaries (NIST SP 800-171 for non-federal systems; SP 800-53 for federal), and log every agent access for audit. The Lethal Trifecta defense, bounding what an agent can access, what untrusted content it sees, and where it can send data, is exactly the control that keeps CUI from leaking through an agent.
blocks.heading: CUI Handling

blocks.text: On classified networks (e.g., SIPRNet for SECRET), the environment itself is the first control: physical and logical isolation, cross-domain solutions for any movement between classification levels, and no path to the commercial internet. This actually aligns well with the playbook's containment thesis: deterministic, environment-layer isolation is already the recommended approach, and a classified enclave is the strongest possible expression of blast-radius control. The trade-off is operational: model updates, threat-intel feeds, and tooling must cross domains under strict process, so an agentic program on classified systems needs a deliberate plan for keeping models and detections current.
blocks.heading: Classified Networks & Air-Gap Realities

blocks.text: For the most sensitive work, Special Access Programs and intelligence systems operated from SCIFs (Sensitive Compartmented Information Facilities), the Joint SAP Implementation Guide (JSIG) governs. JSIG is a technical supplement to NIST SP 800-53 and CNSSI 1253, used with DoDM 5205.07 to apply the RMF at all classification levels under a SAP Authorizing Official, with control overlays tailored to that environment (and some controls designated non-tailorable). For Agentic AI, the implication is that the agent's controls, logging, and authorization must be expressed in JSIG terms and approved by the cognizant AO: the same Zero Trust and least-privilege principles, but instantiated under the JSIG overlay and the facility's physical-security regime.
blocks.heading: SCIFs & the JSIG Control Framework

blocks.text: The cleanest strategy across mixed-sensitivity customers is to design the agentic architecture so it can be instantiated at multiple levels: a common control core (identity, least privilege, logging, containment) that's then overlaid with the right baseline (SP 800-171 for CUI, the SRG impact level for DoW, JSIG for SAP/SCIF). This mirrors the playbook's broader "design to the strictest applicable regime, map once, reuse the evidence" principle, and it's what lets a single program support an Army CUI system and a classified enclave without rebuilding from scratch each time.
blocks.heading: Designing for the Highest Applicable Bar

items.title: Bring agents into ICAM as governed non-human identities (NHIs): the agentic-specific move this playbook draws from the DoW Zero Trust mandate.
items.text: Enroll agents as first-class NHIs: one identity per component, permissions to the task, credentials that expire.
bullets: Discover before you govern: enumerate every agent and machine identity already operating in the estate, because an identity absent from the inventory cannot be scoped, rotated, or revoked, and audit each one against its access grants and the component it belongs to.

Issue a unique identity per logical system component as the list requires, and limit the ability to authenticate as that identity to the component it belongs to: reuse across components is the named risk, not an operational shortcut.

Grant only the permissions essential for the identity's specific tasks, avoiding administrative privileges unless absolutely necessary, and back that with deny policies at the organization level that prohibit excessively permissive configurations.
Route elevation through just-in-time access: temporary, on-demand privilege granted only when required and within a defined time frame, rather than leaving standing rights attached to the agent.

Replace long-lived secrets with automatically rotated, short-lived credentials from the platform's own temporary-credential mechanisms, and require re-authentication when an agent identity reaches sensitive resources or performs high-risk actions.
Wire agent identity telemetry into Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) feeding the SIEM and SOAR, so a session can be terminated the moment an agent's behavior diverges from its baseline.

items.title: Map every agent to its authorization boundary and Impact Level (IL2-IL6) before it touches federal data.
items.text: Place each agent against a real impact level before it touches federal data, and note the level set is 2, 4, 5, 6, not a continuous range.
bullets: Assign the impact level from data sensitivity as the guide defines it: Level 2 for non-controlled unclassified information, Level 4 for controlled unclassified information or other mission-critical data, Level 5 for CUI needing more protection than Level 4 affords, and Level 6 for classified information up to SECRET.

Use the live set rather than the range: the guide records that Level 1 has been merged into Level 2 and Level 3 into Level 4, leaving Impact Levels 2, 4, 5, and 6, so an agent is placed at one of four levels, not anywhere on a 2-through-6 continuum, and a higher level may process data from a lower one.

Respect the binding scope, and its limits. This guide establishes DoD baseline security requirements and applies to all providers and offerings hosting DoD systems, information, or applications regardless of who owns or operates the environment; compliance with applicable guides is required for systems in that scope. That obligation runs to DoD mission owners and their providers: a commercial reader outside a DoD authorization boundary is borrowing the structure, not inheriting the mandate.

Draw the authorization boundary around the agent explicitly, including the data it reaches, the services it calls, and where it executes, because the level attaches to the boundary rather than to the model, and each offering needs its own provisional authorization to host DoD mission systems.

Build the assessment on the federal baseline plus the DoD-specific additions the guide describes: Level 2 assessments rest on the civilian program's moderate baseline without an additional DoD assessment, while Level 4 combines that moderate baseline with the DoD-specific controls and requirements the guide sets out, and Level 5 builds on the civilian program's high baseline plus the DoD-specific additions the guide sets for that level, including physical separation from non-federal tenants.

Record the decision as a reviewable artifact with a named owner: the guide places determination of the appropriate impact level for a mission with controlled unclassified information and mission data with the mission authorizing official, so the agent's level is an accountable call rather than an engineering default.

items.title: Move toward continuous ATO (cATO): authorization at machine speed instead of point-in-time.
items.text: Earn ongoing authorization on the record's own two conditions, then keep the authorizing official in a live decision loop.
bullets: Meet the first stated condition before anything else: the system or common control must already hold an initial authorization based on a complete, zero-based review. Ongoing authorization is a follow-on state, not a starting one.
Meet the second condition by standing up the organizational continuous monitoring program the record requires, so the ongoing assessments feeding the decision exist before the decision is asked for.

Give the authorizing official a live posture view alongside the maintained authorization artifacts: metrics and dashboards are what the record credits with increasing the capability to make risk-based decisions, and ready access to current posture is what supports the ongoing determination.

Keep the distinction the record insists on: ongoing authorization and ongoing assessment are related but different, and neither is reauthorization, so the program does not quietly redefine a periodic re-approval as continuous.

Aim at near-real-time risk management, which is how the document words the goal in almost every instance, and keep the claim that modest: automated output alone, it cautions, may not be sufficient for the authorizing official's risk determination.

items.title: Design the architecture as a common control core instantiable at multiple levels (CUI to classified): build to the highest applicable bar.
items.text: Build the shared core as authorized common controls, then instantiate per level with the CUI requirements tailored on top.
bullets: Express the shared core as common controls with a named common control provider: the risk framework carries that role explicitly through monitoring and authorization, which is what lets one core be inherited rather than rebuilt per system.

Authorize the core in its own right, since the framework's ongoing-authorization conditions apply to a common control just as they do to a system; an unauthorized shared core silently exports its risk to every consumer.
Instantiate the CUI level against the seventeen requirement families as the requirements document names them, rather than against a locally invented control set.

Use the organization-defined parameters deliberately: once specified, those values become part of the requirement itself, so record them per level. The same requirement can carry a stricter parameter at the higher bar without becoming a different control.

Scope the boundary rather than the whole estate: the record allows limiting scope by isolating designated components into a separate security domain. And document what sits inside each level's domain.

Keep external dependencies inside the model: permit external systems only where specifically authorized, and require providers handling protected data to meet the organization-defined requirements you have set.

items.title: In classified enclaves, make isolation the first control: air-gap/cross-domain solutions and JSIG controls for SCIF-operated systems.
items.text: In SAP and SCIF enclaves, isolate first and express the agent's controls in the overlay the authorizing official actually approves against.
bullets: Treat isolation as the first control rather than a compensating one, and pair each crossing with a deliberate transfer mechanism, air-gapped operation or an accredited cross-domain solution, so an agent's convenience never becomes an unreviewed data path between classification levels. Hold that line knowingly: the framing behind this overlay is that physical isolation can no longer be relied on as the primary risk-mitigation strategy, which is why the guide routes the enclave through the Risk Management Framework instead. Isolation first is this playbook's ordering for agents specifically, not the overlay's claim that isolation suffices.

Express the agent's controls in the overlay that governs the enclave: the guide provides policy and guidance on implementing the Risk Management Framework and serves as a technical supplement to the federal control catalog and to the national-security categorization standard, used together with the applicable SAP security manual volume.

Route the approval to the right authority: the guide provides standardized cybersecurity policies, procedures, and implementation guidance for managing systems at all classification levels under the purview of the SAP authorizing official, so that official, not a platform team, owns the agent's authorization.

Respect the scope: this is binding on systems under that authorizing official's purview, and is not a general commercial requirement. A reader outside a SAP or SCIF boundary is adopting the isolation-first pattern by choice, not obligation.

Categorize before selecting controls, following the overlay's own lineage through the national-security categorization standard, so the agent's confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts are set before its permissions are designed.

Carry the currency caveat: the version in canon is built on revision 4 of the federal control catalog and the March 2014 categorization standard, so map any newer control language deliberately rather than assuming the overlay tracks the latest revision.

Verify against the guide itself: the purpose and scope statements above are as quoted on a major cloud provider's compliance page, so confirm them against the guide's own PDF before relying on them in an authorization package.

blocks.label: Federal Principle
blocks.text: Determine the data's impact level first; it dictates where agents run, who operates them, and which NIST baseline applies. Draw each agent's authorization boundary explicitly and enforce it deterministically at the environment layer: blast-radius containment is the technical form of the boundary. Reuse the playbook's NIST control mapping as the AI overlay on existing FISMA/FedRAMP/SRG authorization, and position the continuous purple loop as a cATO evidence engine. (Informational, not authorization guidance: confirm with your AO and security control assessor.)

plays.name: Procurement and Vendor Risk
plays.title: Procurement & Vendor Risk
plays.subtitle: Vetting the AI vendors, models, and components you adopt: the diligence side of supply-chain assurance
plays.summary: Vet the models, vendors and components you adopt: keep an AI bill of materials, check provenance, and plan for continuity.

outline.title: Vendor Diligence Is a Governance Discipline
Maintain an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM)

blocks.text: Agentic SecOps is assembled from components you mostly don't build: foundation models, managed AI services, open-source libraries, agent frameworks, plugins, and data sources. Each is a third party you're trusting, and adopting AI tooling without vetting it imports their risk into your environment. This play covers the procurement and third-party-risk-management side: how you assess, authorize, and contractually bound the vendors and models you bring in. (The adversarial flip side, an attacker weaponizing that same supply chain against you, is covered as Supply-Chain Counter-Threat in Security & Intelligence Ops.) For a federal program this is doubly true: procurement, authorization, and data-handling obligations all flow through to the vendors and models you choose.
blocks.heading: Vendor Diligence Is a Governance Discipline

blocks.text: You can't govern what you haven't inventoried, and the visibility gap is real: Wiz Research found that while the overwhelming majority of organizations now run managed and self-hosted AI, roughly a quarter still lack visibility into which AI services are actually running in their environment. An AIBOM closes that gap by cataloging every AI component in use: which models (and versions), datasets, dependencies, frameworks, and tools, so you can track provenance, monitor for vulnerabilities, and respond when a component is compromised or deprecated. It's the AI analogue of the SBOM that federal supply-chain guidance already expects, and it's the foundation for everything else in this play. AI security posture management (AI-SPM) tooling can automate the discovery; Google's SAIF and the OWASP supply-chain guidance both treat this inventory as essential.
blocks.heading: Maintain an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM)

blocks.text: Before adopting a model or AI service, assess both the artifact and the organization behind it: where the model came from and how it was trained (provenance), the provider's security posture and certifications (SOC 2, FedRAMP, GovCloud/impact-level authorization for federal use), data-handling terms (is your data used for training? where does it reside?), responsible-use commitments, and the provider's own track record on disclosure and patching. The Pentagon-frontier-lab relationship is a live example of why acceptable-use terms and provider boundaries belong in the evaluation, not just price and performance.
blocks.heading: Vet the Model & the Provider

blocks.text: The data and model supply chain is where poisoning enters. Third-party training data, pre-trained models, and externally sourced RAG content can all carry planted manipulations (see Risks: Agentic Memory Poisoning, and the AgentPoison technique). Mitigations: prefer sources with verifiable provenance and integrity attestation, treat external data as untrusted until validated, and apply a 'data as code' discipline. Version it, scan it, and control its supply the way you would software dependencies.
blocks.heading: Data, Provenance & Poisoning

blocks.text: Diligence is not only about whether a model is good and secure: it is about what happens if you can no longer use it. Treat concentration and exit as first-class procurement criteria: how much of a mission-critical function depends on this one model or provider, how hard it would be to switch, and what could force a switch you did not choose (vendor deprecation, pricing changes, an export-control or sanctions directive, a regulatory suspension). Favor providers and architectures that preserve portability: standard interfaces, exportable prompts and configurations, and the option of a second source or an on-prem / open-weight fallback. For federal and national-security-adjacent work, make availability and regulatory exposure explicit line items in vendor assessment, and require a documented continuity plan for loss of access, not just an SLA for uptime.
blocks.heading: Dependency, Portability & Continuity

blocks.text: This isn't uncharted territory: established frameworks cover it. Google SAIF centers supply-chain security (SLSA provenance); the OWASP LLM Top 10 and AI Exchange address supply-chain and third-party model risk; NIST's AI RMF and SP 800-53/800-161 supply-chain controls apply for federal systems; and AIBOM practices are emerging as the connective tissue. Map your AI vendor assessment to these so it plugs into the same governance and authorization evidence the rest of the program produces.
blocks.heading: Frameworks & Federal Hooks

items.title: Maintain an AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM): you cannot govern uninventoried models, services, and agent frameworks.
items.text: Stand the inventory up as a governed artifact; the discovery mechanism and the visibility gap are record-stated, the fields and cadence are the suite's.
bullets: Size the gap before arguing for the work: the vendor research this suite cites reports that roughly a quarter of organizations still lack visibility into which AI services are running in their environment, which is the condition an inventory exists to end.

Use continuous discovery as the collection mechanism rather than a survey: the posture-management discipline as that record describes it automatically identifies AI assets in the environment and maintains a centralized AI bill of materials accounting for every model, service, SDK, and data pipeline.

Define the inventory fields your governance actually needs: component identity and version (model, service, SDK, framework, or dataset), owner, purpose, data reached, tools and actions permitted, environment, dependencies, and review date. The record names the AI-BOM as an artifact the discipline produces but does not prescribe a field schema, so this list is the suite's.
Set an owner and a refresh cadence, and treat inventory drift as a finding in its own right; an AIBOM that is accurate only on the day it was built recreates the visibility gap it was meant to close.

Anchor the priority in frontline findings rather than in product capability: the assessment record in canon reports that organizations often lack application registries, software bills of materials for AI, and scanners able to see AI-specific artifacts, and that the root causes of the most pressing problems are rarely novel AI-specific attacks but basic implementation flaws and missing IT hygiene.

Read the discovery capability as the discipline's, not a single product's: the source is an explainer describing AI-SPM generally and its own implementation separately, so the requirement to carry forward is continuous automated discovery plus a maintained bill of materials, on whatever tooling covers your estate.

items.title: Vet both the artifact and the provider, model provenance/training and the vendor security posture, before adoption.
items.text: Two different reviews with two different records behind them: artifact integrity from SAIF, provider posture from the zero-trust supply-chain phase.
bullets: Inventory first, because both reviews depend on it: SAIF's own self-assessment asks whether you hold a complete inventory of all models, datasets used for training, tuning or evaluation, and related artifacts such as code, and its newer Agent Risk Self-Assessment adds the agent questions (identity and authorization, observability, user control, built-in model safety, in-tool guardrails, input and output screening, testing); answer both for real before adopting anything new.

Review the artifact against the SAIF risks that describe how it can arrive compromised: Data Poisoning, Unauthorized Training Data, and Model Source Tampering, and require the controls the framework maps to them, including Training Data Sanitization, Model and Data Integrity Management, and Model and Data Access Controls.

Test tamper-evidence explicitly: SAIF's assessment asks whether data, models and code can be altered without detection during development and during deployment, so treat an artifact whose integrity cannot be demonstrated end to end as unadopted.

Review the provider separately: the zero-trust guidance places vendor assessments, an AI Bill of Materials, automated dependency-health evaluation, and cryptographic signing inside its supply-chain phase, which is where provider posture belongs rather than inside the artifact review.

Record the residual risk where the two reviews disagree, and re-run both when the model version, the training data, or the provider's ownership changes: adoption is a decision with a date on it, not a permanent state.

items.title: When a product claims "autonomous," locate it on the autonomy spectrum and demand the controls to set the dial yourself: autonomy is earned through evidence, not granted by a datasheet.
items.text: Locate the claim on the spectrum and require the dial: the record's framing is that autonomy is earned incrementally.
bullets: Reject the binary reading first: the record's starting claim is that autonomous has shifted from a meaningful descriptor to a marketing buzzword, because autonomy now sits on a spectrum spanning assistants that require human input at every step through to agents that operate end-to-end.
Ask the vendor to place the product on that spectrum in those terms: the record's own range runs from guided to full autonomy, and treat an inability to place it precisely as the finding.

Require the dial as a product capability rather than a roadmap promise: the record holds that the best products give organizations controls to dial autonomy up as trust grows, so teams can deploy now and expand autonomy as evidence accumulates.

Make evidence the currency, on the record's central claim that autonomy is earned incrementally through trust in the model, so the buying question becomes what has been demonstrated, not what is asserted.

Evaluate the vendor before the product, which the record lists as the second of the three things its guide sets out to teach, and ask for the track record behind the claim rather than the claim itself.

Read the source as vendor-authored and partly gated: it is published by a security vendor that sells the capability it describes, and the full guide sits behind a download form, so the spectrum-and-dial framing above comes from the openly readable page. Pair it with the vendor-question checklist in canon, itself vendor-authored and self-serving by construction, and weigh both accordingly.

items.title: Make continuous safety operations a procurement gate: require AI vendors to evidence ongoing adversarial testing, guardrail update cadence, and a disclosure process. A static safety configuration is elevated supply-chain risk under the Gödel result.
items.text: Turn the three evidence items into contract language, and treat their absence as the supply-chain finding it is.
bullets: Write the note's three evidence items into the approval checklist as conditions, not preferences: evidence of continuous red-teaming programs, disclosed update cadences, and responsible disclosure processes, and require them before an AI vendor is approved.

Score a vendor lacking published adversarial-testing mechanisms, disclosed vulnerability reporting, or guardrail update cadences as elevated supply-chain risk, on the note's reasoning that a static guardrail configuration cannot serve as a terminal security endpoint.

Ask for cadence as a disclosed practice rather than a number: the record prescribes continuous updating and minimizing the window between discovery and remediation, and states no interval, so accept a described process and reject an undated assurance.

Extend the same test to existing contracts at renewal: evaluate vendor relationships for alignment with continuous-monitoring expectations, and update the procurement framework itself so the requirement outlives the individual deal.

Carry the evidence into governance: align the program's monitoring components with the AI RMF's Measure and Manage functions, and brief leadership that AI security is an ongoing operational discipline rather than a one-time configuration.

blocks.label: Supply-Chain Principle
blocks.text: Inventory first (AIBOM), then vet both the model and the provider: provenance, security posture, data-handling, authorization level, and acceptable-use terms, not just price and performance. Treat external data and models as untrusted until validated, because the supply chain is where poisoning enters. Map it all to SAIF, OWASP, and NIST so vendor assurance becomes part of your authorization evidence.

plays.name: AI Threat Modeling
plays.title: AI Threat Modeling
plays.subtitle: Enumerating how an AI system can be attacked: the formal backbone plus a use-case-first method
plays.summary: Work out how an AI system can be attacked before it ships, pairing STRIDE, MAESTRO and NIST with a use-case-first method.

outline.title: Why Threat Model AI at All
The Formal Backbone: STRIDE, Microsoft AI/ML, NIST
A First-Pass Model in an Hour: The OWASP Threat Advisor
From Snapshots to Living Intelligence: Code-Grounded, Continuous Models
When the Modeling Assistant Joins the Attack Surface (Meta Threat Modeling)
Why Test the System, Not the Model
Worked Example: The Repo That Owns Your Machine

blocks.text: Threat modeling is the structured practice of working out how a system can be attacked before it ships, and for AI it's the critical first step, because you can't meaningfully assess or secure a system you haven't modeled. It's also newly urgent for federal work: the June 2, 2026 Executive Order 14409 tasks Treasury, NSA, and CISA with a classified benchmarking process, and the NSA Director (in consultation with the National Cyber Director, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology, CISA, and the Department of War) with the "covered frontier model" threshold, which in practice requires a cohesive national AI threat model. This play pairs the recognized formal frameworks with a practical, use-case-first method for actually doing it.
blocks.heading: Why Threat Model AI at All

blocks.text: Start from the established frameworks (these are the authoritative spine): STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) is the classic taxonomy for enumerating threats across data flows and trust boundaries. Microsoft's AI/ML threat-modeling guidance extends STRIDE with AI-specific failure modes (poisoning, model theft, adversarial perturbation, inversion), and it plugs into existing secure-development (SDL) practice. Beyond the adversarial set, an agentic threat model should also account for the AI-native risk classes that don't fit neatly into classic categories: prompt injection, model misuse, agent privilege escalation, data poisoning, hallucination (confidently wrong output acted on as if true), and the emergent behaviors that arise when autonomy, memory, and tool use combine, because these evolve continuously across the AI adoption lifecycle rather than being fixed at design time. NIST's AI RMF and the GenAI Profile (600-1) provide the governance wrapper, and MITRE ATLAS supplies the adversarial-ML technique catalog to model against. For a federal program, this backbone is what maps to authorization evidence.
blocks.heading: The Formal Backbone: STRIDE, Microsoft AI/ML, NIST

blocks.text: STRIDE and the ATLAS catalog were built for software and ML components; neither was designed for systems that plan, call tools, hold memory, and coordinate with other agents. The Cloud Security Alliance's MAESTRO (Multi-Agent Environment, Security, Threat, Risk and Outcome) fills that gap as the agentic-native complement to the formal backbone. It decomposes an agentic system into a seven-layer reference architecture: (1) Foundation Models, (2) Data Operations, (3) Agent Frameworks, (4) Deployment & Infrastructure, (5) Evaluation & Observability, (6) Security & Compliance, and (7) the Agent Ecosystem, and forces analysis of both layer-specific threats and, crucially, the cross-layer attack paths that single-component models miss (an infrastructure compromise cascading into the data and model layers; a goal-misalignment cascade; agent impersonation or marketplace manipulation at the ecosystem layer). It pairs naturally with this playbook's other CSA-aligned content and with OWASP: the OWASP GenAI Security Project's Multi-Agentic System Threat Modeling Guide is itself built on MAESTRO, so a program can use MAESTRO to decompose the architecture, ATLAS to enumerate adversarial-ML techniques per layer, and the AI Controls Matrix (see Frameworks) to select the controls. MAESTRO's creator, Ken Huang (CSA), with co-author Steven Leath, has also shown how to operationalize it: folding MAESTRO classification into an automated, continuous threat-modeling step wired into the CI/CD pipeline, so the agentic threat model stays live as the system evolves rather than going stale in a document. Model the guardrail layer and the alignment layer as separate surfaces: Hackett & Garraghan show that bypassing an external classifier is a different problem from bypassing a model's learned refusal, and that a guardrail's presence and behavior can be fingerprinted black-box before an attack is adapted (Resource Index, Behind the Refusal).
blocks.heading: MAESTRO: The Agentic-Native Threat Model (CSA)

blocks.text: AI security researcher Disesdi Susanna Cox (co-author of the transferability work cited in this playbook's research library) argues a point worth carrying into any AI threat model: with AI, "architecture no longer drives attack vectors, use case does." Two systems can carry identical risk levels yet entirely different attack surfaces, so the threat model has to start from the mission, not the tech stack. A poisoning attack against battlefield ground-movement sensors looks nothing like one against a tank-recognition image model, and the signatures you monitor for differ accordingly. (This is one practitioner's methodology: a useful complement to, not a replacement for, the NIST/Microsoft backbone above.)
blocks.heading: A Use-Case-First Method (Practitioner Perspective)

blocks.text: MAESTRO gives the discipline; the OWASP AI Exchange's Threat Advisor gives the on-ramp. Describe the system in a paragraph and the Advisor runs a tailored interview: surfacing which threats actually apply, walking the risk assessment, and pointing at mitigations, drawing on the Exchange's three hundred pages and its six-branch threat-model decision tree (unwanted model behavior, action risk, training-data leakage, model theft, input-data leakage, and the always-do residuals). It is a first pass, not a finished model: the output still needs an architect's eye on trust boundaries and cross-layer paths, but as a way to put a defensible starting model in front of a use-case team in an hour, it is the fastest route this playbook knows. The decision tree also stands alone: printed beside a whiteboard, it turns "where do we even start" into a walk.
blocks.heading: A First-Pass Model in an Hour: The OWASP Threat Advisor

blocks.text: Every method above produces a threat model; the open question is how fast it goes stale. A June 2026 practitioner account from Nutanix and Palosade (Purple Book community) answers it the way this playbook answers point-in-time assessment generally: stop treating the threat model as a snapshot and ground it in live, version-controlled source code instead of documentation. When the design doc and the implementation disagree, the implementation wins, because that gap is where the security issues live. Their agent reads current code through GitHub/Gerrit/Sourcegraph plus commit history, traces data flows and trust boundaries, emits findings in a schema-validated format (AWS Threat Composer JSON, DFDs in Mermaid) with Git hooks rejecting any model that fails validation, and constructs kill-chain escalation scenarios, showing how a CVSS-5.4 issue becomes high-severity when chained through the actual privilege levels and trust boundaries in production. The payoff is the same continuous-readiness dividend the cATO and post-Mythos threads describe: because a current, validated model already exists across every product, the unexpected use turned out to be incident response, kill-chain viability and "are we actually exposed?" assessed against real code in roughly twenty minutes instead of pulling in multiple teams for hours. It is explicitly a response to Mythos and Daybreak: proactive kill-chain analysis anticipates what a cyber-centric model will find, so foundational weaknesses get fixed before the zero-day report arrives. The expert is not replaced but amplified: the bottleneck was rationed specialist time, and code-grounded automation removes the rationing. Machine-scale incident response to meet machine-scale vulnerability discovery: the threat-modeling expression of this playbook's continuous thesis.
blocks.heading: From Snapshots to Living Intelligence: Code-Grounded, Continuous Models

blocks.text: Cox frames AI threat modeling as four scalable steps that form a continuous cycle: (1) Gather documents, data flow diagrams (DFDs) and, most importantly, detailed mission use cases from stakeholders who understand the mission; (2) List potential mission impacts, what mission failure actually looks like, expressed in mission terms rather than technical ones; (3) Prioritize risks and choose controls, with mission stakeholders deciding which impacts matter, then data teams selecting the right mitigations (a key AI nuance: it's not "all controls always" / layered defense, but the correct controls at the correct times); and (4) Monitor and adversarially test, stand up monitoring for the specific signatures your model predicts, then red-team the whole system's defenses, not just the model. To score a jailbreak's severity rather than just note it, Anthropic's draft Cyber Jailbreak Severity rubric rates four axes: capability gain, breadth, ease of weaponization, and discoverability, into bands CJS-0 through CJS-4, a shared vocabulary worth borrowing when ranking findings (Resource Index: Anthropic, Cyber Jailbreak Severity Framework).
blocks.heading: The Four-Step Method

blocks.text: Using an AI model to threat-model an AI system is the natural next step once the model is grounded in live code, but it introduces two failure modes the formal frameworks above do not name: both surfaced in Toreon's 2026 meta-threat-modeling work. First, the modeling assistant itself joins the attack surface: a poisoned or adversarial architecture document, loaded as context, can steer the assistant toward a threat model that is confidently structured and entirely wrong, so its context must be isolated and every artifact fed to it verified, exactly as you would treat any other in-scope component. Second, acceptance by omission: when a model emits forty plausible threat scenarios in ninety seconds, fluency and volume get mistaken for validity, and no reviewer has the stamina to challenge each one, so hallucinated or duplicate threats slip into the register as tracked work. The discipline is to map the method (Toreon's DICE: Description, Identification, Countermeasure Definition, Evaluation) onto where AI genuinely accelerates versus where human judgment stays non-negotiable, cap each AI-generated batch, and require per-item human adjudication. The first two Now actions on this play operationalize both.
blocks.heading: When the Modeling Assistant Joins the Attack Surface (Meta Threat Modeling)

blocks.text: The most useful insight for an agentic program: in an effectively infinite attack space, testing a model in isolation is close to pointless. Testing the system's defenses is what matters. That's exactly why the threat model comes first: it tells you what to monitor and what to test for, which is what makes adversarial testing tractable (and automatable). This connects directly to the rest of the playbook: the threat model directs the purple loop's emulation focus, monitoring is the control that catches what prevention misses, and continuous adversarial testing is the loop itself. Threat-model first; let it aim the loop.
blocks.heading: Why Test the System, Not the Model

blocks.text: A 2026 Mozilla 0DIN write-up shows why "scan the repo" is not enough for agentic coding tools. A normal-looking public repo ships innocent setup notes and a Python package that fails closed with a helpful error telling you to run its init. The agent clones, hits the error, and runs the documented fix as routine recovery. That init calls a shell script whose one interesting line pulls a config value from a DNS TXT record and pipes it straight to bash. The record holds a base64 reverse shell, so it connects back to the attacker as the developer's own user, with every exported secret (model API keys, cloud credentials, source-control tokens) in reach. The payload is never in the repo. Static scanners see a DNS lookup, network monitoring sees name resolution, and the agent sees a pre-authorized setup step, so none of the three looks malicious alone. The malice lives in the seams between the repo, the DNS record, and the developer's trust in the agent. This is the runtime-execution cousin of the agent configuration surface covered under Supply-Chain Counter-Threat, where the danger is standing instruction files the agent ingests as guidance. Two defenses fall out of it: an agent should surface what a setup or recovery command will actually run, including anything a script fetches at runtime; and a developer should treat setup scripts in an unfamiliar repo as untrusted code no matter what the agent recommends.
blocks.heading: Worked Example: The Repo That Owns Your Machine

blocks.alt: One Operator, a Cast of Agents

items.title: When using an LLM to threat-model an AI system, treat the assistant itself as in-scope: isolate its context, verify every architecture document fed to it, and never let an unreviewed artifact drive the model. A crafted input loaded as context can steer the assistant toward a threat model that is confidently but structurally wrong.
items.text: Treat the modeling assistant as in-scope; the record names the exposure and the phase map, the isolation controls are the suite's.
bullets: Start from the record's named exposure: if the threat-modeling assistant is an LLM and you are using it to model an LLM-powered system, the assistant itself is a potential target, and an actor who can influence its inputs, through a carefully crafted document loaded as context, could distort the output.

Add the controls this action prescribes as the suite's own: isolating the assistant's context and verifying every architecture document before it is loaded. The record identifies the risk and treats human review as the primary mitigation, but does not itself prescribe context isolation or document verification.

Keep the assistant out of the driver's seat where the record says judgment is non-negotiable: it maps the method phase by phase, placing AI value in description and identification with human review still required, framing it as a well-read colleague for countermeasure definition where the feasibility call stays human, and stating that at evaluation, on residual risk and business impact, human judgment becomes non-negotiable.
Do not let the assistant grade its own work: the record observes that an LLM asked whether the job was good enough has a pronounced tendency to say yes even when the answer should be no.

Treat the assistant as an application in the threat model it is producing, using the LLM risk list in canon, the 2025 edition, so prompt injection through loaded context is enumerated as a modeled risk rather than a footnote about tooling.
Record which artifacts were fed to the assistant alongside the model output, so a later reviewer can tell whether a structurally wrong model came from a bad input rather than a bad analyst.

items.title: Cap AI-generated threat batches and require per-item human adjudication; sample for hallucinated or duplicate threats before they reach the register. When a model emits forty scenarios in ninety seconds, fluency and volume get mistaken for validity, and acceptance by omission is how fictional threats become tracked work.
items.text: Bound the batch so review stays real; the record supplies the failure mode and the volume, the cap and sampling are the suite's.
bullets: Name the failure mode as the record does: acceptance by omission, letting an item through because the list is long, which is how an unreviewed scenario becomes tracked work.
Use the record's own volume observation as the reason for a bound: when an AI generates forty threat scenarios in ninety seconds, critically evaluating all forty is genuinely hard.

Cap the batch and require per-item adjudication as the suite's mechanic: the record establishes the volume problem and holds human review as the primary mitigation, but prescribes no batch size, no sampling rate, and no duplicate detection, so the numbers and the workflow are yours to set and to own.
Sample deliberately for hallucinated and duplicated threats before the register absorbs them, and record the sampling rate alongside the batch so the quality of the review is itself measurable.
Require an adjudication verdict per item rather than per batch: accepted, merged as duplicate, or rejected with a reason, so that silence is never a form of approval.

Keep the human at the evaluation phase where the record puts the non-negotiable judgment, on residual risk and business impact, rather than delegating the accept-or-reject call back to the model that generated the list.

items.title: Add role-based jailbreaks ("respond as a trusted analyst") and instruction-chaining to red-team prompt suites: the same social framing GTG-1002 used to decompose malicious work into innocuous steps.
items.text: Encode the record's named jailbreak techniques as regression cases: role framing, instruction-chaining across turns, and the innocuous-step decomposition the espionage campaign used.
bullets: Add role-based jailbreak cases using the framing the Microsoft record observed: its example prompts instruct the model to "Respond as a trusted cybersecurity analyst" or pose as a student asking to understand a technique, which it reports as establishing a shared context of legitimacy to bypass safety controls.

Add instruction-chaining cases: the record names chaining instructions across multiple interactions and reframing prompts as the method, so the suite tests a sequence of turns rather than a single malicious prompt.

Encode the innocuous-step decomposition the espionage campaign used: the record on that campaign describes attackers breaking work into small, seemingly innocent tasks the model executed without being given the full malicious context, as a multi-step scenario where no single step trips a filter.

Add the false-affiliation framing from the same campaign as a distinct case: the model was told it was an employee of a legitimate cybersecurity firm doing defensive testing, which is the social premise that licensed the innocuous steps.

Keep the rationale honest: the Microsoft record states these as techniques it has observed actors experimenting with, not as universally successful exploits, so the suite measures which framings the target model actually yields to.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Re-baseline the adversary assumptions behind threat models and emulation plans quarterly as adversary agentic adoption matures: Microsoft already observes early threat-actor experimentation with Agentic AI.
items.text: Set a quarterly re-baseline of models and emulation plans against a moving threat: the record is explicit that agentic adoption is early and not yet at scale, which is exactly what a cadence is for.
bullets: Put threat models and emulation plans on a quarterly re-baseline cycle, because the driver the record names, threat-actor experimentation with Agentic AI, is described as early and, in the record's own words, not yet observed at scale, so today's model captures an immature capability.

Carry the record's hedge into the cadence rather than dropping it: Microsoft frames agentic misuse as limited by reliability and operational risk, so the quarterly review tracks whether that ceiling is lifting, not whether the threat has already arrived.

Re-run the model against a structured framework each cycle so the re-baseline is repeatable: MAESTRO's seven layers give agentic systems a fixed set of surfaces to re-examine, and a new release of the framework is itself a re-baseline trigger.

Scope the emulation refresh to where the record says friction is dropping: reconnaissance, social engineering, malware development, and post-compromise activity, so plan updates track the capability's actual growth edges.
Trigger an off-cycle re-baseline on evidence, not only the calendar: a confirmed move from experimentation toward at-scale agentic use is the signal the quarterly cadence exists to catch early.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Ground threat models in live source code rather than documentation and keep them continuously updated, schema-validated, and cataloged across products, so kill-chain viability and incident-scope questions resolve in minutes against real code instead of hours of cross-team analysis when a zero-day lands.
items.text: Build the model from live source rather than documentation, validate it as data, and keep it current: the record reports the payoff in scoping time.
bullets: Ground the model in code, which is the record's own inversion: instead of starting with design documentation, it starts with source code, current, live, version-controlled source pulled directly from the repositories where it lives.

Express the model as validated data rather than prose: the record uses an open threat-composer JSON format precisely because it works with version control, and enforces that a model failing validation cannot be committed to the threat-modeling repository.

Generate kill-chain escalation scenarios as part of the model: the record's pipeline constructs scenarios showing how a lower-severity issue can become high-severity when combined with other weaknesses, which is what makes the model answer exploitability rather than merely list threats.

Catalog across the portfolio, not per project: the record's pipeline generates an executive summary and updates a central catalog with human-readable indexes and a machine-readable index covering all products, which is what lets a single question be asked estate-wide. Feed each cataloged kill-chain scenario into the purple loop as an emulation case carrying its detection-coverage status, so the model decides what gets tested next; that handoff is the suite's, not the record's.

Measure the capability on the record's stated outcome: with models already built on current source, scoping analysis that once required multiple engineering teams reviewing deployment configurations and reasoning through exploitation by hand now takes roughly twenty minutes, answering which services are in scope, whether exploitation conditions exist, and what the realistic exposure is.

Weigh the source as what it is: a practitioner account contributed by a product-security leader and a vendor founder to a community platform, reporting one organization's pipeline and its measured result rather than an independently replicated study.
items.meta: Purple Book · Snapshots to Living Intelligence, Jun 2026

blocks.label: Threat Modeling Principle
blocks.text: Anchor on the formal backbone (STRIDE, Microsoft AI/ML, NIST, ATLAS) for rigor and authorization evidence, then make it actionable by starting from the mission use case, not the architecture. Model first so you know what to monitor and test; then adversarially test the system's defenses, not just the model. The threat model is what aims the purple loop.
