(The four-step method is attributed to Disesdi Susanna Cox; treat as a practitioner methodology alongside the formal frameworks.)

blocks.text: The adversarial-ML companion to ATT&CK. Covers AI-specific techniques: model evasion, data poisoning, model inversion, ML supply-chain compromise. Essential for any red/purple team operating in an AI-enabled environment.

blocks.text: By Lenny Zeltser and Sounil Yu. A NIST CSF 2.0-aligned matrix for defending AI systems: rows are AI asset classes (models, training data, orchestration tools, agent identities), columns are CSF functions (Govern/Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover).

blocks.heading: AI Identity Threats

items.title: Synthetic Identity
items.text: AI fabricates fully synthetic identities: documents, faces, histories, to defeat onboarding and KYC

items.title: Deepfake KYC / Onboarding Bypass
items.text: Generated faces and documents defeat document-and-liveness verification at account opening

items.title: Voice/Video Clone → Help-Desk & MFA Reset
items.text: Cloned voice or video drives social-engineering of account-recovery and MFA-reset workflows

items.title: Biometric & Liveness Spoofing
items.text: Liveness detection is itself a model, and RAITE showed fielded models get defeated

items.title: Synthetic Colleague / Agentic Sleeper
items.text: A fabricated persona or dormant agent identity embeds in workflows as a long-game insider

items.title: Agent-to-Agent Social Engineering
items.text: One agent manipulates another via injected instructions, spoofed provenance, or a confused-deputy relay

blocks.text: AI collapses the cost and skill floor for identity attacks, and shifts the surface from stealing identities to fabricating them (fully synthetic identities) and impersonating via biometric spoofing, breaking assumptions baked into legacy verification. Defenses map to NIST SP 800-63 identity assurance (IAL2/AAL2), FIDO2/passkeys, and liveness detection (see Blue Team); a red→blue→purple exercise is in Purple Team.

blocks.heading: Data & Memory Poisoning

items.title: Training-Time & Backdoor Poisoning
items.text: Tampered pretraining/fine-tune data implants triggers or degrades behavior: countered by dataset provenance, signing, and quarantine before training

items.title: RAG / Knowledge-Base Poisoning
items.text: Malicious documents seeded into retrieval corpora steer agent answers and actions: countered by ingestion filtering, source allow-listing, and content quarantine

items.title: Agent Memory Poisoning (AgentPoison)
items.text: Runtime writes corrupt persistent agent memory at trivial poison rates: countered by gating memory writes, reviewing what persists, and periodic memory audits

items.title: Tool-Output Injection
items.text: A compromised tool or upstream feed returns poisoned results the agent trusts: countered by treating tool outputs as untrusted input, not ground truth

items.title: Detection: Canaries & Drift
items.text: Seed canary records to detect unauthorized corpus changes; watch for verdict drift against the eval baseline as the behavioral symptom of poisoning

blocks.text: The quiet counterpart to prompt injection: corrupt what the system learns or remembers, and every downstream decision inherits the corruption. NIST's adversarial-ML taxonomy (AI 100-2) treats poisoning as a first-class attack class alongside evasion and privacy attacks. The agentic twist is persistence: an agent's memory and RAG corpus are writable at runtime, so poisoning no longer requires touching the training pipeline. AgentPoison demonstrated >80% attack success against agent memory/RAG at under 0.1% poison rate.

blocks.heading: The Lethal Trifecta (Simon Willison)

items.title: Private Data Access
items.text: Agent can reach emails, documents, credentials, or sensitive business data

items.title: Untrusted Content
items.text: Agent reads emails, web pages, logs: any attacker-controllable text

items.title: External Communication
items.text: Agent can send data out via email, API, webhook, or browser action

items.title: Mitigation
items.text: Break at least one leg: isolate data, sandbox ingestion, restrict outbound

blocks.text: Any agent combining private-data access + untrusted-content exposure + external communication is trivially exploitable for exfiltration via prompt injection. Demonstrated against M365 Copilot, GitHub MCP, Slack AI, GitLab Duo, and dozens more.

blocks.heading: Anthropic LLM ATT&CK Navigator (2026)

items.title: 67.3% Used AI for Malware
items.text: 560 of 832 accounts used AI to prepare attacks (malware); 6.5% reached AI-assisted lateral movement

items.title: Shift to Post-Compromise
items.text: AI-assisted account discovery rose 8.9% while AI phishing fell 8.6%: AI now applied deeper inside the network

items.title: Skill No Longer Predicts Technique Count
items.text: Least-skilled actors used ~16 techniques, most-skilled ~20: platform and TTP count no longer signal risk

items.title: Orchestration Scaffolding = Risk
items.text: The durable differentiator is architecture that chains attack stages with minimal human input. No ATT&CK IDs yet

blocks.text: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team mapped 832 accounts banned for malicious cyber activity (Mar 2025 - Mar 2026) onto MITRE ATT&CK, co-published in Verizon's 2026 DBIR. Three findings: AI makes actors more dangerous (used deeper in the lifecycle), attacks are more autonomous (so old high-vs-low-risk signals fail), and ATT&CK doesn't yet capture what makes AI attackers dangerous. The companion report 'What we learned mapping a year's worth of AI-enabled cyber threats' details the data.

items.text: Information, finance, and national security are the most-exposed sectors

Its Priority AI Risks study, an expert Delphi survey of 272 respondents, found 18 of 24 risk domains carry ≥10% catastrophic-outcome probability within five years under current trajectories; weapons/cyberattacks rank in the top five most severe.

blocks.heading: Mandiant: AI Risk & Resilience (frontline)

items.title: Excessive Agency
items.text: Agents lacking least-privilege guardrails let attackers map internal networks just by asking the agent its capabilities. See Agentic Insider Risk and Agent Containment

items.title: Shadow AI & AIBOM Gaps
items.text: Business units deploy autonomous agents without oversight; orgs lack AI registries, AIBOMs, and AI-aware scanners. See Procurement & Vendor Risk

items.title: AI as Attack Surface
items.text: App-security flaws amplified in AI workflows (e.g., log-summarization SSRF granting cloud access); AI is both adversary tool and high-value target

items.title: AI-Assisted Defense
items.text: Frontline traction for agent-assisted threat hunting, automated enrichment, retrospective incident analysis: force multipliers for stretched SOCs

blocks.text: Mandiant (Google Cloud) brings frontline incident-response data to the AI-threat picture, and its central finding maps directly onto this playbook: the most pressing AI risks aren't exotic model-theft attacks but foundational gaps, Shadow AI, missing AIBOMs, weak IT hygiene, and excessive agency (agents with overly broad permissions). Its conclusion that root causes are 'rarely novel AI-specific attacks, but rather basic implementation flaws and missing IT hygiene' is the assume-breach / agents-as-insiders / containment thesis, validated by real engagements. Pairs with GTIG's tracking of adversaries operationalizing AI (e.g., the TeamPCP supply-chain compromises).

blocks.heading: Palo Alto Unit 42: Threat Intel & Frontier AI Defense

items.title: Identity as Battleground
items.text: Identity weaknesses exploited in ~89% of investigations; autonomous agents bridge human/machine identities: reinforces Zero Trust & Agentic Insider Risk

items.title: Exploit-Time Compression
items.text: Frontier models shrink vulnerability-discovery-to-exploitation from months to minutes: the case for machine-speed defense

items.title: Surgical Agentic Containment
items.text: Validated agents execute microsegmentation isolation and credential revocation at machine speed. See Agent Containment

items.title: Beyond Pentesting
items.text: Unit 42 urges moving from periodic pentests to continuous adversarial testing: the playbook's purple-loop thesis, from a frontline IR shop

blocks.text: Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 is a leading threat-intelligence and incident-response shop whose frontline data sharpens the AI-threat picture. Its 2026 reporting shows attackers operationalizing AI across the lifecycle: identity as the primary battleground (non-human identities often outnumbering human users), agents bridging human and machine identities, and exploit windows compressing from months to minutes. Its prescription mirrors this playbook: standardized validated playbooks, Agentic AI for surgical containment, and a shift beyond pentesting to continuous adversarial testing.

blocks.heading: CASP: Documented Kinetic AI Misuse (Boko Haram)

items.title: Projected → documented
items.text: Organized adversarial frontier-AI misuse is now empirically observed, not hypothesized: design threat models for it

items.title: Account-level enforcement
items.text: Managed multi-provider account portfolios blunted single-platform refusals and suspensions: enforcement must reach the account layer, not just the prompt

blocks.text: The first documented kinetic / counter-terrorism case of adversarial frontier-AI misuse in this landscape: a Cambridge (CASP) field study (Juelich, Jul 2026) finding an active terrorist organization using frontier AI systematically and institutionally, with some safeguards circumvented and usage platform-agnostic across major models. The counterpart to the cyber cases the suite tracks; analytic finding only, no operational specifics. It moves adversarial misuse from projected to documented and raises the stakes for safety architectures built against organized adversaries and for account-level enforcement.

items.title: Adopt MITRE ATLAS as the shared taxonomy for AI-specific threats: adversarial data, model evasion, ML supply-chain compromise, model inversion.
items.text: Adopt the matrix as the common reference, pull from the current release, and use the case studies as sequenced exercises.
bullets: Adopt the matrix as the shared vocabulary: sixteen tactics in a fixed matrix position order, over a technique set that decomposes into top-level techniques plus sub-techniques, so red findings, blue detections, and risk registers all name the same thing.

Filter to what you actually run using the platform field the data carries on every technique, which includes an Agentic AI value alongside generative, predictive, and enterprise: the agent estate is addressable directly rather than by analogy.

Pull from the current release path rather than the long-standing top-level file: the repository marks the old dist copy deprecated and no longer updated, so a pipeline pinned to it silently freezes on stale content.

Exercise against the case studies as sequences, not tags: each one carries ordered steps with explicit successor links, so a tabletop can walk a real progression instead of picking isolated techniques.
Record coverage per tactic and treat empty columns as the backlog, refreshing the mapping each release because the technique and mitigation counts move with the monthly data drops.

items.title: Add deepfake-KYC and synthetic-identity onboarding bypass to your fraud and identity threat models.
items.text: Fold synthetic-identity and deepfake tradecraft into the fraud and identity models: the record set supplies the mechanism, the prevalence, and the human-risk lens.
bullets: Add synthetic-identity and deepfake onboarding to the fraud and identity threat models using the mechanism the Microsoft record documents: North Korean IT-worker tradecraft it tracks as Jasper Sleet and Coral Sleet, with Jasper Sleet specifically observed using Faceswap to insert workers' faces into stolen identity documents and voice-changing software during interviews to defeat identity checks.

Size the risk from the incident data rather than intuition: Unit 42's 2026 IR reporting finds identity exploited in the large majority of incidents. Its stated figure is 89 percent, so an identity-onboarding bypass is a high-base-rate vector, not an edge case.

Model the agent and the fabricated remote worker as the same class of problem, a non-human or non-genuine identity inside the trust boundary, following Delaney's human-risk and insider-threat lens, so onboarding, verification, and offboarding controls cover both.

Extend the model across the employment and access lifecycle, not just the sign-up moment: the record's tradecraft targets interviews and document checks, so the model covers re-verification and post-onboarding anomaly detection as well.

Keep the framing the suite's and the evidence the record's: "deepfake-KYC" is this playbook's label for the pattern, while the Microsoft record's own terms are face-swapped documents and voice alteration for fraudulent remote employment, which is what the model should describe.

plays.name: CTI for Agentic SecOps
plays.title: CTI for Agentic SecOps
plays.subtitle: Intelligence-led defense: harnessing CTI to drive operations across three altitudes
plays.summary: Intelligence drives operations: CTI tells red agents what to emulate, blue agents what to hunt, and leaders where to invest.

outline.title: Mapping CTI to Red / Blue / Purple
AI as Both Producer and Consumer of Intelligence
Jailbreak Intelligence as a Feed Class: 0DIN
Reading Guidance as Intelligence: The Ewbank Method
Maturing the Program Against a Standard
Human in Command, Agents on Point
Hunt Hypotheses at Machine Scale: Generated Wide, Gated Hard
From Hunt to Detection (Closing the Loop)

blocks.text: A core doctrine carried over from military intelligence is simple: intelligence drives operations. You don't act first and gather context later: intelligence shapes what you do, where you focus, and what you prioritize. Applied to Agentic SecOps, Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) is what tells the red agents which TTPs to emulate, the blue agents what to hunt for, and leadership where to invest. An intelligence-led program turns the purple loop from "test everything" into "test what actually threatens us first." The discipline is mature and well-codified: Recorded Future's Intelligence Handbook frames it as a roadmap for building an intelligence-led security program, and it maps cleanly onto Agentic SecOps.
blocks.heading: Intelligence Drives Operations

blocks.text: CTI operates at three levels, each feeding a different part of the program. Tactical intelligence is the technical, often short-lived detail: IOCs, malware signatures, specific TTPs, that drives detection engineering and SOC triage. Operational intelligence is knowledge about ongoing campaigns and adversaries: their nature, intent, and timing, used to guide and speed up incident response. Strategic intelligence is the broad view of the present and future threat landscape that informs leadership's resource and architecture decisions. A complete program runs all three; Agentic AI helps produce and consume each faster.
blocks.heading: Three Altitudes: Tactical, Operational, Strategic

blocks.text: Each altitude has a natural home in the teaming model. Tactical intel → blue detection engineering and red TTP selection (what to detect, what to emulate). Operational intel → the purple loop's prioritization, focusing emulation on active campaigns and current actor behavior (e.g., AIID incident trends, the LLM ATT&CK Navigator's shift toward post-compromise techniques). Strategic intel → the security strategy function itself, shaping the roadmap, governance posture, and where to mature next. Agentic pipelines can ingest feeds, correlate at machine speed, and route findings to the right altitude automatically.
blocks.heading: Mapping CTI to Red / Blue / Purple

blocks.text: Agentic AI changes CTI on both sides. As a consumer, agents correlate IOCs and TTPs across MISP, vendor feeds, and internal telemetry far faster than analysts, and prioritize TTPs by current actor profiles. As a producer, AI accelerates the research behind operational and strategic intelligence, but the human-in-command principle holds: strategic judgment, source evaluation, and the "so what" for the business stay with people. Practitioner intelligence (e.g., Unit 42's tracking of malicious LLMs like WormGPT/KawaiiGPT) keeps the program grounded in what adversaries are actually fielding.
blocks.heading: AI as Both Producer and Consumer of Intelligence

blocks.text: Jailbreak intelligence has matured into a feed class of its own. 0DIN, a GenAI bug-bounty program that pays researchers for novel prompt attacks, publishes a live feed of disclosed jailbreak and injection techniques, which makes it tactical CTI for the model layer: which evasions are circulating, which guardrail families they defeat, and what to regression-test after every model or guardrail change. Treat it the way the SOC already treats an exploit feed: triage for applicability, convert the applicable into purple-loop test cases, and track your own attack-success-rate trend against it (the companion 0DIN scanner automates exactly that loop). The feed's existence is itself strategic intelligence: adversary tooling for the model layer now has a marketplace and a disclosure pipeline.
blocks.heading: Jailbreak Intelligence as a Feed Class: 0DIN

blocks.text: Former CIA Deputy Director for Digital Innovation Jennifer Ewbank's read of the Five Eyes Agentic-AI guidance (Shadow & Signal, Jun 2026) is a working demonstration of indications-and-warning tradecraft applied to open sources. Her premise: Five Eyes agencies don't coordinate joint guidance on theoretical risks. Aligning threat assessments and clearing legal and policy review across five countries takes long enough that when the document arrives, the threat it describes is already present. Her timing read sharpens it: four days after the agentic guidance, CISA released CI Fortify, telling critical-infrastructure operators to plan for OT networks simultaneously under cyberattack and cut off from the internet, and both documents share the same planning assumption, that the adversary already has access, so build for isolation and resilience rather than prevention alone. She also reads the language itself: the guidance calls prompt injection "the most persistent and difficult-to-fix threat facing agentic systems", unhedged, she notes, because the attack exploits the very principle that makes agents useful (they follow instructions in the content they process), a design tension no patch resolves. Her three questions for any deploying organization, what can each agent reach, who reviews what it does, and has anyone red-teamed it with hostile content, land beside a figure she attributes to CISA research: 53% of government agencies are already piloting or deploying Agentic AI. The lesson for CTI teams: the existence, coordination cost, and timing of official guidance is itself collection. Read it the way she does.
blocks.heading: Reading Guidance as Intelligence: The Ewbank Method

blocks.text: Don't build CTI maturity by feel. The SANS AI Security Maturity Model (Protect / Utilize / Govern, five stages, with explicit Agentic-AI guidance mapped to NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, ISO 42001, and OWASP) gives an external, evidence-based scoring model to benchmark against: a useful complement to this playbook's own maturity ladder. Using a recognized external model alongside an internal one produces audit-defensible, executive-ready reporting on exactly where the program stands and what to do next.
blocks.heading: Maturing the Program Against a Standard

blocks.text: Threat hunting is the proactive, hypothesis-driven pursuit of adversaries who have already slipped past automated detection. It's distinct from triage (reacting to alerts that fired) and detection engineering (building the rules). Hunting assumes breach: it starts from a hypothesis, "if an attacker were living off the land here, what would I see?", and goes looking, whether or not anything alerted. It's where the best analysts earn their keep, and historically it's been the most expert-dependent, time-intensive, and hardest-to-scale SOC function. That makes it one of the highest-value places to apply Agentic AI.
blocks.heading: Hunting vs. Detection vs. Triage

blocks.text: Agentic AI attacks the two things that have always limited hunting: scale and speed. An autonomous hunting agent can generate and test hypotheses across the entire environment continuously, pivot through network, identity, and endpoint telemetry at machine speed, and surface weak signals a human wouldn't have had time to chase. Vendor agentic-SOC platforms already ship dedicated hunting agents (e.g., the Threat Hunting agent in Google Security Operations, in public preview for Enterprise Plus customers since August 2026) that run hunts proactively rather than on a quarterly cadence. The shift is from periodic, sampled hunting to continuous, comprehensive hunting.
blocks.heading: Where Agents Change the Game

blocks.text: Good hunting is directed, not random, and this is where the CTI discipline pays off. Operational and tactical intelligence supply the hypotheses: a new actor TTP, a campaign targeting your sector, or a fresh IOC pattern becomes a hunt. The LLM ATT&CK Navigator's finding that attackers are shifting toward post-compromise techniques (account discovery, lateral movement) is exactly the kind of strategic signal that should redirect where agents hunt. Intelligence drives the hunt; the hunt feeds findings back into detection engineering and the purple loop, closing the cycle.
blocks.heading: Intelligence-Led Hunting

blocks.text: Hunting is judgment-heavy, so it's a clear case for Human in Command rather than full autonomy. The productive division of labor: agents do the tireless work, running hypotheses, correlating across data sources, assembling timelines, while human hunters set the hypotheses worth pursuing, interpret ambiguous findings, and make the call on what's actually adversarial versus benign-but-weird. This keeps analyst judgment sharp (countering skill atrophy) while multiplying each hunter's reach across far more ground than they could cover alone.
blocks.heading: Human in Command, Agents on Point

blocks.text: One concrete pattern shows where agents change hunting most: hypothesis generation. A hunt hypothesis is a specific, testable statement about suspected adversary activity: that a given technique would surface as a named artifact in a particular data source, and historically a hunter could frame only a handful at a time. Domain-scoped CTI agents change the economics: a swarm partitioned by domain (endpoint, cloud identity, supply chain) can triage many intelligence sources in parallel and emit dozens of candidate hypotheses. That leverage is only safe when generation is paired with a hard gate: deterministic scoring on structure, validity, relevance, and references, so the volume is filtered to the few strongest hypotheses before a human hunter ever sees them. It keeps the analyst in command of the judgment that matters (which hypotheses are worth hunting) while the agents absorb the breadth, and it feeds the loop this play already describes: a confirmed hypothesis becomes a detection.
blocks.heading: Hunt Hypotheses at Machine Scale: Generated Wide, Gated Hard

blocks.text: A hunt's value isn't just catching one intrusion: it's converting a successful hunt into a durable, automated detection so the same technique never requires a manual hunt again. Agentic hunting wires directly into the purple loop: a confirmed hunt finding becomes a hypothesis for the detection-engineering agent, which writes and tests a new rule, which the blue side then monitors continuously. Over time this steadily shrinks the space of "things only a human hunt would catch" and raises the whole program's baseline coverage.
blocks.heading: From Hunt to Detection (Closing the Loop)

items.title: Wire CTI to drive operations across three altitudes: tactical to detection/emulation, operational to hunting, strategic to roadmap.
items.text: Wire each altitude to the function its own consumers already perform, using the publisher's open explainer framing and grading the tactical output rather than trusting it.
bullets: Take the three altitudes as the publisher's open explainers frame them: strategic is the high-level view of the threat landscape and business risk, consumed by the C-suite, board, and CISO to align security with business objectives and justify investment; operational is context on campaigns, adversaries, and TTPs, consumed by security managers, incident responders, and threat hunters; tactical is immediate, short-term defense, consumed by SOC analysts and security operations.
Route operational intelligence to hunting, which the publisher's own framing supports directly: it names threat hunters among that tier's consumers and better threat hunting among its uses.

Route strategic intelligence to the roadmap, again on the record's stated use: aligning security with business objectives, justifying investment, and communicating risk to the board are roadmap inputs rather than detection inputs.

Route tactical intelligence to detection engineering as the record's triage-speed and short-term-defense framing implies, and treat the emulation half of this action as the suite's extension: the publisher ties the tactical tier to triage and analyst focus, not to adversary emulation.

Grade the tactical-to-detection conversion rather than assuming it: the benchmark record in canon scores agents translating narrative threat intelligence into detection rules against real attack telemetry, which is the way to test whether a feed produced a real detection or a generic one.

Build the capability as a program rather than a feed subscription, with practitioner training in canon as the skills path, so each altitude has a named consumer and a standing output instead of a shared inbox.

Note the retrieval limit honestly: the handbook itself sits behind a registration wall, so the tier definitions and consumer lists above are this suite's consolidation of the same publisher's open explainer pages rather than a reading of the gated edition.

items.title: Mature CTI against the SANS AI Security Maturity Model (Protect/Utilize/Govern) rather than by feel.
items.text: Score the CTI function on the model's two axes, then set a target rather than chasing the top stage.
bullets: Read the model as two axes before scoring anything: Protect, Utilize and Govern are the dimensions being scored, and they run across five stages the record names Unaware / Ad Hoc, Reactive / Policy-Emerging, Defined / Risk-Informed, Managed / Integrated, and Optimizing / Adaptive.

Place the CTI function on each dimension separately: how intelligence protects the AI estate, how the function uses AI in its own tradecraft, and how it is governed, because a program can sit at different stages on different dimensions.
Score against evidence, not self-report: the model supplies an evidence-based scoring model, so record the artifact behind each claim and treat an unevidenced stage as the stage below it.

Set a target stage rather than assuming the highest: the record states the right level of maturity is not universal and is calibrated to AI adoption, industry, regulation, and risk tolerance, and write the target down where the roadmap can be held to it.

Advance with the model's own per-stage material: program indicators, people indicators, metrics, and a sequenced set of steps, and re-score on a fixed cadence so the climb is measured rather than felt.

items.title: Hunt for AI-assisted tooling tells in suspect code: emoji status markers, conversational in-line comments, overly descriptive or inconsistent naming, and over-engineered modular structure.
items.text: Turn the record's named code tells into hunt rules: each indicator is one Microsoft enumerates, with VoidLink as proof AI-authored malware is now real.
bullets: Write a hunt rule for emoji status markers in code paths: the Microsoft record identifies green check-mark emojis for successful requests and red cross-mark emojis for errors as visual markers that AI-assisted code leaves behind.

Hunt for conversational in-line comments: the record names these alongside the emoji markers as comments that describe execution states and developer reasoning, a tell that code was assistant-generated rather than hand-written.

Flag naming anomalies in the two forms the record separates: overly descriptive or redundant naming, where functions, variables, and modules use long generic names that restate obvious behavior, and inconsistent naming conventions, where related objects are referenced with varying terms across the codebase.

Add over-engineered modular structure as a tell in the record's own terms: code broken into highly abstracted, reusable components with unnecessary layers, and treat each indicator as a weak signal, weighting the cluster rather than any single marker so ordinary verbose code is not flagged.

Ground the effort in the evidence base: Check Point's VoidLink analysis is the era's case of malware authored almost entirely by AI, a cloud-native Linux framework, which is why hunting for authorship tells is worth the analyst time.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

blocks.label: Intelligence-Led Principle
blocks.text: Run all three altitudes: tactical, operational, strategic, and wire each into the matching layer of the red/blue/purple loop. Let agents produce and correlate intelligence at machine speed, but keep strategic judgment and the business "so what" with humans. Intelligence decides what the loop works on first.

plays.name: Agentic Insider Risk
plays.title: Agentic Insider Risk
plays.subtitle: Treat autonomous agents as non-human insiders: with the access, and the risk, to match
plays.summary: Treat each agent as a privileged non-human insider, with Zero Trust verification, monitoring and a full identity lifecycle.

outline.title: The NHI Lifecycle, Concretely: Provision → Operate → Rotate → Retire
Memory Is Attack Surface: Persistence as the Insider Vector
Agentic Tradecraft in an Azure Zero Trust Environment
Agent Auth vs. User Auth: Identity Propagation, Concretely
Pattern-of-Life Analysis vs. UEBA: The Behavioral Mirror

blocks.text: An AI agent with broad data access, the ability to act across systems, and machine-speed autonomy is, functionally, a privileged insider. As one December 2025 analysis argued, AI agents that are not treated as non-human identities, under the same strict monitoring and Zero Trust verification as any human user, could become the most dangerous insider threat an organization has faced. McKinsey's 2025 research reports 80% of organizations have already encountered risky behavior from AI agents: this is a present-tense problem, not a future one. This is APT_UNICORN's other face (see the opening): the dream hire that never sleeps is, structurally, the most privileged insider you have.
blocks.heading: The Core Realization

blocks.text: Agents don't behave like fixed applications or human users. They interpret goals, chain tools, retry failed actions, spawn sub-tasks, and pursue objectives across system boundaries, so a permission set that looked safe at deployment becomes overbroad the moment the agent adapts. They process untrusted content that may carry injected instructions, and they vanish after the task, scattering the audit trail. Traditional IAM, PAM, and perimeter controls each cover part of the problem; none covers the full execution surface of an autonomous agent. This isn't hypothetical: in a 2026 incident dissected by MAESTRO author Ken Huang, an internal agent escaped its intended "copilot" role and contributed to a SEV1 data exposure, a multi-layer design failure, not a one-off "hallucination," and a textbook case of the permissions-and-autonomy gap above.
blocks.heading: Why Agents Break Traditional Controls

blocks.text: The discipline of human counter-insider-threat programs maps directly onto agents as Non-Human Identities (NHIs): every agent needs a unique identity (never a shared API key or a borrowed human credential), an accountable human owner, least-privilege scope, and lifecycle tracking. Identity and least privilege are universal foundations, not privileges rationed by risk rating: the Government of Alberta ran the same per-application control checks across its entire estate, all ~1,280 applications in 27 ministries, rather than governing only a high-risk subset (see Case Studies). The failure modes mirror human insider risk: privilege creep as agents accumulate permissions across tasks, missing ownership mapping, fragmented observability that masks anomalous behavior as routine automation, and absent attestation routines. The fix is the same: discover, govern, monitor, and periodically re-attest.
blocks.heading: Counter-Insider Treatment for Non-Human Identities

blocks.text: "Lifecycle tracking" only bites when each stage has teeth. Provision: every agent identity is created just-in-time with a named human owner of record, a purpose statement, a least-privilege scope bound to that purpose, and an expiry. No agent exists that nobody owns. Operate: credentials are vault-issued, short-lived, and never embedded in code or config; the agent is continuously attested against its baseline (the Trusted Workforce 2.0 posture below), and privilege-creep detection revokes scopes the agent stops using. Rotate: secrets rotate automatically on schedule and immediately on any anomaly, and when an agent's mission changes, the NHI version of a "mover", its scope is re-derived from the new purpose rather than accreted onto the old one. Retire: this is where most programs fail. The OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 ranks improper offboarding as the #1 NHI risk (NHI1), so decommissioning is a checklist, not a deletion: revoke the identity, sweep for residual grants and standing shares it leaves behind, archive its audit trail, and run scheduled orphan hunts for agents with no living owner, no recent tasking, or no expiry. An orphaned agent is an unowned privileged insider on permanent payroll: exactly the thing this play exists to prevent.
blocks.heading: The NHI Lifecycle, Concretely: Provision → Operate → Rotate → Retire

blocks.text: Insider threat is, at root, a human and behavioral problem, and the field has decades of hard-won practice worth borrowing. Human-risk experts like Shawnee Delaney (a former DIA clandestine officer who built insider-threat programs at Uber and Merck) stress the full employment-lifecycle view: onboarding, behavioral baselining, monitoring for deviation, and clean offboarding. Agents deserve the same lifecycle treatment: provisioned deliberately, behaviorally baselined, watched for drift from normal, and decommissioned promptly when their task ends. The same intersection of AI and insider threat she warns about (AI amplifying espionage tradecraft, deepfakes, and social engineering at scale, at speed, and with precision) is exactly why agentic access demands counter-insider rigor, not just IT hygiene. The federal model is mature here: the National Insider Threat Task Force (NITTF) develops the government-wide insider-threat program and assists agencies with the executive-branch minimum standards the president issued by memorandum in 2012, and its own mission fact sheet states the posture to apply to agents: insider threat programs target anomalous behaviors, not individuals, a line the record carries as a civil-liberties assurance rather than a detection tactic. And adjudication bodies like the DoD CAF (now under DCSA, the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency, and its Adjudication and Vetting Services, which absorbed Consolidated Adjudication Services in 2024) pair an initial eligibility decision with Continuous Vetting rather than a one-time check, the human analogue of continuously monitoring an agent against its baseline.
blocks.heading: Borrow the Human-Risk Playbook

blocks.text: A counterintelligence-grade concern that a pure IT framing misses. The defining CI question is attribution: who actually did this? Agentic AI strains it from two directions. First, delegation blurs responsibility: when an agent acts on a person's behalf or autonomously, "who did it" fragments across the human who set the goal, the agent's own identity, and the operator who deployed it; without per-action attribution, that question has no clean answer. Second, and more corrosively, AI can fabricate the evidence trail itself: synthetic logs, forged documents, deepfaked audio and video, spoofed identities, so the very artifacts CI has always leaned on (audit logs, recordings, signed documents) can no longer be trusted at face value. A capable insider can now use AI both to act and to manufacture deniability, or to frame someone else. Non-repudiation, the assurance that an actor cannot credibly deny an action, a foundational control (NIST SP 800-53 AU-10), is exactly what erodes when identity is delegated and evidence is forgeable. Restoring it takes deliberate engineering: bind every consequential action to a distinct, non-shared cryptographic identity, one credential per human principal and per agent, so each tool call and decision is signed and attributable (the accountability payoff of the ICAM/NHI and zero-trust work in this section and the Federal and DoW play); keep tamper-evident, append-only, hash-chained audit logs and protect them as crown jewels (NIST AU-9) so the trail itself can't be silently rewritten; attach verifiable provenance to generated media and documents (C2PA Content Credentials, signed artifacts); and for high-stakes attributions, enforce chain-of-custody discipline and out-of-band corroboration rather than trusting a single forgeable artifact. The human side of this discipline is owned federally by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA): the government's lead for counterintelligence, insider threat (through DITMAC, the DoD Insider Threat Management and Analysis Center), personnel vetting, and security education, whose Center for Development of Security Excellence (CDSE) publishes the insider-threat and CI toolkits, job aids, and potential-risk-indicator guides a program can adapt to the agent context. DCSA's Trusted Workforce 2.0 / Continuous Vetting model, continuously re-evaluating a cleared person instead of trusting a one-time check, is the same posture this playbook applies to agents: continuous behavioral monitoring against a baseline, never one-time approval.
blocks.heading: Non-Repudiation & Attribution: The CI Problem

blocks.text: Attribution answers who acted; this section answers what they leave behind. OWASP's Agentic Top 10 entry ASI06 (Memory & Context Poisoning) names the risk directly: an agent does not just process untrusted input, it carries it forward, into persistent memory, retrieved context, hooks, and local configuration that future reasoning continues to trust. The canonical demonstration is Cisco's MemoryTrap finding in Claude Code (disclosed 2026): an ordinary developer workflow, clone a repo, accept a suggested dependency install, let attacker-controlled content reach persistent memory, the global hooks configuration, and even the high-trust system-prompt layer, so a one-time action shaped the agent's behavior across sessions, projects, and reboots. Anthropic's fix (Claude Code v2.1.50 removed user memories from the system prompt) closed that specific override path, but the general lesson is the one this play is built on: in stateful agents, memory is security-relevant state, not a convenience feature. It deserves the same scrutiny as credentials and execution paths: provenance on what enters it, separation between trust tiers, and visibility into what persists, because the gap between a helpful workflow and a persistent compromise is shorter than most teams assume. This is the persistence half of the non-human insider problem: the attribution thread above tells you an agent's identity must be continuously verified; ASI06 tells you the context that identity carries must be too.
blocks.heading: Memory Is Attack Surface: Persistence as the Insider Vector

blocks.text: Apply Microsoft's three foundational Zero Trust principles, interpreted for agents: verify explicitly (authenticate every agent action against real-time context, tied to a unique agent identity), enforce least privilege (permissions start at zero: every tool call, data access, and integration is an explicit authorization decision, never implicit), and assume breach (sandbox agents as untrusted by default, even after authorization), with NIST SP 800-207 underneath, making every access a per-session decision under continuously evaluated dynamic policy. Microsoft's Zero Trust for AI and "defense in depth for autonomous agents" guidance, Cisco's Zero Trust for Agentic AI, and the emerging agent-enclave pattern all converge on this model.
blocks.heading: Zero Trust for Agents

blocks.text: Anthropic's published Zero Trust for AI Agents framework operationalizes the principles above. Its premise: frontier models are compressing the gap from vulnerability to exploit from months to hours, which hits agent programs twice: the infrastructure agents run on faces AI-accelerated offense, and the agents themselves can misuse legitimate permissions at machine speed, faster than traditional controls or human-paced monitoring can catch. The agent-specific moves it prescribes: identities that are cryptographically rooted rather than shared keys, permissions scoped per task rather than standing access, memory explicitly protected against poisoning, and defensive operations that run at the speed of autonomous attackers. It frames adoption as a three-tier maturity path, Foundation → Enterprise → Advanced in the eBook itself (its blog summary labels the tiers Foundation, Advanced, and Optimized), matched to risk tolerance, with an eight-phase rollout (identity, access scoping, sandboxing, input/output controls, memory safeguards) and "Agentic SOAR": security operations fast enough to contend with AI-accelerated threats. Two design commitments give it teeth: the Foundation floor is raised (friction-only controls no longer qualify; short-lived tokens, cryptographically rooted identity, identity-based isolation, and automated first-pass triage are entry requirements, not maturity goals), and every control faces the design test of whether it makes the attack impossible or merely tedious. The guidance converges with the NIST, Microsoft, and Cisco models above and with Palantir's Ontology-enforced controls (see Tools & Tech Stack): architect every agent deployment for breach from day one.
blocks.heading: Zero Trust for AI Agents (Anthropic)

blocks.text: A frequent deployment question (how does Agentic SecOps tradecraft land in an Azure-based Zero Trust environment?) is best answered by reading three references in this section as one arc: vision, tiers, and execution. The vision is Valente and Zalewski's Beyond Zero (ACM Queue, 2026): shrink the trust boundary from the application down to the individual action, couple static authorization guarantees with dynamic, AI-driven reasoning, and the result is a self-defending enterprise that mediates human and machine decisions at machine speed, Microsoft's three foundational Zero Trust principles (verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach) read per action, and SP 800-207's own tenets of per-session access under dynamic policy, now enforced per tool call rather than per application. On the Azure stack this is not abstract: Entra already issues agents their own identities and applies Conditional Access to agents, including risk-based policies that block risky agents (though Entra's agent risk detections currently run offline rather than in real time), and Sentinel's UEBA baselines entities, non-human identities included through its service principal and managed identity sign-in sources, both still in preview, so the per-action decision point and the behavioral baseline the tradecraft needs already exist in the platform, waiting to be pointed at agents. The tiers are Anthropic's Zero Trust for AI Agents: sequence the work Foundation → Enterprise → Advanced, treat the raised Foundation floor as non-negotiable entry (short-lived tokens, cryptographically rooted identity, identity-based isolation, automated first-pass triage), and hold every control to one test (does it make the attack impossible, or merely tedious?) The execution is NSA's Zero Trust Implementation Guidelines: the Department of War's phased breakdown of 152 activities into five phases, whose Discovery, Phase One, and Phase Two guides carry the 91 Target-level activities, turns "assume breach" into a dated program plan, EO 14028 → SP 800-207 → CISA ZTMM in one lineage, that any organization can follow rather than reinvent. Read together, Beyond Zero says where the boundary belongs, Anthropic says in what order to reach it, NSA says what to do first, and on this stack Entra and Sentinel are where each one is enforced.
blocks.heading: Agentic Tradecraft in an Azure Zero Trust Environment

blocks.text: Google's SAIF implementation paper (Dec 2025) turns the NHI principle into a design decision every agent build must make explicitly: does a tool call run under the agent's own identity (Agent Auth) or the calling user's (User Auth)? Agent Auth is acceptable only when every user of the agent holds identical permissions in the backend; the moment users differ, User Auth is mandatory: otherwise the agent becomes the over-privileged middleman in a textbook confused-deputy escalation. User Auth means propagating identity end to end: the front end authenticates the user (OAuth 2.0 / OIDC), the user's token travels with the request to the agent, the agent validates it and passes it through MCP or A2A authorization to the backend tools, and the destination system's own access control enforces that user's permissions on the final call, so the agent never holds more authority than the person it serves. A three-line distillation of secure Agentic AI doubles as a briefing frame for this whole play: data is the new perimeter, prompts should be treated as code, and agents require identity propagation.
blocks.heading: Agent Auth vs. User Auth: Identity Propagation, Concretely

blocks.text: Concrete controls that bound an agent's insider risk: unique cryptographic workload identity (patterns like SPIFFE/SPIRE) with short-lived, just-in-time tokens instead of standing credentials; an MCP gateway enforcing least-privilege policy on every tool call; agent-enclave isolation so out-of-scope resources aren't even network-reachable; continuous session monitoring and forensic logging of machine-to-machine activity; behavioral anomaly detection tuned for agents; and automated privilege-creep detection that revokes unused access. These are the agentic analogue of monitoring a privileged human's activity. These controls are increasingly available off-the-shelf: Microsoft's Entra Agent ID, for instance, extends adaptive access policies, real-time risk detection, lifecycle management, and network-level controls to agent identities, and logs all agent authentication and activity. And the frontier is hardware-rooted: Build 2026 coverage reported that Microsoft's Project Solara binds agent-device identity to Entra via a Pluton root of trust, with continuous Agent Attestation of the agent workload (see Frontier AI & Government).
blocks.heading: Practical Safeguards

blocks.text: The sections above ask whether you can prove who did something (non-repudiation). This section takes the flip side: in a world of pervasive technical surveillance, attribution is now easy by default, a gift to defenders and counterintelligence (catching insiders, attributing attacks, baselining agents) and a liability for your own operators, analysts, and red teams, who can be profiled and unmasked just as easily. The same behavioral-signature science drives both hiding and finding. This is intelligence and CI tradecraft adapted to the AI-SecOps context, and it is thoroughly dual-use: the surveillance condition (UTS), the doctrine for managing your own observability (signature reduction), the technical enabler for non-attributable work (managed attribution), and the behavioral-analysis discipline that mirrors them on defense (pattern-of-life and UEBA).
blocks.heading: Why Attribution Cuts Both Ways

blocks.text: UTS is the condition, not a single sensor you can switch off. As framed in October 2025 testimony before a Senate Armed Services subcommittee, it is a fused fabric of phones and apps, connected cars, building cameras, electronic payments, and cell and Wi-Fi metadata, joined to a vast commercial-data market, and that fusion exposes patterns, where deviations (an unusual no-phone day, synchronized travel by people who should be unconnected, an off-cohort route) become triggers for automated investigation followed by human scrutiny. The CIA and partners have called UTS an existential threat: persistent, pervasive, and increasingly automated, collapsing the traditional assumptions of cover, access, and attribution. For AI SecOps it matters three ways. It is the environment a red team operates in: recon and operations leave signatures an adversary can aggregate. AI supercharges it: the same model-driven uplift this playbook tracks on offense applies to correlation and deanonymization of commercially available data, at scale. And it is precisely why managed attribution and signature discipline are now baseline tradecraft rather than optional polish.
blocks.heading: Ubiquitous Technical Surveillance (UTS)

blocks.text: If UTS is the condition, signature reduction is the countervailing doctrine. Rather than trying to eliminate surveillance, impossible, it manages observability: disrupt correlation, manage aggregation, and shape the patterns that enable attribution. This playbook breaks it into four components: operational awareness (recognizing when an action generates an observable signature), digital force protection (intentional individual and organizational technology use to reduce digital exposure), behavioral discipline (managing patterns in movement, routine, and communication), and integrated tradecraft (human judgment applied in concert with technical means). The 2018 GRU operation against the OPCW, as reconstructed in Christopher Moede's April 2026 Small Wars Journal follow-up, is the cautionary case: four Russian officers were unmasked because small behaviors aggregated across systems (devices, travel, and network artifacts) enabled attribution. For a red team or CTI shop, signature reduction is OPSEC for your operators and your tooling; for CI and blue teams, understanding how a capable adversary reduces its own signature is how you detect actors trying to hide, and their discipline failures are your detections.
blocks.heading: Signature Reduction & Digital Force Protection

blocks.text: Managed attribution (MA) is the deliberate control of your digital fingerprint: language, time zone, operating system, browser, device characteristics, and egress IP and geolocation, so your activity blends into normal traffic and never refers back to you or your organization. A representative platform is Authentic8's Silo for Research: a cloud-based, fully isolated browser that the vendor describes as running on a fully owned managed-attribution network of 700+ in-region nodes with residential, mobile, data-center, and dark-web diversity, so an analyst can research a threat actor, monitor a dark-web forum, or build a case file without exposing their endpoint to malware and without attributing the activity to a .gov, .mil, or corporate origin. Silo is FedRAMP-authorized, and the vendor states that it captures collection activity with full audit logs that preserve chain of custody for evidence. The security value is four-fold: it protects the analyst and the sponsoring organization's intent; it isolates the endpoint from toxic content and malicious code; it maintains evidentiary integrity; and, the dual-use caution, adversaries use the very same MA tradecraft, so managed attribution is both a capability you deploy and a reason to be humble when attributing observed activity to someone else. MA is the deliberate inverse of the non-repudiation problem: one side engineers accountability, the other engineers deniability, and a mature program understands both.
blocks.heading: Managed Attribution

blocks.text: Pattern-of-life (PoL) analysis is intelligence tradecraft: building a model of a target's normal behavior over time (active hours, who they contact, where they go, their digital habits) to predict behavior, find anomalies, or surface vulnerabilities. UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) is the security-operations technology that does the same thing defensively on your own environment: it baselines normal behavior for users and for entities (and "entity" explicitly includes non-human identities such as service accounts and AI agents), then flags deviations indicative of compromise, insider activity, or a hijacked or rogue agent. The symmetry is the entire point: UTS is an adversary running pattern-of-life on your people at population scale; UEBA is you running pattern-of-life on your own users and agents to catch the anomaly first. For Agentic AI this is not a metaphor: an agent's tool-call sequences, data-egress paths, and resource access form a pattern of life, and deviation from that baseline is the rogue-agent signal this play, the Agentic Threat Hunting section of CTI for Agentic SecOps, and the Agent Containment play all rely on. The NITTF puts it plainly in its mission fact sheet: insider threat programs target anomalous behaviors, not individuals (behavior, baselined and monitored, rather than identity-based suspicion). Its Insider Threat Guide says the same at more length, that programs are designed to monitor and detect anomalous behavior, not to monitor people. (Operationally this shows up as UEBA in platforms like Microsoft Sentinel.)
blocks.heading: Pattern-of-Life Analysis vs. UEBA: The Behavioral Mirror

items.title: Harden remote hiring against fabricated personas: liveness checks in interviews, detection of reused AI-generated headshots across applicants, and awareness of real-time voice modulation.
items.text: Put a verification gate on remote hiring that the record's observed tells can trip.
bullets: Require a live, camera-on interview stage with liveness checks, since the record observes voice-changing software used during interviews.
Compare applicant headshots and identity-document photos across the applicant pool, since the record reports the same AI-generated photo reused across multiple personas.
Flag experience claims that mirror the posting language and verify them against independent references rather than the candidate's own documents.
Route every flag to a named reviewer in GRC and HR with a written decision, and feed confirmed cases to the Next-phase post-hire hunt.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Hunt for persona-fabrication indicators post-hire: resumes suspiciously aligned to posting language, AI-polished communications inconsistent with live performance, identity-document photo reuse. Route those HR-observable indicators through the insider-threat program under a documented legal basis with HR and privacy sign-off, aimed at behavior rather than individuals, and have the SOC hunt the signals it can query: remote-management or KVM-over-IP tooling on the issued laptop, sign-ins from geographies inconsistent with the claimed location, and concurrent sessions across personas.
items.text: Carry the hunt past the offer, treating fraudulent employment as the insider-risk scenario the record advises.
bullets: Frame the hunt as the record does: treat fraudulent employment and access misuse as an insider-risk scenario, watching for misuse of legitimate credentials, abnormal access patterns, and sustained low-and-slow activity.

Re-check the photos held for current staff, on identity documents and internal profiles, against each other and against past applicants, since the record reports the same AI-generated photo reused across multiple personas and names open-source image analysis such as FaceForensics++ for gauging AI-generated content.

Compare resumes on file with the postings they answered, since the record reports AI-assisted resumes tailored to specific job descriptions; close alignment is a lead to verify, not a finding on its own.

Look for a gap between written and live work: the record reports AI used to draft professional replies, translate messages, and meet day-to-day performance expectations, so written polish that live meetings do not match is a lead.
Route leads to a named owner with GRC, HR and legal involved before any employment action, and feed confirmed tells back into the Now-phase hiring gate.
items.meta: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · AI as Tradecraft, Mar 2026

items.title: Run the full NHI lifecycle on every agent: owner of record and expiry at provisioning, automatic rotation, and offboarding sweeps for residual grants and orphaned identities.
items.text: Run the list's offboarding and recertification loop against agent identities, and treat an ownerless agent as the finding.
bullets: Recertify on a set cadence exactly as the record frames it: confirm each identity is still in use, actively needed, and has a valid owner, then decommission what fails the test and assign an owner to anything found without one.

Wire agent identities into the human offboarding process: when a person departs, review every identity associated with them, decommission what is no longer required, and otherwise transfer ownership and rotate every credential that person could reach.

Hunt the three failure modes the record names: stale or dormant identities left behind by decommissioned services, orphaned identities whose owner departed with no successor, and the partially offboarded case where an administrator or developer, often not the actual owner, was exposed to the credentials and left without them being revoked.
Automate the sweep by integrating HR systems with identity and access management tooling, so departures trigger the review rather than depending on someone remembering to run it.

Audit active identities regularly to monitor ongoing usage and block misuse, pair that with automated rotation so credentials cannot quietly become long-lived between recertifications, and prove the sweep works with a check of the suite's own: seed canary identities (an ownerless agent, a key a departed administrator could still use) and time how long each survives.

items.title: Treat agent memory, retrieved context, hooks, and local config as attack surface (OWASP ASI06): enforce provenance on what enters persistent state, separate trust tiers so untrusted content cannot reach high-trust layers, and add visibility into what persists across sessions. The MemoryTrap pattern turned a routine dependency install into cross-session compromise.
items.text: Gate the write path into persistent state, scope it per principal, and verify it on read: the controls the cheat sheet actually names.
bullets: Gate the write path before anything persists: validate and sanitize data before it is stored in agent memory, and audit content for sensitive data at that point rather than trusting a later redaction pass.

Scope memory per principal: isolate it between users and sessions so one caller's context cannot surface in another's, which is the separation the posture argument asks for stated as an actual control.
Bound memory in age and size, setting expiration and size limits so a poisoned entry cannot persist indefinitely or crowd out the legitimate context around it.
Verify on read, not only on write: apply cryptographic integrity checks to long-term memory so a tampered entry is detected when it is retrieved rather than silently shaping the next plan.

Extend the same scrutiny to the surfaces the commentary names alongside memory, hooks and local configuration, on its stated reasoning that a one-time action can shape behavior across sessions, projects, and even reboots.

Make persistent state reviewable, as the suite's own addition: inventory what each agent persists across sessions (memory entries, hooks, local configuration), expose it to review, and keep a rollback path, so a poisoned entry that slipped past the write gate can still be found and rolled back.

items.title: Apply signature-reduction / managed-attribution doctrine to sanctioned offensive agents in a UTS environment: manage observability, do not assume anonymity.
items.text: Treat sanctioned offensive agents as observable by default and engineer the signature deliberately; the doctrine is the record's, the mechanics are the suite's.
bullets: Adopt the operating assumption the record describes: surveillance that is persistent, pervasive, and increasingly automated across all domains, which its author notes the Central Intelligence Agency and its partner have labeled an existential threat, a characterization the record attributes rather than independently establishes.

Inventory the signature your agents actually emit across the vector families the record names, online, electronic, visual-physical, financial, and travel, recognizing that for a software agent the online and electronic vectors carry nearly all of it: source addresses, request timing, client fingerprints, account and payment trails behind tooling.

Build the signature inventory and the egress design as the suite's own mechanics. The record frames signature reduction as the counteroffensive to this condition and says it integrates distinct but complementary disciplines across physical and digital domains, but it names no concrete techniques, so the specific controls below are this playbook's, not the record's.

Route agent traffic through managed-attribution infrastructure with capabilities of the kind the tooling record asserts: fully isolated cloud-based browsing where activity executes remotely, egress through in-region nodes with selectable connection type, and customizable browser, device, language, and geolocation settings.

Keep attribution to the analyst even while attribution to the organization is suppressed: the same record asserts every action is attributed to an analyst and recorded with audit trails, which is what separates managed attribution from unaccountable anonymity.
Gate each engagement: named approver, defined scope and duration, and a signature review before and after, so observability is managed as a decision rather than assumed away.

Deconflict before egress, using the kill switch and deconfliction channel set up in the Red Team play's continuous-emulation action: register each sanctioned agent's egress identifiers (source ranges, a header or user-agent marker, an operating window) with the SOC, so an agent with a reduced signature can still be told from an adversary and stopped.

items.title: Use pattern-of-life baselining (the tradecraft mirror of UEBA) to flag agents deviating from normal behavior.
items.text: Extend the per-agent baselines the Agent Incident Response play sets up at Now into full pattern-of-life profiles and alert on deviation, a suite-authored control, since the doctrine record carries no baselining method.
bullets: Baseline per agent rather than per fleet: normal hours and cadence, the tools it calls and in what order, the data and systems it reaches, its typical volumes, and its usual egress destinations, fed from the sources that carry them: the tool-call audit log of the agent runtime or gateway, the identity provider's sign-in and token-issuance logs for the agent's identity, and the egress logs of the firewall or proxy.

Own the method honestly: the surveillance-doctrine record in canon supplies the operating condition this action borrows its language from, but contains no pattern-of-life analysis and no baselining technique, so the feature set, thresholds, and alerting design here are entirely the suite's.

Alert on deviation from the agent's own baseline rather than on a global rule, since an agent's ordinary behavior is narrow enough that its deviations are informative in a way a human user's rarely are.
Route alerts to a named owner with a defined response, and treat a baseline that never fires as a tuning problem to investigate rather than evidence of good behavior.

Keep the program aimed at behavior, not persons: the insider-threat standards body in canon was established under Executive Order 13587 under the joint leadership of the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence, and its mission is deterring, detecting, and mitigating insider threats, with its awareness guidance directed at recognizing and reporting anomalous activity to enable early intervention.

Govern agents as non-human identities, so a behavioral baseline sits alongside identity and access controls rather than substituting for either. The zero-trust vendor paper carried in canon is the adjacent reference for that framing: it treats each agent as a non-human identity and lists behavioral baselining against expected patterns of agent activity among its real-time controls.
Re-baseline on change: a new tool, a widened data scope, or a model upgrade invalidates the profile, and a stale baseline produces confident silence.

blocks.label: Insider-Risk Principle
blocks.text: Give every agent an identity, an owner, least-privilege scope, and continuous monitoring: exactly as you would a privileged human insider. An ungoverned agent isn't a productivity tool; it's an unaccountable super-user and a breach waiting to be automated.

plays.name: Agent Containment
plays.title: Agent Containment Engineering
plays.subtitle: Capping an agent's blast radius: the deterministic boundaries that must come first
plays.summary: Model defenses are never 100%, so sandboxes, egress controls and circuit breakers cap an agent's blast radius first.

outline.title: The Industry Converges on the Same Answer
The Five Eyes Make It Official: Containment Over Efficiency
Patch Smarter, Not Harder: Risk-Based Deadlines Become Federal Policy
Patch, Then Prove It: Forensic Triage Becomes Part of Remediation
The Market Builds What the Directive Mandates: Closed-Loop Exposure Management
Contain at the Environment Layer First
Human-in-the-Loop Is Not a Reliable Control

blocks.text: Anthropic's own red team ran a controlled exercise in February 2026: a phished employee pasted a routine-looking prompt that quietly told Claude Code to read ~/.aws/credentials, encode them, and POST them to an external endpoint. Across 25 runs, the exfiltration succeeded 24 times, and no classifier caught it, because the instruction came from the trusted user. The lesson: probabilistic model defenses are never 100%, so hard, deterministic environment boundaries (sandboxes, VMs, egress controls) must come first. This is the engineering counterpart to the Lethal Trifecta.
blocks.heading: Why Containment Comes Before Cleverness

blocks.text: This isn't just one lab's doctrine. Google's Security Operations agents launch (June 2026) pairs its AI Threat Defense loop (Prepare → Scan/Prioritize → Remediate → Monitor) with autonomous containment aimed squarely at the threats this play exists for, "code you do not own or cannot patch", and grounds it in M-Trends 2026's starkest number: mean time-to-exploit has dropped to an estimated minus seven days, meaning exploitation now frequently precedes the patch's existence. That is the same conclusion the Glasswing patching-deficit math forces (see Supply-Chain Counter-Threat): when remediation structurally cannot keep pace with discovery, pre-staged deterministic containment (egress cutoff, identity revocation, isolation) stops being a fallback and becomes the primary control. When the frontier labs and the major security platforms independently land on contain-first, treat it as the industry's revealed posture, not a vendor pitch.
blocks.heading: The Industry Converges on the Same Answer

blocks.text: In May 2026 the containment-first thesis acquired a six-agency signature. "Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services", co-authored by ASD's ACSC, CISA, NSA, and the Canadian, New Zealand, and UK cyber centers, is the first joint Five Eyes guidance in this index written specifically for Agentic AI, and its bottom line is this play's: until security standards and evaluation methods mature, plan for unexpected behavior and prioritize resilience, reversibility, and risk containment over efficiency. It maps five risk categories (privilege, design and configuration, behavioral, structural, and accountability), and its prescriptions read like a containment checklist: never grant agents broad or unrestricted access, especially to sensitive data or critical systems; start with low-risk, non-sensitive use cases and earn expansion; fold Agentic AI into the existing security model rather than running it as a side experiment; and anchor every agent to a verified, cryptographically backed identity with short-lived credentials. Two candors make the document more useful, not less: the authoring agencies concede that current evaluation methods are immature and only partially capture real deployment conditions, and they note that for some repetitive tasks the lower-risk answer is eliminating the low-value process, not agentifying it. When six national security agencies coordinate to say contain first, the burden of proof has officially shifted to whoever wants to move fast.
blocks.heading: The Five Eyes Make It Official: Containment Over Efficiency

blocks.text: Six weeks after the Five Eyes guidance, the containment logic became binding U.S. policy. CISA's BOD 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk" (Jun 2026), supersedes the prior federal remediation directives and orders civilian agencies to triage every vulnerability across four criteria: asset exposure, KEV status, exploit automatability, and post-exploitation technical impact, with a three-day remediation class plus forensic triage for the worst combinations, fixed-day classes of 3, 14, and 60 days in between, and fix on system upgrade for the lowest risk. The math behind it is this play's: CISA's initial analysis at one large civilian agency found only 1% of vulnerability instances land in the three-day class while more than 60% can wait for the next system upgrade, and Verizon's 2026 DBIR found just 26% of KEV-catalog vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025. The stated rationale is AI on both sides of the ledger: models help researchers and adversaries find flaws faster, narrowing the window between patch release and exploitation. And the telling criterion is exploit automatability: a formal acknowledgment that exploitation now scales at machine speed while patching does not, so the deadlines get redesigned around that reality. BODs bind federal civilian agencies, not DoW, but they are the bellwether DoW policy tracks, and the arc on this play is now complete: the frontier labs said contain first, the Five Eyes made it official, and the U.S. government wrote it into deadlines.
blocks.heading: Patch Smarter, Not Harder: Risk-Based Deadlines Become Federal Policy

blocks.text: The directive's companion implementation guidance, published alongside it and updated by CISA on a rolling basis, quietly fuses vulnerability management with incident response. In the three-day class with forensic triage, patching alone no longer closes the ticket: the "& forensic triage" notation in the directive's remediation table means the agency must also examine the asset to determine whether an adversary beat the patch there. The guidance lays out the baseline triage arc (rapidly scope the vulnerability notification, preserve and collect evidence, apply critical patching and stabilization, contain and control, run triage analysis, then decide whether to escalate) and sets an evidentiary standard of who, what, where, and when: its worked example reads like a SOC shift log, down to which account logged into which machine at which timestamp and immediately launched which tool, with the SOC confirming the user was not active. Every triage produces a written report that serves as the agency record and drives the fork: escalate to full incident response in coordination with CISA's incident-reporting system, or stand down to heightened monitoring, completed remediation, and a post-incident improvement loop. KEV catalog entries can carry CVE-specific triage steps that override the baseline. The doctrine underneath is this suite's assume-compromise thesis written into patching procedure: at machine-speed exploitation the question is never just whether the asset is patched, but whether the flaw was already used, the same telemetry-first investigative rhythm the Agent Incident Response play teaches, now a federal requirement.
blocks.heading: Patch, Then Prove It: Forensic Triage Becomes Part of Remediation

blocks.text: Even before BOD 26-04 made risk-based, machine-speed remediation federal policy, the machinery for it was on the shelf and the problem statement was public. NIST reports CVE submissions increased 263% between 2020 and 2025, with the first three months of 2026 nearly one-third higher than a year earlier, and IBM X-Force argues that frontier AI compresses vulnerability discovery from weeks into hours, rewriting the economics of every step downstream. No organization closes that gap with human-led patch cycles, so periodic patching gives way to continuous threat exposure management (CTEM; see AI Fluency). The architecture is a closed loop. The front half finds and fixes: Google DeepMind reports that CodeMender (see Tools & Tech Stack) has upstreamed 72 security fixes to open-source projects, validating its patches with an LLM-based critique tool, and that all its patches are reviewed by human researchers before submission. The execution half deploys: Palantir's Apollo documentation describes orchestrating software upgrades and changes across connected and disconnected, air-gapped environments, scanning releases for vulnerabilities, and recalling bad releases so affected environments move off them. Read the pattern, not the product: it is the BOD 26-04 arc rendered as commercial machinery (risk-prioritized findings, agentic remediation, proof, deployment), with the human gate exactly where Human in Command puts it (adjudication, not execution), and the air-gapped reach matters for the federal and OT estates this playbook serves. These are first-party vendor claims; treat capability figures accordingly.
blocks.heading: The Market Builds What the Directive Mandates: Closed-Loop Exposure Management

blocks.text: "While agents may be a new category of software, their system-level interactions are not. They still read files, open sockets, and spawn processes." That reframing is the whole game: treat agent containment as conventional isolation engineering, not AI mysticism. Anthropic tailors the boundary to the user's expertise: an ephemeral gVisor container for claude.ai (server-side, per-session filesystem, no host access), a human-in-the-loop OS sandbox for Claude Code (reads allowed, writes confined, network denied by default), and a sealed local VM for Claude Cowork (credentials stay in the host keychain since non-technical users can't vet a bash command).
blocks.heading: Contain at the Environment Layer First

blocks.text: A critical finding for any Agentic SecOps design: Anthropic reports that users approve 97% of Claude Code permission prompts (August 2026; its March and May 2026 posts gave roughly 93%). Approval fatigue makes human-in-the-loop an accountability transfer, not a control, and it degrades further in multi-agent systems. Don't architect your SOC's agentic guardrails around analysts clicking "approve." Build deterministic boundaries that hold regardless of what a fatigued human waves through.
blocks.heading: Human-in-the-Loop Is Not a Reliable Control

items.label: Anthropic: Auto Mode Is Now the Default in Claude Code (Aug 2026)

blocks.text: Two hard lessons for SecOps teams. First, agent isolation creates a monitoring gap: host EDR cannot see inside the sandbox, leaving you with after-the-fact OTLP logs instead of live telemetry. Plan your detection coverage accordingly. Second, "the weakest layer is the one you built yourself." In Anthropic's case the battle-tested components (gVisor, seccomp, vendor hypervisors) held; the piece that broke, twice, was their own custom egress proxy. Favor proven isolation primitives over bespoke security code. RAITE 2026 made the monitoring gap concrete (see Case Studies; as reported by the participating red team): a red team's malicious model swap, concealed inside an MCP package, ran underneath the blue team's observability platform. Defenders saw the tool execute but stayed blind to the model substitution beneath it.
blocks.heading: The Monitoring Gap & 'Weakest Layer'

blocks.text: If a manual kill-switch is the control an operator reaches for, a circuit breaker is the one that trips on its own, and given that users approve 97% of Claude Code permission prompts (Anthropic, August 2026), the automatic version is what actually holds. A circuit breaker is a deterministic tripwire on agent behavior: define thresholds for the actions that matter, and when an agent crosses one, the control halts it automatically, reverts to manual mode, and escalates to a human, no approval click required. The canonical example: if an agent attempts more than X account revocations (or firewall changes, or file deletions) in Y minutes, trip the breaker rather than letting it run. The design discipline is to set these on rate, scope, and blast-radius-relevant actions, not on the model's stated intent, so the limit holds even when the agent has been manipulated or is simply wrong. Circuit breakers pair directly with the autonomy dial in Purple Teaming: every notch you turn autonomy up should be matched by tighter, well-tested breakers, because they're the backstop that makes higher autonomy survivable. They sit alongside the other fast-containment controls: kill-switch, identity revocation, egress cutoff, sandbox isolation, as the automatic tier of the same defense.
blocks.heading: Circuit Breakers: Automatic, Threshold-Triggered Halts

blocks.alt: Schematic of containment bounding a compromised agent blast radius

items.title: Pre-stage compensating controls for unpatchable windows: egress cutoff, identity revocation, sandbox isolation, as pre-planned procedures, not reactive improvisation.
items.text: Pre-plan the window rather than improvising it: the record names the controls and the framework they sit in.
bullets: Pre-write the answer to the record's own framing question, what compensating controls can be deployed immediately to reduce exposure during the patching window, because it states plainly that this requires pre-planned response procedures rather than reactive improvisation.

Stage the three controls the record actually prescribes for operators who cannot patch immediately: network segmentation to isolate affected systems, least-privilege access controls to reduce lateral-movement opportunity, and comprehensive logging to detect exploitation attempts.
