The headline's egress cutoff, identity revocation, and sandbox isolation are this suite's agent-layer instances of the same containment logic rather than the record's own list, so stage them alongside and record which set each staged control belongs to.

Anchor them in zero trust, which the record names as the foundational compensating-control framework for the window between vulnerability disclosure and patch deployment, so the staged controls are an instance of an existing architecture rather than a bolt-on.

Rehearse the deployment path so the controls can actually land inside the window, and have the red team play a hijacked agent against them to time the cutoff: an unpracticed segmentation change is a proposal, not a compensating control.

Feed the window into detection: review detection rules for the vulnerability classes most frequently documented, on the record's reasoning that a disclosure in one component is a signal to audit the same pattern across related codebases.

items.title: For OT/ICS assets on quarter-to-year patch cycles, define per-system exposure-reduction playbooks: the operative question is what you deploy now, not how fast you patch.
items.text: Write the exposure-reduction plan per system for the slow-cycle estate the record names, and measure control deployment alongside patch speed.
bullets: Scope the estate using the record's own categories: industrial control systems, medical devices, and communications infrastructure, in the hands of critical infrastructure operators, and inventory which of them cannot absorb a patch inside the exposure window.
Write one exposure-reduction plan per system rather than one for the estate, since the compensating controls that fit a protocol gateway are not the ones that fit a bedside device.

Populate each plan from the controls the record prescribes for the unpatchable case: segmentation, least-privilege access, and logging sufficient to detect exploitation attempts, and record who deploys each one and how long it takes.

Hold both halves of the record's framing: not solely how quickly the organization can patch, but equally what compensating controls it can deploy immediately to reduce exposure during the patching window, and track time-to-compensating-control alongside time-to-patch.

Over the next three to six months, establish the direct communication channels with the maintainers of your most critical open-source dependencies that the record files under its short-term mitigations, using private security advisory mechanisms; for the vendor-supplied systems that make up most of this estate, the equivalent is subscribing to each supplier's product security incident response team (PSIRT) advisories and the sector's advisory channels, with pre-disclosure notice negotiated for critical suppliers, so a coordinated disclosure reaches the operator before the public announcement does.

items.title: Baseline every agent deployment against the Five Eyes 'Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services' guidance: audit what each agent can reach (least privilege), anchor agents to verified short-lived credentials, and adopt its containment-over-efficiency defaults.
items.text: Run the joint guidance as a deployment baseline: registry, entitlements, ephemeral credentials, internal-process logging.
bullets: Give every agent its own identity as the guidance words it, a distinct principal with a cryptographically anchored identity holding its own unique keys or certificates, and bind it in a trusted registry of identities and authorized roles, reconciling that registry against the live set of agents and denying any agent or key it does not carry.

Audit reach as entitlement, not intent: limit entitlements to the exact resources, operations and timeframes needed, scope privilege dynamically for sub-tasks, and revoke elevated rights immediately when the sub-task finishes. The guidance is explicit that agents are never granted broad or unrestricted access, especially to sensitive data or critical systems.

Replace static, long-lived secrets with ephemeral credentials that expire when the job is complete, require just-in-time credentials for high-impact or privileged actions, and authenticate every agent-to-agent and agent-to-service call with mutual TLS so actions are non-repudiable.

Log the inside of the agent, not just its edges: monitor all agent operations including internal processes, record which tools ran and what they retrieved, restrict tool use to an approved allow list, and audit regularly for drift, impersonation or misconfiguration.

Set the guidance's default posture where the trade-off is decided: prioritize resilience, reversibility and risk containment over efficiency gains, keep the human control points in the workflow, live monitoring and interruption, mandatory approval for decision-making steps, auditing and reversibility afterwards, and keep the approval threshold a decision for designers and operators, never delegated to the agent.
items.meta: Five Eyes · Careful Adoption of Agentic AI, May 2026

items.title: Adopt BOD 26-04's four-criteria triage for your own vulnerability program even outside the Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB): asset exposure, KEV status, exploit automatability, post-exploitation impact, with a three-day class plus forensic triage for the worst, fixed-day classes of 3, 14, and 60 days in between, and fix on system upgrade for the lowest.
items.text: Stand up the four-criteria triage as the program's decision layer, with the forensic-triage fork wired behind it.
bullets: Name the feed behind each criterion first (the asset inventory or attack-surface data for exposure, the KEV catalog for KEV status, exploit-availability and threat-intelligence feeds for automation, vulnerability enrichment data rating total or partial control for technical impact), then score every incoming vulnerability across the directive's four criteria as CISA names them: Asset Exposure, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Status, Exploit Automation, and Technical Impact, and let that composite set the remediation clock; the directive supersedes BOD 19-02 and BOD 22-01 with these defined timelines.

Treat the three-day class marked for forensic triage as a compromise-assessment trigger, not just a patch deadline: the companion guidance expects a check for whether the system was compromised before the patch landed, and asks that systems not be altered or remediated before evidence is collected where possible, because patching may jeopardize the artifacts.

Adopt the guidance's six forensic-triage steps as the runbook spine: scoping, evidence preservation and collection, critical patching and stabilization, containment and control, triage analysis, escalation decision, and close with a written triage report in who/what/where/when terms that serves as the record and drives the escalate-to-IR-or-stand-down call.

Use deferral deliberately: reserve it for the lowest-risk findings, which the directive routes to the fix-on-system-upgrade class, so effort concentrates where the four criteria put the risk; CISA strongly encourages partners beyond the FCEB to adopt the same posture.
Before running the baseline steps, check the KEV entry itself: where the catalog carries CVE-specific triage steps, those take precedence.

items.title: Prototype a closed-loop exposure-management pattern (BOD 26-04's four criteria prioritize findings, agents draft remediations, a human adjudicates, deployment automates with rollback), and benchmark build-vs-buy against a commercial execution layer such as Palantir Apollo.
items.text: Prototype the closed loop as a four-stage reference pattern, with the prioritization criteria named and the human adjudication supplied by this suite.
bullets: Prioritize with the four criteria the federal directive names: asset exposure, known-exploited status, exploit automatability, and post-exploitation impact, noting the directive binds federal civilian agencies and is adopted here as a model rather than an obligation.

Split the loop into two halves: a sensing and prioritizing half that applies the directive's criteria to findings, and an execution half that deploys fixes, which Apollo's documentation describes as orchestrating software upgrades and changes across connected and disconnected, air-gapped environments.

Require rollback as a property of the execution half: Apollo's documentation describes recalls that block a bad release from further roll-out and move affected environments onto non-recalled releases; in a closed loop the reversal path is what makes automated deployment survivable.

Insert the human adjudication step deliberately: Google DeepMind reports that all CodeMender patches are reviewed by human researchers before they are submitted upstream, and the gate between a drafted remediation and its deployment is a control you add, not one an execution platform supplies.

Frame the destination as continuous exposure management rather than a patch calendar, and carry the context figure from its primary source: NIST reports CVE submissions increased 263 percent between 2020 and 2025, with the first three months of 2026 nearly one-third higher than a year earlier.

Benchmark build-versus-buy against the pattern, not the products: vendor documentation describes capability rather than measured outcomes, so treat it as a reference architecture to compare your own sense-prioritize-draft-adjudicate-deploy-rollback chain against.

items.title: Require agents to surface the full effect of a setup or recovery command before running it, including the contents of any script it invokes and anything that script fetches at runtime (DNS, HTTP, package hooks), not just the command string. A pre-authorized step is not a safe step.
items.text: Make the agent show what a setup command actually does, including what it fetches at runtime: the record's own recommendation, from an attack that hid the payload outside the repo.
bullets: Require the disclosure the record itself calls for: agents need to surface what a setup command will actually run, including the contents of any script it invokes and anything that script fetches at runtime.

Understand why the command string is not enough: in the record's case the malicious instruction was injected at runtime, pulled from DNS, after the agent had already trusted everything else, so nothing in the cloned repository ever contained the payload.

Treat scanner and review coverage as no assurance for this class: the record's point is that the payload which eventually executes was never part of the repository, so code review and dependency scanning had nothing to find.

Break the specific chain the record documents: the agent reads the files and installs requirements, hits an error whose message names a fix, runs that documented fix as routine error recovery, and the setup script then executes a configuration string retrieved from a DNS record, opening a reverse shell to attacker infrastructure.

Distrust pre-authorization by policy, which is this action's point: a step being documented, expected, or previously approved is what made the fix run unexamined, so surfacing must happen at execution time rather than at approval time.

Scope the rule to every agent with authorized shell access, since the record's framing is that agentic coding tools already have access to everything needed: private data, environment variables, credentials, and API keys.

items.title: Treat setup instructions and scripts in unfamiliar repos as untrusted code regardless of what the AI tool recommends. Run agent-driven first-time setup in a sandbox with no standing secrets and egress control, so a fetched payload lands in a throwaway shell with nothing to steal.
items.text: Distrust unfamiliar setup instructions as the record advises, and run first-time setup where a fetched payload lands on nothing. The containment half is sourced elsewhere.
bullets: Take the record's own instruction first: treat setup instructions and scripts in unfamiliar repositories as untrusted code, regardless of whether an AI tool recommended running them.

Note where the rest of this action comes from. The record documents the attack and the disclosure requirement but does not itself prescribe sandboxing, egress control, or removing standing credentials: that containment posture is the suite's, supported by the containment retrospective in canon whose sandboxes, egress controls, and blast-radius bounding are the named mechanisms.

Run agent-driven first-time setup in a disposable environment, so that the reverse shell the record demonstrates lands in a throwaway context rather than on a developer workstation holding live credentials.

Remove standing secrets from that environment rather than scoping them down, because the record's attack path reaches environment variables, credentials, and API keys directly once shell access is obtained.

Apply egress control to the setup environment specifically, since the payload in the record arrived over a name-resolution lookup rather than an obvious download: a default-deny posture with an explicit allowlist for both name resolution and destinations is what makes a runtime fetch fail closed; a web-proxy allowlist alone leaves DNS lookups open.

Keep the rule class-level rather than repository-specific: the exposure follows from an agent having authorized shell access at all, so the sandbox is a property of how first-time setup is run, not a judgment about a particular project.

blocks.label: Containment Principle
blocks.text: Three things to defend: the model, its environment, and external content. Bound the blast radius at the environment layer with deterministic controls so high-utility agentic capabilities can ship safely. (Source: "How we contain Claude across products," Anthropic, May 2026; analysis via The Weather Report, an AI security newsletter.)

plays.name: Agent Incident Response
plays.title: Agent Incident Response
plays.subtitle: When the agent is the incident: detecting, containing, and recovering from agentic failures
plays.summary: When the agent itself is the incident: detect, investigate, contain, preserve, recover and learn, with a runbook for your own agents.

outline.title: Detect: Know When an Agent Goes Wrong
Investigate: Telemetry Before You Need It (Scope → Context → Signal)
Contain: Stop the Blast Radius Fast
Preserve, Rotate, Re-Certify: The Three Steps Teams Skip
Learn: Feed It Back Into the Loop

blocks.text: Most incident-response plans assume a human or external attacker. Agentic AI adds a new category: the agent itself becomes the incident, prompt-injected into harmful action, manipulated by a trusted user, drifting out of scope, or simply making a high-consequence mistake at machine speed. Because agents act faster and more broadly than humans, an agentic incident can escalate before anyone notices. A SOC adopting Agentic AI needs an IR runbook for its own agents, not just for the threats they hunt. The good news: the classic IR lifecycle still applies. It just needs adapting.
blocks.heading: A New Class of Incident

blocks.text: Detection for agent incidents leans on the monitoring and logging already in the stack: an agent reaching unexpected destinations (egress anomaly), escalating its own privileges, looping abnormally, consuming runaway tokens/compute, or taking actions outside its sanctioned scope. Agent 365-style control planes and the non-human-insider monitoring from the Agentic Insider Risk play are the sensors here. The key design choice is observability: every agent step, tool call, and decision should be traced, because you can't investigate what you didn't log.
blocks.heading: Detect: Know When an Agent Goes Wrong

blocks.text: Microsoft's "See What Happened" AI Investigation Playbook (AeGIS, June 2026) is the first vendor-published, practitioner-grade answer this play has found to a question it raises: when something goes wrong with or through an AI system, how do you actually reconstruct what happened? Its discipline transfers beyond the Microsoft stack. First, the telemetry has to exist before the incident: AI interaction logging (Purview audit events, the Sentinel Copilot connector, Defender integration in Microsoft's case) is a configuration step, and an investigation without it is archaeology without a site. Second, the investigation runs a repeatable scope → context → signal sequence: establish who interacted with the AI and when, then determine what it touched (the resources it accessed are the blast radius), then evaluate detection signals (jailbreak flags, credential-exposure alerts, volume anomalies) inside that chain of activity rather than as isolated alerts. Third, audit telemetry is metadata-first: it tells you who, when, and which resources, but not the prompt and response text. Content-level review is a deliberate, permissioned pivot (eDiscovery / DSPM-style tooling), so plan the legal coordination in advance. The playbook's sharper edges generalize too: correlate AI credential-exposure alerts with follow-on key-listing or deployment operations in the same window (the exposure-to-exploitation pattern), and inventory your agents for risk surfaces, agents with external tool/MCP configurations, and agents that accept interactions with no user authentication, whose activity can never be cleanly attributed (the non-repudiation problem from Agentic Insider Risk, found in the wild).
blocks.heading: Investigate: Telemetry Before You Need It (Scope → Context → Signal)

blocks.text: Containment is where agentic IR differs most from traditional IR: the response must be as fast as the agent, so a reversible pause comes first and the scope, context and signal work above runs against a halted agent. This is the operational payoff of the containment architecture: a kill-switch to halt the agent immediately, the ability to revoke its identity (Entra Agent ID) so it can obtain no new tokens, paired with a tool-gateway deny and short token lifetimes because tokens already issued keep working until they expire unless the resource enforces continuous access evaluation, egress cutoff to block exfiltration mid-flight, and sandbox isolation so the damage can't spread. Pre-wiring these controls before an incident is what makes containment a matter of seconds, not a scramble.
blocks.heading: Contain: Stop the Blast Radius Fast

blocks.text: Three runbook steps separate a clean agentic IR from a messy one, and all three are routinely skipped. Preserve before you tear down: capture the agent's full transcript, tool-call log, memory state, and OTLP traces before killing the sandbox. Agent isolation creates a forensic gap (host EDR can't see inside), so if you don't snapshot the evidence at containment time, it's gone, and with it your answer to the counterintelligence question of what actually happened (see Agentic Insider Risk on non-repudiation). Rotate the blast radius: treat every credential, token, and secret the agent could reach as compromised, not just the ones you can prove it used, and rotate them as a set; this is why the credential-blast-radius map belongs in the runbook before the incident, not reconstructed during it (NIST's incident-response guidance, SP 800-61r3, frames exactly this preparation-first posture). Re-certify before return-to-duty: an agent that caused an incident doesn't resume production. It re-earns it by passing its eval regression suite (see Blue Team's continuous-evaluation discipline) with the incident added as a permanent test case. Skipping that last gate is how the same failure ships twice.
blocks.heading: Preserve, Rotate, Re-Certify: The Three Steps Teams Skip

blocks.text: Once contained, eradicate the root cause (revoke the poisoned input source, patch the vulnerable scaffolding, correct the manipulated memory or RAG content) and recover safely: roll back any unauthorized changes the agent made, restore from known-good state, and validate before re-enabling. Agentic actions should be reversible by design: a rule promoted, a config changed, or a ticket actioned by an agent needs an audit trail and a rollback path, which is exactly what the governance logging provides.
blocks.heading: Eradicate & Recover: Undo and Restore

blocks.text: The post-incident review closes the loop: what failed, what control would have caught it sooner, and how to prevent recurrence. In an agentic program this feeds directly back into the purple loop and governance: a new detection for the failure mode, a tightened guardrail or egress rule, an updated acceptable-use boundary, or a scope reduction. An agent incident handled well doesn't just get resolved; it permanently raises the safety baseline, the same way a successful threat hunt becomes a durable detection.
blocks.heading: Learn: Feed It Back Into the Loop

items.title: Replace freeform closure comments with a structured close artifact on every analyst-closed incident: what inputs were weighed, what precedent was cited, what was ruled out and why, and who or what made the call. The outcome already survives as the incident state; this captures the reasoning before it evaporates. Needs no new platform: a comment template or SOAR variable is enough to start.
items.text: Replace freeform closure text with the structured close the record specifies, and start with one repeatable trace rather than a platform.
bullets: Convert incident closure to structured fields, which is the record's own prescription: every analyst-closed incident records what was weighed, what was ruled out, and what precedent was cited, structured fields, not freeform comments.

Add the attribution field explicitly, who or what made the call, since the record's trace schema asks that question directly and an agent-assisted close needs the human-or-agent distinction preserved.

Capture the negative decision above all: the record calls the negative decision trace the most absent artifact in security operations, because a dismissal or no-finding closure keeps the outcome and loses the reasoning.

Time the capture to the close itself, when the decision context still exists; the outcome already survives as the incident state, so what the close artifact adds is the reasoning the record says is otherwise gone minutes later.

Start small on the record's own terms: it states you do not need the full graph to start, only one repeatable trace that survives the close and a place to put it that someone other than the original analyst can find. The specific starting mechanisms this action suggests, a comment template or a SOAR variable, are the record's own examples of how to capture that first trace.
Design the field set so it can later be read as a query rather than a document, which is what allows the same closes to become the precedent corpus a retrieval step draws on.

items.title: Write agent-specific IR runbooks: the agent itself can be the incident, and containment must move at agent speed.
items.text: Base agent procedures on the incident-response policy and plan, and rehearse them: containment is the part that must move at agent speed.
bullets: Base the agent procedures on the incident-response policy and plan as the guidance directs, so they inherit an agreed authority to act rather than inventing one mid-incident.

Organize them against the life-cycle model the organization has actually adopted; where that is the framework's proposed function-based model, the preparation work sits in the govern, identify, and protect functions, while detect, respond, and recover carry the incident itself.

Write containment first and make it executable at machine speed, taking the record's framing that containment prevents the expansion of an incident and that most incidents require some form of it: for an agent that means stopping its loop first, then revoking its credentials and cutting its tool access, and then rotating every credential, token, and secret the agent could reach, as a set, from a blast-radius map prepared before the incident.

Preserve before you eradicate: capture the agent's full transcript, tool-call log, memory state, and traces at containment time, then follow containment with eradication that assumes persistence. The guidance names eliminating persistence mechanisms and entry points, which for an agent estate means poisoned memory, retained context, and configuration the agent can still read.
Exercise the procedures periodically to verify their accuracy. The record also notes they help train new personnel. And treat an unexercised procedure as an assumption rather than a capability.

items.title: Instrument detection for agent-gone-wrong signals: egress anomalies, unexpected privilege escalation, off-pattern tool use, abnormal looping, and runaway token or compute consumption.
items.text: Instrument the gone-wrong signals as first-class detections: the telemetry and the anomaly and privilege primitives exist in the record; the signal list is the suite's.
bullets: Instrument egress-anomaly detection against a per-agent baseline of normal destinations and volumes; the AeGIS playbook supplies the telemetry foundation and usage-volume anomaly heuristics but no egress telemetry, so source this signal from the egress proxy, firewall and DNS logs of the agent's sandbox or network segment, and treat MITRE ATLAS's Exfiltration column as the objective this signal watches for.

Detect unexpected privilege escalation as a standing signal expressed in the record's Sentinel analytic-rule format; the AeGIS playbook does not ship a dedicated privilege-escalation rule but tags its jailbreak-detection rules with the PrivilegeEscalation tactic, so the tactic is where this suite-chosen signal fits rather than a ready-made detection. Source the signal from the identity provider's audit log (role assignments, permission grants and token scope changes on agent identities) and from cloud IAM policy-change events, which is where an agent's permission changes are recorded.

Flag off-pattern tool use, an agent invoking tools or reaching resources outside its established task profile, using the record's agent-inventory surface, which enumerates agents by their configured tools, as the baseline of what on-pattern means.

Set loop and consumption thresholds from platform metering: flag an agent that repeats the same tool call or plan step past a set count, or whose token or compute use per task or per hour breaks its baseline. The AeGIS playbook's A4 volume heuristic, an hourly count of Copilot events per user checked against a threshold you tune to your own baseline, is the record's model for this signal.

Wire the five signals into the same correlation surface the playbook uses, routing audit and connector telemetry into the SIEM so a gone-wrong agent shows as one correlated pattern rather than five unlinked alerts.

Own the baselines: these thresholds drift as agents change scope, so name who re-baselines them. The signal list here is the suite's operational choice, with the record providing the telemetry, the anomaly heuristics, and the privilege-escalation and inventory primitives.

Validate each signal in the purple loop: on a fixed cadence drive a sanctioned test agent through a scripted egress anomaly, a privilege grab, an off-profile tool call and a runaway loop that spikes token use, and report detection rate, time-to-detect and time-to-contain per signal.

items.title: Enable AI-investigation telemetry before you need it: AI interaction audit logging, the SIEM's AI connectors, and agent-inventory risk queries, and adopt the scope → context → signal investigation sequence.
items.text: Stand the telemetry up before an incident and run the record's own A1→A2→A3 sequence: scope, then context, then signal.
bullets: Enable the telemetry foundation the playbook says to complete before any investigation: Purview Unified Audit Logging, the Defender XDR and Defender for Cloud Apps integration, and the Sentinel Copilot data connector, so AI interaction audit logging and the SIEM's AI connectors exist ahead of the incident rather than during it.

Adopt the playbook's investigation sequence as its own sections order it: A1 identify activity scope (who, when, where), A2 determine what the assistant touched (resources and context), then A3 flag jailbreak and prompt-injection signals. Scope, then context, then signal.

Stand up the agent-inventory risk queries the record ships: list active agents, flag agents with a configured MCP tool as a risk surface, and find agents with no user authentication configured, so the inventory of what could go wrong is queryable before it does.

Load the record's Sentinel analytic rules covering both established and preview agentic threat signals after streaming Defender for Cloud alerts into Sentinel, which the rule pack states it assumes, so the connectors carry detections rather than raw log flow.

Keep content-level review as a later, gated step the way the playbook does: its A6 pivots from audit metadata to content via eDiscovery and DSPM for AI, so scoping happens on metadata first and content access is deliberate.
items.meta: Microsoft AeGIS · AI Investigation Playbook, Jun 2026

items.title: Tabletop the storm, not the incident: exercise multiple simultaneous high-severity incidents landing in the same week, with critical-incident playbooks pre-written and remediation automated as far as possible.
items.text: Exercise the pile-up the briefing names, several severe incidents in one week, and pre-write what the exercise proves you lack.
bullets: Run the exercise the briefing prescribes in its own words: tabletop exercises for multiple simultaneous high-severity incidents occurring within the same week.

Staff the exercise for contention, because the failure the storm surfaces is not technical but allocative: two critical incidents competing for one responder pool, one approval chain, and one change window.
Pre-write the critical-incident playbooks the scenario will demand, so the exercise tests the decisions rather than the drafting, and automate remediation as far as the estate allows.

Sequence the follow-up work on the briefing's own horizons: actions that start this week, others over the next 45 days and the next 12 months, so the exercise output becomes a dated plan with owners rather than a list of concerns.
Re-run against the risk register the briefing supplies rather than against last year's scenario set, and refresh the scenarios as its own risk list moves.

items.title: Gate post-incident return-to-duty on the agent's eval regression suite, with the incident added as a permanent test case: an agent that caused an incident re-earns production, it doesn't resume it.
items.text: Make return to production a verified step, not a default: the record already recommends checking restored assets before production use.
bullets: Hold the agent out of production until the recovery subcategory's own gate is met: check restored assets for indicators of compromise and remediate the root causes of the incident before production use, verifying the correctness and adequacy of the restoration actions first.

Find the root cause before writing the test: the response guidance recommends analyzing the incident to find the underlying or systemic root causes, and a regression test written against a symptom re-admits the same agent.

Turn the incident into a permanent case in the agent's eval suite, run on the open eval harness Engineering adopts in the Red Team play; where an agent has no suite yet, the incident case is its first entry and the gate is that case passing plus the recovery checks in step 1. This is the improvement path the record describes: improvements identified from the execution of operational processes, procedures, and activities, including identifying tactics, techniques, and procedures not currently being blocked by safeguards or flagged by detection technologies.

Confirm the return rather than assume it: validate that essential services are restored in the appropriate order, confirm restoration with the system owners, and monitor the performance of restored systems to verify the restoration was adequate.

Close with the after-action report the record recommends, documenting the incident, the response and recovery actions taken, and the lessons learned, and note its guidance that lessons should often be shared as soon as they are identified rather than delayed until after recovery concludes.

items.title: Close the loop automatically: every agent incident root cause opens a purple-loop item that produces a detection, a validation test and a regression case, with repeat-incident rate as the metric.
items.text: Automate the post-incident Learn step, so every root cause becomes tracked work with three outputs and one metric instead of waiting on a review meeting.
bullets: Open the item automatically: when an agent incident closes with a confirmed root cause, create a purple-loop item with a named owner and a due date. The incident-response guidance notes that improvements are often identified in follow-up reports and lessons-learned meetings; the automatic item turns each one into tracked work rather than a meeting note.

Require three linked outputs before the item closes: a detection for the failure mode, a validation test that replays the failure against that detection, and a regression case in the agent's eval suite, which the return-to-duty gate at Next already starts.

Ground the automation in the same guidance, which gives identifying tactics, techniques, and procedures that safeguards do not block or detections do not flag as an example of an improvement incidents can yield; treat each confirmed root cause as a candidate gap of that kind.
Keep a person on the promotion: automation opens and tracks the work, but a named detection engineer approves each new detection before it goes live.

Track repeat-incident rate as the metric, the share of agent incidents whose root cause matches an earlier closed item, and treat a rate that does not fall as a sign the three outputs are not landing.

blocks.label: Agent IR Principle
blocks.text: Plan for your own agents to fail, not just for external threats. Pre-wire the fast-containment controls: kill-switch, identity revocation, egress cutoff, sandbox isolation, because an agentic incident moves at machine speed. Make every agent action logged and reversible, and feed every incident back into the loop so it raises the baseline rather than just getting closed.

plays.name: Supply-Chain Counter-Threat
plays.title: Supply-Chain Counter-Threat
plays.subtitle: Cyber Supply-Chain Risk Management through a counterintelligence lens: when an adversary weaponizes the AI supply chain
plays.summary: C-SCRM through a counterintelligence lens: how an adversary would weaponize your AI supply chain, and how to disrupt it.

outline.title: A Counterintelligence Problem, Not Just a Procurement One
The Agent Configuration Surface: Files That Steer the Swarm
Provenance, Attestation & Zero Trust for the Supply Chain

items.label: high/critical vulns found in Glasswing's first month
of newly exploited CVEs in Q1 2025 hit within 24h of disclosure
rise in CVE submissions straining NVD (2020 - 25)

blocks.text: Procurement and vendor diligence (see Procurement & Vendor Risk) ask "is this vendor trustworthy?" Counter-threat C-SCRM asks a different, adversarial question: "how would a capable adversary use my AI supply chain to get to me, and how do I detect and disrupt that?" This is the counterintelligence framing the military-intelligence community already applies to human and technical supply chains, now turned on the AI stack. The supply chain isn't just a risk to be assessed once at purchase; it's a persistent attack surface an adversary actively probes: model weights, training data, dependencies, plugins, and update channels are all targets.
blocks.heading: A Counterintelligence Problem, Not Just a Procurement One

blocks.text: Distinct from generic software supply-chain attacks, the AI supply chain adds new adversary vectors: data poisoning (planted manipulations in training or RAG sources, see AgentPoison, >80% success at <0.1% poison rate), model tampering and trojaned weights (a pre-trained model carrying a hidden backdoor), compromised model/dependency registries (typosquatted or backdoored packages and model hubs), malicious or hijacked agent plugins/tools, and poisoned update/fine-tuning channels. Because these manipulations can be statistically invisible until triggered, they're especially appealing to sophisticated, patient actors: exactly the threat profile a counterintelligence posture is built to counter.
blocks.heading: The AI Supply-Chain Attack Surface

blocks.text: There is a supply-chain surface specific to agentic systems that never appears on a software bill of materials: the configuration surface, the instruction files (AGENTS.md, now an open standard stewarded under the Linux Foundation and used across tens of thousands of repositories), persona and identity files (SOUL.md), system prompts, and the skills, tools, and memory a swarm shares. These artifacts define how the agents behave, which makes them simultaneously a first-class attack surface and a governance artifact: whoever can edit one of these files, or poison a shared resource the agents read at runtime, can redirect the swarm without ever touching a model weight or tripping a CVE. Treat them the way you treat code and secrets: version-controlled, access-controlled, integrity-checked, and review-gated on every change, and pull them explicitly into threat-modeling and supply-chain review. The first Next action on this play makes that inventory-and-govern step concrete, and the AGENTS.md and SOUL.md entries in the Resource Index point to the standards themselves.
blocks.heading: The Agent Configuration Surface: Files That Steer the Swarm

blocks.text: Treat the supply chain as a hunting ground, not a checklist. Apply the intelligence cycle to it: prioritize which supply-chain elements matter most (PIRs for your most mission-critical models/data), then hunt. Integrity-verify model weights and artifacts against known-good baselines, monitor for anomalous model behavior that could indicate a planted trigger, watch dependency and registry activity for tampering, and treat externally sourced data/models as untrusted until validated. Findings feed Agent Incident Response and back into AI Threat Landscape, closing the loop. This is the active, ongoing counterpart to the one-time vetting that procurement performs.
blocks.heading: Detect & Disrupt (the Counter-Threat Cycle)

blocks.text: The structural defenses mirror Zero Trust: never trust a component because of where it nominally came from, verify it. Demand verifiable provenance and integrity attestation (SLSA-style) for models, data, and dependencies; cryptographically sign and verify model artifacts; pin and scan dependencies; and apply the "data as code" discipline so external data is versioned, scanned, and supply-controlled like software. SAIF centers provenance, and it pairs with the capability-based, treat-the-model-as-untrusted approach (CaMeL) covered in Frontier AI & Government.
blocks.heading: Provenance, Attestation & Zero Trust for the Supply Chain

blocks.text: This maps to recognized C-SCRM standards so it plugs into authorization evidence: NIST SP 800-161 (Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management) is the federal backbone, alongside NIST SP 800-53 supply-chain control families; the OWASP LLM Top 10 and AI Exchange address third-party model and supply-chain risk; and Google SAIF supplies the provenance controls. For DoW/federal work, supply-chain provenance and integrity are increasingly explicit authorization requirements, making a counter-threat C-SCRM capability both a security and a compliance asset.
blocks.heading: Frameworks & Federal Hooks

blocks.alt: The patching deficit, drawn to scale

items.title: Inventory and govern the agent configuration surface, instruction files (AGENTS.md), persona files (SOUL.md), system prompts, and the skills, tools, and memory a swarm shares: version-control it, access-control it, integrity-check it, and review-gate every change, and bring it into threat-modeling and supply-chain review. Whoever edits these files, or poisons a shared resource the agents read, redirects the agents.
items.text: Govern the configuration surface as code and run the play's supply-chain hunt around it: verify artifacts on every pull, watch registries, and test for planted triggers.
bullets: Govern the configuration surface as code: keep instruction files, persona files, system prompts, and the shared skills, tools, and memory under version control and access control, integrity-check them, and review-gate every change. The AGENTS.md and SOUL.md entries in canon define two of these formats; the controls around them are the suite's.

Verify every model, dataset, and artifact on every pull, checking hashes and signatures against known-good baselines before promotion. This is the integrity verification the play's counter-threat cycle prescribes, and SAIF asks for verifiable integrity protection of data, models, and code through its Model and Data Integrity Management control, which it maps to its Data Poisoning and Model Source Tampering risks.
Watch registry and dependency activity for tampering, including typosquatted or backdoored packages and model-hub uploads, and treat externally sourced models and data as untrusted until validated.
Test adopted models for planted triggers before promotion and monitor them for anomalous behavior after it, since a trojaned model can look clean until its trigger fires.
Route every finding into Agent Incident Response and back into the AI Threat Landscape, so the hunt closes the loop rather than ending at a report.

items.title: Audit direct and transitive dependencies against the 281 open-source projects with Glasswing-disclosed vulnerabilities as of May 22, 2026: prioritize anything internet-facing or handling auth, crypto, or protocol parsing.
items.text: Run the dependency audit the record calls for, prioritized by the criteria it names, against a dated snapshot.
bullets: Audit direct and transitive dependencies against the 281 open-source projects in which the program has disclosed vulnerabilities as of May 22, 2026, which is the immediate action the record itself prescribes.

Prioritize within the hit list on the record's stated criteria: dependencies that are internet-facing, or that handle authentication, cryptography, or network protocol parsing, rather than by dependency popularity.

Carry the snapshot date with the number: the 281 projects and the 1,596 disclosed findings behind them are stated as of May 22, 2026, so an audit run later needs a refreshed list rather than a remembered one; the note does not enumerate the projects, so take the list from Anthropic's coordinated vulnerability disclosure dashboard, which as of August 26, 2026 listed 392 projects.

Fix the intake path as well as the inventory: the record directs auditing vulnerability-management workflows for dependence on the national database, supplementing or replacing that scoring with GitHub Security Advisories, direct vendor security advisories, and established private advisory channels.
Treat one disclosure as a pattern signal, auditing the same weakness class across related codebases rather than closing the single reported component.

items.title: Treat available Glasswing patches (97 confirmed as of May 22, 2026) as emergency changes, not scheduled maintenance: median disclosure-to-exploit has collapsed to hours.
items.text: Route the confirmed remediations through the emergency path, on the record's own reaction-time arithmetic.
bullets: Route the confirmed remediations that your dependency audit against the 281 open-source projects shows you consume, 97 upstream fixes as of May 22, 2026, through the emergency-change path rather than scheduled maintenance, which is the record's explicit instruction for them.

Justify the routing with the reaction time the record cites: the median from public disclosure to weaponized exploit has fallen from 771 days in 2018 to single-digit hours, and carry the finding it cites with its original scope: per VulnCheck, 28.3% of the CVEs newly confirmed exploited in Q1 2025 had exploitation evidence within 24 hours of disclosure.

Read the remediation rate as the record denominates it, as a May 22, 2026 snapshot that Anthropic's coordinated vulnerability disclosure dashboard has since overtaken: the 97 confirmed patches are roughly a six percent remediation rate on disclosed findings, and under one percent of total discovery volume, so most of the surface is still unpatched, not merely unscheduled.
Pre-authorize the emergency path before it is needed, since a change process that requires a meeting cannot execute inside a single-digit-hour window.
Evaluate tooling that compresses the validation cycle between patch development and deployment, which the record names as the lever on the part of the window you actually control.

items.title: Audit vulnerability-management tooling for NVD/CVSS dependency and add vendor advisories + CTI as primary triage signals: NVD can no longer enrich everything it receives.
items.text: Rewire vulnerability triage off single-database enrichment: audit the tooling's NVD/CVSS dependence and add the signals that still resolve at exploit speed.
bullets: Inventory where vulnerability-management tooling depends on NVD or NVD-derived CVSS enrichment; the Glasswing note's relevant finding is that the national database is under structural strain and can no longer enrich everything it receives, which NIST formalized in April 2026 by enriching KEV, federal-software, and critical-software CVEs first and marking the rest not scheduled for immediate enrichment, so a pipeline that blocks on that enrichment inherits the backlog.

Add vendor security advisories as a primary triage input rather than a supplement, since affected-version and fix data arrive there first when the national database lags: a supplementation the Glasswing note itself names among its alternative sources. Treat the CISA KEV catalog and an exploit-probability score such as EPSS as primary inputs as well, a suite addition that gives the queue an exploitation-likelihood axis beside severity.

Wire threat intelligence in as a standing triage signal, run as a program along the Intelligence Handbook's tactical, operational, and strategic tiers rather than as an ad-hoc feed, so exploited-in-the-wild status can drive priority ahead of a score that may never be assigned.

Reuse the four BOD 26-04 criteria the Agent Containment play already installs as the program's decision layer (asset exposure, known-exploited status, exploit automatability, and post-exploitation impact) as the ranking axes, noting the directive is binding on FCEB agencies and offered here as a model rather than an obligation for everyone else.

Keep CVSS as one input, not the gate: the deficit the record documents, roughly six percent of its disclosed findings patched as of May 22, 2026, while the originating VulnCheck data shows 28.3% of the CVEs newly confirmed exploited in Q1 2025 were exploited within 24 hours of disclosure, is a gap that a score-blocked queue cannot close when enrichment stalls.

items.title: Report mean-time-to-remediate alongside discovery volume so leadership sees the patching deficit, not just the find count.
items.text: Put remediation rate next to discovery volume on the leadership dashboard: the record's whole thesis is that the first number outruns the second.
bullets: Define mean-time-to-remediate and remediation coverage as first-class metrics reported alongside discovery and find volume, computing coverage as the share of your own in-scope findings closed inside their assigned remediation windows, so a rising find count is never read as progress on its own.

Anchor the target on the record's measured gap: the Glasswing note's framing is discovery outpacing patching, with roughly six percent of the findings disclosed to open-source maintainers patched as of May 22, 2026, so the deficit, not the find count, is the number leadership tracks.
Name an owner and a reporting cadence so the metric survives past one board cycle; the AI Vulnerability Storm briefing is pitched at exactly this CISO and board audience.
Report the deficit as a trend rather than a snapshot: whether remediation rate is closing or widening against discovery over time, which is the signal a find-count alone hides.

blocks.label: Counter-Threat Principle
blocks.text: Procurement asks whether a vendor is trustworthy; counter-threat C-SCRM assumes an adversary is already targeting your AI supply chain and asks how you detect and disrupt them. Treat model weights, data, dependencies, and update channels as a live attack surface: verify provenance, hunt for tampering and planted triggers, and feed findings into incident response and threat intel. It's the counterintelligence complement to vendor diligence. Map it to NIST 800-161, OWASP, and SAIF.

blocks.text: These programs show what Agentic AI security looks like at the frontier, and why the public-private partnership model matters for any SecOps team adopting these capabilities.

blocks.heading: Claude Mythos Preview & Project Glasswing

items.title: Zero-Day Discovery
items.text: Found exploitable vulns across major OSes/browsers, including a 27-year-old OpenBSD bug

items.title: Exploit Chaining
items.text: Wrote a 4-vuln browser exploit chaining JIT heap spray and dual sandbox escapes

items.title: Project Glasswing
items.text: Restricted defensive deployment: an estimated 6,000+ high/critical open-source vulns found by May 22, 2026

items.title: Watershed Moment
items.text: Capabilities emerged from general gains in code/reasoning/autonomy, not security training

items.title: The bottleneck is now patching
items.text: Anthropic's 'When AI Builds Itself' analysis reports Glasswing has surfaced enough high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities across the world's most important systems that the constraint in cyber defense has already shifted from finding vulnerabilities to patching them fast enough (see Risks & Ethics and the Resource Index)

blocks.text: At its April 2026 announcement, Mythos Preview was Anthropic's most capable frontier model, restricted from public release over cyber concerns. It autonomously finds and exploits zero-days across every major OS and browser, chaining multi-stage exploits. Project Glasswing deploys it defensively with trusted orgs, finding an estimated 6,000+ high/critical open-source vulns by May 22, 2026, and on June 2, 2026 expanded to about 150 more organizations in over 15 countries. Per Anthropic's Project Glasswing launch page, Mythos Preview scored 83.1% on CyberGym. The later Mythos 5.1 (Sep 2026) is also restricted, available only through Anthropic's trusted access programs. Anthropic reports that a June 12, 2026 US export-control directive led it to disable its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models for all customers, that Mythos 5 returned for a set of US organizations after US government approval, and that with the controls lifted on June 30, Fable 5 returned globally on July 1.

blocks.heading: Anthropic Frontier Red Team: Cyberdefense Program

items.title: Autonomous Vuln Discovery
items.text: Using Claude Opus 4.6, found and validated 500+ high-severity vulnerabilities in production open-source code: bugs undetected for decades despite expert review

items.title: Capture-the-Flag Testing
items.text: Enters Claude in competitive CTF events to systematically benchmark offensive/defensive cyber capability

items.title: Strategic Warning & ASL
items.text: Tracks dual-use capability trajectory against AI Safety Level thresholds to trigger heightened safeguards in advance

items.title: External Red-Team (METR)
items.text: Invites independent third parties (e.g. METR) to adversarially test its own agent-monitoring systems: defense-in-depth on the defenders

blocks.text: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team (within its Policy org) runs an evidence-based cyberdefense research program: stress-testing Claude's offensive and defensive capabilities in competitive Capture-the-Flag events, partnering with national labs, and refining autonomous vulnerability discovery and patching. Its strategic-warning work tracks dual-use capability against AI Safety Level (ASL) thresholds. The throughline: understand what frontier models can do, then build the defenses that matter, and put them in defenders' hands first.

blocks.heading: Anthropic + NNSA: Nuclear Safeguards

items.title: 96% Nuclear Classifier
items.text: Co-developed with NNSA, deployed live to detect nuclear-proliferation misuse

items.title: Year-Long Red Team
items.text: NNSA staff red-teamed Claude in a secure environment before classifier build

items.title: FMF Blueprint
items.text: Shared as a replicable model for all frontier AI labs

items.title: Dual-Use Precedent
items.text: Sets the pattern for governing dual-use AI capabilities

blocks.text: Anthropic and DOE's National Nuclear Security Administration co-developed a classifier distinguishing concerning vs. benign nuclear conversations at 96% accuracy in preliminary testing, now live on Claude traffic. After a year of NNSA red-teaming in a secure environment, the blueprint was shared with the Frontier Model Forum.

blocks.heading: Anthropic + PNNL: Critical Infrastructure

items.title: 3 Hours vs. Weeks
items.text: AI-accelerated adversary emulation against an OT environment

items.title: Autonomous Adaptation
items.text: Claude switched UAC-bypass techniques on its own when one failed

items.title: DHS/CISA Relevance
items.text: PNNL operates the Control Environment Lab Resource for CISA

items.title: Public-Private Model
items.text: Frontier AI + national-lab cyber-physical assets: neither could do it alone

blocks.text: Anthropic and Pacific Northwest National Lab demonstrated AI-accelerated adversary emulation against a high-fidelity water-treatment plant simulation: three hours instead of multiple weeks. When a UAC-bypass tool failed, Claude autonomously found and used an alternative. PNNL runs the platform for DHS/CISA.

blocks.heading: Microsoft AI Red Team & PyRIT

items.title: AI Red Team
items.text: Dedicated team for adversarial-ML, RAI failures, and novel attack patterns

items.title: PyRIT
items.text: Open-source automation for AI red teaming, also in the OWASP AI Exchange tool list

items.title: Playground Labs
items.text: Hands-on adversarial-ML training; basis of Microsoft Learn AI Red Teaming 101

items.title: AI as Tradecraft
items.text: MS Threat Intel: AI now appears across the full attack lifecycle

blocks.text: Microsoft's AI Red Team stress-tests AI for adversarial-ML and Responsible-AI failures beyond traditional security testing. PyRIT (Python Risk Identification Tool) is their open-source framework for proactively finding generative-AI risks, with hands-on AI Red Teaming Playground Labs.

blocks.heading: Microsoft MDASH & MAI

items.title: Prepare→Scan→Validate→Dedupe→Prove
items.text: A pipeline of specialized agents that discovers, validates, and proves software vulnerabilities end-to-end

items.title: 96.5% on CyberGym
items.text: Any-crash score on the 1,507-vulnerability benchmark; now in production across Windows, Azure, and identity systems, and in preview in Azure Government for select US government customers and authorized partners since September 8, 2026

items.title: Two CVSS 9.8 RCEs
items.text: June 2026 Patch Tuesday, Windows kernel and HTTP.sys, routed into GitHub Advanced Security, Azure DevOps, and Defender

items.title: The System Is the Product
items.text: Led by Taesoo Kim (VP, Agentic Security); the model is one input: the system around it is the product

blocks.text: Microsoft AI (MAI), led by Mustafa Suleyman, builds the MAI model family (Build 2026). MDASH (codename), Microsoft Security's multi-model agentic scanning system, runs a Prepare→Scan→Validate→Dedupe→Prove pipeline of specialized agents to discover, validate, and prove software vulnerabilities end-to-end, routing findings into GitHub Advanced Security, Azure DevOps, and Defender as a closed discover→validate→prove→fix loop. Now in production across Windows, Azure, and identity systems, and in preview in Azure Government for select US government customers and authorized partners since September 8, 2026; scored 96.5% (any crash, by June 17, 2026) on the 1,507-vulnerability CyberGym benchmark, and its June 2026 Patch Tuesday cohort included two CVSS 9.8 RCEs (Windows kernel, HTTP.sys). Led by Taesoo Kim (VP, Agentic Security); the stated principle is that the model is one input: the system around it is the product.

blocks.heading: Microsoft Project Solara: Agent-First Devices

items.title: Hardware-rooted agent identity
items.text: As reported in Build 2026 coverage, Pluton binds device identity to Entra ID at manufacturing: a hardware root of trust, the literal form of the per-agent, non-human identity this playbook argues for (see Reference Architecture and Agentic Insider Risk)

items.title: Agent Attestation
items.text: As reported in Build 2026 coverage, a continuous-integrity service for the agent workload: zero-trust 'verify continuously, never trust-once' applied to agents, echoing the CISA zero-trust-for-OT principle

items.title: Agents as the interaction layer
items.text: Microsoft frames a shift from operating a device to authorizing a network of agents: agent identities about to walk around the building, including industrial and point-of-sale spaces

items.title: Watch, don't procure yet
items.text: An early platform preview: no general availability, pricing, or commercial hardware announced, external pilots only. Track the direction; specifics are as reported at Build 2026, not confirmed deployment detail

blocks.text: Unveiled at Build 2026, Project Solara is a chip-to-cloud platform for agent-first devices: endpoints that run AI agents instead of apps, built on the AOSP-based Microsoft Device Ecosystem Platform (not Windows) and managed through Intune, Defender, and Entra ID. Microsoft's post names Intune management, Entra ID sign-in and Hello for Business; Build 2026 coverage also reported a Pluton security processor binding each device's identity to Entra at manufacturing and an Agent Attestation service validating the agent workload, details that post does not state. Concept reference designs, a wearable badge and a desk companion, point at where this is heading.

blocks.heading: Google DeepMind: CaMeL, CodeMender & Frontier Safety

items.title: CaMeL: Capability-Based Control
items.text: Metadata on every value restricts data/control flows via fine-grained policy; LLM treated as untrusted, guarantees come from the framework: no retraining needed

items.title: CodeMender (defensive agent)
items.text: Autonomously root-causes vulns (fuzzing, SMT solvers) and self-validates patches via 'critique' agents before human sign-off. See Tools & Tech Stack

items.title: AI Vulnerability Reward Program
items.text: Dedicated AI VRP with unified reward tables; $430K+ already paid for AI-related issues, incentivizing high-impact disclosure

items.title: Frontier Safety Framework v3.1
items.text: Critical/Tracked Capability Levels across risk domains (incl. cyber) trigger heightened mitigations as models approach dangerous capability

blocks.text: Google DeepMind's CaMeL (Capabilities for Machine Learning) abandons the failed strategy of having models police themselves, treating the LLM as an untrusted component inside a secure software framework with capability-based access control, solving 77% of the AgentDojo benchmark with provable guarantees against data exfiltration. Google has since shipped CodeMender (an autonomous Gemini-powered agent that finds and fixes code vulnerabilities), launched a dedicated AI Vulnerability Reward Program, and strengthened its Frontier Safety Framework (v3, September 2025; v3.1, April 2026) with Critical/Tracked Capability Levels including a cyber domain. Together these show security treated as a data-flow problem plus AI used as an active defender.

blocks.heading: Wiz (Google Cloud): AI-APP & Agentic Defense

items.title: Red / Blue / Green Agents
items.text: Adversarial-testing, defensive-monitoring, and posture/compliance agents: agentic defense of agentic systems, the playbook's teaming model in a product

items.title: AI-SPM (Posture Management)
items.text: Agentless discovery of AI assets across Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), and self-hosted models: the visibility layer behind an AIBOM

items.title: AI-APP Runtime Protection
items.text: Risk posture + runtime analysis for AI applications across clouds and AI studios; integrates with Google SecOps workflows

items.title: Model Armor for Agents
items.text: Extended to cover agentic risks: prompt injection, tool poisoning, with MCP server support

blocks.text: Wiz, acquired by Google Cloud in March 2026 (the largest cybersecurity acquisition to date), brings cloud-native AI security posture management (AI-SPM) and the AI-Application Protection Platform (AI-APP) into the Google stack. Its standout architectural choice mirrors this playbook's red/blue/purple thesis: Wiz fields its own security agents, red agents (adversarial testing), blue agents (defensive monitoring), and green agents (posture/compliance), using AI agents to defend AI systems. AI-APP integrates with Google Security Operations and Model Armor (extended to agentic risks like prompt injection and tool poisoning).

blocks.heading: Google Cloud: AI Threat Defense

items.title: Prepare / Scan and Prioritize / Remediate / Monitor
items.text: A continuous loop, not a point-in-time scan: the continuous-validation posture in a product

items.title: Collection of Models, Multiple Passes
items.text: No single model catches everything; ensemble passes under human supervision

items.title: Mandiant + Wiz + Gemini + CodeMender
items.text: Threat intel, posture, reasoning, and autonomous code-fixing in one stack

blocks.text: Google Cloud's always-on autonomous defense platform (May 2026), unifying Mandiant threat intelligence, Wiz posture management, Gemini, and CodeMender across a Prepare / Scan and Prioritize / Remediate / Monitor loop, predicting attack paths and shipping verified fixes at machine speed. Its operating premise restates this playbook's multi-model thesis from the platform side: no single model catches everything, so it runs a collection of models across multiple passes, under human supervision.

blocks.heading: OpenAI: Agentic Safety & Preparedness

items.title: Frontier Challenge Framing
items.text: OpenAI: deterministic guarantees are hard; defenses must co-evolve with capability

items.title: Product-Level Guardrails
items.text: Logged-out mode, action confirmation, Watch Mode keep the user aware and in control

items.title: Automated Red-Team Loop
items.text: Internal automated attacker finds new injection classes before they appear in the wild

items.title: Safety Bug Bounty (2026)
items.text: Dedicated program formalizing an agent-safety vulnerability taxonomy worth adopting

blocks.text: OpenAI publicly frames prompt injection as a 'frontier security challenge' that may never be fully 'solved' for browser agents, and has responded with layered controls: ChatGPT Atlas logged-out mode, confirmation gates on sensitive actions, 'Watch Mode' for sensitive sites, an automated red-teaming rapid-response loop, a dedicated Safety Bug Bounty (Mar 2026) targeting agent prompt injection and data exfiltration, and Preparedness Framework risk assessments in model system cards. A candid acknowledgment that agentic security is a continuous discipline, not a one-time fix.

blocks.heading: Meta: Purple Llama: Open-Source AI Security

items.title: CyberSecEval 4 (CyberSOCEval / AutoPatchBench)
items.text: Open benchmark for both insecure-code propensity and defensive SOC / auto-patch capability: the agentic-SOC thesis, measured

items.title: LlamaFirewall
items.text: Real-time, modular guardrail framework spanning chat models to autonomous agents: prompt-injection, insecure-code, and plug-in defense

items.title: Llama Guard 4 + Prompt Guard 2
items.text: Multimodal I/O safety classifier plus jailbreak / prompt-injection detection: open, deployable guardrails

items.title: Llama Defenders Program
items.text: Partner access to AI tools for detecting AI-generated scam, fraud, and phishing content

blocks.text: Meta's distinctive contribution is open-source and defensive: Purple Llama, an umbrella of freely available trust-and-safety tools that level the playing field for any team securing LLM and agent systems, no platform lock-in. Two pieces map straight onto this playbook: CyberSecEval 4 now measures defensive capability, not just risk, via CyberSOCEval (can a model reason about incidents, spot malicious activity in logs, and read threat intel?) and AutoPatchBench (can an agent auto-patch native-code vulnerabilities found by fuzzing?). Scale AI's founder, Alexandr Wang, moved to Meta in 2025 to lead its superintelligence effort.

blocks.heading: DOE Genesis Mission

items.title: 17 Labs + 41 Partners (Jul 2026)
items.text: Public-private platform connecting supercomputers, data, AI, and quantum systems

items.title: Anthropic's Role
items.text: Claude access + engineers building AI agents and MCP servers for lab researchers

items.title: National-Security Mandate
items.text: Explicitly strengthens national security alongside science and energy

items.title: PNNL Key Partner
items.text: Pacific Northwest National Lab anchors the cyber-physical security work

blocks.text: DOE's national AI initiative uniting all 17 national labs with industry AI partners (Anthropic, Microsoft, Google, AWS, OpenAI, NVIDIA) to accelerate discovery science, strengthen national security, and drive energy innovation. At the inaugural Genesis Mission Summit (Jul 22, 2026) the Genesis Mission Consortium (17 labs, 5 NNSA sites, 41 partner organizations) reported $800M+ in committed partner support, with the first RFA projects selected.

blocks.heading: White House: AI Innovation & Security EO (Jun 2026)

items.title: AI Cybersecurity Clearinghouse
items.text: Treasury + NSA + CISA coordinate vuln scanning, validation, and patch prioritization with industry & critical infrastructure

items.title: AI-Enabled Federal Defense
items.text: CISA Binding Operational Directives to expand AI-enabled defensive tools for agencies, state and local authorities, and critical infrastructure: incl. rural hospitals, community banks, local utilities

items.title: Classified Frontier Benchmark
items.text: Treasury, NSA, and CISA build a classified process to flag models with 'advanced cyber capabilities'; voluntary pre-release access up to 30 days

items.title: Implies a National Threat Model
items.text: Tasking Treasury, NSA, and CISA to benchmark capability and the NSA Director (w/ National Cyber Director, Assistant to the President for Science and Technology, CISA, Dept. of War) to set the 'covered frontier model' threshold effectively requires a cohesive AI threat model (see AI Threat Modeling play)

items.title: Enforcement & Hiring
items.text: AG to prioritize AI-driven cybercrime enforcement; OPM expands US Tech Force cyber-specialist hiring pathways within 60 days

blocks.text: Signed June 2, 2026 as EO 14409, 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security' sets the current US federal posture: advance AI leadership while addressing national-security risk from increasingly capable models, via two tracks, (1) strengthening government and private cyber defenses against 'advanced AI,' and (2) a voluntary benchmarking/review framework for 'covered frontier models.' It explicitly avoids mandatory licensing or preclearance, reflecting a permissive-but-security-conscious stance. Key terms ('advanced AI,' 'covered frontier models') are left for agencies to define, so impact hinges on implementation.

blocks.heading: Palantir AIP / Foundry

items.title: Ontology-Enforced Security
items.text: The same controls govern data, logic, and action for human and agent actors: per-task authorization grants, human-in-the-loop on destructive actions, Ontology MCP for external agents

items.title: Government & Defense Heritage
items.text: Palantir reports two decades in national security and says AIP powers real-time human-agent decision-making in critical government and commercial environments

items.title: A Real-World Zero Trust Pattern
items.text: AIP embodies the per-task-permission, human-or-agent, assume-breach controls this playbook teaches (see Agentic Insider Risk)

blocks.text: Palantir is a marquee government and defense AI vendor; the company describes its Ontology-based AI Platform (AIP) as enforcing the same per-task, human-or-agent security controls this playbook advocates.

blocks.heading: XBOW: Autonomous Offensive Security

items.title: Autonomous Agentic Pentesting
items.text: AI agents discover and validate exploitable risks continuously: continuous validation, not point-in-time

items.title: Exposure Management at Scale
items.text: Surfaces and prioritizes real exploitable paths across complex, AI-driven estates

blocks.text: XBOW reports that its autonomous penetration tester reached the top of HackerOne's US leaderboard in June 2025 after submitting nearly 1,060 vulnerabilities, with its security team reviewing findings before submission to comply with HackerOne's policy on automated tools. XBOW is the red-team half of this playbook's thesis as a product: AI agents hunting exploitable paths continuously rather than in a once-a-year engagement.

blocks.heading: U.S.-UK Frontier AI Security Framework (RAND-Oxford)

items.title: Hardened Access & Interfaces
items.text: Maps to Governance (per-agent NHI, least privilege) and Network & Security Controls (gateway, egress discipline).

items.title: Secure Development & Supply Chain
items.text: Maps to Supply-Chain Counter-Threat (Glasswing-era dependency auditing) and Procurement & Vendor Risk (AIBOM, provenance vetting).

items.title: Monitoring, Detection & Incident Response
items.text: Maps to Blue Team and Agent Incident Response: telemetry-first, contain-first.

items.title: Personnel Security
items.text: Maps to Agentic Insider Risk: the report urges extending government personnel-security practice (continuous vetting) to frontier labs, the Trusted Workforce 2.0 posture this playbook applies to agents as NHIs.

items.title: Physical & Environmental Security
items.text: The one cluster outside this playbook's software scope, touched here only at the IT/OT boundary (OT, ICS & SCADA).

blocks.text: An interim RAND-Oxford Programme for Cyber and Technology Policy report (June 8, 2026) arguing frontier AI security must be elevated to the level of strategic national assets, and proposing a five-cluster framework for U.S.-UK coordination, with bilateral recommendations including joint threat-intelligence infrastructure for AI security, expanded support for red-teaming and model evaluations, personnel-security practices extended from government to frontier labs, and regular joint AI crisis exercises. The significance for this playbook: allied governments are converging at policy level on exactly the posture operationalized here, continuous adversarial testing, tabletop-exercised response, vetted people, hardened supply chains. Each cluster lands on plays this playbook already runs.

plays.name: Frameworks
plays.title: Frameworks & Standards
plays.subtitle: The governance and threat-modeling references that structure an AI security program
plays.summary: The authoritative references for an AI security program, from the NIST AI RMF and OWASP to MAESTRO, and what each anchors.

outline.title: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1 + AI Companion Guides
OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet

blocks.text: These are the authoritative frameworks to anchor governance, detection coverage, compliance, and threat modeling.

blocks.heading: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI 100-1)

items.title: GOVERN
items.text: Cultivate a risk-aware culture, policies, accountability, and oversight across the AI lifecycle

items.title: MAP
items.text: Establish context and identify risks tied to the system's purpose and deployment

items.title: MEASURE
items.text: Assess, analyze, and track AI risks with quantitative and qualitative methods

items.title: MANAGE
items.text: Prioritize and act on risks; allocate resources; monitor and respond over time

items.title: Trustworthy AI Traits
items.text: Valid/reliable, safe, secure/resilient, accountable/transparent, explainable, privacy-enhanced, fair

items.title: Companion Resources
items.text: The AI RMF Playbook, Roadmap, and crosswalks; extended by the GenAI Profile (600-1) and paired with CSF 2.0

blocks.text: The foundational US framework for trustworthy AI (NIST AI 100-1, Jan 2023), voluntary and widely adopted across the federal public sector and beyond. It organizes AI risk management into four functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE, and defines the characteristics of trustworthy AI. The GenAI Profile (600-1) extends it and the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF 2.0) runs alongside it; together they form the NIST backbone a federal-facing program is expected to align to.

blocks.heading: NIST AI 600-1: GenAI Profile

items.title: CBRN Information
items.text: LLM uplift toward chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons

items.title: Confabulation
items.text: Plausible-but-false outputs: dangerous in security and medical contexts

items.title: Information Security
items.text: Lowered barrier to vulnerability discovery, malware dev, and phishing

items.title: Human-AI Configuration
items.text: Automation bias, over-reliance, anthropomorphism degrade human judgment

items.title: Value Chain & Integration
items.text: Supply-chain risk from third-party models, data, APIs, and fine-tuning

items.title: Four Response Strategies
items.text: Mitigate, transfer, avoid, or accept: adapted to the GenAI context

blocks.text: Published July 2024 under EO 14110 (since rescinded, January 2025), the official GenAI companion to the NIST AI RMF. Identifies 12 risk categories unique to or exacerbated by generative AI, mapping 200+ suggested actions to GOVERN / MAP / MEASURE / MANAGE. An AI RMF critical-infrastructure profile concept note followed in April 2026.

blocks.heading: NIST CSF 2.0: AI Defense Matrix

items.title: Govern + Identify
items.text: AI platform standards, posture management, AIBOM, agent-framework discovery

items.title: Protect
items.text: System-prompt hardening, plugin allowlisting, RAG sanitization, model firewalls

items.title: Detect
items.text: Prompt-injection testing, agent anomaly detection, RAG-leakage egress detection

items.title: Respond + Recover
items.text: Agent runtime IR, plugin disable, prompt rollback, model version restore

blocks.text: Zeltser & Yu's matrix mapping AI asset classes to the six NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions. The companion to the Cyber Defense Matrix for the AI era: use it to identify gaps, assign ownership, and select controls across your AI estate, aligned to the NIST CSF structure public sector programs already use.

blocks.heading: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1 + AI Companion Guides

items.title: AI & LLM Companion Guide
items.text: "What does the model know and do?" Secures models and text-centric generative AI by mapping CIS Safeguards (data, configuration hardening, access, monitoring, supplier governance) to LLM- and SLM-enabled systems.

items.title: AI Agents Companion Guide
items.text: "How does the system reason, plan, and act?" Applies CIS Controls v8.1 to the agent layer (planning, reasoning, tool invocation, multi-step workflows) across identity, endpoint execution, knowledge stores, integration pipelines, and monitoring. Frames excessive agency as excessive functionality + permissions + autonomy, with human-approval gates on high-impact actions.

items.title: MCP Companion Guide
items.text: "How does the AI interface with tools and data?" Secures the Model Context Protocol layer: secure tool access, non-human identity management, and auditable protocol-layer interactions.

items.title: Implementation-Group prioritization
items.text: Keeps the CIS IG1/IG2/IG3 tiering, so you scope AI controls to org maturity instead of adopting a parallel AI-only framework.

blocks.text: The CIS Controls you likely already run, extended to AI. In April 2026 CIS (with Astrix and Cequence) released three Companion Guides to CIS Controls v8.1 that reinterpret existing Safeguards for AI rather than inventing a new framework, so the same prioritized controls (asset management, secure configuration, identity, logging, vulnerability management, supplier governance) carry over to AI/LLM, agentic, and MCP environments. For a shop already standardized on CIS Controls or SANS SEC566, this is the lowest-friction, defensible path to covering agentic systems.

blocks.heading: OWASP AI Exchange (324-page guide)

items.title: Threat Map with Controls
items.text: Every threat mapped to applicable controls, general and ready-made-model variants

items.title: Three-Move Threat Summary
items.text: New assets (add to ISMS) → new suppliers (supply-chain mgmt) → input threats (resilience + zero model trust)

items.title: Agentic AI Threats
items.text: Dedicated section beyond LLM-only threat models

items.title: Periodic Table of AI Security
items.text: The most scannable control catalog for finding coverage gaps

blocks.text: A free AI security reference OWASP describes as the go-to comprehensive resource: 324 pages spanning the full lifecycle, feeding directly into the EU AI Act and ISO standards. Its essentials sort AI controls into four categories (Manage, Have resilient models, Watch, Limit); this playbook summarizes its threat view in three moves: (1) new AI assets facing conventional threats, (2) new suppliers, and (3) input threats via the model's own interface. The prescription: resilience + what this playbook calls zero model trust + blast-radius control. (See the AI Security Essentials section of the Fundamentals play for the full mental model.)

blocks.heading: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2026)

items.title: LLM01 Prompt Injection
items.text: Direct/indirect injection hijacks behavior via untrusted input: #1 risk, hardest to fix

items.title: LLM02 Sensitive Info Disclosure
items.text: Model leaks PII, credentials, or proprietary data through outputs

items.title: LLM03 Excessive Agency
items.text: Over-permissioned agents act on malicious instructions without oversight

items.title: LLM05 Data & Model Poisoning
items.text: Training/fine-tuning manipulation distorts behavior and plants backdoors

items.title: LLM06 Unbounded Consumption
items.text: Resource-exhaustion / DoS / cost-amplification via large or recursive requests

items.title: LLM08 Hidden Context Exposure
items.text: Formerly System Prompt Leakage: adversarial queries extract confidential system-prompt logic

items.title: LLM09 Vector & Embedding Weaknesses
items.text: RAG systems vulnerable to poisoned embeddings and cross-context leakage

items.title: LLM10 Improper Output Handling
items.text: Downstream systems trust LLM output → XSS, SSRF, privilege escalation

blocks.text: The definitive list of the ten most critical LLM-application security risks, re-ranked in the August 2026 edition; the playbook's action tags keep the 2025 numbering.
