LLM vulnerabilities differ structurally from traditional app flaws: they hinge on data integrity, model behavior, and autonomous interaction. Detailed 2025-edition breakdown via the Oligo Security Academy.

blocks.heading: OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet

items.title: Tool Security & Least Privilege
items.text: Scope tools tightly and gate them; excessive agency is the core agent risk

items.title: Input Validation
items.text: Treat retrieved and untrusted content as hostile: the prompt-injection surface

items.title: Memory & Context Isolation
items.text: Memory, hooks, and retrieved context persist across sessions: isolate and provenance-tag them

items.title: Human-in-the-Loop
items.text: Gate consequential actions on human judgment; don't automate the irreversible

items.title: Output Validation & Guardrails
items.text: Verify before acting; keep enforcement hot-updateable, not static

items.title: Monitoring · Multi-Agent Trust · Data Protection
items.text: Log agent reasoning; treat inter-agent messages as untrusted; propagate identity, don't over-share

blocks.text: OWASP's concise, implementation-focused companion to the LLM and Agentic Top 10 lists: worth loading directly into an agent as a skill so the controls apply at design time. It maps the key agent risks to nine control categories (as of September 2026), turning the threat lists into something an engineer (or an agent) can act on while building.

blocks.heading: AWS AI Security Framework

items.title: Right Controls / Layers / Phases
items.text: Phase controls in as workloads evolve (Foundational for prototype → Enhanced for production → Advanced for scale) rather than bolting on at the end

items.title: Threat-Model AI Workloads
items.text: AWS stresses existing threat models miss probabilistic outputs, prompt injection, and autonomous agent behavior

items.title: Model-Agnostic Controls
items.text: Bedrock's consistent API + Guardrails apply the same security across first- and third-party models

items.title: Audit Manager GenAI Framework
items.text: 110 prebuilt controls (72 automated, 38 manual) for evidence collection; AWS reports Audit Manager is moving to maintenance mode and closed to new accounts from April 30, 2026, so this is an existing-customer option only

blocks.text: AWS's framework (May 2026, Goodman & Rae) for applying the right controls, at the right layers, at the right phases: built on the premise that security compounds from day one as a workload moves from prototype to production to scale. Assess-first, then phase in controls. Decouples model choice from security infrastructure: Bedrock provides a consistent API and consistent security controls across Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, OpenAI, and others, with AgentCore Gateway extending those controls to externally hosted models. Relevant for public sector teams: Bedrock Guardrails is available in GovCloud.

blocks.heading: Google SAIF 2.0 (Secure AI Framework)

items.title: Three Agent Principles (2.0)
items.text: Agents must have well-defined human controllers, carefully limited powers, and observable actions/planning: the backbone of agent governance

items.title: Agent Risk Map (2.0)
items.text: Maps agentic threats across a full-stack view of AI risk; SAIF risk-map data donated to the CoSAI Risk Map initiative

items.title: Supply-Chain Integrity
items.text: SLSA-style provenance, attestations, model signing, reproducible pipelines for data/models/weights

items.title: AI Firewall Pattern
items.text: Inspect every input for malicious intent and every output for data leaks (e.g. Model Armor, guard models)

blocks.text: Google's enterprise framework (community-driven via CoSAI), extended in October 2025 to SAIF 2.0 with explicit guidance for securing autonomous agents. Its defining insight: in AI, data takes on the role code plays in traditional software, so the attack surface extends to the data and model supply chain, not just code. SAIF 2.0 adds an agent risk map and three core agent principles, making it a strong fit for both the supply-chain/provenance side and the agentic-governance side of an AI program; pairs BeyondCorp zero-trust and SLSA supply-chain lineage with AI-specific controls.

blocks.heading: Microsoft AI/ML Threat Modeling (STRIDE)

items.title: STRIDE Taxonomy
items.text: Six categories to systematically enumerate threats per data-flow and trust boundary

items.title: AI/ML-Specific Threats
items.text: Adversarial perturbation, data/model poisoning, model stealing, membership inference, model inversion

items.title: Trust-Boundary Mapping
items.text: Diagram where untrusted input, augmentation data, and agent tool-calls cross boundaries

items.title: Fits Existing SDL
items.text: Extends current secure-development threat modeling rather than replacing it; pairs with MITRE ATLAS

blocks.text: Threat modeling is the structured practice of enumerating how a system can be attacked before it ships. STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) is the classic taxonomy; Microsoft's AI/ML threat-modeling guidance extends it with AI-specific failure modes so existing SDL practices cover the model, its data, and its pipeline. Do this in Roadmap Phase 0 - 2, before agents touch production.

blocks.heading: Zero Trust for AI Agents (Anthropic)

items.title: Agents Hit Twice
items.text: Exposed infrastructure plus autonomy that can misuse legitimate permissions: traditional access controls and human-paced monitoring can't keep up

items.title: Three-Tier Architecture
items.text: Foundation → Enterprise → Advanced (the eBook's tier names; Anthropic's blog summary says Foundation, Advanced, Optimized), matched to organizational maturity and risk tolerance

items.title: Eight-Phase Rollout
items.text: Identity, access scoping, sandboxing, input/output controls, and memory safeguards

items.title: Agent-Specific Controls
items.text: Cryptographically rooted identities, per-task-scoped permissions, and memory protected against poisoning

items.title: Agentic SOAR + Compliance
items.text: Security operations run fast enough to contend with AI-accelerated attackers; alignment for healthcare, finance, and government

blocks.text: Anthropic's Zero Trust framework for deploying autonomous AI agents in the enterprise. Its premise: frontier models compress the vulnerability-to-exploit window from months to hours, hitting agent programs twice. The infrastructure they run on faces AI-accelerated offense, and the agents themselves can abuse legitimate permissions at machine speed. It adapts 'never trust, always verify, assume breach' for agents and maps adoption to organizational maturity and risk tolerance. The floor is raised at Foundation. Friction-only controls no longer qualify: short-lived tokens, cryptographically rooted identity, identity-based isolation, and automated first-pass triage are entry requirements, and every control faces one design test: impossible, or merely tedious?

blocks.heading: SANS AI Security Maturity Model (2026)

items.title: Protect / Utilize / Govern
items.text: Three scored dimensions: secure the AI, use AI for security, and govern both

items.title: 5 Stages with Controls & Metrics
items.text: Defined controls, metrics, and actions at each level; a 'Determine Your Target Maturity' table

items.title: Agentic-AI Guidance
items.text: Original coverage of agent identity, ownership, and permission boundaries

items.title: Audit-Defensible Reporting
items.text: Produces executive-ready language and evidence for regulators, customers, partners

blocks.text: SANS's operational companion (Chris Cochran, 2026) to its Secure AI Blueprint: a 5-stage, evidence-based path from ad hoc AI use to a fully governed program, scored across Protect / Utilize / Govern, with original Agentic-AI guidance. Explicitly mapped to NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, ISO 42001, and the OWASP AI Exchange + Agentic Top 10 (via the SANS-OWASP partnership). An excellent external benchmark to validate this playbook's own maturity model against.

blocks.heading: CSA AI Controls Matrix (AICM) & MAESTRO

items.title: 243 controls (247 in v1.1) / 18 domains
items.text: Vendor-agnostic AI control set built on the Cloud Controls Matrix; each control analyzed across five pillars (type, ownership, architecture, lifecycle, threat category); maps to ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF/600-1, and BSI AIC4

items.title: Control Applicability and Ownership
items.text: One of the five pillars each control objective is analyzed across, alongside control type; the matrix ships implementation and auditing guidelines in role-specific versions: model provider, orchestrated service provider, application provider, AI customer, and cloud service provider, the ownership clarity GenAI procurement usually lacks (pairs with Procurement & Vendor Risk)

items.title: AI-CAIQ + STAR for AI
items.text: A consensus self-assessment questionnaire plus a pathway to third-party-validated STAR for AI certification, with a Catastrophic Risk Annex now in development (kickoff June 2026, target December 2027) aligned to NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, and ISO 42001

items.title: MAESTRO + CSAI Foundation
items.text: CSA also stewards MAESTRO (the seven-layer agentic threat model) and, via the CSAI Foundation, runtime/zero-trust agent specifications and MITRE CVE Numbering Authority status (initial scope CSA's own software tools, building toward Agentic-AI vulnerability coordination)

blocks.text: The Cloud Security Alliance, the body behind the widely adopted Cloud Controls Matrix and the STAR assurance registry, has become a central standards player for AI. Its AI Controls Matrix (AICM) is a vendor-agnostic control framework of 243 control objectives in v1.0, expanded to 247 in v1.1 (June 2026), across 18 security domains (Model Security, Data Security & Privacy, IAM, Supply Chain, GRC, and more), built on the CCM and mapped to ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF / AI 600-1, and the BSI AIC4 catalog. Alongside it sits MAESTRO (the seven-layer agentic threat model, see AI Threat Modeling), the AI-CAIQ assessment questionnaire, the STAR for AI certification pathway, and the CSAI Foundation's 2026 'Securing the Agentic Control Plane' program. Together they give a public sector or enterprise program an auditable, standards-aligned way to specify and prove AI controls, complementing the NIST/OWASP/ATLAS backbone rather than replacing it.

plays.name: Research Library
plays.title: Research Library
plays.subtitle: The university labs and independent research, plus the key arXiv papers, grounding Agentic AI security
plays.summary: Independent university research and key arXiv papers that ground the playbook's claims, a counterweight to vendor sources.

outline.title: Alan Turing Institute: CETaS & Defence AI

blocks.text: University research centers provide independent evidence and benchmarks (peer-reviewed where noted) that anchor this playbook's claims: a counterweight to vendor and frontier-lab sources. Below are the leading academic institutions working on Agentic AI security, followed by key arXiv papers (including work from Disesdi Susanna Cox, an OWASP AI Exchange core author) underpinning agentic red/blue/purple teaming.

blocks.heading: Stanford HAI: AI Index & Cybench

items.title: Security is the #1 scaling barrier
items.text: AI Index 2026: 62% of orgs cite security/risk as the top blocker to scaling Agentic AI, a 24-point margin over the next factor

items.title: Cybench: 15% → 93% in a year
items.text: Unguided AI solve rates on Stanford's cyber-agent benchmark leapt from 15% (2024) to 93% (2025): the dual-use curve, quantified

items.title: Transparency is declining
items.text: The Foundation Model Transparency Index fell from 58 to 40; vendor-reported benchmarks are a weaker basis for procurement: independent eval matters

items.title: Incidents rising
items.text: 362 documented AI incidents in 2025 (up from 233); responsible-AI benchmark reporting remains inconsistent and voluntary

blocks.text: The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI) produces the field's most-cited independent benchmarks and its annual AI Index. The 2026 edition put hard numbers behind this playbook's core premises, and HAI's Cybench benchmark tracks how fast AI cyber-capability is rising.

blocks.heading: Carnegie Mellon (CyLab): Autonomous Attack & Defense

items.title: Autonomous multi-host attack
items.text: "On the Feasibility of Using LLMs to Autonomously Execute Multi-host Network Attacks": LLM-as-strategist over specialized agents replicated the 2017 Equifax breach in a controlled environment

items.title: Hierarchical agent architecture
items.text: The LLM plans and issues high-level instructions; a mix of LLM and non-LLM agents handle scanning, exploitation, and exfiltration, mirroring real-world complexity

items.title: Pivot to autonomous defense
items.text: CyLab is now studying LLM agents that detect and respond to attacks in real time. Singer: "We're entering an era of AI versus AI in cybersecurity"

items.title: Democratizing red teaming
items.text: Points toward continuous, AI-powered network testing affordable for small orgs, not just annual human red-team engagements

blocks.text: CMU's CyLab (its university-wide security & privacy institute) produced one of the most important academic demonstrations of agentic offensive capability, in collaboration with Anthropic. Brian Singer et al.'s study showed LLMs structured with hierarchical planning can autonomously execute multi-host network attacks, and the team is now pivoting the same architecture toward autonomous defense: an academic anchor for the dual-use thesis.

blocks.heading: MIT: AI Risk Repository & FutureTech

items.title: 1,700+ cataloged risks
items.text: A structured, citable taxonomy of AI risks and harms: use it to ensure a threat model covers documented failure modes, not just imagined ones

items.title: Priority Risks (272-expert Delphi study)
items.text: Ranks the 5 most-severe risks and the most-vulnerable sectors: Information, Finance, and National Security, and surfaces a responsibility gap between who is exposed and who is accountable; complements the Risks and Ethics play

items.title: Governance-document analysis
items.text: An LLM pipeline classifies 1,000+ AI governance documents (e.g., CSET's AGORA archive): useful for compliance landscape mapping

items.title: Independent grounding
items.text: A neutral academic source to validate vendor claims and anchor the threat-model 'list mission impacts' step in evidence

blocks.text: MIT's FutureTech / AI Risk Initiative maintains the AI Risk Repository: a living, comprehensive database of 1,700+ documented AI risks with an expert-scored taxonomy (also referenced in this playbook's AI Threat Landscape play). It's the most rigorous academic catalog for grounding an AI threat model in evidence rather than anecdote, and it feeds broader governance-document analysis across the field.

blocks.heading: Agents of Chaos (Multi-University Study)

items.title: "Vulnerable to conversation"
items.text: Agents fell not to novel exploits but to social engineering: the human-manipulation vector content filters don't catch

items.title: Representative case
items.text: A researcher renamed themselves to match an agent's owner, opened a private channel, and convinced it to delete memory, rename itself, and reassign admin access

items.title: Structural deficits identified
items.text: No reliable way to distinguish legitimate users from manipulators; no self-awareness of competence limits; no private deliberation surface

items.title: Reinforces agents-as-insiders
items.text: Backs the playbook's Insiders + Containment thesis: deterministic boundaries, not model trust, are what hold against manipulation

blocks.text: A February 2026 multi-institution study (Northeastern, Harvard, MIT, Stanford, Carnegie Mellon, and others) put AI agents in a live laboratory environment, where twenty AI researchers tested them. Its memorable finding: agents are vulnerable less to sophisticated exploits than to plain conversation, social manipulation. The clearest academic backing for treating agents as manipulable non-human insiders and bounding them at the environment layer.

blocks.heading: Alan Turing Institute: CETaS & Defence AI

items.title: Autonomous Cyber Defence (CETaS + Georgetown CSET)
items.text: Joint report assessing AI agents for autonomous cyber defense via reinforcement learning: the academic/policy backbone of the agentic blue-team thesis

items.title: DARe & AIDA: Defence AI
items.text: Defence AI Research Centre and AI for Data-Driven Advantage: responsible, resilient, effective AI for UK Defence. Aligns with the federal/DoW lens here

items.title: Research-Security & Insider Threat
items.text: CETaS work on securing the AI research ecosystem against state espionage, theft, and dual-use reverse-engineering: backs Supply-Chain Counter-Threat & counterintelligence

items.title: Indirect Prompt Injection & Assurance
items.text: CETaS analysis of indirect prompt injection plus the Turing's Trustworthy & Ethical Assurance (TEA) work on argument-based AI assurance: supports Mission Assurance (GRC)

blocks.text: The UK's national institute for data science and AI, and a leading allied voice on defense and national-security AI: a useful counterweight to the US-centric vendor and academic sources elsewhere in this playbook. Its Centre for Emerging Technology and Security (CETaS) researches autonomous cyber defense, AI evaluation frameworks, and research-security threats, while its Defence AI Research Centre (DARe) and AI for Data-Driven Advantage (AIDA) programs work directly with the UK MoD and British Army on adopting responsible, resilient, and effective AI. The framing, evidence-based, hype-cutting, assurance-led, closely tracks this playbook's own stance.

items.title: Securing Agentic AI: ATFAA + SHIELD
items.text: The threat model purpose-built for GenAI agents. ATFAA organizes 9 primary threats across 5 domains: cognitive architecture, temporal persistence (memory), operational execution, trust-boundary violations, governance circumvention. SHIELD maps mitigations. Argues OWASP/NIST/ATLAS treat LLMs as isolated components and miss the emergent risks of autonomy + memory + tool use combined. The single best paper for designing your Agentic SecOps security.

items.title: Quantifying the Risk of Transferred Black Box Attacks
items.text: Cox (OWASP AI Exchange) and Bunzel (Fraunhofer) build a framework to quantify risk from transferred adversarial attacks using surrogate models selected by Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity. The core argument behind Cox's 'AI red teaming is fake' thesis: the input space is too high-dimensional for exhaustive coverage, so prompt-spraying can't work. You need mathematical risk estimation. Directly relevant to building red-team programs that actually scale.

items.title: AgentPoison: Red-Teaming LLM Agents via Memory Poisoning
items.text: The authors present it as the first backdoor attack on generic and RAG-based LLM agents by poisoning long-term memory or the knowledge base: no fine-tuning required. >80% attack success with <0.1% poison rate and <1% benign impact. Featured in Disesdi's analysis as the canonical example of why agentic memory is a critical, hard-to-detect security vector. Essential reading for both red (offense) and blue (RAG-poisoning detection).

items.title: Red-Teaming for Generative AI: Silver Bullet or Security Theater?
items.text: Surveys AI red-teaming practice and finds it diverges wildly: vague purposes, inconsistent artifacts and criteria, often functioning as 'security theater' rather than rigorous testing. Cited heavily in the AI-security-operationalization debate. The cautionary counterpoint that keeps an agentic red-team program honest: define purpose, artifact, and success criteria up front.

items.title: AI Red Teaming Has a Subspace Problem (analysis)
items.text: Cox's argument that real attackers don't keep prompt repos: they develop repeatable mathematical processes to perturb any input into an attack set. Reframes red teaming away from prompt collections toward subspace coverage and transferability math. Pairs with her transferred-black-box-attacks paper to form a coherent 'red teaming that actually works' thesis.

items.title: Systematic Review of Algorithmic Red-Teaming Methodologies
items.text: Consolidates research on automated red teaming: methodologies, tools, benefits, and limitations, arguing that manual red teaming is too resource-intensive and unscalable for frequent assessment, and that AI-driven automation delivers adaptive, efficient evaluation. The literature backbone for justifying an agentic, continuous red-team program to leadership.

items.title: RED-AI: A Red-Teaming Framework for Real-World AI Systems
items.text: A framework for red teaming and evaluating real-world (not just lab) AI systems, applied to maritime autonomous systems as a test case. Includes a practical RED-AI checklist (Appendix A) adaptable to a range of AI evaluations: a useful template when standing up structured AI red-team engagements.

items.title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL)
items.text: Introduces CaMeL: capability-based access control that treats the LLM as an untrusted component and enforces data/control-flow policies via a custom interpreter, no model retraining required. Solves 77% of AgentDojo with provable guarantees against exfiltration, and explicitly bolsters insider-threat and malicious-automation defense by making security a data-flow property. The leading example of 'don't ask the model to police itself.'
items.meta: Debenedetti et al., Google DeepMind / ETH Zurich, 2025

items.title: The Attacker Moves Second (Joint Adversarial Study)
items.text: A rare joint study across the three leading frontier labs on adaptive attacks against LLM defenses. Headline finding: adaptive attacks bypassed 12 recent defenses, with attack success above 90% for most; the International AI Safety Report's November 2025 key update separately finds attackers given ten tries still succeed at prompt injection about half the time, and Claude Opus 4.6's system card quantified a single GUI-agent prompt injection succeeding 17.8% of the time without safeguards. The empirical case for assume-breach and structural (not model-only) defenses.

blocks.label: Why Academic Sources Matter
blocks.text: Independent research (peer-reviewed where noted) is the counterweight to vendor benchmarks, and the Stanford AI Index makes the case directly: as model transparency declines, independent evaluation stops being optional. These sources ground the playbook's threat model, benchmark the dual-use curve, and validate the assume-breach and agents-as-insiders stances with evidence no single vendor could provide alone.

plays.name: Case Studies
plays.title: Case Studies: Evidence in Action
plays.subtitle: What real, documented incidents prove about Agentic AI in offense and defense
plays.summary: Documented cases from 2025 to 2026, in offense and defense, each told as what happened and what it proves.

outline.title: Government of Alberta: Red/Blue Agents Securing a Public Estate at Scale
Mexican Government Breach: APT_UNICORN in the Wild
A Year of AI-Enabled Threats (ATT&CK Mapping)
Claude Code Security: 500+ High-Severity Vulns in Production
Accenture Cyber.AI: Agentic SecOps at Scale (Powered by Claude)
RAITE 2026: Navy Red/Blue AI Test Event
Unit 42 Global IR Report 2026: Fastest Attacks at 4x Speed

blocks.text: The playbook's thesis isn't theoretical: it rests on documented, public cases from 2025 - 2026. These mini case studies translate the sources cited throughout the playbook into 'what happened and what it proves.' Each is drawn from primary reporting. (Figures are as reported by the cited source; verify before quoting in formal settings.)

blocks.heading: Government of Alberta: Red/Blue Agents Securing a Public Estate at Scale

items.title: What happened
items.text: A red-team agent probed each application from the outside the way an attacker would and mapped how a vulnerability might be exploited; a blue-team agent then assessed defenses against an international security standard and wrote a remediation plan pointing to the exact files to fix. Every app was checked against roughly 95 security controls per pass, with additional agents checking code quality: all built on the Claude Agent SDK.

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: External, primary-source validation of this playbook's core thesis: the red/blue/purple agent loop is not theoretical. A peer government deployed it at scale and treated adversarial evaluation as continuous, not episodic.

items.title: Human in Command
items.text: Before any patch shipped it was reviewed and approved by engineers at Alberta's Ministry of Technology and Innovation: the same human-in-command discipline this playbook requires. The agents proposed; people approved.

items.title: The lesson
items.text: The defensive answer to agent-speed offense is agent-speed defense under human control, and building it in the open, so other teams can replicate rather than reinvent. The full method is published as the open-source Velocity White Papers.

blocks.text: The clearest real-world demonstration to date of the red/blue agent loop this playbook argues for, on Anthropic's and Alberta's own figures: a government used Claude to run it throughout its development process. Around 50 agents worked autonomously and in parallel to scan 466 million lines of code in about 20 hours, a review the team estimates could otherwise have taken roughly 6.5 years, across about 1,280 applications and 3,400 repositories in 27 ministries. (Anthropic case study; figures as reported.)

blocks.heading: GTG-1002: AI-Orchestrated Espionage

items.title: What happened
items.text: An agent autonomously executed multi-stage intrusion activity across targets, with minimal human direction

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Proves agentic attacks at scale are here now, not hypothetical: the core premise of the Dual-Use Reality section in Fundamentals

items.title: Playbook link
items.text: Anchors Dual-Use Reality; justifies assume-breach, continuous teaming, and the urgency framing

items.title: The lesson
items.text: Defenders must operate at the same machine speed and autonomy attackers now wield

blocks.text: Anthropic disclosed disrupting what it described as the first documented large-scale cyber-espionage operation run largely by an AI agent: a state-linked actor using an agentic model to conduct intrusions with up to 80 - 90% of the work performed autonomously, humans intervening only at a few key decision points. The defining real-world example of agentic dual-use: the same capabilities that power defensive teaming were turned to offense.

blocks.heading: Mexican Government Breach: APT_UNICORN in the Wild

items.title: What happened
items.text: One operator plus two commercial AI tools breached nine agencies; the AI wrote exploits, automated exfiltration, and turned raw server dumps into clean network maps and next-target plans

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: APT_UNICORN made literal: a lone actor operating at the speed and scale of a full team; the reaction-time collapse this playbook is built around

items.title: How it got in
items.text: Gambit attributes success to unpatched software, infrequent credential rotation, and flat (unsegmented) networks: the tools were novel but the techniques (known CVEs, stolen creds, lateral movement) were basic

items.title: The lesson
items.text: You cannot out-react agent-speed offense with human-speed defense: the answer is hardened fundamentals plus agentic detection/containment plus behavioral monitoring of agent-tempo activity

blocks.text: 'APT_UNICORN' is this playbook's fictional framing device (see the opening), not a real designation; this is the real, documented incident that made it literal. The Israeli firm Gambit Security reported that, between December 2025 and February 2026, a single operator compromised nine Mexican government agencies using Claude Code and OpenAI's GPT-4.1 as the operational team: Claude Code generating ~75% of remote commands, with 1,088 prompts producing 5,317 commands across 34 live sessions. A custom tool piped data from 305 internal servers through GPT-4.1 to auto-generate ~2,600 'what to attack next' reports; over 150GB and roughly 195 million identities were exposed (including the SAT tax authority and Mexico City's civil registry). The unicorn turned: the same machine-speed capability that makes Agentic AI the perfect analyst let one person operate like a nation-state. (As reported by Gambit Security and SecurityWeek; verify before quoting externally.)

blocks.heading: A Year of AI-Enabled Threats (ATT&CK Mapping)

items.title: What happened
items.text: Hundreds of real misuse cases analyzed; ~67% used AI for malware, with measurable shifts in technique mix

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Empirical evidence of how attackers actually use AI: directs where defenders should focus the loop

items.title: Playbook link
items.text: Feeds AI Threat Landscape, CTI, and Agentic Threat Hunting (the post-compromise hunting hypotheses)

items.title: The lesson
items.text: Orchestration is the leverage point: defenders should target detection at the post-compromise stage

blocks.text: Anthropic's review of a year of real misuse attempts, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and co-published with Verizon DBIR context. It found that 67.3% of the 832 accounts banned for malicious cyber activity used AI to write malware, with activity shifting toward the post-compromise lifecycle (account discovery, lateral movement), and that scaffolding/orchestration, not raw model skill, was the durable differentiator among capable actors.

blocks.heading: MDASH: Autonomous Vulnerability Discovery

items.title: What happened
items.text: Coordinated AI agents found numerous real vulnerabilities, including 16 new flaws in the Windows networking and authentication stack, with high benchmark scores

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Shows the defensive upside is as real as the offensive threat: agents materially augment security work

items.title: Playbook link
items.text: Supports Red Team, Tools & Tech Stack, and the Frontier picture; evidence for the maturity payoff

items.title: The lesson
items.text: The same autonomous capability cuts both ways, which is why governance and containment are non-negotiable

blocks.text: Microsoft's research on agentic systems for security demonstrated AI agents autonomously discovering software vulnerabilities at scale, including 16 new flaws in the Windows networking and authentication stack, and strong performance on cyber-reasoning benchmarks. A concrete example of Agentic AI's defensive (and dual-use) power in the hands of a major vendor, validating the capability the playbook builds on.

blocks.heading: Claude Code Security: 500+ High-Severity Vulns in Production

items.title: What happened
items.text: 500+ high-severity vulnerabilities surfaced and validated in widely used open-source code with Opus 4.6; released as a defender product in limited preview, since followed by Anthropic's Claude Security (public beta)

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Reasoning-based discovery finds the subtle, context-dependent flaws rule-based static analysis misses, at machine scale

items.title: Playbook link
items.text: Concrete instance of the Tools & Tech Stack defensive agents and the Frontier Red Team program; Human in Command by design

items.title: The lesson
items.text: Defenders who move fast can find and patch the same bugs attackers would, if AI is put to work on defense first

blocks.text: Using Claude Opus 4.6, Anthropic's Frontier Red Team found and validated over 500 high-severity vulnerabilities in production open-source codebases, bugs that had gone undetected for decades despite years of expert review, then began responsible disclosure with maintainers. The capability shipped as Claude Code Security (Feb 2026), which reasons about code like a human researcher, self-verifies each finding to filter false positives, and suggests patches for human approval. The clearest evidence yet that Agentic AI puts a decisive, scalable tool in defenders' hands.

blocks.heading: Accenture Cyber.AI: Agentic SecOps at Scale (Powered by Claude)

items.title: Scan time: 3 - 5 days → under an hour
Coverage: ~10% → over 80%
items.text: Security-testing coverage expanded roughly eight-fold, with a dramatic cut to the critical-vulnerability backlog and a 35% service-delivery improvement (year-over-year cost-reduction framing): the patching/throughput bottleneck attacked directly

items.title: Agent Shield (the 'secure the agents' half)
items.text: Real-time identity controls, threat detection, and runtime protection to protect, monitor, and govern autonomous agents in line with organizational policy and risk tolerance: a productized version of this playbook's agent-as-NHI and containment controls

items.title: Both questions, one platform
items.text: Cyber.AI uses agents to do security work AND secures the agents doing it, on top of Claude's built-in guardrails plus enterprise governance: the red/blue/purple-plus-governance model, deployed

blocks.heading: Critical-Infrastructure Emulation (PNNL)

items.title: What happened
items.text: AI-driven emulation against an ICS/water-treatment sim reconstructed an attack in about three hours instead of multiple weeks

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: A concrete demonstration of the weeks-to-hours compression at the heart of the agentic teaming value case

items.title: Playbook link
items.text: Backs the Use Case & Value Stream Map lead-time story and the Federal/critical-infrastructure relevance

items.title: The lesson
items.text: Agentic teaming makes continuous, comprehensive testing feasible where manual cadence couldn't keep up

blocks.text: An Anthropic + PNNL exercise applied AI adversary emulation against a simulated water-treatment environment (a CISA-relevant critical-infrastructure scenario), compressing what would traditionally take weeks of expert red-teaming into about three hours. A direct demonstration of the lead-time compression the Value Stream Map describes, in a federal/critical-infrastructure context.

blocks.heading: RAITE 2026: Navy Red/Blue AI Test Event

items.title: Scenario 1: Beating a computer-vision detector
items.text: Tasked with defeating a competitor's AI person-detection model, the team built a custom suite of video-stream manipulation attacks on-site and won 5 of 7: video looping (replaying benign footage to hide live activity), gradual feed degradation until detection silently failed, and a steganographic payload hidden in the stream that forced a mission-kill, all built fast by people, not pulled from a product

items.title: Scenario 2: A GenAI 'Model Downgrade' via a poisoned MCP package
items.text: Against a Blue Team with deep observability into its LLM application, the team concealed malicious code inside a benign-looking MCP package: defenders saw the tool run but stayed blind to a malicious model swap underneath it, then watched the team re-adapt the MCP code to a different LLM provider within minutes. A multi-stage enterprise-AI attack, not a simple prompt injection

items.title: Scenario 3: A 360° physical + cyber + ICS attack
items.text: With DIU and MITRE observers watching, the team blended physical tradecraft (ghillie suit, smokescreens, picked locks) with a Wi-Fi foothold and a purpose-built ICS exploit to subvert security cameras, disable a water pump, and deliver a simulated contaminant strike on a water tank, leaving a self-destructing microcontroller implant for persistence

items.title: Why it matters / playbook link
items.text: One federal exercise validates several playbook themes at once: Human in Command, MCP/agentic-supply-chain risk and the observability blind spot (Scenario 2 → Agent Containment's monitoring gap), and combined physical-plus-cyber attacks on OT/ICS water systems (Scenario 3 → the OT, ICS and SCADA play, mirroring the PNNL water-treatment case)

items.title: The lesson
items.text: A capable adversary attacks on several fronts at once: physical access, cyber footholds, and AI manipulation woven into one coordinated operation, so the defense has to be just as integrated. The team's bottom line: mission-ready AI security comes from rigorous, human-led adversarial testing

blocks.text: RAITE (Robust Artificial Intelligence Test Event) is a U.S. Navy AI test-and-evaluation exercise run by Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane. It brings government and industry together for time-boxed, hackathon-style exercises where teams alternate Red (attacker) and Blue (defender) roles against live AI/ML systems to find and expose vulnerabilities before fielding; the 2026 event was held at Playas, New Mexico. An industry red team fielded a cross-functional 'Fusion Cell' built on a deliberate people-over-products philosophy (their framing: 'Crew Over COTS'), building custom attacks on-site with AI-assisted coding rather than relying on a pre-packaged toolkit. Across three red-team scenarios: a computer-vision person-detector, a GenAI/LLM application, and a full-spectrum critical-infrastructure target, the team's self-reported results make this the playbook's most direct account of human-in-command adversarial AI testing in a federal setting. (Source: John Herren, "What RAITE 2026 Taught Us About Mission-Ready AI"; specifics as reported by the author.)

blocks.heading: The 50% Bypass: Why Assume-Breach

items.title: What happened
items.text: Attackers given ten tries still succeed at prompt injection ~50% of the time (International AI Safety Report key update, Nov 2025); the cross-lab study's adaptive attacks beat 12 recent defenses, above 90% for most

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Model-layer guardrails alone are insufficient: quantified proof, not opinion

items.title: Playbook link
items.text: Underpins Agent Containment, Network & Security Controls, and the zero-model-trust stance

items.title: The lesson
items.text: Bound the blast radius with deterministic environment controls; never rely on the model behaving

blocks.text: A cross-lab study on adaptive attacks bypassed 12 recent LLM defenses with attack success above 90% for most, and the International AI Safety Report's November 2025 key update finds that prompt-injection attackers given ten tries still succeed about half the time; a frontier system card separately quantified a single GUI-agent prompt injection succeeding ~17.8% of the time without safeguards. The empirical foundation for the playbook's insistence on structural, not model-only, defenses.

blocks.heading: Mandiant M-Trends 2026: Frontline Reality

items.title: What happened
items.text: Frontline data: ~22-second access hand-offs at initial access, recovery-denial ransomware, and AI woven into adversary workflows

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Independent, real-world confirmation that the threat-to-impact window is collapsing: the case for continuous, machine-speed defense

items.title: Playbook link
items.text: Benchmarks for Metrics & ROI; reinforces Agentic Threat Hunting and the detect→contain→respond lifecycle

items.title: The lesson
items.text: Map your dwell times and recovery dependencies against Mandiant's frontline figures to turn vague concern into targeted investment

blocks.text: Mandiant's flagship annual report, built from real incident-response engagements, is the field's frontline benchmark. The 2026 edition documents attackers moving at machine speed, initial-access hand-offs measured in seconds, alongside stealthy multi-year intrusions and recovery-denial ransomware engineered to defeat restoration. It grounds the playbook's machine-speed thesis in observed adversary behavior, and gives security leaders external benchmarks to map their own dwell times and response capability against.

blocks.heading: Unit 42 Global IR Report 2026: Fastest Attacks at 4x Speed

items.title: What happened
items.text: 750+ incidents analyzed: AI accelerated the fastest attacks ~4x; identity exploited in 89%; multi-surface in 87%; access-to-exfiltration in 72 minutes for the fastest quartile

items.title: Why it matters
items.text: Frontline confirmation that human-speed response can't keep pace, and that identity is the primary battleground for agentic threats

items.title: Playbook link
items.text: Benchmarks for Metrics & ROI; reinforces Zero Trust, Agentic Insider Risk, and surgical Agent Containment

items.title: The lesson
items.text: Centralize human/machine/agent identity governance, eliminate implicit trust, and move to continuous adversarial testing

blocks.text: Palo Alto's Unit 42 analyzed 750+ high-stakes incidents and found adversaries leveraging AI across the attack lifecycle, accelerating the fastest attacks roughly 4x over the prior year, with initial-access-to-exfiltration down to 72 minutes in the fastest quartile. Identity weaknesses were exploited in 89% of investigations and 87% of attacks spanned multiple attack surfaces. A second independent frontline benchmark (alongside Mandiant M-Trends) confirming the threat-to-impact window is collapsing, and that identity and complexity are the adversary's leverage.

blocks.label: Evidence Principle
blocks.text: Every pillar of this playbook traces to documented reality: agentic attacks at scale (GTG-1002), how attackers actually use AI (the ATT&CK mapping), the defensive upside (Microsoft's MDASH vuln-discovery harness), the lead-time compression (PNNL), and why model-only defense fails (the 50% bypass). The strategy isn't a bet on the future: it's a response to what's already happened.

plays.name: Risks and Ethics
plays.title: Risks, Ethics & Guardrails
plays.subtitle: Deploying Agentic AI in SecOps responsibly
plays.summary: The critical risks of agentic SecOps, from the lethal trifecta to blast radius and trusted-user abuse, with guardrails for each.

outline.title: The Lethal Trifecta: Prompt Injection & Exfiltration
How the Field Prioritizes These Risks: MIT Expert Delphi (272 Experts)

items.title: The Lethal Trifecta: Prompt Injection & Exfiltration
items.text: Any security agent combining private-data access + untrusted-content exposure + external communication is trivially exploitable. A malicious log entry, email, or web page can instruct the agent to exfiltrate data: demonstrated against M365 Copilot, GitHub MCP, and Slack AI.
bullets: Break at least one trifecta leg: isolate data, sandbox content, restrict outbound
Separate model calls for ingestion vs. action: never let untrusted content drive privileged actions
Red-team your own agents for prompt injection before production
Monitor agent outbound traffic for anomalous exfiltration patterns

items.title: Autonomous Action & Blast Radius
items.text: Agents that can isolate hosts, block IPs, or change firewall rules can cause outages on false positives. This is OWASP LLM06:2025 (Excessive Agency). Autonomous response needs strict blast-radius limits.
bullets: Explicit 'approval required' gates for high-impact actions
Dry-run mode: agent plans, human approves execution
Least-privilege agent identities (per AI Defense Matrix)
Log every action with full reasoning chain for audit

items.title: Trusted-User Instruction Abuse
items.text: Classifiers and content filters key on untrusted input, but a phished employee pasting a malicious prompt is a trusted-user instruction. Anthropic's red team got Claude Code to exfiltrate AWS keys 24 of 25 times this way, with no classifier catching it. The model layer cannot save you here.
bullets: Deterministic environment containment: sandboxes, VMs, egress controls before model defenses
Deny network by default; confine writes to the workspace; isolate credentials in host keychain
Don't rely on human-in-the-loop approval: ~97% of Claude Code permission prompts get approved (Anthropic, August 2026; approval fatigue)
Defer config/hook parsing until after explicit trust is granted (avoid pre-trust code execution)

items.title: Over-Trust & Over-Automation: The Meta-Risk
items.text: The honest counter-case the skeptics get right: deployed carelessly, Agentic AI makes security worse, not better. This playbook does not claim a lights-out SOC, that agents replace analysts, or that the technology is mature everywhere. Model-only defenses are still bypassed roughly half the time within ten attempts, per the International AI Safety Report's November 2025 key update; agents are confidently and fluently wrong; and naive automation amplifies those errors at machine speed while analyst skills atrophy. The biggest risk in the whole program is believing the demo and over-delegating before the foundations, guardrails, and evaluation are in place.
bullets: Foundations first: sequence AI onto solid triage, tuning, and data quality; never automate a broken process
Human in Command with real escalation thresholds: oversight that cannot quietly become a rubber stamp
Bound blast radius with deterministic containment, not model promises (model-only defenses are bypassed ~50% of the time within ten attempts)
Continuously evaluate the agents (regression suites, drift, verdict quality): an unmeasured agent is an untrusted one
Treat capability claims as indicative and start supervised; expand autonomy only as evidence earns it

items.title: Agentic Memory Poisoning
items.text: Per AgentPoison (arXiv:2407.12784), attackers can backdoor RAG/memory-based agents with <0.1% poison rate and >80% success, no fine-tuning. Poisoned memory creates 'forever-day' risks that are stealthy and hard to find in a sea of data.
bullets: Validate and provenance-check all knowledge-base / RAG content
Monitor memory writes for anomalous embeddings or trigger patterns
Isolate and quarantine memory across sensitive workflows
Apply AI Defense Matrix runtime-data controls: RAG sanitization, memory-poisoning defense

items.title: Agentic Scaffolding as Attack Surface
items.text: Anthropic's research finds that the durable differentiator among high-risk actors is their orchestration scaffolding. Your own MCP servers, tool integrations, and pipelines are themselves an attack surface, covered by OWASP LLM03:2025 (Supply Chain) and Agentic Top 10 ASI04 (agentic supply chain).
bullets: Treat agent orchestration as critical security infrastructure
Audit MCP servers, tool APIs, and plugins for injection and supply-chain risk
Apply MITRE ATLAS ML supply-chain techniques to your own stack
Maintain an AIBOM to track every AI component

items.title: Dual-Use Red-Team Capability
items.text: Agents that autonomously chain exploits are dual-use: the WormGPT/KawaiiGPT pattern shows how fast offensive capability commoditizes. If agent credentials or prompts are compromised, your red-team tooling becomes an attacker's.
bullets: Isolate red-team agents in air-gapped or segmented environments
Require human approval before any execution against production
No production credentials in red-team agent context
Enforce scope: the agent cannot exceed defined target boundaries

items.title: Offense-Defense Asymmetry & the Open-Weight Reality
items.text: A structural asymmetry the field is actively debating: centralized, API-level safety controls don't bind adversaries who run open-weight or jailbroken models, which, once released, can't be recalled and can have their safeguards stripped. So defenders can't assume attackers face the same guardrails they do. The same controls can also impose one-sided friction on legitimate defenders (approval processes, usage policies, occasional over-refusals on offensive-security research). The honest framing is industry-wide, not vendor-specific, and it's documented in the International AI Safety Report 2026 (the offense-defense balance) and reporting on safety constraining defenders more than attackers. It is not an argument against guardrails: probabilistic model defenses fail often (see the International AI Safety Report's ~50% ten-attempt bypass figure), so deterministic, environment-layer controls remain essential regardless of what any single model will or won't say.
bullets: Model the adversary as unconstrained: assume attackers use open-weight/jailbroken models, so design detections and threat models for capabilities the API guardrails wouldn't expose
Use vendor safe-harbor / cyber-verification pathways (e.g., provider verification programs) to authorize legitimate defensive and red-team use rather than routing around controls
Plan for usage-policy and authorization friction in procurement and operating model: pick providers and contract terms that support sanctioned defensive use (see Procurement & Vendor Risk)
Don't rely on model-layer refusal as a security control in either direction; bound capability at the environment layer (containment, least privilege, egress) where the guarantee is deterministic

items.title: Model Availability & Regulatory Dependency
items.text: A frontier capability your program is built around can become unavailable with little warning through forces you don't control: a vendor deprecating or restricting a model, a government export-control or sanctions directive, or a regulatory suspension. Unlike a technical threat, no control prevents the action itself: the exposure is the dependency, and it sharpens precisely where you lean hardest on a single model or provider for a mission-critical function. There is a real tension here: the most capable model is often the one most exposed to being pulled. Treat model access as a single point of failure in critical infrastructure, not a procurement footnote.
bullets: Avoid single-model / single-vendor dependency for mission-critical agentic functions: design for portability so a model can be swapped without re-architecting
Maintain a tested fallback posture: a secondary model (ideally a different provider, or an on-prem / open-weight option) the function can degrade to
Add 'a model or provider becomes unavailable' as an explicit scenario in continuity and DR planning, with a defined switchover RTO
Keep prompts, tools, and guardrails behind a model-abstraction layer rather than hard-wired to one vendor's API
Track regulatory and export-control exposure for the models you depend on, especially for federal and national-security-adjacent work, where directives can apply abruptly

items.title: Recursive Self-Improvement & Self-Modifying Agents
items.text: A fast-emerging, forward-looking risk. As agents become able to write and modify code, including their own scaffolding, tools, and eventually their successors, self-modification erodes the very assumptions containment depends on: a stable behavioral baseline to detect drift against, a fixed tool and permission set, and a known-good version to roll back to. Anthropic's own data shows AI now authoring the large majority of its code and beginning to propose and run its own experiments; the same trajectory in an operational agent means behavior can change between runs without a human ever in the loop, and any latent misalignment can compound rather than stay static. This is not a present-day Critical for most deployments, but it is the risk the whole 'autonomy is a dial, not a cliff' stance exists to manage.
bullets: Treat any self-modification, self-update, or code-deployment capability as a high-impact, human-gated action, never auto-approved (see Agent Containment circuit breakers)
Version-pin and cryptographically sign agent code, prompts, and configs; require explicit human approval and re-authorization to change them
Re-baseline and re-test behavior after every change, and monitor for capability and behavior drift over time, not just point-in-time policy violations
Keep immutable known-good snapshots so any change is reversible, and bound the agent at the environment layer so a self-modified agent still cannot exceed its sandbox

items.title: Multi-Agent Compounding & Trust Chains
items.text: Risk compounds when agents call other agents. A prompt injection or compromised tool in one agent can propagate through inter-agent trust (ATFAA's trust-boundary violations), and human-in-the-loop oversight degrades fastest exactly here: no one reviews agent-to-agent calls at machine speed.
bullets: Enforce per-agent identity and least privilege on every inter-agent call, not just user-facing ones
Sanitize and validate content passed between agents; carry provenance/trust metadata across hops
Constrain agent-to-agent topology: explicit allowlists, no open delegation
Apply agent-enclave isolation so a compromised agent can't reach out-of-scope peers or resources

items.title: Attribution & Non-Repudiation Collapse
items.text: A counterintelligence problem, not just an IT one. When agents act under delegated or shared credentials and AI can fabricate logs, documents, and media, the question 'who actually did this?' can become unanswerable, eroding non-repudiation (NIST SP 800-53 AU-10), incident forensics, and CI attribution. A capable insider can use AI both to take an action and to manufacture deniability or frame another party, and synthetic evidence can mislead an investigation outright.
bullets: Bind every consequential action to a distinct, non-shared cryptographic identity (one credential per human principal and per agent) so each action is signed and attributable: no shared service accounts
Keep tamper-evident, append-only, hash-chained audit logs and protect them as crown jewels (NIST AU-9); a forgeable or rewritable log is no evidence at all

Attach verifiable provenance to generated media and documents (C2PA Content Credentials, signed artifacts); for high-stakes attributions, require chain-of-custody and out-of-band corroboration, not a single artifact
Adopt DCSA/CDSE insider-threat and CI practices and a Continuous-Vetting posture for agents (see Agentic Insider Risk)

items.title: Regulatory Non-Compliance (EU AI Act / NIS2)
items.text: EU AI Act high-risk obligations are deferred to Dec 2, 2027 for Annex III systems by the AI Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since July 2026), but transparency duties still apply from Aug 2, 2026, GPAI obligations are already live, penalties reach €35M / 7% of revenue, and NIS2 enforcement is active. Specific critical-infrastructure, essential-public-service, credit-scoring, and law-enforcement use cases are listed as high-risk in Annex III: an ungoverned, undocumented agentic program is a direct compliance exposure.
bullets: Maintain audit-ready documentation: model cards, data-provenance records, risk assessments, agent action logs
Design to the strictest applicable regime; map controls once to a recognized framework and reuse the evidence
Use continuous control validation to keep the audit trail current rather than scrambling pre-audit
Register high-risk systems where required; engage counsel on specific obligations and scope

items.title: Sequencing Gap: Automating Before Foundations
items.text: Scaling Agentic AI ahead of basic SOC maturity limits the return: on an environment full of false positives, undocumented processes, and noisy telemetry, automation surfaces more to chase rather than less. The fix is sequencing: apply AI first to help build the fundamentals, then scale autonomy on top of them.
bullets: Fix the five fundamentals first: triage discipline, alert tuning, detection optimization, playbook maturity, data fabric
Gate agentic rollout on Maturity Levels 1 - 2 being genuinely met, not just claimed
Ask before automating: would this multiply signal or multiply noise?
Measure detection quality (signal-to-noise) before measuring agent throughput

items.title: Overreliance & Skill Atrophy
items.text: If analysts defer entirely to AI verdicts, judgment atrophies and the team can't operate when AI fails. MIT's AI Risk Repository tracks overreliance and unsafe use as a distinct risk subdomain under human-computer interaction.
bullets: Require analysts to review and challenge AI reasoning, not just approve
Run regular manual-only exercises to keep skills sharp
Policy: AI verdicts are recommendations, not decisions
Train on AI failure modes and known blind spots

items.title: 'Security Theater' Red Teaming
items.text: Per Feffer et al. (arXiv:2401.15897) and Cox's work, AI red teaming often has vague purpose and inconsistent criteria, looking rigorous while proving little. Prompt-spraying can't cover a near-infinite input space.
bullets: Define purpose, artifact, and success criteria before every engagement
Use mathematical risk estimation (e.g. surrogate/transferability methods) over prompt collections
Tie red-team findings to measurable detection-coverage outcomes via the purple loop
Avoid vendors selling 'agentic auto-fix' as a silver bullet

items.title: Data Privacy & Legal
items.text: Security agents handle PII in logs, credential fragments, and personal emails. Sending this to external LLM APIs may violate data-handling obligations, and some workloads now face data-residency/sovereignty requirements.
bullets: Evaluate on-prem or private-cloud LLM deployment for sensitive or regulated data
Data minimization: strip PII before external API calls
Review vendor DPAs for AI security tools; confirm data-residency where required
Apply NIST AI 600-1 data-privacy actions and AI Defense Matrix runtime controls

items.title: How the Field Prioritizes These Risks: MIT Expert Delphi (272 Experts)
items.text: MIT FutureTech's AI Risk Initiative ran a 272-expert Delphi study (its 'Priority AI Risks') on top of the 1,700-entry AI Risk Repository. Headline findings: under current trajectories, 18 of 24 risk domains carry ≥10% probability of a catastrophic outcome within five years (with pragmatic mitigations, experts judged five would remain above that line); the five most-severe risks are dangerous capabilities, competitive dynamics, weapons & cyberattacks (incl. CBRNE), power centralization, and false information; and the three most-vulnerable sectors are Information, Finance, and National Security: the last facing compound exposure as both a target for AI-enabled attacks and a domain where failures cascade. Experts also flagged a responsibility gap: the users and public most exposed are not the developers and governance actors most responsible for addressing the risks. (Expert-judgment Delphi elicitation, not empirical frequency: attribute to MIT FutureTech and verify before quoting.)
bullets: Treat National Security-sector exposure as a design assumption for this program, not an edge case: it is one of the three most-vulnerable sectors
Prioritize controls and detections against the top-five severe risks, especially weapons/cyberattacks and dangerous capabilities, which intersect this playbook's threat model
Use the responsibility gap to frame governance asks: as a deployer, close it with enforceable controls rather than relying on upstream developers' voluntary action
Anchor the 'why now' case in independent expert consensus (MIT) alongside the incident evidence, not vendor claims
