plays.name: AI Fluency
plays.title: AI Fluency: Key Terms
plays.subtitle: A working glossary of the AI security and threat-intelligence vocabulary used in this playbook
plays.summary: A working glossary of the terms that recur across the plays: agentic foundations, attacks, defense, CTI, and federal and DoW.

blocks.text: Shared language keeps a cross-functional program aligned. These are the terms that recur across the plays, grouped for quick reference: agentic foundations, the attack surface, defense and governance, the cyber threat intelligence vocabulary (including CCIRs and PIRs), and federal and DoW terms.
For the public sector framework abbreviations, see the Framework Maps glossary.

items.title: Agent configuration surface
items.text: The files and shared resources that define how an agent behaves: instruction files (AGENTS.md, an open standard now under the Linux Foundation), persona files (SOUL.md), system prompts, and the skills, tools, and memory a swarm shares. For a defender it is both a first-class attack surface and a governance artifact: whoever edits these files, or poisons a shared resource a swarm reads, redirects the agents, so it must be versioned, access-controlled, integrity-checked, and review-gated.

items.title: Agency vs. Autonomy
items.text: Two separately governed axes of an agent: agency is the scope of actions it is permitted to take (needs boundaries and permission systems); autonomy is its independence in deciding when to act (needs oversight and behavioral controls). The axes of AWS's four-scope agentic matrix.

items.title: Agent
items.text: An LLM (or system of them) given tools, memory, and an objective so it can take multi-step actions across systems.

items.title: Agentic AI
items.text: AI that pursues a goal autonomously: it plans, calls tools, observes results, and re-plans, rather than producing a single response. The basis of autonomous red/blue/purple teaming.

items.title: Agentic Memory
items.text: Persistent state an agent carries across steps or sessions; a stealthy attack surface (see memory poisoning / AgentPoison).

items.title: Autonomy Spectrum
items.text: The range from guided assistant to end-to-end agent. Autonomy is earned through eval evidence, and every notch up the dial pairs with tighter circuit breakers.

items.title: Human-in-the-Loop vs. Human in Command
items.text: In-the-loop = a person approves individual actions (degrades under approval fatigue). In-command = people own strategy, policy, and exceptions while agents do the repeatable work.

items.title: LLM (Large Language Model)
items.text: A model trained on vast text that generates and reasons over language; the engine inside most current security agents.

items.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
items.text: An open standard for connecting agents to tools and data sources. Convenient, and itself part of the agentic supply-chain attack surface.

items.title: Orchestration / Scaffolding
items.text: The architecture that chains an agent's steps and decisions. Anthropic's research identifies this, not raw model skill, as the durable differentiator of high-risk actors.

items.title: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
items.text: Augmenting a model's input with retrieved documents/knowledge at query time; powerful, but a poisoning and data-leakage surface.

items.title: SOC
items.text: Security Operations Center: the team and function that monitors, detects, and responds to threats. The operating environment this whole playbook is built to modernize.

items.title: Tool Use / Function Calling
items.text: An agent's ability to invoke external functions or APIs (scanners, SIEM queries, ticketing) to act on the world, not just describe it.

items.title: AI Red Teaming
items.text: Structured adversarial testing of an AI system to find safety and security failures (prompt injection, jailbreaks, harmful outputs) before attackers do. Distinct from classic network red teaming; increasingly automated and continuous.

items.title: Confused Deputy
items.text: A privileged component tricked into using its authority on an attacker's behalf, the classic frame for most agent abuse: the agent is the deputy, the injected content is the trick.

items.title: Context Flooding
items.text: Overwhelming a model's limited context window with bulk or repetitive input so the real payload is pushed out of the analysis, and, secondarily, to inflate compute cost and trip rate limits. A denial-of-analysis technique against AI triage pipelines; the operational face of OWASP LLM10:2025 (Unbounded Consumption).

items.title: CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration)
items.text: The standard MITRE taxonomy of software-weakness types, e.g. CWE-89 SQL injection, CWE-918 SSRF, that gives corpora, scanners, and scoring a shared vocabulary so findings line up. Labeled test suites tag each case by CWE; the OWASP Benchmark and NIST SARD / Juliet are organized around it.

items.title: Data / Model Poisoning
items.text: Manipulating training, fine-tuning, or RAG data to distort behavior or plant backdoors. OWASP LLM04:2025.

items.title: Deception Prompt
items.text: Harmful-looking content (apparent weapon or exploit instructions) planted in an artifact to trip a defensive AI's safety guardrails, forcing a refusal or abort before it reaches the real payload. Weaponizes the defender's own safety behavior as a denial-of-analysis vector, distinct from prompt injection, which hijacks behavior rather than halting it.

items.title: Dual-Use
items.text: The property that the same AI capability serves defense, sanctioned offense, and adversary attack alike: only intent and guardrails differ.

items.title: Encoding Evasion
items.text: Hiding malicious content from filters and AI analysis with ROT13, Base64, foreign-language, or other transformations so the payload decodes only downstream. Also called prompt encoding; countered by normalizing and decoding input before analysis.

items.title: Excessive Agency
items.text: OWASP LLM06 in the 2025 list (LLM03 in 2026): an over-permissioned agent taking consequential actions on malicious or mistaken instructions. The core blast-radius risk.

items.title: Indirect Prompt Injection
items.text: Malicious instructions planted in content the agent will later read (web page, email, document, tool output) rather than typed by a user: the primary exploitation path for tool-using agents.

items.title: Jailbreak
items.text: Input crafted to bypass a model's safety guardrails so it produces restricted output or behavior.

items.title: Memory Poisoning (Agentic)
items.text: Implanting false or malicious entries in an agent's persistent memory or knowledge store so the corruption survives sessions and steers future actions (e.g., AgentPoison).

items.title: Model / Data Extraction
items.text: Using a system's normal interface to exfiltrate the model itself or the data it holds.

items.title: Model Evasion (Adversarial Example)
items.text: Input that looks normal to humans but forces a wrong model prediction, e.g., to slip past an ML detector.

items.title: Model Inversion / Membership Inference
items.text: Querying a model to reconstruct sensitive training data or determine whether a record was in the training set.

items.title: Non-Human Identity (NHI)
items.text: A machine/agent identity (service account, workload, agent) that needs the same governance as a privileged human: unique ID, least privilege, monitoring.

items.title: Prompt Injection
items.text: Malicious instructions, direct or hidden in retrieved/user content, that hijack a generative model's behavior. OWASP LLM01 and the hardest agentic problem to fully solve.

items.title: Slopsquatting
items.text: Registering packages under names LLMs tend to hallucinate so AI-generated code imports attacker malware: supply-chain squatting aimed at machine-written software.

items.title: The Lethal Trifecta
items.text: Simon Willison's term: any agent combining private-data access + untrusted-content exposure + external communication is exploitable for exfiltration. Break at least one leg.

items.title: Tool Poisoning (MCP)
items.text: Hiding malicious instructions or behavior inside a tool's description or output so any agent that loads the tool is compromised: the MCP-era supply-chain variant of injection.

items.title: TRAIT&R (Taxonomy of Rogue AI Tactics and Routines)
items.text: Google DeepMind's threat-modeling taxonomy for a hypothetical misaligned internal AI agent, built on MITRE ATT&CK. It maps the tactics and techniques such an AI insider could use: inserting vulnerabilities, entrenchment, persisting context and goals across memory resets, evading AI monitors via collusion or obfuscated reasoning, across three objective classes: loss of control, work sabotage, and direct harm. The Agentic-AI counterpart to ATT&CK/ATLAS for the insider-threat case.

items.title: Decision trace
items.text: The full provenance of a triage, hunt, or response decision: what inputs were weighed, what alternatives were considered, what precedent was cited, what was ruled out and why, the outcome, and who or what made the call. Today this trace evaporates the moment an incident closes or a playbook completes; only the outcome survives. Coined for security operations by Mike Palitto, adapting the rules-versus-decision-traces distinction from Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg.

items.title: Context graph (security context graph)
items.text: Decision traces joined to the security entity graph, so that querying an entity (a user, device, application, or address) returns both the history of what happened to it and the reasoning behind every decision made about it. Precedent becomes searchable, and finding prior decisions for an alert pattern becomes a graph traversal. Named by Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg (Foundation Capital, 2025) as the missing system of record that captures not just what happened but why; the security-operations translation is Mike Palitto.

items.title: Decision plane
items.text: The reasoning layer of security operations, distinct from the data plane. The data plane (events, alerts, normalized incidents) is what the SIEM and XDR deliver well. The decision plane is the missing layer: the record of how judgments were made, why hypotheses were ruled out, and what precedent governed the call. Detection platforms have largely solved the data plane; the decision plane is still unbuilt in most environments.

items.title: Negative decision trace
items.text: The record of why an action was not taken: why an alert was dismissed, why a hunt concluded without findings, why a suppression was applied. It is the most absent artifact in security operations, because platforms capture the outcome (no action taken) but not the reasoning that led there. It is also the artifact a breach review most needs, since the unanswerable question after an incident is usually why the activity was never seen.

items.title: Meta threat modeling
items.text: Using an AI model to threat-model an AI system, while recognizing that the modeling assistant itself joins the attack surface. A document loaded as context can steer the assistant toward a confidently but structurally wrong threat model, so its inputs must be verified and its context isolated like any other in-scope component. Named in the 2026 Toreon guide on AI-assisted threat modeling.

items.title: Acceptance by omission
items.text: The failure mode where AI-generated security findings, dozens of threat scenarios produced in seconds, are accepted into the register because no reviewer has the stamina to challenge each one. Volume and fluency get mistaken for validity, and hallucinated or duplicate threats become tracked work. The countermeasure is bounded batches with per-item human adjudication.

items.title: DICE
items.text: A four-step threat-modeling method from Toreon: Description of the context, Identification of threats, Countermeasure definition, and Evaluation. It maps cleanly onto where AI accelerates (scaffolding the system description, populating STRIDE tables, cross-referencing OWASP LLM and MITRE ATLAS) and where human judgment stays non-negotiable (validating completeness and owning residual-risk decisions).

items.title: AI Firewall / LLM Gateway
items.text: An inspection layer in front of the model that screens prompts and outputs for injection, data leakage, and policy violations: it pairs with, never replaces, network egress controls.

items.title: AI threat boundary
items.text: The line around the model and its data pipeline inside which everything is treated as untrusted, because the model's behavior can't be verified deterministically. Authorization decisions stay outside it (CoSAI).

items.title: AIBOM (AI Bill of Materials)
items.text: An inventory of every AI component: models, datasets, dependencies, tools, used to track and govern the AI supply chain.

items.title: Automated Reasoning (Formal Verification)
items.text: Proving an AI output correct against a formal logic model of policy rather than sampling it for quality: deterministic where evals are probabilistic; the guardrail class behind Cedar-style verified authorization. Requires formalizable policy and a sound model of the environment.

items.title: Blast-Radius Control
items.text: Limiting the damage an agent can do if misused or compromised, via sandboxes, egress controls, least privilege, and approval gates.

items.title: Capability-Based Control
items.text: Granting an agent explicit, scoped capabilities (what data may flow where) instead of trusting model judgment; the design behind DeepMind's CaMeL. Deterministic bounds over probabilistic defenses.

items.title: Chain-Detection Score
items.text: Of N planted vulnerability chains, cases whose components are each individually low or medium but combine into a critical exploit, how many the scanner identifies as chains rather than as isolated findings. Tests the scanner's hardest and most over-claimed capability: reasoning across findings to report emergent severity.

items.title: Circuit Breaker
items.text: An automatic, threshold-triggered halt on agent activity (spend, action rate, anomaly score): the machine-speed kill switch pre-wired before an incident, not improvised during one.

items.title: Containment / Agent Enclave
items.text: Deterministic environment isolation (gVisor, VMs, sealed enclaves) so out-of-scope resources aren't even reachable: defense that doesn't depend on the model behaving.

items.title: Continuous Control Validation
items.text: The compliance analogue of the purple loop: continuously testing that controls (least privilege, egress limits, logging) still hold, producing a living audit trail.

items.title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM)
items.text: A program model that replaces periodic, cycle-based patching with a standing loop (discover exposures, prioritize by real-world exploitability and asset exposure, validate, remediate, verify) run continuously. Coined by Gartner (2022); now the organizing frame for machine-speed vulnerability management as discovery-to-exploit windows compress from weeks to hours.

items.title: Egress Filtering
items.text: Default-deny outbound network control with destination allowlisting: the concrete defense that breaks the lethal trifecta's external-communication leg.

items.title: Ground-Truth Set
items.text: A curated corpus of code targets where every vulnerability, and every clean spot, is already labeled, so a scanner's output can be scored objectively as a true positive, false positive, or miss. The foundation of any accuracy measurement; assembled from pre-labeled corpora (SARD, Juliet, the OWASP Benchmark), real code pinned at known-vulnerable CVE versions, deliberately benign 'looks-scary-but-safe' code, and hand-built vulnerability chains.

items.title: Guardrails
items.text: Layered controls (input/output filters, policy checks, allowlists, confirmation gates) that constrain agent behavior at runtime.

items.title: Least agency
items.text: OWASP's extension of least privilege to agents (Agentic Top 10, 2026): give an agent only the autonomy a task needs, limiting what each tool can do, how often, and where, not just what it can reach.

items.title: Least Privilege
items.text: Granting an identity only the access it needs for its task, nothing more: the antidote to privilege creep in long-running agents.

items.title: Model Cards / Provenance
items.text: Documentation of a model's training, intended use, and limitations; provenance/attestation records prove where models and data came from (supply-chain integrity).

items.title: Red / Blue / Purple Teaming
items.text: Red emulates adversaries; Blue defends and detects; Purple closes the loop, turning red findings into blue improvements. Agentic AI lets the purple loop run continuously.

items.title: Severity-Tiered False-Positive Rate
items.text: False-alarm rate broken out by severity rather than reported as one blanket number, because a false 'critical' in front of a decision-maker is far more damaging than a false 'low.' The false-positive metric that most determines a scanner's credibility in a demo or a report (see the Quality Metrics group on the Metrics and ROI play).

items.title: Shadow AI / Shadow Agents
items.text: Ungoverned models, bots, or agents adopted outside security's view: unowned non-human identities with real access and no lifecycle; the agentic twin of shadow IT.

items.title: Threat Modeling (STRIDE)
items.text: The structured practice of enumerating how a system can be attacked before it ships. STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) is the classic taxonomy, extended for AI/ML to cover poisoning, model theft, and inversion.

items.title: Token exchange
items.text: Swapping one security token for another scoped to a specific downstream resource, standardized in OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693). For agents, it produces a short-lived token that represents the user plus the agent, instead of reusing the user's own token.

items.title: VulnOps
items.text: Operating vulnerability response as a continuous, AI-accelerated discipline: triaging, patching, and validating at the cadence AI-driven discovery now forces (CSA's Mythos-ready framing).

items.title: Zero Model Trust
items.text: Treat the model as an untrusted component: assume it can be misled, exhausted, or extracted, and bound what it can do (this playbook's term).

items.title: Zero Trust (NIST SP 800-207)
items.text: NIST's Zero Trust architecture standard: every access is a per-session decision under continuously evaluated dynamic policy, no implicit trust. The familiar verify-explicitly / least-privilege / assume-breach triad is Microsoft's formulation. Applied to agents: authenticate every action, start permissions at zero, sandbox by default.

items.title: Hunt hypothesis
items.text: A specific, testable statement about suspected adversary activity that scopes a threat hunt: for example, that a given technique would surface as a named artifact in a particular data source. Increasingly produced at scale by domain-scoped CTI agents that triage many sources into candidate hypotheses, then gated by deterministic scoring (structure, validity, relevance, references) so only the strongest reach a human hunter.

items.title: CCIR (Commander's Critical Information Requirement)
items.text: Borrowed from military doctrine: the critical information leadership needs to make timely decisions. In security, the small set of things that must escalate immediately, typically composed of PIRs (threat) plus friendly-force and decision requirements.

items.title: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI)
items.text: Evidence-based knowledge about threats: actors, capabilities, intent, TTPs, used to inform security decisions. Directs what the red/blue/purple loop works on first.

items.title: Intelligence-Led Security
items.text: An operating model where CTI drives detection priorities, emulation focus, and strategy, rather than testing everything equally.

items.title: IOC (Indicator of Compromise)
items.text: An artifact: hash, IP, domain, registry key, that signals a likely intrusion. The raw material of tactical intelligence and detection.

items.title: IoPC (Indicator of Prompt Compromise)
items.text: Thomas Roccia's term for patterns or artifacts inside a prompt, or the model's output, that signal an attempt to exploit, abuse, or misuse an LLM (injection, jailbreak, adversarial tokens, data extraction). The prompt-layer analogue of the IOC; lets defenders hunt adversarial prompts with detection rules such as NOVA instead of IP, domain, or hash indicators.

items.title: MITRE ATT&CK / ATLAS
items.text: ATT&CK is the knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques; ATLAS is its adversarial-ML extension. Both anchor coverage measurement in the purple loop.

items.title: Operational Intelligence
items.text: Knowledge about ongoing campaigns and adversaries: their nature, intent, and timing, used to guide and speed up incident response.

items.title: PIR (Priority Intelligence Requirement)
items.text: A prioritized question the intelligence effort must answer to support a decision (e.g., 'Which threat actors are targeting our sector with AI-enabled techniques?'). PIRs scope and focus collection.

items.title: Strategic Intelligence
items.text: The broad view of present and future threat landscape that informs leadership's resource, architecture, and roadmap decisions.

items.title: Tactical Intelligence
items.text: Technical, often short-lived detail (IOCs, malware signatures, specific TTPs) that drives detection engineering and SOC triage.

items.title: Time-to-Exploit / Patching Deficit
items.text: The collapsing gap between disclosure and exploitation (M-Trends 2026 estimates a mean of minus seven days) set against fixed patching capacity: Glasswing's core math, and why containment comes before cleverness.

items.title: Tradecraft (Agentic)
items.text: The practiced discipline of operating without exposing yourself: sourcing, validating, and acting on intelligence while leaving no exploitable trail. In Agentic SecOps, the habits that separate operators from tool users: identity hygiene, containment-first defaults, eval-gated autonomy, and evidence preserved before action.

items.title: TTP (Tactics, Techniques & Procedures)
items.text: How an adversary operates, from high-level goals (tactics) to specific methods (procedures). The shared language of MITRE ATT&CK and adversary emulation.

items.title: ATO / cATO
items.text: Authorization to Operate: formal sign-off that a system may run at an accepted risk level. Continuous ATO (cATO) replaces point-in-time certification with ongoing, monitoring-backed authorization.

items.title: CUI
items.text: Controlled Unclassified Information: sensitive but unclassified data requiring safeguarding; governed by NIST SP 800-171 on non-federal systems, SP 800-53 on federal ones.

items.title: DoD Impact Levels (IL2 - IL6)
items.text: DISA Cloud Computing SRG tiers by data sensitivity: IL2 (public), IL4 (CUI and other mission-critical data), IL5 (higher-sensitivity CUI / unclassified NSS), IL6 (classified up to SECRET).

items.title: DoW
items.text: Department of War: the secondary title the Department of Defense has used since September 2025, under Executive Order 14347. Its name in law is still Department of Defense, and documents issued before then say DoD.

items.title: FedRAMP
items.text: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program: standardized security authorization for cloud services used by the federal government, with continuous monitoring.

items.title: FISMA
items.text: Federal Information Security Modernization Act: requires US agencies to secure information systems against a NIST control baseline, authorized via the Risk Management Framework.

items.title: JSIG
items.text: Joint SAP Implementation Guide: the RMF control overlay for Special Access Programs and SCIF/classified systems; a technical supplement to NIST SP 800-53 and CNSSI 1253 under a SAP Authorizing Official.

items.title: NSS (National Security System)
items.text: A system handling national-security functions or data; subject to CNSS policy and, for classified work, tighter control overlays than ordinary federal systems.

items.title: RMF (Risk Management Framework)
items.text: NIST SP 800-37's lifecycle for categorizing systems, selecting and assessing controls (SP 800-53), authorizing, and monitoring: the spine of FISMA and DoW authorization.

blocks.label: Why Fluency Matters
blocks.text: A program that spans red, blue, purple, governance, and leadership only works if everyone shares the vocabulary. Tactical/operational/strategic intelligence, PIRs and CCIRs, zero model trust, and blast-radius control aren't jargon: they're the common language that lets the loop run and the strategy hold together.

outline.title: A Field Guide to Getting Fluent
The Two Questions That Frame Everything
Build It to Believe It: Hands-On Labs
Frameworks and Tools to Know Cold
Red · Offense: attacking AI, and adversary emulation
Blue · Defense: securing the GenAI stack
Purple · Automation across red, blue & purple

blocks.text: The rest of this playbook is a reference and a strategy; this play is a curriculum: a structured path to get fluent enough to contribute to a red/blue/purple Agentic-AI project. It assumes you already know SOC fundamentals (alerts, telemetry, the kill chain, MITRE ATT&CK, EDR/SIEM) but are newer to AI/ML security specifically, and it builds from "what is an AI agent" up to running exercises against agentic systems. A realistic pace is three to four weeks part-time. The companion Study Guide document expands every part below with a full glossary, a deeper attack-surface walk-through, and active-recall self-check questions; treat the linked primary sources (OWASP, MITRE ATLAS, NIST, CSA) as the authority, since this space renumbers frameworks and ships tools monthly.
blocks.heading: A Field Guide to Getting Fluent

blocks.text: Almost everything in Agentic-AI security falls into one of two questions, and a teaming project touches both. Question A: how do we secure the AI agents themselves? Here the agent is the target: you protect an autonomous system against prompt injection, tool/MCP misuse, memory poisoning, jailbreaks, and model/weight theft. Question B: how do we use AI agents to do security work? Here the agent is the tool: autonomous triage, investigation, and response (the "agentic SOC") on defense, and AI-accelerated recon, exploitation, and attack simulation on offense. The red/blue/purple lens applies to both. The crucial insight is that the two converge: a defensive AI agent (Question B) is itself an agentic system that needs securing (Question A). The agent that triages your alerts can be prompt-injected through a single malicious log entry.
blocks.heading: The Two Questions That Frame Everything

blocks.text: A realistic pace is three to four weeks part-time. Each week builds on the last, and every phase maps to the plays that go deeper. The track below is the route, with Case Studies (including the RAITE 2026 federal exercise) as the Week 4 capstone.
blocks.heading: A Three-to-Four-Week Path

blocks.text: Reading makes you fluent; building makes you dangerous, in the good way. Work the ladder below in order, foundational to advanced, and run every exercise only in an isolated, explicitly authorized lab, never against production or systems you don't own.
blocks.heading: Build It to Believe It: Hands-On Labs

blocks.text: Seven bodies of work define the vocabulary (covered in depth across Frameworks, AI Threat Modeling, and Agentic Insider Risk): the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (app-level LLM risk) and the OWASP Agentic Security Initiative / Agentic Top 10 (autonomous-agent risk: goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity/privilege abuse, agentic supply chain, memory poisoning, inter-agent attacks, blast radius, rogue agents); the OWASP Non-Human Identities Top 10 (per-agent identity, secrets, and privileges); MITRE ATLAS (the "ATT&CK for AI"); the NIST AI RMF plus the AI 100-2 adversarial-ML taxonomy (evasion, poisoning, privacy); Google SAIF; and CSA's MAESTRO seven-layer threat model plus the AI Controls Matrix. On tooling, know PyRIT (Microsoft's open-source AI red-teaming toolkit, the de facto starting point: RAMPART and Azure's AI Red Teaming Agent are built on it, and Clarity ships alongside RAMPART as a design-stage planning aid), plus garak and DeepTeam as scanners. The automation/purple side leans on Atomic Red Team, Caldera, and CrewAI-style red-team agents, orchestrated through SOAR and detection-as-code pipelines.
blocks.heading: Frameworks and Tools to Know Cold

blocks.text: Training maps onto the two framing questions and across all three teaming colors. The grid below lays out the SANS AI-security courses by team: offense (attacking AI and adversary emulation), defense (securing the GenAI stack), and the purple/automation backbone, each with its GIAC certification, where one exists. Confirm current offerings and prerequisites on the SANS AI focus-area page, since these are new and evolving. Beyond the grid: SEC595 (Applied Data Science and AI/Machine Learning for Cybersecurity Professionals) adds a foundational footing and the wider catalog carries defensive certs (continuous monitoring, SOC, DFIR); for self-paced, hands-on practice the Hack The Box AI Red Teamer path, now capped by the Certified Offensive AI Expert (COAE), launched April 2026, is ML-heavy, with Microsoft Learn connecting these concepts to the product stack. TryHackMe adds two browser-based, exam-backed credentials worth noting: AI1 (offensive AI security: prompt injection, RAG attack and defense, AI supply chain and data poisoning against live systems, mapped to the OWASP LLM Top 10) and SAL1 (a hands-on, entry-level SOC-analyst cert), both affordable and practical. Separately, for teams that already hold enterprise licenses, Immersive (formerly Immersive Labs) adds hands-on offensive and defensive ranges: adversary-simulation, offensive-malware, and exploit-development tracks plus live CVE labs in paired attack/defend variants mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, for building muscle memory on the tradecraft beneath the AI-specific work here. For a standardized, exam-validated benchmark of this skill set, CompTIA's SecAI+ (CY0-001, launched February 2026) maps almost one-to-one onto these two questions: 40% securing AI systems, 24% AI-assisted security, plus AI-for-cyber fundamentals and AI governance/risk/compliance.
blocks.heading: Certifications & Courses

blocks.text: Formal certifications are one track; the Black Hills Information Security (BHIS) / Antisyphon / Active Countermeasures ecosystem is the other: practical, instructor-led, and radically accessible (a select group of courses run on a Pay-What-You-Can model). Two courses map directly onto this playbook's AI focus: Antisyphon's "Agentic AI for Threat Hunting" (Faan Rossouw) teaches harness engineering and the seven systems of an agentic hunting architecture (the Question-B "use AI agents for SecOps" skill set, hands-on), and BHIS's "Attacking, Defending, and Leveraging AI-LLM Systems" (Derek Banks and Brian Fehrman) covers leveraging AI for security tasks (log parsing, discovery and exploitation, code review) through agentic assistance, custom tooling, and automated security validation, with both Questions A and B in one course. Their free weekly AntiCasts add focused AI sessions: adapting incident response to AI threats; AI's effect on cloud IAM, monitoring, and governance, that count toward CPE. For tabletop practice, Backdoors & Breaches (BHIS and Active Countermeasures' incident-response card game) runs structured IR exercises, free online or with physical decks, that pair naturally with the Agent Incident Response play's playbooks; and REKCAH Publishing's security comics and zines are a low-friction way to carry security-awareness narrative to a broader team. Treat this as the affordable, hands-on complement to the SANS/GIAC track above: strong for building real skills and for upskilling a team on a budget.
blocks.heading: Hands-On & Community Training (BHIS / Antisyphon)

items.label: Antisyphon: Agentic AI for Threat Hunting
Antisyphon: Attacking, Defending & Leveraging AI-LLM Systems

blocks.text: A short, curated listen-list is the ambient layer of this path: for real-world grounding and for keeping pace with a field that moves weekly, not a substitute for the hands-on work above. Four shows at different altitudes: Darknet Diaries (Jack Rhysider) for narrative case studies of how breaches actually unfold, general infosec, but the tradecraft, social engineering, and incident dynamics make the abstract concrete (BHIS / REKCAH even adapted an episode into a comic); the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Podcast (Microsoft Threat Intelligence; Sherrod DeGrippo signed off as host in July 2026) for current threat intelligence and the AI threat landscape from a major CTI shop; the MLSecOps Podcast (Protect AI, now part of Palo Alto Networks) for AI/ML-security depth, prompt injection, model poisoning, Agentic AI, and the same frameworks this playbook cites; and Daniel Miessler's Unsupervised Learning for offensive-AI strategy and the security / AI / national-security intersection. Kept deliberately to four: a listen-list earns its place by pointing to the few that matter, the same discipline the Resource Index follows. Find each show through its own site rather than a single platform.

items.title: Foundations
items.text: What agents are (a reasoning core plus tools, memory, and orchestration, running a perceive → reason → act → observe loop), the two framing questions, and the core frameworks.

items.title: The Attack Surface
items.text: How agentic and AI systems fail, layer by layer: prompt/input, tool/MCP, memory/RAG, multi-agent, identity, model/supply-chain, vision, and infrastructure.

items.title: Offense & Defense
items.text: Red-team methodology and tooling, then the defensive controls and the agentic SOC that answer them.

items.title: Integration & Practice
items.text: Purple-team automation, the hands-on labs below, and the certification and course map.

items: PyRIT: Install PyRIT and run a scored red-team pass against a model endpoint you control.
Prompt injection: Stand up a deliberately vulnerable agent (an LLM with web-fetch and send-message tools) and achieve indirect prompt injection through content it ingests.
MCP: Attack a local MCP setup: tool shadowing via a homoglyph name, a name collision, and a parameter-injection path.
Adversarial ML: Run a vision-evasion attack and build a simple adversarial patch against an image classifier you own.
Model extraction: Run a model-extraction experiment, then add rate-limiting and watch the detection signal appear.
IaC range: Stand up a disposable firing range with infrastructure-as-code (Terraform / Ansible).
Adversary emulation: Run continuous adversary emulation (Atomic Red Team or Caldera) and confirm what your logging catches.
Detection-as-code: Wire one detection-as-code rule and prove it fires in a pipeline: add a RAMPART / pytest check so a known injection is caught on every build.
Mapping: Map every successful attack to its OWASP / ASI and ATLAS IDs.
Purple loop: Run a mini purple loop: take one red finding, build a detection and a guardrail, and prove the detection fires on re-attack.

blocks.label: Learning Principle
blocks.text: Reading gets you fluent; building gets you dangerous, in the good way. Use the companion Study Guide's self-check questions for active recall, treat the primary sources (OWASP, ATLAS, NIST, CSA) as the authority over any summary, and run every hands-on exercise only in isolated, explicitly authorized environments. This is a study aid, not operational authorization.

plays.name: Resource Index
plays.title: Resource Index
plays.subtitle: 243 key sources, organized for quick reference
plays.summary: All 243 key sources behind the playbook, grouped by theme, from frameworks and federal standards to threat intelligence.

items.title: NIST SARD: Software Assurance Reference Dataset
items.text: NIST's public-domain ground-truth corpus for testing software-assurance tools: 450,000+ labeled test cases across C, C++, Java, PHP, and C#, covering 150+ weakness classes (CWEs), from small synthetic cases to production code. The authoritative, federally credible source of labeled targets for measuring scanner precision and recall (NIST IR 8561).

items.title: Juliet Test Suite (within NIST SARD)
items.text: The widely used CWE-tagged collection inside SARD, built by the NSA's Center for Assured Software for testing static-analysis tools: tens of thousands of cases across C/C++, Java, and C# (this link opens the C/C++ suite; the Java and C# suites are separate SARD records), each shipping paired 'bad' (vulnerable) and 'good' (fixed) variants with manifests marking exact flaw locations, so you measure both detection and false alarms. Public domain (CC0).

items.title: OWASP Benchmark: SAST/DAST Accuracy Testbed
items.text: A fully runnable Java and Python testbed (Java v1.2: 2,740 cases across 11 CWE categories) where each case carries a single intentional weakness marked true- or false-positive in an answer-key CSV (expectedresults), with automated scorecard tooling that scores SAST/DAST tools on precision, recall, F1, and false-positive rate. Purpose-built to put a number on detection accuracy.

items.title: AISI: Engineering Playbook (Frontier-Eval Infrastructure)
items.text: The UK AI Security Institute's open guide to building frontier-AI evaluation infrastructure, in five layers: Evaluate (a reproducible, agentic-capable test framework), Isolate (containment matched to the risk of the work), Connect (audited, cost-controlled model-provider access), Run (the researcher's compute and data platform), and Scale (supercomputer-scale inference for the largest open-weight models). Built on the open-source Inspect toolkit; usable component-by-component or as a reference architecture for standing up an evaluation platform from scratch.

items.title: AGENTS.md: Open Standard for Agent Instructions
items.text: A simple, open Markdown format that gives coding and agentic tools a predictable home for task context, build and test conventions, and security considerations: a README-style file for agents, used across 60,000+ repositories and now stewarded under the Linux Foundation via the Agentic AI Foundation. The defender frame: this file is part of the agent configuration surface and must be governed and integrity-checked, not just authored.

items.title: SOUL.md: Agent Persona and Identity Format
items.text: Captures who an agent is: its values, boundaries, and persona, rather than what it can do; a convention from the OpenClaw agent project (the site is written in an AI agent's own voice) for giving agents continuity of identity across sessions. It matters to defenders because persona files shape agent behavior and therefore belong inside the same versioning, integrity, and review controls as the rest of the configuration surface.

items.title: CSA: AI Controls Matrix (AICM)
items.text: Vendor-agnostic framework for cloud-based AI systems: this is the v1 record (released July 2025, updated October 2025), which links AICM v1.1 (June 2026, 247 control objectives) as the newest version. The v1 record holds 243 control objectives across 18 security domains, analyzed by five pillars including control type and control applicability and ownership, built on CSA's Cloud Controls Matrix. Ships the AI-CAIQ questionnaire, implementation and auditing guidelines in role-specific versions, and a STAR for AI Level 1 submission guide for filing a self-assessment to the STAR Registry; maps to ISO 42001, ISO 27001, NIST AI RMF 1.0, and BSI AIC4.

items.title: CSA: MAESTRO (Agentic AI Threat Modeling)
items.text: Seven-layer threat-modeling framework purpose-built for Agentic AI (Multi-Agent Environment, Security, Threat, Risk and Outcome); the basis for OWASP's Multi-Agentic System Threat Modeling Guide.

items.title: NIST: AI 100-1 (AI Risk Management Framework)
items.text: The foundational US trustworthy-AI framework (AI RMF 1.0, January 2023; NIST states the 1.0 text is being revised under the White House AI Action Plan): GOVERN / MAP / MEASURE / MANAGE, plus the AI RMF Playbook.

items.title: NIST: AI 100-2 (Adversarial Machine Learning Taxonomy)
items.text: The standard taxonomy of attacks on predictive and generative AI: evasion, poisoning, privacy, and misuse, with mitigations; the shared vocabulary behind this playbook's poisoning and evasion coverage.

items.title: NIST: AI 600-1 (GenAI Profile)
items.text: 12 GenAI risk categories + 200+ suggested actions; the GenAI companion to the AI RMF.

items.title: NIST: Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF)
items.text: The Govern/Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover backbone the AI Defense Matrix maps AI controls onto.

items.title: NIST: SP 1800-35 (Implementing a Zero Trust Architecture)
items.text: NCCoE practice guide, final June 2025: 24 collaborators built 19 example zero trust implementations aligned to SP 800-207, from enhanced identity governance to software-defined perimeters, microsegmentation and SASE. It has no AI or agent content; its Use Case G, a non-person subject calling an API, is the nearest to agent access.

items.title: NIST: SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture)
items.text: The foundational Zero Trust architecture standard: seven tenets, every access a per-session decision under continuously evaluated dynamic policy, no implicit trust from network location or asset ownership.

items.title: NIST: SP 800-61r3 (Incident Response Recommendations)
items.text: The CSF 2.0-aligned incident-response framing (Apr 2025): preparation-first and lifecycle-integrated; the backbone for the Agent IR runbook anatomy.

items.title: OWASP: Agentic Top 10 (2026)
items.text: The OWASP GenAI Security Project's Top 10 for Agentic Applications (December 9, 2025), whose ASI01 to ASI10 identifiers this playbook cites: agent goal hijack, tool misuse and exploitation, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain vulnerabilities, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, and rogue agents. It extends least privilege to least agency.

items.title: OWASP: AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet
items.text: Concise, implementation-focused best practices for securing Agentic AI, key agent risks (prompt injection, tool abuse, memory poisoning, goal hijacking, excessive autonomy, cascading failures, denial-of-wallet, supply chain) mapped to nine control categories as of September 2026: tool least-privilege, input validation, memory isolation, human-in-the-loop, output validation, monitoring, multi-agent trust boundaries, data protection, and secure agent testing. Worth loading as an agent skill so the assistant applies the controls during agent design.

items.title: OWASP: AI Exchange (324-page PDF)
items.text: OWASP's self-described go-to comprehensive AI security guide; the four-category 'essentials' model, now the foundation for its AI Security Essentials overview under the SANS/OWASP alignment.

items.title: OWASP: AI Exchange Threat Advisor
items.text: Interactive AI threat-modeling assistant from the OWASP AI Exchange: describe a system and it runs a tailored interview to surface applicable threats and guide risk assessment and mitigation, drawing on the Exchange's 300-plus pages and decision tree. A fast first-pass Agentic-AI threat model. Access note: the advisor runs on NotebookLM and requires Google sign-in. The link points at the Exchange overview page that describes and launches it.

items.title: OWASP: AI Exchange Threat Model & Decision Tree
items.text: The OWASP AI Exchange's structured threat-model decision tree: a six-branch walk across model-behavior, training-data, model-theft, and input-data risks, mapping each decision point to threats, controls, and notes. The reference flow behind the Threat Advisor and a clean scaffold for modeling agentic systems by hand.

items.title: OWASP: AI Security Verification Standard (AISVS) 1.01
items.text: Community-driven catalog of testable security requirements for AI-enabled systems: 12 requirement categories, from training-data integrity and model supply chain through orchestration/agentic and MCP security to adversarial robustness and monitoring, across three assurance levels; the AI counterpart to OWASP's Application Security Verification Standard. The verification layer of the OWASP AI stack: where the Top 10s enumerate risk, AISVS specifies what to test to prove a control works. Led by Jim Manico (founder) with Otto Sulin, Rico Komenda, and Russ Memisyazici.

items.title: OWASP: GenAI Security Project (hub)
items.text: The top community hub for GenAI security: LLM Top 10, Agentic Top 10, red-teaming and security solutions guidance.

items.title: OWASP: LLM Top 10 (2025)
items.text: The ten critical LLM-application risks in their 2025 numbering, which the playbook's framework tags keep; the 2026 edition re-ranks them.

items.title: OWASP: LLM Top 10 (2026)
items.text: The 2026 edition: the same ten risks re-ranked, eight changed ordinal, none added or dropped, with System Prompt Leakage re-scoped as Hidden Context Exposure. It draws the boundary this suite works either side of: this list owns the model as a component, the Agentic Top 10 owns it once it becomes an actor. Framework tags here remain 2025-numbered.

items.title: OWASP: LLM Top 10 Deep Dive (Oligo)
items.text: Examples + mitigations for each LLM Top 10 entry.

items.title: OWASP: MCP Top 10 (2025, beta)
items.text: The canonical OWASP security reference for Model Context Protocol deployments, official project led by Vandana Verma Sehgal, the 2025 list (MCP01:2025 to MCP10:2025), in beta release and pilot testing. Ten risk categories, including Token Mismanagement & Secret Exposure (MCP01), Tool Poisoning (MCP03), Shadow MCP Servers (MCP09), and Context Injection & Over-Sharing (MCP10). This suite leans on MCP throughout: gateways, tool-call mediation, agent enclaves, and this is its dedicated security primary; AISVS category 10 (MCP Security) carries the verification side.

items.title: OWASP: Memory Is a Feature, and an Attack Surface (ASI06, May 2026)
items.text: Agentic Top 10 ASI06 (Memory & Context Poisoning) via Cisco's MemoryTrap finding in Claude Code: a routine dependency install reached persistent memory, hooks, and the system-prompt layer, surviving across sessions and reboots (fixed in v2.1.50). Treat memory and retrieved context as security-relevant state, not convenience features.

items.title: OWASP: Non-Human Identities (NHI) Top 10
items.text: Ranked risks for the service accounts, API keys, and agent identities that outnumber humans in production: NHI1 improper offboarding, secret leakage, overprivileged NHIs, long-lived secrets. The identity frame this playbook applies to agents as governed non-human insiders.

items.title: AI Defense Matrix (Zeltser & Yu)
items.text: NIST CSF 2.0-aligned control matrix across AI asset classes; now crossmaps nine AI security frameworks (NIST IR 8596, CSA AICM, ISO 42001, SAIF, SANS, MITRE ATLAS v5.6.0, OWASP AI Exchange, LLM Top 10, Agentic Top 10 Dec 2025) with a change log and a Considered-and-Rejected scope section. Zeltser and Yu's origin blog (SANS, Jul 2026) adds the design rationale, conceived at RSAC 2026 as the dedicated security-for-AI companion to Yu's Cyber Defense Matrix: CSF's six functions crossed with eight AI asset classes (workload platforms, orchestration tools, generated code, gateways and routers, models, training data, runtime data, agent identities; the matrix has since renamed orchestration tools to "coding and orchestration tools" and gateways and routers to "AI traffic"), downloadable as CSV/YAML/Markdown. Companion to the Cyber Defense Matrix for the security-FOR-AI half; AI FOR security stays with CDM. CC BY-SA 4.0.

items.title: CIS: CIS Controls v8.1 AI Companion Guides (AI/LLM, Agents, MCP)
items.text: Three companion guides (Apr 2026, with Astrix and Cequence) that extend the CIS Critical Security Controls to AI: securing models/LLMs, autonomous agents (planning, tool-use, excessive agency), and the MCP protocol layer, reinterpreting existing Safeguards rather than inventing a new framework.

items.title: CMU SEI: AI Adoption Maturity Model (Jun 2026)
ENISA: Multilayer Framework for Good Cybersecurity Practices for AI (FAICP)
items.text: The EU cybersecurity agency's layered framework for securing AI across its lifecycle: a base ICT/infrastructure layer, an AI-specific layer for machine-learning-unique properties, and a sector-specific layer. The European counterpart to the NIST and OWASP material here.

items.title: GAIA Top 10 (Mandiant): Good AI Assessment
items.text: Mandiant's Good AI Assessment (GAIA) Top 10: a risk-based framework from frontline offensive-security engagements, paired with the Secure Development of Generative AI Applications report. Field lessons from that report: secure the whole SDLC not just the prompt, sign conversation context with HMAC, drop user-supplied system messages, keep appsec basics, and build an AI early-warning system.

items.title: Google: SAIF (Secure AI Framework)
items.text: Enterprise AI security framework with an AI agent security section, the SAIF Map, 15 cataloged risks with mapped controls, and the risk self-assessment, now joined by a newer Agent Risk Self-Assessment (saif.google/agent-risk-self-assessment). Implementation-side detail lives in the OCISO paper (cf. Google: Implementing SAIF Controls in Google Cloud).

items.title: Microsoft: Threat Modeling AI/ML Systems
items.text: Extends STRIDE and the SDL to AI/ML-specific threats: poisoning, model stealing, adversarial perturbation, inversion.

items.title: MITRE: ATLAS
items.text: Adversarial-ML extension to ATT&CK.

items.title: SANS: AI Security Maturity Model (2026)
items.text: 5-stage Protect/Utilize/Govern model with Agentic-AI guidance; mapped to NIST, EU AI Act, ISO 42001, OWASP.

items.title: Toreon: Meta Threat Modeling: Using AI to Threat Model Your AI System
items.text: By Asma Oualmakran (Toreon, June 2026). Walks the DICE method phase by phase for an AI system, mapping where an LLM accelerates threat modeling (system-description scaffolding, STRIDE population, OWASP LLM and MITRE ATLAS cross-referencing) against where human judgment is non-negotiable, and names two failure modes this suite now carries: the threat-modeling assistant becoming part of the attack surface, and acceptance by omission under AI-generated volume.

items.title: AI Incident Database (AIID)
items.text: Real-world AI harm catalog.

items.title: Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills (community; NOT Anthropic)
items.text: Independent, Apache-2.0 skills library for security agents by Mahipal Jangra (@mukul975): 800+ agentskills.io-format skills across 30+ domains, mapped to ATT&CK, ATLAS, D3FEND, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST AI RMF and MITRE F3. Widely misattributed to Anthropic by its name and branding; the repo itself states it is unaffiliated. Cited as the worked case for third-party skill-pack provenance risk: treat as untrusted code, pin the audited commit, diff updates. COMMUNITY tier.

items.title: Mapping AI
items.text: Open-source map of the U.S. AI policy landscape: the people and organizations shaping AI governance, what they believe, and how they connect.

items.title: MIT: AI Incident Tracker (Jun 2026 update)
items.text: The MIT AI Risk Initiative's operational companion to the AI Risk Repository: an LLM pipeline classifies 1,600 real-world reports from the AI Incident Database across five taxonomies, Harm Severity (10 harm types), EU AI Act risk tier, Causal, Domain, and Subdomain, turning raw incident reports into queryable trend data already cited by the 2026 World Disasters Report and Time. The tracker's June 30, 2026 update post, AI Incident Tracker June 2026 Update, is the methodological headline: a pilot validation set a human-human expert baseline (itself only 0.31 QWK on Harm Severity, expert disagreement is real), scored eight models against consensus labels, and after targeted prompt refinement Claude Opus 4.6 matched or exceeded the human baseline on all five taxonomies on the pilot sample, with a held-out review set planned as the tracker scales. Read it twice: once as an incident-trend resource, and once as a worked example of validating an LLM-as-analyst pipeline against expert baselines before trusting it, the same ground-truth-and-scoring discipline this playbook's evaluation thread advocates.

items.title: MIT: AI Risk Repository
items.text: 1,700+ risks; plus a 272-expert 'Priority Risks' Delphi study ranking severity, the most-vulnerable sectors (incl. National Security), and a responsibility gap.

items.title: Responsible AI Collaborative
items.text: Non-profit behind the AI Incident Database.

items.title: DISA: DoD Cloud Computing SRG (Impact Levels)
items.text: Defines IL2/IL4/IL5/IL6 by data sensitivity; builds DoD-specific controls on top of FedRAMP.

items.title: DoD: JSIG (Joint SAP Implementation Guide)
items.text: RMF overlay for SAP/SCIF classified systems; technical supplement to NIST SP 800-53 and CNSSI 1253.

items.title: FedRAMP: Program & Marketplace
items.text: Standardized authorization for cloud services; IL2 by reciprocity to FedRAMP Moderate.

items.title: NIST: SP 800-171 (Protecting CUI)
items.text: Controls for Controlled Unclassified Information in non-federal systems.

items.title: NIST: SP 800-37 (Risk Management Framework)
items.text: The RMF lifecycle underpinning FISMA authorization and ATO/cATO.

items.title: NIST NCCoE: Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization (Concept Paper, Feb 2026)
items.text: NCCoE concept paper (February 5, 2026; Booth, Fisher, Galluzzo and Roberts) scoping a possible demonstration of identity standards for software and AI agents: identifying agents as distinct from people, OAuth 2.0 and policy-based authorization, delegation from user to agent, and logging. Candidate standards named: MCP, OAuth 2.0 and 2.1, OpenID Connect, SPIFFE/SPIRE, SCIM and NGAC. Comments closed April 2, 2026; on September 29, 2026 NIST published a summary of the comments on the project's resource hub. The paper asks questions rather than prescribing a design.

items.title: NIST: IR 8547: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (draft)
items.text: NIST's transition roadmap (initial public draft, November 2024): how quantum-vulnerable algorithms get deprecated and replaced across federal systems, anchored to NSM-10's 2035 primary target with per-algorithm disallow dates. The scheduling layer over the FIPS trio; draft status carried deliberately: watch for the final.

items.title: NIST: Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (FIPS 203/204/205, Aug 2024)
items.text: The August 13, 2024 trio that ended the wait for quantum-safe primitives: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, module-lattice key encapsulation), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, module-lattice signatures), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, stateless hash-based signatures). Framed for the agentic estate: long-lived agent identities, channel crypto, and signed audit trails are exactly the surfaces a harvest-now-decrypt-later adversary records today to break later. Migration is a when, not a whether. Anchor is the FIPS 203 record; 204 and 205 are linked from it.

items.title: NSA: CNSA 2.0 (Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite)
items.text: NSA's quantum-resistant algorithm suite for National Security Systems: the algorithm selections NSA announced in September 2022, required for NSS by the updated CNSS Policy 15 (2025) and detailed in the CNSA 2.0 FAQ, built on the NIST post-quantum standards, with phased, category-specific adoption deadlines set out in the FAQ (software and firmware signing first). Where commercial estates get options, national-security systems get a mandate: the NSS half of this suite's PQC treatment.

items.title: NSA: MCP Security Design Considerations for AI-Driven Automation (May 2026)
items.text: NSA AI Security Center cybersecurity information sheet (May 20, 2026) on Model Context Protocol deployments. It treats MCP's gaps as design problems: the protocol does not bind a session to an identity, authorization is optional, and bearer tokens have no defined lifecycle. Its recommendations include: prefer maintained MCP projects, design for trust boundaries, validate tool parameters, treat dynamic tool discovery with caution, constrain and sandbox tool execution, sign and verify messages, filter and monitor outputs, log every invocation, track and patch MCP vulnerabilities, and scan for exposed MCP servers.

items.title: CDSE: Insider Threat & CI Toolkits (DCSA)
items.text: DCSA's Center for Development of Security Excellence: free insider-threat and counterintelligence toolkits, job aids, and potential-risk-indicator guides, the human-side practices to adapt to the agent (non-human-identity) context.

items.title: DCSA: Adjudication and Vetting Services (AVS)
items.text: The sole authority for security-clearance eligibility of non-IC DoW personnel (formerly the DoD CAF, later DCSA's Consolidated Adjudication Services, which AVS absorbed in 2024); applies the SEAD-4 (Security Executive Agent Directive 4) adjudicative guidelines and pairs an eligibility decision with Continuous Vetting: the human model behind continuous agent monitoring.

items.title: DCSA: Counterintelligence & Insider Threat (DITMAC)
items.text: The federal government's lead for counterintelligence, insider threat (via the DoD Insider Threat Management and Analysis Center), personnel vetting, and Trusted Workforce 2.0 / Continuous Vetting: the model behind continuous behavioral monitoring of agents.

items.title: NITTF: National Insider Threat Policy & Minimum Standards
items.text: ODNI/NCSC hub (an archived page, no longer updated) for the task force established by E.O. 13587 (October 2011) under joint leadership of the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence; the president directed agencies with access to classified information to establish insider-threat detection and prevention programs and the NITTF to assist them, then issued the National Insider Threat Policy and the Minimum Standards by presidential memorandum in November 2012. Its stated primary mission is developing a government-wide insider-threat program for deterring, detecting, and mitigating insider threats, taking into account risk levels and the distinct needs, missions, and systems of individual agencies; the page also carries the program guide, the maturity framework, and hub-operations training.

items.title: Anthropic: DoD / CDAO Partnership
items.text: CDAO prototype agreement (July 14, 2025; $200M ceiling) for frontier AI in national-security missions; Claude Gov + accredited Claude for Enterprise. On March 3, 2026 the Department of War designated Anthropic a supply chain risk, and on September 25, 2026 the D.C. Circuit denied Anthropic's petitions for review.

items.title: ASD ACSC: Opportunities for AI in Cyber Defence (May 2026)
items.text: Joint guidance from the Australian Signals Directorate's ACSC, co-sealed by the Canadian, New Zealand and UK cyber security centers, on using AI to strengthen cyber defense: maps AI use to the ISM security functions, gives principles for secure adoption, and supplies vendor questions for defenders, the defensive-opportunity counterpart to the Five Eyes 'Careful Adoption' risk guidance. Use cases span AI-assisted asset discovery, risk-based patch prioritization, and vulnerability-chain analysis.

items.title: CISA: Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology (Apr 2026)
items.text: Joint guide (April 29, 2026) from CISA, the Department of War, and the Department of Energy, with the Department of State, the FBI, and NIST credited as participating agencies, on applying zero trust principles to operational technology within its legacy, operational, and safety constraints: asset visibility, supply-chain risk management, and identity and access management on an assume-breach footing that puts uninterrupted operations, safety, and reliability first, aligned to the NIST CSF 2.0 functions.

items.title: CISA: BOD 26-04 Implementation Guidance: Forensic Triage (Jun 2026)
items.text: Companion guidance published alongside the directive and updated on a rolling basis: baseline forensic-triage steps for prompt vulnerability response, scoping, evidence preservation and collection, critical patching and stabilization, containment and control, triage analysis, escalation decision, with a who/what/where/when evidentiary standard, a written triage report as the agency record, and the escalate-to-IR-or-stand-down fork. KEV entries may carry CVE-specific triage steps that take precedence.

items.title: CISA: BOD 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (Jun 2026)
items.text: Binding Operational Directive ordering FCEB agencies to triage vulnerabilities across four criteria: asset exposure, KEV status, exploit automatability, post-exploitation impact, with a three-day class plus forensic triage for the worst, fixed-day classes of 3, 14, and 60 days in between, and fix on system upgrade for the lowest; supersedes the prior remediation directives. Explicitly motivated by AI-accelerated discovery and exploitation. FCEB-binding, DoW bellwether.

items.title: CISA: CI Fortify: Advice for Isolating Vital Systems (Jul 2026)
items.text: Joint CI Fortify guidance (July 28, 2026) from CISA and ASD's ACSC with the FBI and international partners: practical steps for critical-infrastructure organizations to identify vital operational technology and enabling systems, map their connections, and set separation points so those systems can be isolated from all other networks and keep essential services running through a cyber incident or geopolitical crisis.

items.title: CISA: Principles for the Secure Integration of AI in OT (2025)
items.text: Joint guidance (December 3, 2025) co-authored by CISA and the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre in collaboration with NSA AISC, the FBI, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, Germany's BSI, and the Netherlands, New Zealand, and UK National Cyber Security Centres: nine authoring agencies. Focuses on ML- and LLM-based AI and AI agents in operational technology, though it may also be applied to traditional statistical modeling and other logic-based automation, and outlines four principles owners and operators can follow: understand AI, consider AI use in the OT domain, establish AI governance and assurance frameworks, and embed safety and security practices into AI-enabled OT systems. Explicitly voluntary: it does not create policies, impose requirements, or mandate actions.

items.title: Five Eyes: Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services (May 2026)
items.text: The first joint Five Eyes guidance in this index written specifically for Agentic AI (ASD ACSC, CISA, NSA, and the Canadian, NZ, and UK cyber centers). Five risk categories (privilege, design & configuration, behavioral, structural, accountability), cryptographically anchored agent identity with short-lived credentials, and an explicit instruction to prioritize resilience, reversibility, and containment over efficiency until evaluation methods mature.

items.title: Microsoft: A CISO's Guide to Securing AI (Federal & DIB)
items.text: Public-sector CISO framing for securing AI across federal, DIB, and defense entities on the Microsoft stack.

items.title: NSA AISC: AI Data Security (May 2025)
items.text: Joint cybersecurity information sheet (May 22, 2025) from NSA's AI Security Center, CISA, the FBI and the Australian, New Zealand and UK cyber centers: data security across the AI lifecycle, three risk areas (the data supply chain, poisoned data and data drift), provenance and signing of training data, and a trusted computing environment built on zero trust architecture. It builds on Deploying AI Systems Securely and predates agent-specific guidance.

items.title: NSA AISC: Deploying AI Systems Securely (Apr 2024)
items.text: Joint cybersecurity information sheet (April 15, 2024) led by NSA's AI Security Center with CISA, the FBI and the Australian, Canadian, New Zealand and UK cyber centers, for organizations deploying AI systems someone else built: apply secure by design and zero trust to the deployment architecture, assume breach, and harden, sandbox and monitor the environment. It covers machine learning systems, not agents.

items.title: Anthropic + NNSA: Nuclear Safeguards
items.text: Nuclear-risk classifier, 96% accurate in preliminary testing, live on Claude traffic.

items.title: Anthropic + PNNL: Critical Infrastructure
items.text: AI adversary emulation against a CISA water-treatment sim: 3 hrs vs. weeks.

items.title: Anthropic: AI models on realistic cyber ranges (Jan 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's January 16, 2026 update on its cyber-range evaluations, work begun with Carnegie Mellon's CyLab and continued with Incalmo: the vendor reports that current Claude models can now complete multistage attacks on simulated networks of dozens of hosts with nothing beyond standard open-source tools.

items.title: Anthropic: Auto Mode Is Now the Default in Claude Code (Aug 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's claude.com post (August 7, 2026): auto mode becomes the default for Pro, Max and Team plans, on Anthropic's data that manual review turns habitual. An update of October 22, 2026 says it rolls out as the default for new sessions in most Claude apps on those plans, and that Enterprise admins get an email before it becomes the default for their organizations. Users approve 97% of permission prompts (Anthropic, August 2026), yet reject 39% of plans presented for approval. Anthropic's earlier engineering posts (March and May 2026) gave 93%; this August 2026 post gives no measurement period or population.

items.title: Anthropic: Claude Code Security (defenders)
items.text: Agentic vuln scanner; 500+ validated high-severity vulns found in production open-source with Opus 4.6, patches for human review.

items.title: Anthropic: Containing Claude (engineering)
items.text: Agent containment retrospective: sandboxes, VMs, egress controls, blast-radius bounding.

items.title: Anthropic: Disrupting AI Espionage (GTG-1002)
items.text: Anthropic reports the GTG-1002 operation as the first documented large-scale AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign, 80 - 90% autonomous by its estimate.

items.title: Anthropic: Fable 5 Cyber Safeguards & Cyber Jailbreak Severity Framework (Jul 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's public draft of a Cyber Jailbreak Severity (CJS) rubric, developed with Glasswing partners, scoring a jailbreak on four axes: capability gain, breadth of capability gain, ease of weaponization, and discoverability, summed into bands from CJS-0 (informational) to CJS-4 (critical), where the computed score is a floor that can be escalated but never reduced. It ships alongside a disclosure of Fable 5's safety classifiers, which sort cyber requests into four tiers rather than blanket-blocking: prohibited (ransomware, wipers, ICS/SCADA sabotage, C2, backbone attacks), high-risk dual-use (penetration testing, exploit development, privilege escalation, container escape), low-risk dual-use, and benign, the last explicitly naming SOC analysis, patch management, malware reverse-engineering, and incident response, behind a deliberately wide safety margin that trades false positives for assurance. Two reasons it earns a place: it is a rare worked severity rubric a red team can actually score findings against, using the same capability-gain-and-discoverability logic an adversarial-evaluation harness needs; and its safety margin, which the post says deliberately blocks some benign uses out of caution, is a documented reason legitimate defensive cyber prompts are sometimes refused. Feedback goes to cyber-safeguards@anthropic.com, and a HackerOne program accepts Fable 5 jailbreak submissions.

items.title: Anthropic: Frontier Red Team
items.text: National-security AI research: cyber capabilities, exploit finding, critical-infrastructure defense, LLM misuse.

items.title: Anthropic: Introducing Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 (Sep 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's September 2026 release page: the vendor states Claude Mythos 5.1 is available only through its trusted access programs, with safeguards designed for cybersecurity and life sciences work, and currently only to a set of US organizations.

items.title: Anthropic: LLM ATT&CK Navigator (2026)
items.text: 832 malicious accounts mapped across all 14 ATT&CK tactics; orchestration is the new risk differentiator.

items.title: Anthropic: Mapping a Year of AI-Enabled Threats
items.text: Companion report: 67.3% used AI for malware, shift to post-compromise, ATT&CK gaps; co-published in Verizon DBIR.

items.title: Anthropic: Measuring LLMs' impact on N-day exploits (Jun 2026)
items.text: Measured frontier-model uplift on N-day exploit development: 8 working Firefox exploits across 18 patches and 8 full Windows kernel privilege-escalation chains from binary diffing alone, first exploit within an hour of patch release. Quantifies the reaction-time collapse: patch diffing falls from expert-weeks to an afternoon and a few thousand dollars.

items.title: Anthropic: Mythos Preview & Project Glasswing
items.text: Frontier model autonomously finding/exploiting zero-days; basis of Project Glasswing, whose open-source findings Anthropic tracks on its coordinated vulnerability disclosure dashboard (red.anthropic.com/2026/cvd).

items.title: Anthropic: Project Glasswing: Securing critical software for the AI era (Apr 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's April 7, 2026 launch page for Project Glasswing: the vendor reports Mythos Preview scoring 83.1% on the CyberGym vulnerability reproduction benchmark, against 66.6% for Opus 4.6.

items.title: Anthropic: Redeploying Fable 5 (Jun 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's June 30, 2026 statement that the US export controls applied to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 12 had been lifted: the vendor reports Mythos 5 restored for a set of US organizations after US government approval and Fable 5 available globally again from July 1.

items.title: Anthropic: When AI Builds Itself (Recursive Self-Improvement)
items.text: The Anthropic Institute's analysis of AI accelerating AI development (Claude authoring 80%+ of the code merged into Anthropic's codebase, proposing experiments) and the implications of recursive self-improvement; notes Glasswing has shifted cyber defense's bottleneck from finding vulnerabilities to patching them.

items.title: Alan Turing Institute: CETaS (Emerging Technology & Security)
items.text: UK national AI institute's national-security center: autonomous cyber defense, AI evaluation frameworks, research-security threats, and Defence AI (DARe/AIDA) with the MoD.

items.title: DOE: Genesis Mission
items.text: National AI initiative launched by Executive Order in November 2025, uniting DOE's 17 national laboratories with industry: Anthropic among the founding collaboration-agreement partners. At the inaugural Genesis Mission Summit (Jul 22, 2026) DOE reported more than $800M in committed partner support through the Genesis Mission Consortium: 17 labs, 5 NNSA plants and sites, and 41 partner organizations; compute and credits, foundational-model access, cloud infrastructure, expertise, and direct funding, alongside the first projects selected through the Genesis Mission RFA.

items.title: FLI: AI Safety Index (Summer 2026)
items.text: Independent frontier-lab safety benchmarking from the Future of Life Institute: an expert panel grades nine leading AI companies across six safety domains and dozens of indicators (evidence cutoff June 2026). Cited here for its framework-maturity findings: published safety frameworks sometimes lack quantitative thresholds, genuinely independent audits, and clear decision authority, and existential-safety scores are weak industry-wide. Useful third-party evidence for the governance case that a framework on paper is not an enforced one.

items.title: Germany: DE-AISI (KI-Sicherheitsinstitut, Jun 2026)
items.text: Announced June 8, 2026 after a National Security Council session chaired by Chancellor Merz, headlined by heise as a possible reaction to Claude Mythos. Bundles German federal capacity to analyze frontier-model capabilities and risks (security and safety alike), launches as a virtual institution on BSI and Bundesnetzagentur structures, and aims at exchange with peer institutes (UK AISI et al.) and common international standards.

items.title: NIST: Gödel Proof: Continuous Monitor-and-Update for AI (Jun 2026)
items.text: NIST's announcement of Vassilev's peer-reviewed proof (IEEE S&P): no finite guardrail set is universally robust against adversarial prompts, so the prescribed model is standing red teams, continuous guardrail updates, and operational resilience, with the defensive goal an economic one: make new exploits cost more than attackers' resources.

items.title: RAND: Advancing U.S.-UK Cooperation to Secure Frontier AI (2026)
items.text: Interim RAND-Oxford report (June 8, 2026) elevating frontier AI security to strategic-asset level: five clusters (hardened access, secure development and supply chain, monitoring and incident response, personnel security, physical security) plus bilateral recommendations for joint AI threat-intelligence infrastructure, red-team and model-evaluation support, and regular joint AI crisis exercises. Policy-level convergence on the continuous-testing, tabletop-exercised posture this playbook operationalizes.

items.title: Small Wars Journal: Ubiquitous Technical Surveillance and the Renewal of Irregular Warfare
items.text: Doctrine for operating under pervasive, AI-correlated surveillance (UTS), the CIA-labeled existential condition, and the countervailing signature-reduction and digital-force-protection practices.

items.title: Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond: Generative AI at Work (NBER, Nov 2023)
items.text: NBER field study of a generative AI assistant for customer-support agents: issues resolved per hour rose 14% on average and 34% for novice and low-skilled workers, with minimal impact on the most experienced. Field evidence that AI augments the people using it rather than replacing them.

items.title: DORA: State of AI-assisted Software Development (Sep 2025)
items.text: Google's DORA research (nearly 5,000 technology professionals): AI's primary role is an amplifier, magnifying high performers' strengths and struggling organizations' dysfunctions; the greatest return comes from platform quality, workflow clarity, and team alignment rather than the tools. AI and maturity compound.

items.title: IBM IBV: 2025 CDO Study (Nov 2025)
items.text: IBM Institute for Business Value survey with Oxford Economics of 1,700 senior data and analytics leaders (Jul to Sep 2025): only 26% are confident their data can support new AI-enabled revenue streams, 79% are early in defining how to scale and govern AI agents, and 84% say their data products already provide significant competitive advantage; the evidence base for sequencing data readiness before autonomy.

items.title: Microsoft: Towards Humanist Superintelligence
items.text: Suleyman's MAI vision: controllable, human-centered AI that serves people, not replaces them.

items.title: Stanford HAI: Human-Centered AI
items.text: Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI: independent academic grounding for the human-in-command, augmentation-not-replacement thesis.

items.title: Anthropic: Expanding Project Glasswing (Jun 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's June 2, 2026 update: the vendor reports extending Project Glasswing to approximately 150 new organizations based in more than 15 countries.

items.title: Anthropic: Project Glasswing: An initial update (May 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's May 22, 2026 progress report: the vendor reports Mythos Preview found an estimated 6,202 high or critical severity vulnerabilities in open-source projects, and the post links the program's coordinated vulnerability disclosure dashboard.

items.title: Cotool: BlueBench (Windows Enterprise Intrusion)
items.text: Blue-team model evaluation on REAL intrusion data (not synthetic): 3.9M+ events across 40 log tables from an actual Windows AD attack chain (RDP spray, Mimikatz, WMI lateral movement, DC replication), with every detection rule re-executed against the live dataset so a rule that does not run scores zero. Key finding (Sep 2026 leaderboard, 24 models, 40 scored tasks each): the best guided detection-engineering score (95.8%) runs well above the best open-ended incident-response report score (83.5%), reinforcing that human judgment stays in the loop. The page also notes that run completion does not rule out a refusal, a concrete reminder to evaluate whether a model will actually perform legitimate defensive work, not just whether it is capable. Vendor research (Cotool, with Threat Hunting Labs data); tier accordingly.

items.title: CSA: NIST's Gödel Proof: Static Guardrails Are Insufficient (Jun 2026)
items.text: Enterprise read of the Vassilev result: point-in-time audits systematically underestimate residual risk, so assess the discovery-to-update cadence rather than control presence; re-architect guardrails to hot-updateable gateway layers (input and output); and treat vendors shipping static safety configurations as elevated supply-chain risk. Cites refuse-then-comply fine-tuning at 72% / 57% success against frontier models.

items.title: CSA: Project Glasswing: Discovery Outpaces Patching
items.text: Research note on the discovery-to-remediation gap: 10,000+ high/critical vulns across partners in month one, ~6% of the findings disclosed to open-source maintainers patched as of May 22, 2026, 28.3% of newly exploited CVEs in Q1 2025 hit within 24h (VulnCheck's figure), NVD under structural strain.

items.title: CSA: The AI Vulnerability Storm (VulnOps / Mythos-ready)
items.text: Board-level CISO briefing (Apr 2026; Gadi Evron, Rich Mogull, and SANS's Rob T. Lee, with contributing authors including Jen Easterly, Bruce Schneier, Chris Inglis, Rob Joyce, Heather Adkins, Joshua Saxe, Sounil Yu, John Stewart, Katie Moussouris, Dave Lewis, and Maxim Kovalsky, plus the 250 CISOs who redlined it live): AI-driven vulnerability discovery is collapsing the disclosure-to-exploit window faster than current operating models can absorb. It frames 'VulnOps' as a permanent organizational capability and structures action across this week / 45 days / 12 months, reinforcing the reaction-time-collapse thesis.

items.title: CSO Online: When AI Safety Constrains Defenders
items.text: Lays out the defender-side friction case: defenders navigate approval processes and occasional refusals while attackers using open-weight or bypass techniques (EchoGram, multi-turn) face no such limits, the 'friction is largely one-sided' argument, with the explicit caveat that the fix is safety designed for defensive use, not removing it. Backs the offense-defense asymmetry risk entry.

items.title: IAPS: Asymmetry by Design (differential access)
items.text: Policy research proposing 'differential access', deliberately giving vetted defenders broader AI access than the open market, as a way to tilt the offense-defense balance toward defense. The constructive counterpart to the asymmetry problem.

items.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
