items.text: The flagship international scientific assessment of frontier AI (second edition, Feb 2026, Bengio-chaired, 100+ experts, 30+ governments). Its offense-defense balance section documents that defenders face adoption barriers attackers don't, and that open-weight models compound the challenge since their safeguards can't be recalled. The authoritative source for the asymmetry framing.

items.title: International AI Safety Report: Second Key Update: Technical Safeguards and Risk Management (Nov 2025)
items.text: The report's November 25, 2025 key update on technical safeguards, which says prompt-injection success rates reported by AI developers have been falling slightly over time, yet attackers given ten tries still succeed about half the time.

items.title: NIST: NVD Operations Update for Record CVE Growth (Apr 2026)
items.text: NIST's April 15, 2026 notice moving the National Vulnerability Database to risk-based enrichment: CVEs in CISA's KEV catalog, in software used by the federal government, and in EO 14028 critical software are enriched first, the rest are marked lowest priority and not scheduled for immediate enrichment, and NIST reports CVE submissions rose 263% between 2020 and 2025.

items.title: OpenAI: GPT-Red: Self-Improvement via Automated Red Teaming (Jul 2026)
items.text: Internal-only automated red-teaming model trained with self-play RL: an attacker co-trained against diverse defender LLMs at the scale of OpenAI's largest post-training runs, folded directly into production training and strong enough to break nearly every model it is pitted against, internal and production alike, up to and including GPT-5.5. OpenAI reports 6x fewer failures on its hardest direct prompt-injection benchmark for GPT-5.6 Sol vs. its best production model four months prior (0.05% failure against GPT-Red's direct injections); on a replicated Dziemian et al. indirect-injection arena GPT-Red succeeded in 84% of scenarios where human red-teamers managed 13% against GPT-5.1; an early version discovered a novel direct-injection class, "Fake Chain-of-Thought" insertion, that ran at ~95% success on GPT-5.1 and now lands below 10% on GPT-5.6 Sol. Live-agent cases: a vending-machine agent (all three malicious objectives achieved; disclosed, safeguards in testing) and a Codex CLI data-exfiltration suite, with the gains verified not to come from over-refusal. The model stays out of deployment, the second-lab proof point for the offense-defense flywheel beside the Anthropic material; the paper, GPT-Red: Automated Red Teaming via Self-Play at Scale (arXiv 2607.26115, July 28, 2026), is the secondary citation.

items.title: Palo Alto Networks: Beyond Human Oversight (Frontier AI Era, Jun 2026)
items.text: Policy point-of-view from Nicole Quinn (Jun 2026): governance and response systems built for human cadence cannot absorb machine-speed compromise. Unit 42 observes data exfiltration inside the first hour in roughly 20% of modern breaches, a tempo at which a 72-hour reporting window ceases to function as a defense, while a single PANW month disclosed 26 CVEs spanning 75 issues. Regulatory lens is JAPAC (APRA and ASIC, MAS, Korea's AI Basic Act). Its landing point is oversight redesigned, not removed: real-time defensive AI under disciplined human supervision, with ultimate accountability remaining with people. Boards still set risk appetite, CISOs set operational thresholds, and security teams decide how much authority autonomous systems hold. Pairs with Human in Command and the containment thesis.

items.title: The Weather Report (AI security newsletter): Anthropic Agent Containment
items.text: Analysis of the AWS-key exfiltration exercise and why the model layer can't stand alone.

items.title: Foundation Capital: Context Graphs: AI's Trillion-Dollar Opportunity
items.text: By Jaya Gupta and Ashu Garg (December 2025): the origin of the rules-versus-decision-traces framing and the term context graph. Argues that systems of record capture what happened but overwrite the reasoning that led there, and that a durable, queryable record of decision traces (the exceptions, overrides, precedents, and cross-system context that today live in chat threads and human memory) is the next enterprise-software layer. A follow-up adds a governance nuance: precedent ages out, so a decision made under different conditions may no longer apply.

items.title: SOCAutomators (Palitto): The Context Graph: The Missing System of Record for the Agentic SOC
items.text: Mike Palitto translates the context-graph thesis to security operations: agents inherit the SOC glue function (synthesizing across SIEM, XDR, IAM, and ITSM) but lose the institutional memory analysts relied on, because the reasoning behind every triage, suppression, and closure evaporates at incident close. Distinguishes the data plane (events and incidents, largely solved) from the decision plane (the reasoning, unbuilt), names the negative decision trace as the most absent artifact, and argues traces must be captured at orchestration time, not downstream in the warehouse.

items.title: Disesdi: Agentic Top 10: ASI04 Supply Chain
items.text: Threat modeling agentic supply-chain vulnerabilities.

items.title: Disesdi: AI Red Teaming Has a Subspace Problem
items.text: Why prompt-spraying fails; subspace/transferability thinking.

items.title: Disesdi: Angles of Attack
items.text: OWASP AI Exchange core author; OWASP Agentic Top 10 series, threat modeling.

items.title: Disesdi: Dear NSA: The AI Threat Model You Need
items.text: A use-case-first, four-step AI threat-modeling method tied to the June 2026 EO's federal tasking (see AI Threat Modeling play).

items.title: Ken Huang: Agentic AI security (Substack)
items.text: Ongoing agentic-threat analyses from MAESTRO's creator, including layer-by-layer dissections of real production agent failures (e.g., a rogue internal agent that broke least privilege).

items.title: Ken Huang: MAESTRO operationalized (CI/CD)
items.text: MAESTRO's creator, with co-author Steven Leath, on folding the framework into an automated, continuous threat-modeling step in the CI/CD pipeline, keeping the agentic threat model live instead of stale.

items.title: Shawnee Delaney: Human Risk & Insider Threat
items.text: Former DIA clandestine officer; built insider-threat programs at Uber & Merck. Work on the AI/insider-threat intersection and employment-lifecycle human risk. (LinkedIn login-walled; background corroborated by her SANS profile entry.)

items.title: Shawnee Delaney: Insider Threat at SANS
items.text: Vaillance Group CEO; SANS resources on defending against AI-powered threats and human risk.

items.title: Adam Krivka & Ondrej Vlcek (AISLE): AI Found 12 Zero-Days in OpenSSL ([un]prompted 2026)
items.text: [un]prompted 2026, Day 1 (March 3). AISLE reports that its AI system found the 12 vulnerabilities OpenSSL fixed on January 27, 2026, each validated by its researchers before coordinated disclosure; OpenSSL's advisory credits all 12 to Aisle researchers (one also reported independently): one High, one Moderate and ten Low. Zero-day here means previously unknown, not exploited in the wild. AISLE is listed as a partner of the conference's October 2026 edition.

items.title: Andrew Bullen (Stripe): Breaking the Lethal Trifecta ([un]prompted 2026)
items.text: [un]prompted 2026, Day 2 (March 4). Stripe's AI security lead on containing the lethal trifecta in production by assuming prompt injection will happen. One guardrail cuts the egress leg: web search with outside access disabled, third-party SaaS reached only through Stripe's central MCP proxy, and CI checks on agent services' egress settings. A second requires human confirmation for sensitive tools, driven by annotations every tool must carry.

items.title: Anton Chuvakin: Stop Building a 2003 SOC with AI (Part 1, Jun 2026)
items.text: Google Cloud Office of the CISO's Chuvakin, writing with Augusto Barros (Prophet Security), opens a people-and-process framework for the agentic SOC with the warning this playbook is built around: bolt AI onto 2003-era processes and you get a somewhat better 2003 SOC, the SOAR story repeated, where a few tasks moved to machines and everything else stayed put. Part 1 deliberately collects the questions before the answers: what humans do in an agentic SOC, which processes vanish outright (triage), what the new validation role looks like, how to run human-in-the-loop without breaking the humans or the machines, how metrics must change, nearly one-for-one the questions the Human in Command and Program and Operating Model plays exist to answer. The ASO lineage (humans build machines; machines do the work) runs straight through it. Part 2 (Triage Must Die) and Part 3 (Local Context, Failure Modes and Your Path) have since been published.

items.title: Avishai Efrat & Roey Ben Chaim (Zenity): Total Recon ([un]prompted 2026)
items.text: [un]prompted 2026, Day 2 (March 4), presented by Roey Ben Chaim. Zenity reports finding tens of thousands of publicly reachable AI agents, mostly Microsoft Copilot Studio bots, thousands of them unauthenticated, by fuzzing default URLs and searching backlinks (2,500 open Copilot Studio agents from backlinks alone), and released new agent-recon modules in its open-source PowerPwn toolset for self-assessment. Vendor research with no exact total; Zenity is listed as a partner of the conference's October 2026 edition.

items.title: Binary Defense: NightBeacon CMD: The Glass-Box SOC Workbench (webinar)
items.text: On-demand webinar making the glass-box case for the agentic SOC: every AI verdict ships with its evidence, reasoning, and steps mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, so analysts stay in command and never have to answer with "the AI said so." Featuring Dave Kennedy, Binary Defense's founder and the workbench's developer, with CTO Jason Vest. Registration-walled (the session sits behind a form) and a product pitch by construction: take the human-in-command, auditable-agent thesis this playbook independently argues, and put the product itself through the Torq 20 questions below.

items.title: Caroline Wong (The AI Cybersecurity Handbook): When You Turn On AI, Who Owns the New Signals? (Jul 2026)
items.text: A crisp operating-model answer to the question every security leader hits when AI turns on: of the flood of new alerts, logs, and telemetry, what is the SOC's job and what is not. Wong, author of The AI Cybersecurity Handbook, draws the line as cybersecurity owns whether AI can safely act, product owns whether it acts correctly, so prompt injection, credential abuse, over-permissioned tools, and rogue-agent behavior sit with cyber, while hallucinations, answer quality, and workflow accuracy sit with product and AI governance. The piece is built for teams embedding AI security into the org they already have rather than standing up a separate function, and it is unusually concrete: a three-stage maturity model (turn AI on, build with AI, AI does the work), the AI gateway as a single policy-enforcement point in front of every model (authentication, prompt inspection, content filtering, tool control, logging), the two flows it enforces (DLP inbound, vaulted short-lived secrets outbound), five rogue-agent scenarios that are all deviations from an agent's baseline rather than malware, the reality that there is no unified agent-behavior view yet, signals scatter across identity, cloud, SIEM, and gateway logs, and MCP treated as privileged middleware to be scoped one job, one identity, one boundary, one owner. It maps directly onto the Program & Operating Model and agent-incident-response material here, giving the ownership boundary a citable source.

items.title: CSO Online: AI Red Teaming Comes of Age (2026)
items.text: Brumfield's June 2026 state-of-the-discipline feature: Microsoft's AI red team founder and technical lead, HackerOne, Cisco, and Palo Alto on probabilistic testing, whole-system scope, the expanded threat-persona roster, and the coming convergence of AI and traditional red teaming.

items.title: Darktrace: State of AI Cybersecurity 2026 (survey, via CSA)
items.text: Darktrace's survey of 1,500+ security leaders, republished on the Cloud Security Alliance blog: 73% say AI-powered threats already significantly affect their organization, and the expansion of generative AI is outpacing the security frameworks meant to govern it. An external benchmark for the agents-as-NHI and governance themes.

items.title: FedRAMP: 2025 AI Prioritization Initiative (Aug 2025)
items.text: FedRAMP's initiative, run from August 2025 to April 2026, prioritized 20x authorizations for AI cloud services offering conversational AI engines for routine federal use, provided they offered enterprise-grade features (single sign-on, SCIM provisioning, role-based access control), guaranteed data separation and protection, showed demand from at least five CFO Act agencies or a CIO Council recommendation, and were on the GSA Multiple Award Schedule: the federal pathway from AI pilots to authorized production.

items.title: Google DeepMind: Introducing CodeMender (Oct 2025)
items.text: Google DeepMind's autonomous code-security agent, both reactive (instantly patching new vulnerabilities) and proactive (rewriting existing code): special-purpose agents plus an LLM-based critique tool validate changes, 72 security fixes upstreamed in six months, and every patch reviewed by human researchers before submission. Agents hunt and fix; humans adjudicate.

items.title: IBM X-Force (Patrick Fussell): The Front of the Cyber Kill Chain Just Moved (Jun 2026)
items.text: A precise argument against both AI-security hype and dismissal: the thing frontier AI actually changes is the front of the kill chain, reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery, historically the slow, expensive, human-bound phase, and compressing it from weeks to hours rewrites the economics of every step downstream. It is grounded in real cases: Google's Big Sleep agent finding a previously unknown memory-safety bug in SQLite, which Google described as the first public instance in widely deployed software; DARPA's AIxCC, where cyber-reasoning systems ran roughly 143 hours autonomously against 53 projects and surfaced 54 of 63 synthetic vulnerabilities plus 18 unknown real-world bugs; and Sean Heelan using OpenAI's o3 to surface a Linux-kernel SMB zero-day (CVE-2025-37899) across 100 runs for about $116. For the red-team spine, this is the empirical case that discovery-to-exploitation is collapsing and that sophisticated capability is now a function of API budget rather than headcount.

items.title: Joshua Saxe: The Hard Part Isn't Building the Agent ([un]prompted 2026)
items.text: [un]prompted 2026, Day 1 (March 3); listed as Meta's AI security technical lead, he said he had just left to co-found a startup. Evaluation is the blocker for autonomous cyber defense: security ground truth is noisy, so grade how an agent works (evidence, reasoning and justification) against a rubric, calibrate an LLM judge on as few as about 100 labeled samples to start, set a deployment bar, and keep monitoring after deployment.

items.title: Matt Maisel (Sondera): Hooking Coding Agents with the Cedar Policy Language ([un]prompted 2026)
items.text: [un]prompted 2026, Day 1 talk (March 3). Sondera's CTO puts a deterministic reference monitor outside the agent and the model: coding-agent hooks in Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Cursor send each event to a Cedar policy engine that allows, modifies or stops it. Demos blocked a destructive SQL command, a web fetch after the session touched personal data, and a malicious skill. Some facts the policies use come from classifiers; the code is open source.

items.title: Microsoft CTI-REALM: Benchmark for CTI-to-Detection Agents
items.text: Checkpoint-scored evaluation of agents translating narrative CTI into Sigma/KQL against real attack telemetry: the model for grading emulation fidelity (did we emulate the actor, or "generic attacker"?) rather than trusting it.

items.title: Microsoft: What Is Microsoft Entra Agent ID? (Learn, Apr 2026)
items.text: Microsoft's identity and security framework for AI agents: agent identities and blueprints over OAuth 2.0, MCP and A2A, with adaptive access policies, real-time risk detection, lifecycle management and network-level controls extended to agents, third-party agents included via workload identity federation, and all agent authentication and activity logged. Vendor documentation: an off-the-shelf instance of the agent-as-NHI controls.

items.title: Nicholas Carlini (Anthropic): Black-hat LLMs ([un]prompted 2026)
items.text: [un]prompted 2026, Day 1 (March 3, San Francisco). Anthropic research scientist Nicholas Carlini ran Claude Code in a VM with permission prompts skipped and a short CTF-style prompt: current models found zero-days, among them a remotely exploitable heap overflow in the Linux kernel's NFSv4 code, present since 2003, and exploited some of them, including a blind SQL injection in Ghost CMS. His point is that this needs no special scaffolding and was not possible a few months earlier. Anthropic's February 5, 2026 write-up reports more than 500 validated high-severity vulnerabilities.

items.title: NIST: SP 800-184: Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery (Dec 2016)
items.text: NIST's recovery-planning guide: include comprehensive recovery planning in risk management, identify and prioritize organization resources to guide plans and realistic test scenarios, develop and test recovery playbooks, and improve continually from past events, so preparation enables rapid recovery. The backbone for deciding what to recover first and exercising reconstitution before an incident.

items.title: NOVA & PromptIntel: Adversarial-Prompt Detection & IoPC Feed (Roccia)
items.text: Thomas Roccia's NOVA ecosystem. NOVA is an open-source rule framework for detecting adversarial-prompt patterns (YARA for prompts); PromptIntel is a free community database of adversarial prompts, Indicators of Prompt Compromise (IoPC), with a live feed, API, and attached NOVA rules. dogesec models it as structured CTI on Cyber Threat Exchange.

items.title: Palantir: Apollo Docs (Introduction)
items.text: Palantir's documentation for Apollo, its platform for managing and deploying software: orchestrates upgrades and changes across connected and disconnected, air-gapped environments with built-in controls for FedRAMP, IL5 and IL6; companion pages document daily vulnerability scanning of releases and recalls that block bad releases and move environments off them. The execution half of a closed exposure-management loop. Vendor documentation.

items.title: Purple Book: From Snapshots to Living Intelligence (Threat Modeling, Jun 2026)
items.text: Nutanix + Palosade on code-grounded, continuously maintained threat models (schema-validated, kill-chain escalation mapping) that cut incident-response scoping to ~20 minutes: explicitly a response to Mythos/Daybreak. The threat-modeling expression of point-in-time to continuous.

items.title: Rob T. Lee: Sleep. Diet. Exercise. AI. (SANS)
items.text: SANS Chief AI Officer and "Godfather of DFIR" (coined DFIR & CTI); author of the SANS Secure AI Blueprint and Critical AI Security Guidelines: the practitioner voice behind the SANS maturity model cited here.

items.title: SANS: The AI-Enabled Vulnerability Analysis Loop (SEC543 × Anthropic, Jun 2026)
items.text: Anthropic's six-step source-code loop (threat model → sandbox → discovery → verification → triage → patch) with SANS's hands-on SEC543 translation: discovery parallelizes, so the skill is adversarial verification, a separate agent tasked to disprove each finding, and exploitation proven on real test beds. 1,596 disclosed / 97 patched as of May 22 corroborates the Glasswing figures this playbook carries.

items.title: Sergej Epp (Sysdig): 8 Minutes to Admin ([un]prompted 2026)
items.text: [un]prompted 2026, Day 2 (March 4). Sysdig's CISO on an intrusion its threat research team caught in the wild: credentials exposed in public S3 buckets, code injected into a Lambda function with an admin role, and AWS administrator access in about eight minutes (Sysdig write-up, February 3, 2026). Sysdig infers AI assistance from LLM-style code, hallucinated account IDs, a hallucinated GitHub repository and a role session named claude-session; the talk frames this as a behavioral method for when proof is impossible.

items.title: Stephen Tate (infosecuriosity): Most SOCs Are Thinking About AI the Wrong Way (Jun 2026)
items.text: Part 1 of a Building the AI-Ready SOC series from a working blue-teamer, and the sharpest short statement of why bolting AI onto existing SOC tasks misses the point: it makes individual tasks faster but leaves the shape of the work untouched, when the real opportunity is scaling the expertise your best analysts already hold across the whole operation. Its most useful contribution is a three-jobs taxonomy worth borrowing: automation handles the certain (known steps, predictable outcomes), AI handles the variable (choosing and running the right investigative steps, then making sense of the results), and people handle the novel (genuinely new attacker behavior, ambiguity, judgment, and deciding what gets captured for AI to use next). Two further points land on this playbook's themes: hand-built detection-tied playbooks break on ambiguity (living-off-the-land activity that only context can resolve) and on volume, so the move is to codify an analyst's line of questioning once and let AI apply it everywhere; and product-embedded AI that sees only its own control, network-only NDR, for example, is a feature, not an investigative capability, because real investigations cross endpoint, network, and identity. Reinforces the human-in-command spine with a clean operating model.

items.title: Sublime Security: Trust, Then Autonomy (Evaluating Security AI)
items.text: A procurement-and-operations framework: autonomy sits on a spectrum, is earned incrementally through demonstrated trust, and the right products expose a dial. Evaluate the vendor's evidence before the product's claims.

items.title: Torq: 20 Questions for AI SOC Vendors (Apocalypse Manifesto, Jun 2026)
items.text: A vendor-evaluation checklist from Torq's AI SOC campaign. The manifesto's 20 questions distill to themes worth asking any agentic SOC vendor: transparent, auditable reasoning; adjustable autonomy; human-on-the-loop control; RBAC and guardrails; immutable audit logs; memory and context handling; native MCP support; provable MTTR impact. Vendor-authored and self-serving by construction: a manifesto built so its author scores perfectly against it; include as a procurement scaffold, not an endorsement or an evaluation. Its footnoted primaries, CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report and Check Point's VoidLink research, have entries of their own (see Threat Intelligence & Industry Reports). Second citation, same campaign (Grounding the AI SOC: The Context Graph Problem, Jun 2026): the AI SOC's binding failure is grounding, not reasoning, and trustworthy context has four properties, current rather than a snapshot, traceable, decision-capturing rather than merely topological, and isolated. Carries SANS 2025's 73% false-positive-burden figure and IBM 2025's $3.62M-vs-$5.52M breach-cost split; the vendor's entry in the context-graph conversation (cf. the Context Graph cluster above).

items.title: Wang et al.: From Sands to Mansions: Towards Automated Cyberattack Emulation with Classical Planning and Large Language Models (Aurora)
items.text: Generates attack chains guided by CTI reports: raises CTI-mentioned-technique fidelity ~30% over report-agnostic chains, and substitutes available tooling when a named tool is absent while preserving the chain's logic. The emulation-fidelity half of intelligence-driven agentic adversary emulation.

items.title: Wes Ring & Josiah Peedikayil (Block): Operation Pale Fire ([un]prompted 2026)
items.text: [un]prompted 2026, Day 2 (March 4). Block reports red-teaming its own open-source agent, goose, end to end: calendar-invite prompt injection failed, a poisoned recipe reached the goose team and ran, and Block's detection and response team caught the payload. The fixes it describes: Unicode stripping, recipe warnings, a command allowlist and an initial prompt-injection detector. Block Engineering's write-up is dated January 15, 2026.

items.title: Wiz: Red Agent POV: Autonomous Offensive AI (2026)
items.text: Wiz Research series on its autonomous AI pentester, the Red Agent. One month of aggregate data: hundreds of thousands of scans across ~1,000 environments, 17,000+ unique findings, 5,500+ high and critical (validated multi-step chains). The SSRF breakdown shows the agent learning from blocked probes across 96 iterations to turn an unauthenticated SSRF into credential and source-code theft: discovery is cheap, proof is the job, demonstrated.

items.title: XBOW: The Road to Top 1 on HackerOne (Jun 2025)
items.text: XBOW reports its autonomous pentester reached #1 on HackerOne's US leaderboard after nearly 1,060 submissions, with human review before submission per HackerOne policy: continuous offensive testing as a product. Vendor-reported.

items.title: EU: AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689)
items.text: Staggered obligations: prohibitions, GPAI duties and, since Aug 2, 2026, transparency duties live; penalties up to €35M / 7% of global revenue. The tracker now carries the Omnibus dates; the AI Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, adopted July 8, 2026 and in force) defers Annex III high-risk obligations to Dec 2, 2027. The Compliance play carries the full status.

items.title: EU: Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
items.text: The enacted record: adopted July 8, 2026, in force since late July. Defers Annex III high-risk obligations to Dec 2, 2027 and embedded-product AI to Aug 2, 2028, while Article 50 transparency holds at Aug 2, 2026 with a four-month transitional period for generative systems already on the market. Supersedes the provisional-agreement status this suite previously tracked.

items.title: EU: NIS2 Directive (2022/2555)
items.text: Cyber risk-management + incident reporting for 160k+ entities; overlaps the AI Act for essential services.

items.title: White House: AI Innovation & Security EO (Jun 2026)
items.text: US federal posture: AI-enabled cyber defense + voluntary frontier-model benchmarking; no mandatory licensing.

items.title: A CPU-Centric Perspective on Agentic AI (Georgia Tech + Intel)
items.text: By Ritik Raj, Hong Wang, and Tushar Krishna (arXiv:2511.00739v1, Nov 2025; CC BY 4.0), the primary research behind the systems framing this suite borrows from. Profiles five representative agentic workloads and finds that tool processing on CPUs can reach up to 90.6% of total agent latency, with throughput bottlenecked by CPU coherence, synchronization, and core over-subscription rather than the model. The security-relevant reframe: the bottleneck and the value sit in the execution stack (orchestration, retrieval, tool calls, guardrail checks), not the model, so that same execution layer is where controls run and where the attack surface concentrates. Version 3 (April 16, 2026) is retitled "Towards Understanding, Analyzing, and Optimizing Agentic AI Execution: A CPU-Centric Perspective", adds two authors and no longer states these figures; this entry cites version 1.

items.title: Agents of Chaos (Northeastern/Harvard/MIT/Stanford/CMU)
items.text: Live-environment study: agents are vulnerable to conversation/social manipulation, not just exploits.

items.title: Chen et al.: AgentPoison
items.text: Agent memory / RAG poisoning; >80% success at <0.1% poison rate.

items.title: Cox & Bunzel: Quantifying Transferred Black-Box Attacks
items.text: Red-team risk math via surrogate/transferability methods.

items.title: Debenedetti et al.: CaMeL (Defeating Prompt Injections)
items.text: DeepMind: capability-based, model-agnostic injection defense.

items.title: Dux et al.: Governance by Design (Agentic AI)
items.text: ESSEC Business School and Accenture Research case study: governance implemented as architecture, allowed actions, reachable tools and data, memory handling, update paths, with seven scaling lessons.

items.title: Feffer et al.: Silver Bullet or Security Theater?
items.text: Critical survey of AI red-teaming practice.

items.title: Forough, Kogias & Haddadi: When Agents Handle Secrets (arXiv)
items.text: Systematic survey mapping hardware confidential computing onto Agentic AI: six TEE platforms (Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, Arm TrustZone/CCA, NVIDIA H100 CC) assessed against agents that plan, call tools, keep memory, and delegate over MCP and A2A. Honest about limits: not a prompt-injection fix, partial-TEE shortcuts have leaked model weights, and no end-to-end framework yet binds the primitives; GPU-TEE throughput penalties of 4 to 8% make confidential inference production-practical.

items.title: Hackett & Garraghan (Mindgard / Lancaster): Behind the Refusal: Determining Guardrail Activation via Behavioral Monitoring (Jul 2026)
items.text: The core contribution is a distinction the jailbreak literature usually blurs: bypassing a guardrail, exploiting gaps in an external classifier, is a different problem from bypassing a model's own learned refusal, and production systems rarely tell an attacker which one blocked them. The paper proposes the first black-box reconnaissance methodology for determining a guardrail's presence and behavioral characteristics assuming zero knowledge of the target: with only 40 prompts it detects guardrail presence with 100% accuracy across 162 lab-built target configurations, ascertains which content categories a guardrail is built to catch, and distinguishes a guardrail block from an LLM refusal on unseen prompts at 98% average F1. For a red team it is a reconnaissance primitive: fingerprint the defense before adapting the attack, and for this playbook it sharpens the threat model by separating the guardrail layer from the alignment layer, two things most tooling conflates.

items.title: MIT: AI Agent Index (2025)
items.text: Independent transparency index of 30 deployed AI agents across origins, design, capabilities, ecosystem, and safety. Useful as non-vendor evidence: autonomy spans L1 to L5, only 4 of 13 frontier-autonomy agents disclose any agentic safety evaluations, and nearly all depend on the GPT, Claude, or Gemini families.

items.title: Narajala & Narayan: Securing Agentic AI (ATFAA+SHIELD)
items.text: The Agentic-AI threat model and mitigation framework.

items.title: Singer et al. (CMU + Anthropic): Incalmo: An Autonomous LLM-assisted System for Red Teaming Multi-Host Networks
items.text: LLM-as-strategist over agent hierarchy autonomously replicated an Equifax-modeled breach in emulation.

items.title: Stanford HAI: AI Index 2026
items.text: Security = #1 barrier to scaling Agentic AI (62%); Cybench 15%→93%; transparency declining.

items.title: Vassilev (NIST): Robust AI Security & Alignment: A Sisyphean Endeavor?
items.text: The proof itself (IEEE Security & Privacy, May/June 2026): formalizes guardrails as a checker function and extends Gödel's incompleteness to show some constraint always exists that any finite guardrail system enforces incorrectly against some adversarial input; finite context windows tighten the bound. The theoretical floor under this playbook's assume-breach and containment stances.

items.title: Wikipedia: Adversarial Machine Learning
items.text: Evasion, poisoning, inversion, extraction taxonomy.

items.title: Wikipedia: Prompt Injection
items.text: Direct/indirect injection mechanics and defenses.

items.title: Anthropic: Government of Alberta Cybersecurity Case Study
items.text: Primary case study (Jul 2026): red-team and blue-team agents built on the Claude Agent SDK secured a government technical estate, ~50 parallel agents, 466M lines of code in ~20 hours (est. 6.5 years manual), ~95 controls per app, human approval before every patch. The clearest real-world demonstration to date of the red/blue/purple agent loop this suite argues for, on Anthropic's and Alberta's own figures.

items.title: Anthropic: Zero Trust for AI Agents (eBook)
items.text: Anthropic primary framework (May 2026): three principles (never trust/verify, assume breach, least privilege), seven control domains across three maturity tiers, an eight-phase workflow, and the design test of whether a control makes attack impossible or merely tedious. The architecture-side anchor for agentic zero trust.

items.title: CASP: How Boko Haram Uses Frontier AI (Juelich, Jul 2026)
items.text: Cambridge Programme on AI Science & Policy field study by Dr. Antonia Juelich: the first case in this index of an active terrorist organization using frontier AI systematically and institutionally, with some safeguards successfully circumvented and use platform-agnostic across major models. The other threat cases here are cyber (GTG-1002, the Gambit breach, Iran AA26-097A); this is the kinetic counterpart. Analytic finding only, no operational specifics: it moves adversarial frontier-AI misuse from projected to documented, raising the stakes for safety architectures designed against organized adversaries rather than isolated users, for safety-team design as a first-class constraint rather than post-launch moderation, and for account-level enforcement, where managed multi-provider account portfolios blunted single-platform refusals and suspensions. HIGH tier: documented academic field study (27 interviews; NYT-covered Jul 2026).

items.title: Check Point Research: VoidLink: AI-Authored Malware Framework (Jan 2026)
items.text: Check Point Research's two-part VoidLink analysis of what it calls the first evidence-based case of advanced malware authored almost entirely by AI. The Jan 13 deep-dive dissects the framework: a stealthy, cloud-native Linux implant with 37 plugins across seven categories, user-mode and kernel-level rootkits (LD_PRELOAD, LKM, eBPF), and a functional C2 server and dashboard integrated into a single ecosystem; the Jan 20 follow-up (the second primary) proves the authorship. A single actor produced a functional implant in under a week, demonstrated through exposed TRAE development artifacts. No evidence of real-world infections at publication: the significance is the authorship bar, not the victim count. First-party vendor research, framed accordingly; the primary source behind the Torq checklist's VoidLink footnote.

items.title: CrowdStrike: 2026 Global Threat Report (Feb 2026)
items.text: CrowdStrike's annual adversary telemetry (Feb 24, 2026), framed as the "Year of the Evasive Adversary": average eCrime breakout time down to 29 minutes, 65% faster year over year, fastest observed 27 seconds, an 89% YoY surge in AI-enabled adversary operations, malicious prompts injected into GenAI tools at 90+ organizations, a 42% rise in zero-days exploited before public disclosure, cloud-conscious intrusions up 37% overall (+266% state-nexus), and 280+ named adversaries tracked. Vendor-authored and self-serving by construction: CrowdStrike sells the platform its telemetry argues for; read the trendlines, verify point figures before quoting. Summary press release Feb 24, 2026; the primary source behind the Torq checklist's CrowdStrike footnote.

items.title: CSA + OWASP: Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide
items.text: The hands-on test manual for autonomous agents (May 2025, 50-plus contributors): twelve agentic threat categories (permission escalation, goal/instruction manipulation, memory poisoning, multi-agent collusion, orchestration flaws, supply-chain risk, and more), each with specific test requirements, attack vectors, example prompts, and defined deliverables. Turns the OWASP Agentic Top 10 into executable engagement plans; the authoritative parent of the requie community guide.

items.title: CSA: Evaluating PyRIT for Agentic AI Red Teaming
items.text: Hands-on gap analysis of PyRIT against the Agentic Red Teaming Guide: strong at prompt-level agentic tests (~80%) and CI/CD integration (~90%), only partial (~40%) at system-level validation because it reads model text responses, not actual tool invocations or state changes. The honest map of what your red-team harness can and cannot see.

items.title: Gambit Security: The AI-Assisted Breach of Mexico's Government Infrastructure (Apr 2026)
items.text: Gambit Security's full technical report on the Mexican government breach (released April 10, 2026): the firm reports that between late December 2025 and mid-February 2026 a threat actor using Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's GPT-4.1 breached at least nine Mexican government organizations, with Claude Code running about 75% of remote command execution across 1,088 logged prompts and 5,317 commands.

items.title: Google GTIG: Adversarial Misuse of Generative AI (Jan 2025)
items.text: GTIG's intelligence-grounded analysis of how government-backed (APT) and information-operations actors actually used Gemini: the empirical counterweight to AI-threat projection. The measured finding: threat actors gained productivity (research, code troubleshooting, content generation and localization, attack-lifecycle support) but not breakthrough or novel offensive capabilities, and jailbreak attempts recycled public prompts and failed. GTIG has sustained this no-breakthrough-capabilities read through follow-up trackers into 2026. Use it to calibrate the machine-speed material: operational automation and scale are real and here now (cf. the GTG-1002 agentic espionage operation), while AI inventing wholly new attack capabilities is not yet observed in the wild.

items.title: Government of Alberta: The Velocity White Papers (open source)
items.text: 21-plus open-source (MIT) technical papers on securing and modernizing a government estate with Agentic AI: strategy, governance, architecture, engineering patterns, security, and code. The published companion to the Alberta case study; a build-in-the-open reference. Note: the site's own imagery and narration are disclosed as AI-generated.

items.title: Mandiant: AI Risk & Resilience (special report)
items.text: Google Cloud's write-up of the Mandiant report: in recent assessments Mandiant found organizations often lack application registries, software bills of materials (SBOMs) for AI, and standard security scanners capable of viewing AI-specific artifacts, and that the root causes of the most pressing challenges are rarely novel AI-specific attacks but basic implementation flaws and missing IT hygiene. Google Cloud recommends robust governance for AI usage defining clear policies and approval workflows, plus regular AI red teaming; separate CSA and Google Cloud research it cites finds organizations with clear guidelines nearly twice as likely (46%) to adopt advanced Agentic AI.

items.title: Mandiant: M-Trends 2026 (frontline IR)
items.text: Annual incident-response benchmark: ~22-sec access hand-offs, recovery-denial ransomware, AI in adversary workflows.

items.title: Microsoft: AI as Tradecraft (2026)
items.text: Microsoft Threat Intelligence on how actors operationalize AI across the attack lifecycle: DPRK IT-worker tradecraft (Jasper/Coral Sleet), role-based jailbreaks, and AI-assisted-code detection tells.

items.title: MOSAIC Standards: AI Security Framework Alignment
items.text: Coordination initiative (founded April 2026) aligning the major AI security standards bodies (NIST, BIML, CIS, CoSAI, OWASP AI Exchange, OWASP GenAI, CSA, and SANS) onto shared principles and a common control-and-threat taxonomy. A precedent among its members: SANS and the OWASP AI Exchange had already aligned their frameworks on one taxonomy (MANAGE / RESILIENT MODELS / WATCH / LIMIT) before MOSAIC formed. The signal that the fragmented AI-security-guidance landscape is converging.

items.title: 0DIN: Clone This Repo and I Own Your Machine
items.text: Mozilla 0DIN research (Jun 2026): indirect prompt injection plus agentic tool abuse against coding agents. The malicious payload lives in a DNS TXT record, not the repo, so code review and scanners never see it; the agent runs a documented setup fix and opens a reverse shell. Class-level for any agent with authorized shell access.

items.title: 0DIN: Jailbreak Feed
items.text: Real-time jailbreak and prompt-attack threat intelligence from 0DIN's GenAI bug-bounty program (the 0-Day Investigative Network): a live feed of disclosed attack techniques for tracking which model evasions are circulating. The threat-intel sibling to the 0DIN scanner; now consumable natively inside Microsoft PyRIT via the 0din_threatfeed loader (live, paginated, incrementally cached), so red teams can pull it without leaving their harness.

items.title: Recorded Future: The Intelligence Handbook
items.text: Roadmap for an intelligence-led security program; the tactical / operational / strategic CTI model.

items.title: requie: AI-Red-Teaming-Guide
items.text: Community red-team field guide: OWASP Agentic Top 10 (ASI01-ASI10) with per-technique test approaches, MCP tool-poisoning coverage, the Microsoft failure-mode taxonomy, attack trees, an eval harness, and RoE templates. Attributed to requie (not OWASP or the similarly titled book); folds in the authors' vendor tooling and directional, non-audited stats, so tier accordingly.

items.title: SANS: Critical AI Security Guidelines v1.4
items.text: Practitioner controls guide (v1.4, March 2026; CC BY 4.0), aligned with the OWASP AI Exchange, a formal SANS partner. Eight control categories: conventional controls, data minimization/obfuscation, AI supply chain, data/model engineering, limit model behavior, model I/O handling, monitoring, and GRC, plus a Secure Agentic Systems section. The SANS-side structure of the SANS/OWASP aligned taxonomy; pairs with the AI Exchange for deep technical detail.

items.title: SANS: Cyber Threat Intelligence (FOR578 / CTI)
items.text: Practitioner training and resources on building and operating a CTI capability.

items.title: SANS: Protocol SIFT & the Find Evil! Hackathon (RSAC 2026)
items.text: Rob T. Lee's [un]prompted 2026 Day 1 talk (March 3, San Francisco), re-shown at RSAC 2026: after about 90 minutes of setup, a two-word tasking drove a complete C-drive forensic analysis in 14m27s, work responders report takes a week or longer. Protocol SIFT is the proof-of-concept wiring AI agents (Claude Code) to the SIFT Workstation's 200+ forensic tools over MCP: the GTG-1002 architecture (agents, MCP, security tools) pointed the other direction (cf. Anthropic: Disrupting AI Espionage). SANS concedes the PoC "hallucinates more than the team would like"; the Find Evil! hackathon (4,413 registered by close; submissions closed Jun 15, 2026; five winners named Aug 27, 2026) was held to harden it: judged on autonomous execution quality, IR accuracy, hallucination management, architectural guardrails, audit-trail quality, and documentation.

items.title: SecurityWeek: Hackers Weaponize Claude Code in Mexican Government Cyberattack (Mar 2026)
items.text: SecurityWeek's March 1, 2026 press report on the Mexican government breach, citing Gambit's initial findings: over 150GB exfiltrated within a month and roughly 195 million identities exposed; its early count of ten government bodies and a financial institution predates Gambit's technical report.

items.title: Torq: 2026 AI SOC Leadership Report
items.text: Sapio Research survey of 450 security leaders (US + EMEA): 94% run AI in the SOC across ~7 tools, 80% on fragmented point solutions; a 97%-confident vs. 35%-deployed triage autonomy gap; 92% cite trust-reducing factors, with exposed agent reasoning the consistent fix; 8.6 hrs/week of oversight nine in ten analysts call worthwhile. Vendor-commissioned: weigh the consolidation finding accordingly.

items.title: Unit 42 (Palo Alto): Dual-Use Dilemma (Malicious LLMs)
items.text: WormGPT 4 & KawaiiGPT: commercialized malicious LLMs.

items.title: Unit 42 (Palo Alto): Global IR Report 2026
items.text: 750+ incidents: AI ~4x speed in the fastest attacks, identity exploited in 89%, access-to-exfiltration in 72 minutes for the fastest quartile.

items.title: Unit 42 (Palo Alto): Threat Research
items.text: Operational/strategic threat intel: actor tracking, incident response, and AI-threat research.

items.title: Verizon: 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report
items.text: Annual breach data; carried Anthropic's AI-enabled-threat ATT&CK analysis in 2026.

items.title: VulnCheck: 2025 Q1 Trends in Vulnerability Exploitation (Apr 2025)
items.text: VulnCheck's Q1 2025 exploitation analysis (Apr 24, 2025): of 159 CVEs first publicly disclosed as exploited in the wild that quarter, the vendor reports 28.3% had exploitation evidence within a day of CVE publication, the originating source of the 28.3% figure the CSA Glasswing note restates as a share of all CVEs.

items.title: WEF: Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026 (Jan 2026)
items.text: World Economic Forum annual insight report: 87% of respondents identified AI-related vulnerabilities as the fastest-growing cyber risk over the course of 2025.

items.title: Zenity Labs: AI Security Research Out of the Lab and Into the Wild (Jun 2026)
items.text: Field telemetry rather than lab research: a global network of AI threat-intelligence sensors, honeypots exposing decoy LLM infrastructure, capturing thousands of real attack attempts against enterprise AI. The findings are concrete adversary tradecraft: hundreds of exploitation attempts against LiteLLM's critical remote-code-execution flaw (CVE-2026-40217) the same day it was patched, six weeks of escalation from reconnaissance to sandbox-escape payloads, a server-side request forgery variant of CVE-2024-6587 with attempted exfiltration, and a coordinated campaign against LiteLLM's admin endpoint (CVE-2026-35029). From March to May 2026 the sensors also recorded three campaigns hijacking exposed Ollama and LiteLLM inference endpoints, no compromise required, just a reachable port, to run attackers' own offensive agents: the autonomous penetration-testing frameworks Strix and HexStrike AI, and an OpenAI Codex agent carrying a persona built to suppress refusals. It is the wild-side counterpart to the lab and frontier-research sources in this index: direct evidence that adversaries are already attacking AI infrastructure and converting it into offensive compute. First in a series; companion Zenity Labs posts carry the specifics: the LiteLLM guardrail-tester post (CVE-2026-40217, the six-week escalation), the connection-test post (the CVE-2024-6587 variant), A Read-Only Account is All it Takes to Own a LiteLLM Server (CVE-2026-35029) and Bring Your Own Agent (the three hijacking campaigns).

items.title: Authentic8: Silo for Research (Managed Attribution)
items.text: Cloud-isolated investigation workspace with managed attribution: composes the Silo for Research browser with analyst apps, routes through a managed-attribution network of 700+ in-region egress nodes for a non-attributable IP, and lets analysts customize browser, device, language, and geolocation; activity executes remotely so endpoints stay clear of malware, and collection carries full audit logs supporting chain of custody. Vendor page for OSINT and digital-investigation use; it does not itself assert FedRAMP status, but the vendor's certifications page (authentic8.com/certifications) states that Silo is a FedRAMP-authorized service.

items.title: AWS + SANS: AI for Security and Security for AI (Nov 2025)
items.text: Joint whitepaper across three lenses: securing generative AI, generative AI for security, and defending against AI-powered threats. Distinctive for its three first-principles LLM concepts (non-determinism, equal-privilege input processing, statistical pattern completion) and for automated reasoning, formal verification, as a deterministic guardrail class.

items.title: AWS: Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix (Nov 2025)
items.text: Four-scope framework (no, prescribed, supervised, full agency) built on the agency-vs-autonomy distinction, with six security dimensions per scope, progressive-autonomy deployment, and graceful degradation: the agentic successor to the widely adopted GenAI Security Scoping Matrix.

items.title: AWS: AI Security Framework
items.text: Right controls, at the right layers, at the right phases; assess-first, prototype→production→scale. Model-agnostic via Bedrock.

items.title: AWS: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
items.text: Model-agnostic safeguards: prompt-attack detection, PII redaction, contextual grounding; AWS reports blocking up to 88% of harmful content; GovCloud-available.

items.title: AWS: Continuum (Jun 2026)
items.text: Machine-speed code-vulnerability loop: discovery, prioritization, validation (builds working exploit examples in a sandbox), and remediation with blast-radius visibility and rollback. Model-agnostic across frontier models; trust graduates from a human-in-the-loop learn mode to an enforce mode; folds in pen-testing and code scanning and adds STRIDE threat modeling. Gated preview.

items.title: Cisco: 8 Years of Security Research in 8 Weeks (2026)
items.text: Cisco's report on pairing frontier models (incl. Claude Mythos Preview and GPT-5.5-Cyber) with a human-guided harness to scan 1.8 billion lines across 25+ languages in eight weeks at under 3% false positives: work it pegs at eight years manually. Notably withholds the vulnerability count, underscoring that scan scale and validated quality, not raw tallies, are the metric that matters.

items.title: Cisco: Shields Up: Defending Against AI-Enabled Attacks (2026)
items.text: Cisco's defense guidance written off the April Mythos hold-back: traces the AI-enabled-attack record from the 2024 Microsoft/OpenAI research through TA547's LLM-generated PowerShell, and models the near-future AI-enabled adversary.

items.title: Splunk: Defending in the Post-Mythos Era (Jun 2026)
items.text: The validation-bottleneck thesis: frontier AI exposes SOC weaknesses rather than replacing the SOC, the constraint moves from finding to validating, and the SOC runs on confidence, not alert volume. Notes Cisco as a launch partner in both Anthropic's Glasswing and OpenAI's Daybreak (GPT-5.5).

items.title: Google: AI Threat Defense
items.text: Always-on agentic security platform (Gemini + Wiz + Mandiant + CodeMender) to detect, prioritize, and remediate at machine speed.

items.title: Google: Implementing SAIF Controls in Google Cloud (Dec 2025)
items.text: OCISO technical paper mapping every SAIF control across six domains (data, infrastructure, model, application, assurance, governance) to concrete implementations, what is inherited versus what you configure, including the Agent Auth vs. User Auth identity-propagation pattern, Model Armor, and the agent observability triad.

items.title: Google: SecOps Agents for AI-Powered Threat Containment (Jun 2026)
items.text: Pairs AI Threat Defense's Prepare → Scan/Prioritize → Remediate → Monitor loop with autonomous containment agents for code you don't own or can't patch, citing M-Trends 2026's mean time-to-exploit at an estimated minus seven days.

items.title: Google: Securing the AI Frontier (CodeMender, AI VRP, SAIF 2.0)
items.text: CodeMender autonomous patching agent, a dedicated AI Vulnerability Reward Program (Google's reward programs had already paid $430K+ for AI-related issues), and SAIF 2.0 for agents.

items.title: Meta: Purple Llama (Llama Guard 4, LlamaFirewall, CyberSecEval 4)
items.text: Open-source trust-and-safety stack: LlamaFirewall (real-time guardrails for chat models through autonomous agents), Llama Guard 4 and Prompt Guard 2 (multimodal I/O safety plus jailbreak/injection detection), and CyberSecEval 4, now measuring defensive capability via CyberSOCEval (SOC reasoning) and AutoPatchBench (agentic auto-patching), not just insecure-code risk.

items.title: Microsoft: Codename MDASH Brings Agentic AI Security Scanning to US Government (Sep 2026)
items.text: Microsoft reports that Codename MDASH has deployed to Azure Government as a Microsoft Defender feature working with FedRAMP High-authorized Microsoft Foundry models, with preview access for select US government customers and authorized partners (Sep 8, 2026).

items.title: Microsoft: MAI-Cyber-1-Flash & Project Perception (Aug 2026)
items.text: Microsoft's first first-party cyber model (announced August 13, 2026), introduced inside the MDASH harness and delivered through Perception: Microsoft's agentic security systems, providing teams of agents for security workflows in MDASH that continuously monitor, patch, and close new threat vectors. The citable pattern is difficulty-tiered routing: the lightweight first-party model is designed to handle up to 90% of tasks, reserving the fleet's largest models (GPT-5.4 at announcement) for the 10% of exceptionally hard tasks that truly need them. First-party vendor announcement: framed accordingly.

items.title: Microsoft: MDASH Agentic Security
items.text: 100+ agent harness that found 16 new vulnerabilities in the Windows networking and authentication stack; 88.45% CyberGym success rate at launch (May 12, 2026).

items.title: Microsoft: See What Happened: AI Investigation Playbook (Jun 2026)
items.text: Microsoft AeGIS's practitioner playbook for investigating M365 Copilot and Azure AI activity: telemetry enablement, the scope → context → signal workflow, KQL hunting and correlation queries, agent-inventory risk checks (MCP tools, missing user auth), and a Sentinel analytic rule pack.

items.title: OpenAI: Trusted Access for Cyber (GPT-5.5 / GPT-5.5-Cyber, May 2026)
items.text: OpenAI's identity- and trust-based access framework (TAC) for verified cyber defenders: the OpenAI counterpart to Anthropic's Glasswing, and the first-party anchor for the Daybreak frontier the suite otherwise cites secondhand. Vetted defenders receive reduced classifier-based refusals for authorized workflows (vulnerability identification and triage, malware analysis, binary reverse engineering, detection engineering, patch validation, red teaming), while the framework keeps blocking malicious activity such as credential theft, persistence, malware deployment, and exploitation of third-party systems. GPT-5.5 is the primary model; GPT-5.5-Cyber is the more-permissive variant for a smaller, highly verified set. GPT-5.5 is rated 'High' for cyber capability under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework. Access is gated on identity hygiene: from June 1, 2026, individual TAC members must enable phishing-resistant MFA (enterprises attest at the SSO level), tying frontier-capability access to zero-trust identity. Completes the cross-lab frontier picture (Glasswing/Mythos · Daybreak/GPT-5.5-Cyber) and reinforces the suite's identity-first and safety-constrains-defenders threads.

items.title: OpenAI: Understanding Prompt Injections: A Frontier Security Challenge
items.text: OpenAI's framing of agentic prompt injection and its layered product controls.

items.title: Palo Alto Networks: Defender's Guide to the Frontier AI Impact on Cybersecurity (May 2026)
items.text: Lee Klarich's May 2026 update after testing Claude Mythos, Opus 4.7, and GPT-5.5-Cyber, a four-step program every organization should run now: find and fix vulnerabilities across code and the open-source supply chain; assess and reduce exposure with attack-surface management; ensure best-in-class layered protections because a vulnerability exploit is one step of a multi-step lifecycle, not the end; and run real-time security operations at single-digit MTTD/MTTR, delivered as a platform rather than point solutions. The production proof: PANW's May 'Patch Wednesday' disclosed 26 CVEs (75 issues) across 130+ products, the majority surfaced by frontier-AI scanning, against a typical sub-five-CVE month, with a stated three-to-five-month window to outpace adversaries. The PANW member of the same vendor-operationalizes-the-closed-loop family as AWS Continuum, Cisco, Splunk, and Google AI Threat Defense.

items.title: SentinelOne: The Autonomous SOC, Revisited (Jul 2026)
items.text: Eighteen months after publishing its Autonomous SOC Maturity Model, SentinelOne returns with field data and an unusually sober verdict: the levels held, but the binding constraint between AI-Assisted Operations and Partial Autonomy is governance, not tooling: rules of engagement, pre-approved policies, audit trails, and a named owner for every AI verdict, defined before automation fires. Two findings earn the entry: Gartner's gap between the 40% of organizations evaluating AI SOC capability and the 18% actually deployed (Feb 2026), and the structural asymmetry the Offense-Defense group names, a defender's trust-building timeline versus an attacker's consequence-free iteration tempo, a gap that compounds. Vendor-reported outcomes (75% faster investigations, 4x more threats handled, 42% fewer false positives) trace to a SentinelOne-sponsored IDC study: treat accordingly. Pairs with the Maturity Model play as the autonomy-specific external benchmark.

items.title: Wiz (Google Cloud): AI-SPM & State of AI in the Cloud
items.text: AI security posture management; ~25% of orgs lack visibility into which AI services run in their environment. Wiz says AI-APP extends AI-SPM across the full AI lifecycle.

items.title: Disesdi Susanna Cox: AI security architect (OWASP AI Exchange)
items.text: Core author of the OWASP AI Exchange (AI Policy Lead; EU AI Act technical requirements) and an AI-security patent holder; her Angles of Attack brief drives the use-case-first threat modeling and the 'new paradigm is purple' arguments this playbook builds on.

items.title: Shawnee Delaney: human risk & insider threat
items.text: Former DIA clandestine officer who built insider-threat programs at Uber and Merck; the human-risk lens behind treating agents as non-human insiders. (LinkedIn login-walled; background corroborated by her SANS profile.)

items.title: Jennifer Ewbank: An Intelligence Warning Hidden in Agentic AI Guidance (Jun 2026)
items.text: Former CIA Deputy Director for Digital Innovation reads the Five Eyes guidance as indications-and-warning: coordination across five governments means the threat predates publication. Pairs it with CI Fortify's assume-access posture and closes with three governance questions (agent reach, oversight, and prompt-injection red-teaming) every deploying organization should answer now.

items.title: Ken Huang: creator of CSA MAESTRO
items.text: Creator of CSA's MAESTRO agentic threat model; co-chairs CSA's AI Organizational Responsibility and AI Control Framework and leads OWASP AIVSS; shows how to wire MAESTRO into CI/CD (see AI Threat Modeling).

items.title: Rob T. Lee: SANS Chief AI Officer
items.text: SANS Chief AI Officer and author of the SANS Secure AI Blueprint and the practitioner voice behind the AI Security Maturity Model this ladder benchmarks against.

items.title: Ipek Ozkaya: Carnegie Mellon SEI
items.text: SEI principal researcher and technical director of the Engineering Intelligent Software Systems group; first-listed author of the SEI's AI Adoption Maturity Model v1.0 (see Maturity Model).

items.title: Wendi Whitmore: Chief Security Intelligence Officer, Palo Alto Networks
items.text: Palo Alto Networks' Chief Security Intelligence Officer: formerly the leader of Unit 42, with prior executive roles at IBM, CrowdStrike, and Mandiant, and an inaugural member of DHS's Cyber Safety Review Board. Her Frontier AI for Boards newsletter translates frontline threat intelligence into executive decisions, anchored on a framing this playbook shares: separate what's new from what's important. The datapoint that earns the follow: by May 2026 the majority of PANW's vulnerability findings came from frontier AI scanning rather than human researchers, with similar capability, as of May 2026, expected in adversary hands within two to four months, a diffusion window that turns find-and-fix-first and attack-surface reduction into scheduling problems. Her one-mandate-two-halves frame (defend against weaponized frontier models; secure the AI your enterprise deploys at pace) is this playbook's two questions, stated for the boardroom.

items.title: Cisco: Zero Trust for Agentic AI (white paper)
items.text: White paper (updated March 23, 2026) extending Zero Trust to AI agents, which it treats as a rapidly growing class of Non-Human Identities that must be discovered, governed, and mapped to accountable owners. Risk concentrates across three dimensions (identity, access, and behavior), and the framework's stated promise is to know every agent, authorize every action, and adapt to risk in real time: inventory agents, MCP servers, and connected tools; apply least-privilege, time-bound access for NHIs; and run runtime guardrails on requests, responses, and tool invocations. Vendor-authored, and its remedy is Cisco's own integrated networking, identity, and security stack.

items.title: CoSAI: Zero Trust for AI Systems (v1.0, Sep 2026)
items.text: Why authorization can't live inside the model. Places the LLM inside an untrusted "AI threat boundary," treats every tool call as its own authorization event, and gives a three-step maturity path for agent authorization, plus a Zero Trust control matrix for AI systems mapped to the DoD Zero Trust Reference Architecture and the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model.

items.title: Google DeepMind: AI Control Roadmap (v0.1)
items.text: A defense-in-depth framework for operating untrusted, possibly misaligned internal AI agents by treating them as insider threats: a second line of security that holds even if model alignment is imperfect. Introduces TRAIT&R (a rogue-AI tactics-and-techniques taxonomy built on MITRE ATT&CK), two control invariants (reliable detection of misaligned intent or actions; effective prevention and response), and capability-mitigation ladders: four Detection tiers (D1 - D4) and three Prevention/Response tiers (R1 - R3), across 15 tiered mitigations from chain-of-thought monitoring to AI access control, untrusted monitoring, and shutdown infrastructure. GDM reports an internal asynchronous monitor prototype that has analyzed a million coding-agent tasks.

items.title: Google DeepMind: Three Layers of Agent Security
items.text: The policymaker-facing companion to the AI Control Roadmap, arguing agent security must be addressed at three levels: hardening individual agents, governing multi-agent systems at scale, and empowering cyber defenders to keep their edge as agent capabilities grow. Pairs the internal-controls engineering of the Roadmap with an ecosystem and governance frame.

items.title: IETF: RFC 8693 (OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange)
items.text: IETF Standards Track specification (January 2020) for swapping one security token for another scoped to a specific downstream resource. CoSAI's Zero Trust for AI Systems cites it for agent token exchange at each hop.

items.title: Ken Connell: Lensatic Field Guides: Zero Trust (Sep 2026)
items.text: My companion study guide: an eight-week plan with a shared Zero Trust core (NIST SP 800-207 and the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model), then DoW, federal civilian and private-sector tracks, with one-page quick references. Public sources only; it links back to this playbook for the agentic view.

items.title: Microsoft: Announcing Zero Trust for AI
items.text: Verify explicitly and least-privilege for agents, workloads, and users.

items.title: Microsoft: Defense in Depth for Autonomous Agents
items.text: Bounded scope + progressive permissioning starting at zero trust.

items.title: NSA: Zero Trust Implementation Guidelines (ZIGs, 2026)
items.text: NSA's implementation tier for zero trust: modular phase guides, a Primer plus Discovery, Phase One, and Phase Two published to Target level, with further phases planned toward Advanced, organizing the DoD ZT Strategy's 152 activities into executable steps, the published set carrying the 91 Target-level activities; developed with and approved by the DoW CIO Zero Trust Portfolio Management Office, with pillar views and Cybersecurity Information Sheet alignment on the hub and updates planned through 2026. The lineage runs EO 14028 → NIST SP 800-207 → CISA ZTMM → the DoD ZT Reference Architecture and Strategy; these guides are the how-to layer under all four: the government primary for the rollout the vendor zero-trust guidance in this group assumes. Guide PDFs (Primer, Discovery, Phase One, Phase Two) on media.defense.gov.

items.title: OpenID Foundation: Identity Management for Agentic AI (Oct 2025)
items.text: OpenID Foundation whitepaper (October 7, 2025), compiled by its AI Identity Management Community Group with lead editor Tobin South. Agents should act on explicitly delegated authority rather than impersonating users, with scope attenuated at each hop: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange online, attenuable tokens offline. OAuth 2.1 fits single-domain, synchronous cases; cross-domain, asynchronous and shared agents remain open problems. The hosted file was revised after release, adding the full author list and minor edits, to match arXiv 2510.25819.

items.title: Valente & Zalewski: Beyond Zero: Enterprise Security for the AI Era (May 2026)
items.text: Preprint (arXiv, May 2026; formal version in ACM Queue, DOI 10.1145/3819083) arguing the application-centric model of zero trust is breaking under autonomous agents and machine-speed data access. Its move: shrink the trust boundary from the application to the individual action, and couple static authorization guarantees with dynamic, AI-driven reasoning, so per-resource-and-method decisions are made for humans and agents at machine speed, a self-defending enterprise mediating thousands of decisions per second. The academic vision end of this group's zero-trust arc: the Anthropic eBook supplies the maturity tiers and NSA's ZIGs the phased execution, while Beyond Zero makes the case for the per-action trust boundary this playbook's agent controls already assume.
